Name: commitment_stop_gap
Title: The Commitment-Stop Gap: Overthinking as a Decoupling Between Answer-Knowing and Stop-Deciding Circuits
Short Hypothesis: Reasoning LLMs overthink not because they lack the answer, but because an internal 'answer-commitment' signal stabilizes long before a separate 'stop-decision' circuit fires. Overthinking is the temporal gap between these two internal events, and it can be measured, mechanistically localized, and closed with a lightweight commitment monitor.
Related Work: Prior efficient-reasoning interpretability work either (a) finds a single linear 'verbosity/length' direction and steers along it (ASC, Efficiency Steering, Manifold Steering, ThinkEdit), (b) characterizes overthinking behaviorally via triggers such as self-doubt, internal bias, or first-impression conflict, or (c) detects completion reactively by monitoring termination-token rank dynamics (RCPD). All treat 'answer-knowing' and 'when-to-stop' as a single conflated phenomenon. Our proposal is the first to explicitly separate two internal subprocesses: an answer-commitment readout (when the model's latent predicted final answer stabilizes) and a stop-decision circuit (what actually drives generation of the termination token). We test whether overthinking is precisely the gap between these two, localize the stop-decision circuit via attention/head attribution, and use the earlier commitment signal—rather than a length direction—to trigger stopping. This is a mechanistic decomposition and causal account, not another steering vector.
Abstract: Large reasoning models routinely 'overthink,' expending tokens long after they could correctly answer. Existing interpretability work explains this via a single verbosity direction or reactive termination signals, implicitly treating knowing the answer and deciding to stop as one process. We hypothesize instead that these are two distinct internal events: an answer-commitment signal, when the model's latent predicted final answer stabilizes across reasoning steps, and a stop-decision, when a control circuit finally emits the termination token. We define the commitment-stop gap as the number of tokens between these events and argue overthinking is largely this gap. Using linear probes and logit-lens-style readout on the residual stream, we measure per-step answer commitment on math and science benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, GPQA) across open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills, Qwen3). We show commitment stabilizes far before termination for overthought instances, and that the gap predicts wasted tokens better than length or verbosity-direction metrics. We then localize the stop-decision circuit via head-level attribution and activation patching, finding heads that attend to termination cues and whose ablation shifts stop timing. Finally, we build a training-free commitment monitor that early-exits when the probed answer is stable and confident for k steps, and show it reduces tokens with minimal accuracy loss, outperforming length-based and reactive baselines. Our work reframes overthinking as a circuit-level decoupling and offers a principled, interpretable efficiency mechanism.
Experiments:
All experiments use open reasoning models on a single 8xA100-80GB (or smaller) node, well within an academic budget. Primary model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (transformer decoder, all weights frozen; only lightweight linear probes are trainable). Scale sweep uses the 1.5B/7B/14B/32B R1-Qwen distills and Qwen3-8B. Decoding: temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 16k thinking tokens, 3 seeds (0,1,2) for every reported number. Reasoning traces are segmented into steps by newline/step delimiters. Datasets (used as released, as is): GSM8K test (1319 items), MATH500 (500), AIME 2024+2025 (60), GPQA-Diamond (198). A trace is 'correctly solved' if the extracted final answer matches gold; probing and gap analysis are run on correctly solved traces only, so the question is when the answer was known, not whether.

Experiment 1 (H1 — Commitment precedes stopping): Test whether an answer-commitment signal stabilizes strictly before the termination token is emitted. For each step we read the model's current implicit final answer two ways: (a) logit-lens projection of the last-token residual onto the vocabulary, (b) a trained linear probe. Probe data: for each dataset we hold out 40% of correctly solved traces to train one probe (ridge logistic regression on the layer-L residual predicting the gold final-answer token(s)); the other 60% is the evaluation set, never seen in training. The 'commitment step' is the first step after which the decoded answer equals the eventual final answer and stays unchanged to termination. Systems compared: commitment-step distribution vs. termination-step distribution, per dataset. Decisive metric: fraction of correctly solved traces whose commitment step is at least 15% of the trace earlier than the termination step. Convincing result: this fraction exceeds 0.60 on MATH500 and GSM8K with the mean commitment-to-termination separation > 20% of trace length. Indecision band: fraction in [0.45, 0.60], or mean separation in [10%, 20%] of trace length — this neither confirms nor refutes early commitment, and we would report the phenomenon as weak/dataset-dependent rather than claim it. Negative result (fraction < 0.45): commitment does not generally precede stopping, and the core premise of the hypothesis fails.

Experiment 2 (H2 — The gap IS the overthinking): Test whether the commitment-stop gap (tokens between commitment step and </think>) accounts for wasted tokens better than length or a verbosity direction. 'Wasted tokens' is defined operationally by truncate-and-resume: for each trace we truncate at each step, force </think>, and take the last step after which forced-exit accuracy stops changing; wasted tokens = tokens after that step. Systems compared as predictors of wasted tokens, via out-of-sample regression R^2 (5-fold): (i) commitment-stop gap, (ii) total tokens, (iii) projection onto a reproduced ASC verbosity direction, (iv) Failed-Step Fraction. Decisive metric: R^2 of the gap predictor minus R^2 of the best competing single predictor. Convincing result: gap R^2 exceeds the best competitor by >= 0.10 on at least three of four datasets. Indecision band: advantage in [0.02, 0.10] — gap is competitive but not clearly superior; we would report it as one useful signal among several, not the explanation. Negative result (advantage <= 0.02, or gap R^2 below a competitor): overthinking is not primarily this gap.

Experiment 3 (H2/H3 — Causal check that commitment is real): Truncate generation at the probed commitment step, force </think>, and measure accuracy retention against truncating at matched random earlier and later steps. Decisive metric: accuracy at commitment-step truncation minus accuracy at same-token-budget random-step truncation. Convincing result: commitment-step truncation retains within 2 accuracy points of full-generation accuracy while random earlier truncation loses > 8 points at equal budget. Indecision band: retention gap vs. full generation in [2, 5] points — the probe locates an approximately-but-not-exactly sufficient point; we soften claims about commitment being a clean event. Negative result (> 5 point loss): the probed commitment step is not the point at which the answer is actually decided.

Experiment 4 (H4 — Localizing the stop-decision circuit): Localize heads/layers that drive the termination token via activation patching and attention attribution, and test decoupling from the commitment readout. Method: for correctly solved traces, patch clean-run activations into a run where </think> is delayed, ranking heads by their effect on termination-token logit; ablate the top-k heads (k in {1,4,16}) and measure the shift in termination timing. Decisive metric: change in mean termination step under top-head ablation vs. random-head ablation of equal count. Decoupling test: measure Experiment-1 probe accuracy on the same traces with stop heads ablated; if commitment readout is preserved while stop timing shifts, the two subprocesses are dissociable. Convincing result: top-head ablation shifts mean termination by >= 15% of trace length (vs. < 3% for random ablation) while probe answer-decoding accuracy drops by < 5 absolute points. Indecision band: termination shift in [5%, 15%], or probe accuracy drop in [5, 10] points — partial or entangled localization; we report a candidate circuit without the clean-decoupling claim. Negative result (shift < 5% or probe collapses with stop heads): the stop decision is not localized to identifiable heads, or is inseparable from answer computation, weakening H4.

Experiment 5 (H5 — Training-free commitment monitor): Build an early-exit that forces </think> once the probe-predicted answer is stable and probe confidence exceeds threshold tau for k consecutive steps, and test that it saves tokens at minimal accuracy cost. Hyperparameters tau and k are selected on the Experiment-1 training split only (grid tau in {0.7,0.8,0.9}, k in {2,3,5}); the 60% eval split is used for reporting. Systems compared on all four datasets: commitment monitor vs. (a) full generation, (b) fixed-fraction truncation matched to the monitor's mean token budget, (c) verbosity steering (ASC), (d) RCPD reactive exit, (e) budget forcing. Decisive metric: token reduction at equal accuracy — percent token reduction relative to full generation while accuracy stays within 1 point. Secondary: mean tokens, accuracy, wall-clock speedup. Convincing result: monitor achieves >= 30% token reduction within 1 accuracy point on GSM8K and MATH500 and beats every baseline on the token-reduction-at-equal-accuracy frontier. Indecision band: token reduction in [15%, 30%] within 1 point, or a tie with the strongest baseline (difference < 5% reduction at matched accuracy) — the monitor works but is not clearly better; per the hypothesis's own framing the primary contribution then rests on the mechanistic decomposition (Experiments 1-4), not the intervention. Negative result (< 15% reduction, or > 1 point accuracy loss to match baseline budgets): the commitment signal does not yield a usable efficiency mechanism.

Experiment 6 (H3 — Generality of the signal across scale): Test whether commitment is a shared, cheaply readable signal by transferring probes and the monitor across datasets and the 1.5B/7B/14B/32B/Qwen3-8B models. Decisive metric: cross-dataset and cross-scale probe transfer accuracy (train on one dataset/scale, evaluate on another) relative to the in-domain probe. Convincing result: transferred probe retains >= 80% of in-domain answer-decoding accuracy across at least three model scales, and the monitor's token savings hold within 10 relative percent under transfer. Indecision band: transfer retention in [60%, 80%] — the signal exists but is partly model-specific; we scope the claim to per-model probes. Negative result (< 60% retention): commitment is idiosyncratic per model/dataset, contradicting the 'shared low-cost readout' claim.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The linear probe for latent answer commitment may be unreliable for open-ended or multi-token answers, limiting to tasks with extractable final answers; mitigated by focusing on math/multiple-choice. Commitment and stop-decision may not be cleanly separable circuits—if patching shows they share heads, the decoupling framing weakens (though this is itself an informative negative result). Probe confidence may correlate with problem difficulty, risking premature exit on hard problems (underthinking); the k-step stability and confidence threshold aim to control this. Steering/early-exit gains may not exceed strong existing baselines; the primary contribution remains the mechanistic decomposition even if the intervention only matches prior methods. Results may be model-family specific.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims: (1) overthinking is a temporal gap between internal answer-commitment and stop-decision; (2) these are separable circuits rather than one conflated process; (3) commitment can be probed early and used for early exit; (4) stop-decision heads can be localized/ablated to dissociate them. The underlying early-stopping/answer-convergence idea is crowded and close prior work already exists, so the monitor itself is not novel. The potentially novel part is the two-circuit decomposition plus causal dissociation experiment. That is a non-trivial framing, but it is still an incremental mechanistic refinement of known termination/early-exit phenomena rather than a clearly new task or theory.

impact.reasoning: The phenomenon under study is whether reasoning models know an answer before they decide to stop, and whether that gap drives wasted tokens. This matters to inference efficiency, interpretability, and prompt/control design, especially for expensive CoT systems. The 'so what' is real: if true, it could justify earlier stopping and a new way to analyze overthinking. However, practical uptake depends on beating strong existing early-exit baselines; if not, the main value is conceptual/mechanistic. So the work is important and citable, but not obviously direction-changing unless the decomposition proves robust and general.

The causal story risks conflating correlation with mechanism, and the planned head localization/ablation may be fragile given distributed representations. Experiments are feasible, but key controls are missing: comparison to confidence, entropy, answer repetition, and termination-token rank; robustness across prompting, decoding, and answer formats; and analysis of probe calibration and leakage. Executed well, it could be a solid interpretability/efficiency paper, but not yet fundable as written without tighter definitions and stronger controls.

Name: decorative_step_router
Title: Skip the Filler: A Mechanistic Router that Predicts and Suppresses Decorative Reasoning Steps Before They Are Generated
Short Hypothesis: Reasoning LLMs interleave a small number of causally-load-bearing 'true-thinking' steps with many 'decorative' steps that have near-zero causal influence on the answer. We hypothesize that the model's residual stream at the boundary of a reasoning step already linearly encodes whether the upcoming step will be decorative or load-bearing, before that step is generated. If so, a lightweight probe-based router can proactively skip decorative steps at generation time, cutting tokens without harming accuracy.
Related Work: Recent interpretability work (True Thinking Score / TTS, 2025) shows only a tiny fraction of CoT steps causally drive predictions and identifies a steerable 'TrueThinking' latent direction, but does so post-hoc and per-step by corrupting already-generated steps; it does not predict or prevent decorative steps in advance. NLDD/Reasoning-Horizon work (2026) finds late steps (70-85% mark) lose causal influence but only measures this retrospectively. 'Think Clearly' (2025) prunes redundant tokens using attention-to-end-of-thinking but requires generating the tokens first, then evicting and resuming; it is reactive and content-agnostic. Length-based methods (When More is Less, 2025) target a global optimal length rather than which specific steps to keep. Our proposal is distinct: it is the first to test whether the decorative-vs-load-bearing status of a step is *predictable in advance* from the pre-step residual stream, and to convert that predictive signal into a *proactive generation-time router* that never generates the filler in the first place. This is prospective causal decomposition + intervention, not post-hoc scoring or reactive pruning.
Abstract: Large reasoning models produce long chains of thought in which only a small minority of steps causally affect the final answer; the rest are 'decorative.' Prior interpretability work can identify decorative steps only retrospectively, by corrupting steps after they are generated, and existing efficiency methods either prune tokens reactively or target a single global length. We ask a sharper mechanistic question: does the model already 'know', at the boundary just before emitting a reasoning step, whether that step will be load-bearing or decorative? We first quantify per-step causal influence via resample-ablation (measuring the drop in answer log-probability when a step is removed) to label each step decorative or load-bearing across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3). We then train lightweight linear probes on the residual stream at step boundaries to predict the label of the *upcoming* step, testing whether decorative status is prospectively encoded. Using this probe as a training-free router, we skip predicted-decorative steps at generation time by forcing continuation past them, and measure accuracy vs. token savings against reactive pruning, length-aware filtering, and TTS-style post-hoc baselines. We further localize the circuit that determines step status via activation patching and characterize when the predictive signal fails (e.g., near the reasoning horizon). Our work reframes overthinking as a per-step, predictable planning decision and turns a purely diagnostic interpretability finding into a proactive, interpretable efficiency mechanism.
Experiments:
Compute fits an academic node (<= 8xA100-80GB). Primary model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, all weights frozen; only linear probes are trainable. Scale sweep: R1-Qwen distills 1.5B/7B/14B and Qwen3-8B. Decoding: temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 16k thinking tokens, seeds 0/1/2 on every reported number. CoT is segmented into steps by newline/step delimiters plus sentence splitting. Datasets, used as released: GSM8K test (1319), MATH500 (500), AIME 2024+2025 (60), GPQA-Diamond (198). Unless stated, analysis is on correctly solved traces.

Experiment 1 (H1 — Load-bearing steps are sparse): Quantify per-step causal influence and confirm most steps are decorative. For each step, run resample-ablation: replace the step with a semantically neutral connector, and separately delete it and resume, then measure the normalized drop in final-answer log-probability. A step is 'load-bearing' if the drop exceeds a fixed threshold theta, else 'decorative'; theta is fixed a priori as the drop that changes the argmax answer with probability 0.5 on a 200-step calibration subset. Decisive metric: median decorative fraction (share of steps labeled decorative) per dataset. Robustness: label agreement (Cohen's kappa) between the connector-replacement and deletion ablation variants. Convincing result: median decorative fraction > 0.5 on all four datasets with variant kappa > 0.6. Indecision band: decorative fraction in [0.35, 0.5], or kappa in [0.4, 0.6] — sparsity is weak or label-noisy; we report it as tendency, not fact, and downstream router claims are scoped accordingly. Negative result (fraction < 0.35 or kappa < 0.4): steps are not predominantly decorative, or labels are unreliable, undercutting the premise.

Experiment 2 (H2 — Decorative status is prospectively encoded): Test whether a linear probe on the pre-step residual predicts the upcoming step's label before it is generated. Probe data: 40% of labeled step-boundaries (from Experiment 1) train per-layer ridge logistic probes; 60% held out for evaluation, split by problem so no trace appears in both. Systems compared: (i) prospective probe on the boundary residual, (ii) bag-of-words baseline on preceding text, (iii) a retrospective probe that sees the generated step (upper bound). Decisive metric: prospective-probe AUROC for upcoming-step label on the held-out split. Layer sweep localizes the strongest signal. Convincing result: prospective AUROC >= 0.75 on at least three datasets and >= 0.10 above the bag-of-words baseline. Indecision band: AUROC in [0.62, 0.75], or advantage over bag-of-words in [0.03, 0.10] — weak or partly lexical prospective signal; the router is unlikely to help much and we say so. Negative result (AUROC < 0.62 or no advantage over bag-of-words): decorative status is not linearly pre-encoded, refuting H2 (an informative negative — the decision may form mid-step).

Experiment 3 (H2 — Circuit behind the prediction): Localize components that determine the probe's decorative prediction via activation patching and head attribution, then ablate the top components and test whether the model emits fewer/different decorative steps. Decisive metric: change in decorative fraction (Experiment-1 labeling) under top-component ablation vs. equal-count random ablation. Convincing result: top-component ablation changes decorative fraction by >= 10 absolute points while random ablation changes it by < 3, with task accuracy preserved within 3 points. Indecision band: change in [3, 10] points — partial localization; a candidate circuit is reported without strong causal claims. Negative result (< 3 points or accuracy collapse): the prospective signal is not tied to an identifiable, intervenable circuit.

Experiment 4 (H3 — Proactive router saves tokens without hurting accuracy): Use the Experiment-2 probe as a training-free generation-time router: at each boundary, if predicted decorative with confidence > tau, force continuation past the step. tau is selected on the Experiment-2 training split only (grid {0.6,0.7,0.8,0.9}); reporting is on held-out problems. Systems compared on all four datasets: router vs. (a) no intervention, (b) fixed truncation matched to router mean budget, (c) length-aware voting (When More is Less), (d) reactive attention pruning (Think Clearly), (e) post-hoc TTS pruning. Decisive metric: token reduction at equal accuracy — percent token reduction vs. no intervention while accuracy stays within 1 point. Secondary: mean tokens, accuracy, wall-clock speedup. Convincing result: router achieves >= 25% token reduction within 1 accuracy point on GSM8K and MATH500 and lies on or above every baseline's accuracy-vs-token frontier. Indecision band: reduction in [10%, 25%] within 1 point, or a tie with the best reactive baseline (< 5% reduction difference at matched accuracy) — the router works but is not clearly superior; the standalone contribution is then the mechanistic finding (Experiments 1-3). Negative result (< 10% reduction or > 1 point accuracy loss to match baselines): the predictive signal does not convert into a usable router.

Experiment 5 (H3 — Failure and safety analysis): Characterize where the router harms accuracy. Measure router accuracy as a function of tau, separately on the final 15-30% of the chain (reasoning horizon) and on the hardest quartile of items (by base pass-rate), and audit false-skip cases. Decisive metric: accuracy drop attributable to skips in the final 30% of the chain vs. the first 70%, at the deployed tau. Convincing result: no region shows > 2 points of accuracy loss beyond the aggregate at deployed tau, so a single tau is safe. Indecision band: a region shows 2-5 points extra loss — a horizon-aware tau schedule is needed and reported. Negative result (> 5 points concentrated loss): the router is unsafe without step-position gating, bounding H3.

Experiment 6 (H2/H3 — Generality across data and scale): Transfer the probe/router across datasets and the 1.5B/7B/14B/Qwen3-8B models without retraining. Decisive metric: transferred-probe AUROC relative to in-domain AUROC, and router token-savings retention under transfer. Convincing result: transfer retains >= 80% of in-domain AUROC across at least three scales and router savings hold within 10 relative percent. Indecision band: retention in [60%, 80%] — signal is partly model-specific; claims are scoped to per-model probes. Negative result (< 60% retention): prospective decorative-encoding is idiosyncratic, contradicting the 'shared low-cost signal' claim.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Step boundaries may be ambiguous for models without clean delimiters, complicating labeling; mitigated by using consistent newline/step segmentation and sentence splitting. Resample-ablation labels are noisy proxies for causal influence and depend on the neutral replacement; we will validate with multiple ablation variants. Decorative status may only be weakly predictable in advance (the model may decide mid-step), which would be an informative negative result but weaken the router. Skipping steps could disrupt downstream coherence or trigger error cascades on hard problems (underthinking); the confidence threshold and horizon-aware analysis address this. Router gains may not exceed strong reactive baselines, but the mechanistic finding (prospective encoding of step utility) stands independently. Results may be model-family specific.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims: (1) decorative vs load-bearing CoT steps can be labeled by resample-ablation; (2) the pre-step residual stream linearly predicts whether the *upcoming* step will be decorative; (3) this prediction can drive a generation-time router that skips filler before it is emitted; (4) circuit-level localization via patching may explain the router. The first claim is not novel relative to Thought Anchors / True Thinking Score / reactive pruning, which already identify sparse causally important steps post-hoc. The actual delta is the prospective, pre-generation predictability claim and the router, which is a meaningful but fairly narrow extension. Closest prior family: post-hoc step importance / decorative-CoT analyses and generate-then-prune methods. The delta is moving from retrospective importance measurement to proactive prediction/control. That is non-trivial, but it is still an incremental mechanism layered on an established setup rather than a new task, theory, or dataset.

Name: recompute_loop_forgetting
Title: Recompute Loops: Overthinking as Retrieval Failure of the Model's Own Scratchpad
Short Hypothesis: A large fraction of wasted reasoning tokens are spent re-deriving intermediate results the model already computed earlier in the same chain-of-thought. This 'recompute loop' arises because the model fails to retrieve its own prior conclusions from context, and it is mechanistically detectable at the point of recomputation via degraded attention to the earlier result. Restoring that retrieval with a lightweight memory-injection intervention eliminates the redundant recomputation and cuts tokens without hurting accuracy.
Related Work: Prior efficiency work treats redundancy as a scattered-attention or verbosity phenomenon: Think Clearly (2025) prunes low-attention tokens reactively; TTS (2025) labels steps decorative vs. load-bearing post-hoc; NLDD (2026) shows a reasoning horizon where late steps stop mattering; When More is Less (2025) targets a global optimal length. Separately, cognitive-science-flavored interpretability shows LLMs lack persistent working memory (Language Models Do Not Have Human-Like Working Memory, 2025; Self-Attention Limits Working Memory Capacity, 2024; Strong Memory Weak Control, 2025), causing self-contradiction and concept drift. No existing efficiency paper connects these two literatures: we are the first to identify a *specific, structured* redundancy pattern—recomputation of previously-derived intermediate quantities—and attribute it to a *retrieval/working-memory failure* (weak attention back to the earlier result) rather than to generic verbosity or decorativeness. Our intervention (memory injection to restore self-retrieval) is causal and targeted, distinct from content-agnostic pruning or length control.
Abstract: Reasoning models often 'overthink,' but the structure of the wasted computation is poorly understood. We identify a concrete and pervasive pattern we call recompute loops: within a single chain of thought, the model re-derives an intermediate quantity (an equation, a partial sum, a constraint, a candidate answer) that it already established earlier in the same trace. We hypothesize that recompute loops are a symptom of the model failing to retrieve its own prior conclusions from context—a working-memory/retrieval failure—rather than generic verbosity. First, we build an automatic detector for recomputed intermediate results by matching semantically-equivalent value-producing statements across a reasoning trace, and quantify what fraction of tokens recompute loops account for across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3). Second, we test the retrieval-failure hypothesis mechanistically: at the token position where recomputation begins, we measure attention back to the original derivation and compare against matched non-recomputing positions, and use activation patching to test whether injecting the earlier result's representation suppresses recomputation. Third, we turn the diagnosis into a training-free intervention—memory injection—that, upon detecting the onset of a recompute loop, appends a terse reminder of the already-derived result (or steers hidden states toward it) so the model can continue instead of re-deriving. We evaluate token savings at equal accuracy against reactive pruning, verbosity steering, and length-aware baselines, and analyze failure cases. Our work reframes a slice of overthinking as self-retrieval failure and offers a targeted, interpretable efficiency mechanism.
Experiments:
Compute fits an academic node (<= 8xA100-80GB). Primary model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, frozen; only a cheap onset probe is trainable. Scale sweep: R1-Qwen distills 1.5B/7B/14B and Qwen3-8B. Decoding: temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 16k thinking tokens, seeds 0/1/2 on every reported number. CoT segmented into steps by newline/step delimiters. Datasets, used as released: GSM8K test (1319), MATH500 (500), AIME 2024+2025 (60), GPQA-Diamond (198).

Experiment 1 (H1 — Recompute loops exist and are costly): Build a detector for recomputed intermediate results and quantify their token cost. Detector: parse value-producing statements (equations, computed numbers, named intermediates, candidate answers) and flag a statement as a recompute when an LLM-judge deems its value semantically equivalent to one produced earlier in the same trace. Detector validity: two human annotators label a 300-statement sample; we report detector precision/recall against the majority label (target precision >= 0.8). Decisive metric: fraction of thinking tokens attributable to recompute loops per dataset. Convincing result: recompute loops account for >= 15% of thinking tokens on average across datasets, at detector precision >= 0.8. Indecision band: token fraction in [7%, 15%], or detector precision in [0.65, 0.8] — the pattern is real but minor or noisily measured; we report it as a small named waste category rather than a large one. Negative result (< 7% of tokens, or precision < 0.65): recompute loops are not a material or reliably measurable source of waste, undercutting the premise.

Experiment 2 (H1 — Distinct from generic waste): Show recompute loops are a distinct waste category, not a relabeling of decorativeness. Correlate recompute-token fraction with total tokens and with 'wasted tokens' (tokens after the last accuracy-changing step, via truncate-and-resume), and compute overlap with TTS-style decorative-step labels. Decisive metric: share of recompute tokens that fall on steps labeled load-bearing (non-decorative) by TTS-style labeling. Convincing result: > 40% of recompute tokens sit on non-decorative steps, establishing recompute loops as partly orthogonal to decorativeness. Indecision band: overlap such that 25-40% of recompute tokens are non-decorative — partial distinctness; we present recompute loops as a refinement, not a separate axis. Negative result (< 25% non-decorative): recompute loops are largely a subset of decorative waste, weakening the novelty claim.

Experiment 3 (H2 — Retrieval-failure signature): Test whether recompute onsets show degraded attention to the earlier derivation. At each detected recompute onset token, measure attention mass directed at the tokens of the original derivation; compare against matched control positions where the same result is instead referenced/reused without recomputation. Decisive metric: difference in mean attention-to-original between recompute onsets and matched reuse controls (paired, across heads/layers). Convincing result: recompute onsets show significantly lower attention to the earlier result (paired difference with p < 0.01 and effect size Cohen's d > 0.5), localized to a small set of heads. Indecision band: 0.2 < d < 0.5 — a weak signature consistent with but not strong evidence for retrieval failure. Negative result (d < 0.2 or no significant difference): recomputation is not accompanied by degraded self-attention, refuting the retrieval-failure mechanism (recomputation may be a deliberate strategy) — an informative negative.

Experiment 4 (H2 — Causal patching): At a recompute onset, patch in the residual-stream representation of the original result (from its derivation position) and measure whether the model reuses rather than re-derives. Decisive metric: drop in probability of continuing the recomputation (next-token / next-step recompute continuation) under the patch vs. a norm-matched random patch. Convincing result: the true-result patch reduces recompute-continuation probability by >= 20 absolute points, vs. < 5 for the random patch. Indecision band: reduction in [8, 20] points — the representation influences but does not control recomputation. Negative result (< 8 points): injecting the earlier result does not causally suppress recomputation, undercutting the mechanism and the intervention's premise.

Experiment 5 (H3 — Memory-injection saves tokens without hurting accuracy): Run the detector online via a cheap residual-stream onset probe (trained on Experiment-1 labels, 40% train / 60% eval split by problem); on predicted onset, inject a terse natural-language reminder of the prior result and continue. Systems compared on all four datasets: memory injection vs. (a) no intervention, (b) fixed truncation matched to injection mean budget, (c) Think Clearly reactive pruning, (d) verbosity/CREST-style steering, (e) length-aware filtering. Decisive metric: token reduction at equal accuracy — percent reduction vs. no intervention while accuracy stays within 1 point. Secondary: recompute-loop count reduction, mean tokens, wall-clock speedup. Convincing result: >= 15% token reduction within 1 accuracy point on GSM8K and MATH500 with recompute-loop count cut by >= 50%, matching or beating every baseline on the accuracy-token frontier. Indecision band: reduction in [7%, 15%] within 1 point, or a tie with the best baseline (< 5% reduction difference at matched accuracy) — injection works but is not clearly superior; the diagnosis (Experiments 1-4) is then the standalone contribution. Negative result (< 7% reduction or > 1 point accuracy loss): the intervention does not yield usable savings.

Experiment 6 (H3 — Preserving corrective re-derivation): Distinguish blind recomputation from beneficial self-correction and ensure the trigger does not suppress the latter. Label a sample of recompute onsets as corrective (fixes an earlier error) vs. blind, then measure accuracy impact of suppressing each class. Decisive metric: accuracy change on items containing corrective re-derivations when injection is applied vs. withheld. Convincing result: with the corrective-aware trigger, accuracy on corrective-containing items drops by < 1 point while token savings on blind-recompute items are retained. Indecision band: 1-3 point drop on corrective items — the trigger imperfectly separates the two; we report the tradeoff curve. Negative result (> 3 point drop): blind and corrective recomputation cannot be separated cheaply, bounding H3 to easy items.

Experiment 7 (H1/H2 — Generality across data and scale): Transfer detector and onset probe across datasets and the 1.5B/7B/14B/Qwen3-8B models without retraining. Decisive metric: transferred onset-probe AUROC relative to in-domain, and recompute-token-fraction stability across scales. Convincing result: transfer retains >= 80% of in-domain AUROC on at least three scales and recompute prevalence stays within a factor of 2 across scales. Indecision band: retention in [60%, 80%] — partly model-specific; scoped to per-model probes. Negative result (< 60% retention or prevalence varying by more than a factor of 3): the phenomenon is idiosyncratic across models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Detecting semantically-equivalent recomputations is nontrivial and may be noisy; we mitigate with parsing plus LLM-judge and human validation, but false positives could over-trigger the intervention. Some recomputation is beneficial (self-correction, verification), so blindly suppressing it may hurt accuracy on hard problems; the trigger must distinguish blind recompute from corrective re-derivation, and this may be hard. The retrieval-failure hypothesis may not hold—recomputation might be a deliberate learned strategy rather than an attention failure—which would be an informative negative result but weaken the mechanistic framing. Memory injection alters the context and could introduce distribution shift or new errors. Gains may not exceed strong reactive-pruning baselines, though the structured diagnosis (recompute loops as a named, quantifiable waste category linked to working-memory limits) is a standalone contribution. Results may be model-family specific and biphasic across scales.

novelty.reasoning: Core claim is not reuse instead of recompute in general; that space is crowded. The proposal's real delta is narrower and more specific: detect within-trace recomputation loops, argue they come from self-retrieval/working-memory failure, and intervene at onset. That mechanism-level framing and onset-triggered memory injection are meaningfully distinct from prior efficiency work, but the underlying idea of avoiding redundant reasoning via reuse is already present in adjacent work. Closest prior family: Reuse Don't Recompute / Memory-of-Thought / Thought-Retriever on the reuse axis, plus redundancy/pruning papers and working-memory interpretability. The non-trivial novelty is the mechanistic attribution and structured redundancy target, not the broad problem.

Name: stale_uncertainty_gate
Title: Stale Uncertainty: Overthinking as a Failure to Update the Internal Confidence Signal That Gates Reflection
Short Hypothesis: Reasoning models keep reflecting not because they are still genuinely uncertain, but because the internal uncertainty signal that gates continued reasoning is stale: it lags the model's actual, freshly-computable confidence. Overthinking is the gap between a lagging gating-uncertainty and an up-to-date evidence-uncertainty, and forcing an uncertainty 'refresh' breaks the reflection loop.
Related Work: A wave of 2025 work links reflection to uncertainty: ReflCtrl and SEAL steer reflection/transition thoughts with a latent direction; 'Reasoning Models Better Express Their Confidence' and 'Trace Length is a Simple Uncertainty Signal' correlate calibration and length with an internal confidence state and identify high-entropy 'forking' tokens; 'Calibrating Reasoning with Internal Consistency' and the Verbal Uncertainty Feature (VUF) find linear uncertainty directions. Crucially, ALL of these treat the gating uncertainty as an accurate reflection of the model's current knowledge state, and either steer it down bluntly or use it to early-exit. Our proposal advances a fundamentally different mechanistic claim: the uncertainty signal that drives continued reflection is a STALE, lagging estimate that fails to incorporate evidence the model has already produced. We distinguish two internally-decodable quantities — a 'gating-uncertainty' (the signal upstream of reflection-onset tokens) and an 'evidence-uncertainty' (uncertainty recomputed over the freshest reasoning state) — test whether they diverge, show the divergence predicts wasted tokens, and design a targeted 'uncertainty refresh' intervention. This is a lag/update-failure account, not another steering vector or exit rule.
Abstract: Reasoning LLMs often continue to reflect and verify long after they have effectively solved a problem. Prior interpretability work ties this behavior to an internal uncertainty signal, but implicitly assumes that signal accurately tracks the model's current confidence and simply remains high. We propose a different mechanism: the uncertainty signal that gates continued reflection is stale. It lags behind the confidence the model could compute from its most recent reasoning, so the model keeps triggering verification against an out-of-date sense of doubt. We formalize two residual-stream-decodable quantities: gating-uncertainty, read just before reflection-onset tokens, and evidence-uncertainty, read after conditioning on the freshest reasoning state. Across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we train lightweight probes for both and test whether gating-uncertainty systematically lags evidence-uncertainty during overthinking, using granger-style temporal analysis and the identified 'forking' tokens. We show the lag magnitude predicts wasted tokens better than absolute uncertainty or trace length. We then localize where the gating signal is read via activation patching, and introduce a training-free 'uncertainty refresh': at reflection-onset, we patch the stale gating representation with the fresh evidence-uncertainty representation, testing whether this suppresses the redundant reflection loop. We evaluate token savings at equal accuracy against ReflCtrl/SEAL-style steering, trace-length exit, and internal-consistency exit, and analyze failures on genuinely hard items. Our work reframes a slice of overthinking as an uncertainty-update failure and offers a targeted, interpretable efficiency fix.
Experiments:
Compute fits an academic node (<= 8xA100-80GB). Primary model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, frozen; only linear uncertainty probes are trainable. Scale sweep: R1-Qwen distills 1.5B/7B/14B and Qwen3-8B. Decoding: temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 16k thinking tokens, seeds 0/1/2 on every reported number. CoT segmented into steps; reflection-onset tokens marked by lexical cues (wait / let me check / but) plus a reflection-direction classifier reproduced from ReflCtrl. Datasets, used as released: GSM8K test (1319), MATH500 (500), AIME 2024+2025 (60), GPQA-Diamond (198).

Experiment 1 (H1 — Two separable uncertainty readouts): Establish that gating-uncertainty and evidence-uncertainty are distinct, decodable signals. Train two linear probes to predict eventual answer correctness from the residual stream: (a) gating-uncertainty at the token immediately preceding a reflection-onset, (b) evidence-uncertainty at the end of the most recent completed step. Probe data: 40% of traces train, 60% held out, split by problem. Decisive metric: held-out AUROC of each probe for eventual correctness. Separability check: correlation between the two probe outputs at matched positions (they must not be near-identical to support a lag account). Convincing result: both probes reach AUROC >= 0.70 and their outputs correlate at r < 0.8 (distinct signals). Indecision band: either probe AUROC in [0.6, 0.7], or output correlation in [0.8, 0.9] — the readouts are weak or partly redundant; the lag framing is reported tentatively. Negative result (AUROC < 0.6 or correlation > 0.9): the two signals are not separable/useful, undercutting the whole framing.

Experiment 2 (H1 — Gating uncertainty lags evidence uncertainty): Test staleness directly. For each reflection episode, compare gating-uncertainty to evidence-uncertainty at the same point, and estimate the lag as the offset k for which evidence-uncertainty at step t-k best matches gating-uncertainty at step t (cross-correlation). Also test whether reflection-onset preferentially fires when gating exceeds evidence (large lag), linking to high-entropy forking tokens. Decisive metric: mean signed difference (gating minus evidence) at reflection onsets during overthought traces, and the modal best-fit lag k. Convincing result: gating exceeds evidence at onsets by a significant margin (paired p < 0.01, d > 0.5) with modal lag k >= 1 step, and onset firing rate is higher in high-lag windows. Indecision band: 0.2 < d < 0.5, or modal lag k = 0 with a small positive difference — weak or zero-lag staleness; we report a small effect, not a lag mechanism. Negative result (d < 0.2 or gating <= evidence): no staleness, refuting H1 (reflection may reflect genuine current doubt or deliberate exploration).

Experiment 3 (H2 — Lag predicts wasted tokens): Test that the lag explains overthinking better than absolute uncertainty or length. 'Wasted tokens' = tokens after the last accuracy-changing step (truncate-and-resume). Compare out-of-sample regression R^2 (5-fold) of predictors of wasted tokens: (i) per-trace mean lag, (ii) absolute gating-uncertainty, (iii) trace length, (iv) internal-consistency score. Decisive metric: lag-predictor R^2 minus best competitor R^2. Convincing result: lag beats the best competitor by >= 0.10 on at least three datasets. Indecision band: advantage in [0.02, 0.10] — lag is a useful but not dominant predictor. Negative result (advantage <= 0.02): the lag does not specifically explain waste, weakening H2.

Experiment 4 (H2 — Localizing where the gating signal is read): Use activation patching to find layers/heads where gating-uncertainty feeds the reflection-onset decision; ablate them and measure change in reflection frequency and lag. Decisive metric: change in reflection-onset rate under top-component ablation vs. equal-count random ablation. Convincing result: top-component ablation changes reflection rate by >= 10 absolute points (vs. < 3 for random) while task accuracy holds within 3 points. Indecision band: change in [3, 10] points — partial localization. Negative result (< 3 points or accuracy collapse): the gating read is not localized/intervenable.

Experiment 5 (H3 — Uncertainty-refresh breaks the loop): At reflection-onset, patch the residual components carrying gating-uncertainty with the fresh evidence-uncertainty representation, then continue; test that redundant reflection is suppressed without accuracy loss. Systems compared on all four datasets: refresh vs. (a) no intervention, (b) fixed truncation matched to refresh mean budget, (c) ReflCtrl/SEAL reflection steering, (d) trace-length early-exit, (e) internal-consistency early-exit. Decisive metric: token reduction at equal accuracy — percent reduction vs. no intervention while accuracy stays within 1 point. Secondary: reflection-count reduction, mean tokens, wall-clock speedup. Convincing result: >= 20% token reduction within 1 accuracy point on GSM8K and MATH500 with reflection count cut >= 40%, on or above every baseline frontier. Indecision band: reduction in [10%, 20%] within 1 point, or a tie with the best steering baseline (< 5% difference at matched accuracy) — refresh works but is not clearly superior; the lag diagnosis (Experiments 1-4) is then the standalone contribution. Negative result (< 10% reduction or > 1 point accuracy loss): refresh does not yield usable savings.

Experiment 6 (H3 — Preserving genuine reflection): Verify refresh does not suppress reflection when evidence-uncertainty is genuinely high (guard against underthinking). On the hardest quartile of items and on cases where reflection is corrective, gate refresh by an evidence-uncertainty threshold and measure accuracy. Decisive metric: accuracy change on hard/corrective items with refresh vs. without, at the deployed threshold. Convincing result: accuracy on hard/corrective items drops < 1 point while savings hold on easy items. Indecision band: 1-3 point drop — threshold trades savings for safety; we report the curve. Negative result (> 3 point drop): refresh harms genuine reflection, bounding H3.

Experiment 7 (H1/H2 — Generality across data and scale): Transfer both probes and the refresh trigger across datasets and the 1.5B/7B/14B/Qwen3-8B models without retraining. Decisive metric: transferred-probe AUROC relative to in-domain, and refresh token-savings retention. Convincing result: transfer retains >= 80% of in-domain AUROC on at least three scales and savings hold within 10 relative percent. Indecision band: retention in [60%, 80%] — partly model-specific; scoped to per-model probes. Negative result (< 60% retention): the lag signal is idiosyncratic across models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The distinction between 'gating' and 'evidence' uncertainty relies on read-position choices that may be entangled; if the two probes are not separable, the lag framing weakens (an informative negative result). Confidence probes are noisy for open-ended answers, so we focus on math/multiple-choice with extractable answers. The stale-uncertainty hypothesis may be wrong — reflection could be a deliberate learned exploration strategy rather than an update failure — which would still yield a publishable mechanistic characterization. The uncertainty-refresh patch alters internal state and may introduce new errors or overconfidence, causing underthinking on hard items; the evidence-uncertainty threshold aims to guard against this. Intervention gains may not exceed strong steering baselines, but the lag diagnosis is a standalone contribution. Results may be model-family specific and vary non-monotonically with scale.

novelty.reasoning: Core claim is the stale/lagging uncertainty account: reflection is triggered by an outdated gating-uncertainty signal that lags a fresher evidence-uncertainty signal, and an uncertainty-refresh patch can break the loop. That is a real delta from prior confidence-gating/early-exit/steering work, which largely assumes the internal confidence is current. However, the idea is still tightly adjacent to active 2025-26 work on uncertainty during reasoning, so the novelty is mainly in the temporal-lag mechanism and intervention, not a new task or theory family.

Name: difficulty_contraction_failure
Title: Difficulty That Won't Shrink: Overthinking as a Failure of the Internal Difficulty Signal to Contract as Reasoning Progresses
Short Hypothesis: LLMs carry a linearly-decodable, attention-head-mediated 'difficulty' representation. Prior work reads it only once, before generation. We hypothesize this difficulty signal should contract during a chain of thought as sub-goals are resolved and the problem becomes effectively easy, and that overthinking occurs precisely when this contraction fails—the internal difficulty stays high even after the problem is essentially solved. Forcing the difficulty signal to contract (via targeted head steering) at the point where residual work is minimal should curtail redundant reasoning without hurting accuracy.
Related Work: A recent cluster of interpretability work establishes that LLMs linearly encode problem difficulty in pre-generation activations, localize it to specific final-layer attention heads (Probing the Difficulty Perception Mechanism, 2025; A Shared Geometry of Difficulty, 2026; LLMs Encode Their Failures, 2026), and use it to allocate compute at the input level (ACTSC 2026, FR-Ponder 2025, AdaCtrl 2025, CODA 2026, UAB 2026). Critically, ALL of these treat difficulty as a static, pre-generation property of the input and use it to set a budget or sample count before or independent of the actual reasoning trace. None examine how the difficulty representation evolves *during* generation, nor connect overthinking to a failure of that representation to update. Our contribution is orthogonal: (1) we show the same difficulty direction/heads can be read at intermediate points in the CoT and that it normally contracts as work is completed; (2) we identify overthinking with a specific dynamical failure—non-contracting difficulty despite resolved residual work; and (3) we intervene on the difficulty heads mid-generation to induce contraction. This is a temporal-dynamics + causal-intervention account of an established static representation, not another budget-allocation method or steering-vector-for-length.
Abstract: Recent interpretability work shows that large language models linearly encode a notion of problem difficulty in their activations, mediated by specific attention heads, and that this signal can be read before generation to allocate compute. But difficulty is not static: as a reasoning model works through a problem and resolves sub-goals, the *residual* problem should become easier, and its internal difficulty should shrink. We hypothesize that overthinking is a failure of this contraction—the internal difficulty signal remains elevated even after the problem is effectively solved, driving the model to keep reasoning. We first replicate a linear difficulty probe and localize difficulty-sensitive heads on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), then read the difficulty signal at each step of a chain of thought on GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA. We test whether difficulty normally contracts as residual work (measured by truncate-and-resume accuracy) decreases, and whether overthought traces exhibit stalled, non-contracting difficulty. We show the contraction-failure metric predicts wasted tokens better than absolute difficulty or trace length. We then causally validate the difficulty heads by patching/steering them mid-generation toward the 'easy' pole once residual work is low, and measure whether this induces early, correct termination. We compare token savings at equal accuracy against input-level difficulty budgeting (CODA/AdaCtrl-style), length steering, and confidence early-exit, and analyze failure cases where genuine difficulty persists. Our work reframes a static difficulty representation as a dynamical control signal and locates overthinking in its update failure.
Experiments:
Compute fits an academic node (<= 8xA100-80GB). Primary model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, frozen; only linear probes are trainable, and interventions are activation edits (no weight updates). Scale sweep: R1-Qwen distills 1.5B/7B/14B and Qwen3-8B. Decoding: temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 16k thinking tokens, seeds 0/1/2 on every reported number. CoT segmented into steps by newline/step delimiters. Datasets, used as released: GSM8K test (1319), MATH500 (500), AIME 2024+2025 (60), GPQA-Diamond (198); difficulty labels from Easy2Hard-AMC-style annotations plus empirical per-item pass-rates (32 samples/item).

Experiment 1 (H1 — Difficulty is decodable and head-mediated, including mid-trace): Replicate a linear difficulty probe and localize difficulty-sensitive final-layer heads, then test readability at intermediate positions. Train the probe on pre-generation activations (40% of items) to predict difficulty (pass-rate bucket); evaluate on 60% held out. Identify difficulty heads by ablation impact on probe output. Then fine-tune/evaluate the probe on intermediate step-boundary states. Decisive metric: held-out probe AUROC/R^2 for difficulty, pre-generation and at intermediate positions. Convincing result: pre-generation AUROC >= 0.75 (replication) and intermediate-position AUROC >= 0.70, with a small head set (<= 10) whose ablation drops probe AUROC by >= 0.1. Indecision band: intermediate AUROC in [0.6, 0.7] — difficulty is only weakly readable mid-trace; the dynamical framing is reported tentatively. Negative result (intermediate AUROC < 0.6): difficulty is encoded only pre-generation, refuting the premise that it can be tracked during reasoning (an informative negative).

Experiment 2 (H2 — Difficulty normally contracts): Read step-wise difficulty and test whether it declines as work is done. For each trace, form the difficulty trajectory over step boundaries. Decisive metric: mean signed change in decoded difficulty from first to last step across correctly solved traces. Convincing result: difficulty contracts on average by a significant margin (paired p < 0.01, mean drop > 0.3 in normalized probe units) on the majority of correctly solved traces. Indecision band: mean drop in [0.1, 0.3] — weak contraction; we report a mild trend. Negative result (mean drop < 0.1 or increasing): difficulty does not contract during reasoning, refuting H2.

Experiment 3 (H3 — Contraction failure tracks residual work and predicts waste): Measure residual work by truncate-and-resume (truncate at each step, force termination, answer; residual work = steps still needed to reach the correct answer), then define contraction failure = area between difficulty and residual-work trajectories after residual work hits zero. Steps subsampled (every 2nd boundary) to control compute. First test that difficulty tracks residual work (correlation), then test that contraction failure predicts waste. Decisive metric: out-of-sample R^2 (5-fold) of contraction failure predicting wasted tokens (tokens after the last accuracy-changing step), minus best competitor R^2 among absolute pre-generation difficulty, trace length, and a confidence probe. Convincing result: difficulty-vs-residual-work correlation r > 0.4, and contraction failure beats the best competitor by >= 0.10 R^2 on at least three datasets. Indecision band: correlation in [0.2, 0.4], or R^2 advantage in [0.02, 0.10] — the account is suggestive but not dominant. Negative result (r < 0.2 or R^2 advantage <= 0.02): overthinking is not the specific contraction-failure pattern, weakening H3.

Experiment 4 (H4 — Difficulty heads causally gate continuation): At low-residual-work / high-difficulty boundaries, patch/steer the localized difficulty heads toward their easy pole (or add the negative difficulty direction) and measure the effect on termination-token probability and continuation length, vs. control heads and norm-matched random directions. Decisive metric: increase in termination-token probability under difficulty-head steering minus that under control-head steering. Convincing result: difficulty-head steering raises termination probability by >= 15 absolute points and shortens continuation by >= 20%, both significantly above control/random steering, while accuracy on already-solved items holds within 2 points. Indecision band: termination-probability gain in [5, 15] points over control — heads influence but do not clearly gate continuation. Negative result (< 5 points over control, or indistinguishable from confidence-probe steering): difficulty heads are not a distinct causal gate, blurring the claim vs. confidence early-exit.

Experiment 5 (H4 — Training-free intervention saves tokens without hurting accuracy): Online, read step-wise difficulty; when difficulty fails to contract but a lightweight residual-work probe (trained on Experiment-3 labels, 40/60 split by problem) predicts low residual work for k consecutive steps, steer difficulty heads toward easy to induce termination. k and the residual-work threshold selected on the training split (grid k in {2,3,5}). Systems compared on all four datasets: intervention vs. (a) no intervention, (b) fixed truncation matched to intervention mean budget, (c) input-level difficulty budgeting (CODA/AdaCtrl-style), (d) length steering, (e) confidence-based early-exit. Decisive metric: token reduction at equal accuracy — percent reduction vs. no intervention while accuracy stays within 1 point. Secondary: mean tokens, accuracy, wall-clock speedup. Convincing result: >= 25% token reduction within 1 accuracy point on GSM8K and MATH500, on or above every baseline frontier. Indecision band: reduction in [10%, 25%] within 1 point, or a tie with the best budgeting baseline (< 5% difference at matched accuracy) — the intervention works but is not clearly superior; the dynamical characterization (Experiments 1-4) is then the standalone contribution. Negative result (< 10% reduction or > 1 point accuracy loss): the intervention does not yield usable savings.

Experiment 6 (H4 — Underthinking guard): On the hardest quartile of items where residual work truly stays large, verify the trigger does not fire and does not induce premature termination. Decisive metric: underthinking rate (accuracy drop on hard items) as a function of the residual-work threshold. Convincing result: at the deployed threshold, hard-item accuracy drops < 1 point. Indecision band: 1-3 point drop — threshold trades savings for safety; report the curve. Negative result (> 3 point drop): the residual-work gate cannot protect hard items, bounding H4.

Experiment 7 (H1/H3 — Generality across data and scale): Transfer probe, head set, and trigger across datasets and the 1.5B/7B/14B/Qwen3-8B models without retraining. Decisive metric: transferred-probe AUROC relative to in-domain, and intervention token-savings retention. Convincing result: transfer retains >= 80% of in-domain AUROC on at least three scales; savings hold within 10 relative percent. Indecision band: retention in [60%, 80%] — partly model-specific; scoped to per-model probes/heads. Negative result (< 60% retention): the difficulty-dynamics signal is idiosyncratic across models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The difficulty direction may entangle with confidence/uncertainty, blurring the distinction from prior 'confidence early-exit' work; we control by comparing difficulty-head steering against confidence-probe steering and require the difficulty heads to be causally distinct. Difficulty may not be cleanly readable at intermediate positions (the probe was trained pre-generation); we mitigate by fine-tuning the probe on intermediate states, but if difficulty is only encoded pre-generation, the dynamical framing weakens (an informative negative result). The truncate-and-resume residual-work measure is noisy and compute-heavy; we subsample steps. Steering difficulty heads could disrupt genuine hard-problem reasoning (underthinking); the residual-work-gated trigger and threshold analysis address this. Intervention gains may not exceed strong difficulty-budgeting baselines, but the dynamical, causal characterization of difficulty contraction is a standalone contribution. Results may be model-family and scale specific.

novelty.reasoning: Core claim is a temporal shift from static difficulty readouts to mid-generation difficulty dynamics, plus a causal steering test. Closest prior family already shows difficulty is linearly decodable and steerable, but mostly as a pre-generation property for compute allocation. The actual delta - difficulty contraction during CoT, overthinking as failure to contract, and intervention mid-trace - is genuine and non-trivial. The main novelty risk is that it is a refinement of an established representation rather than a wholly new mechanism.

Name: answer_oscillation_settling
Title: Settling Time: Overthinking as Under-Damped Oscillation in the Model's Latent Answer Trajectory
Short Hypothesis: Reasoning models often overthink because their internal latent answer does not converge monotonically but oscillates between a small set of competing candidate answers before settling. Overthinking is largely the time spent in this under-damped oscillation, the amplitude/frequency of oscillation is linearly decodable step-by-step, and a lightweight 'settling detector' that stops once the latent answer has stopped oscillating (rather than merely become stable once) reduces tokens without harming accuracy.
Related Work: Prior work reads a single latent-answer or confidence signal and treats stabilization as a one-time event (Chain-of-Probe on early answering; Beyond the Last Answer on subthought answer distributions; commitment/uncertainty probes). Latent-reasoning work (Emergent Search and Backtracking, 2026) documents exploration-commitment-backtracking phases in continuous space but for non-verbal latent transformers, not deployable verbal reasoning models, and offers no efficiency intervention. Overthinking-cause work attributes it to internal bias/first-impression conflict, self-doubt, or a single verbosity direction (Manifold Steering, CREST, First Impression Problem). None characterize overthinking as an oscillatory dynamical signature in the step-wise latent answer of verbal reasoning models, nor use oscillation-damping (settling-time) rather than one-shot stability as the stopping criterion. Our contribution is a dynamical-systems reframing: measure per-step latent-answer trajectories, quantify oscillation (amplitude, dominant switch pairs, damping), show oscillation-time predicts wasted tokens better than one-shot stability, and design a settling detector that distinguishes genuine convergence from transient stability that will oscillate again. This directly addresses the failure mode of naive early-exit methods (exiting during a lull before the answer flips back).
Abstract: Existing interpretability accounts of overthinking read a single latent signal (a committed answer, a confidence, a verbosity direction) and treat the moment it stabilizes as the point past which reasoning is wasted. But models frequently stabilize on a wrong answer, flip, restabilize, and flip again, meaning one-shot stability is a dangerous stopping criterion. We propose a dynamical-systems view: the model's step-wise latent answer follows a trajectory that is often under-damped, oscillating among a small set of competing candidates before settling. We hypothesize that a large share of overthinking is the settling time of this oscillation, and that oscillation is cheaply decodable from the residual stream. Using logit-lens and trained linear probes, we decode the implicit final answer at every reasoning step on GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA across open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3). We characterize each trace's answer trajectory: number of distinct candidates, switch count, dominant switch pairs, and a damping coefficient fit to the switch amplitude over time. We show settling time predicts wasted tokens (via truncate-and-resume) better than one-shot stability, absolute confidence, or trace length. We then build a training-free settling detector that early-exits only when the latent answer is not merely stable but has entered a low-amplitude, converged regime (no predicted future flip), and compare token savings at equal accuracy against one-shot stability exit, confidence exit, and verbosity steering. We further localize heads that drive candidate switching via activation patching. Our work reframes a slice of overthinking as under-damped answer dynamics and yields a flip-aware efficiency mechanism.
Experiments:
Compute fits an academic node (<= 8xA100-80GB). Primary model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, frozen; only linear probes are trainable. Scale sweep: R1-Qwen distills 1.5B/7B/14B and Qwen3-8B. Decoding: temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 16k thinking tokens, seeds 0/1/2 on every reported number. CoT segmented into steps by newline/step delimiters; analysis restricted to items with extractable answers (math / multiple-choice). Datasets, used as released: GSM8K test (1319), MATH500 (500), AIME 2024+2025 (60), GPQA-Diamond (198).

Experiment 1 (H2 — Step-wise latent answer is decodable): Decode the current implicit final answer at every step boundary via (a) logit-lens at the last position and (b) a trained linear probe on the residual stream predicting the eventual answer token(s). Probe data: 40% of traces train, 60% held out, split by problem. Decisive metric: held-out probe accuracy for the eventual answer, and agreement between logit-lens and probe trajectories. Convincing result: probe accuracy >= 0.70 for the eventual answer by mid-trace and logit-lens/probe trajectory agreement (fraction of steps with matching decoded answer) >= 0.7. Indecision band: probe accuracy in [0.55, 0.70] or agreement in [0.5, 0.7] — trajectories are noisy; oscillation claims are reported tentatively. Negative result (accuracy < 0.55 or agreement < 0.5): the latent answer trajectory is not reliably decodable, undercutting the dynamical analysis.

Experiment 2 (H1 — Trajectories are oscillatory, among few candidates): Characterize each trace's answer trajectory: number of distinct candidates, total switch count, dominant switch-pair identity, and a damping coefficient fit to inter-switch spacing/amplitude. Report distributions per dataset; test concentration among few competing candidates. Decisive metric: fraction of traces with >= 2 answer switches, and, among those, the share of switches confined to the top-2 candidate answers. Convincing result: >= 40% of correctly solved traces show >= 2 switches, with >= 70% of switches confined to 2-3 candidates (structured oscillation, not diffuse drift). Indecision band: 20-40% of traces with >= 2 switches — oscillation exists but is uncommon; settling-time will be a weak lever and we say so. Negative result (< 20% oscillating, or switches diffuse across many candidates): overthinking is not characteristically oscillatory, refuting H1.

Experiment 3 (H1 — Settling time predicts waste): Define settling time = tokens from first commitment to the final flip. Measure wasted tokens via truncate-and-resume (tokens after the last accuracy-changing step). Decisive metric: out-of-sample R^2 (5-fold) of settling time predicting wasted tokens minus best competitor R^2 among one-shot stability point, absolute confidence probe, and trace length. Convincing result: settling time beats the best competitor by >= 0.10 R^2 on at least three datasets. Indecision band: advantage in [0.02, 0.10] — settling time is useful but not dominant. Negative result (advantage <= 0.02): settling time does not specifically explain waste, weakening H1.

Experiment 4 (H3 — One-shot stability is dangerous, motivating settling): Quantify how often the answer is stable for k steps and then flips. Decisive metric: expected accuracy loss of a naive k-step one-shot stability exit (fraction of traces where the answer flips to the correct value after a k-step stable window), for k in {2,3,5}. Convincing result: naive one-shot exit at k=3 would forfeit >= 5 accuracy points on at least one hard dataset (AIME/GPQA), establishing the failure mode the settling detector targets. Indecision band: forfeit in [2, 5] points — the danger is modest; the settling detector's advantage over one-shot exit is expected to be small. Negative result (< 2 points): one-shot stability is already safe, so the flip-aware criterion adds little (an informative negative for H3's motivation).

Experiment 5 (H1 — Switching is head-mediated): Use activation patching / head attribution at switch onsets to find heads driving candidate switching; ablate them and measure change in switch count and settling time. Decisive metric: change in mean switch count under top-head ablation vs. equal-count random ablation. Convincing result: top-head ablation changes switch count by >= 30% (vs. < 10% random) while accuracy holds within 3 points. Indecision band: change in [10%, 30%] — partial head-mediation; a candidate circuit is reported without strong claims. Negative result (< 10%): switching is not cleanly head-mediated; the dynamical characterization stands but the circuit claim does not.

Experiment 6 (H3 — Settling detector saves tokens without missing beneficial flips): Online, decode step-wise answer; a lightweight residual-stream probe (trained on Experiment-2 trajectories, 40/60 split by problem) predicts P(future flip); early-exit only when the answer is stable for k steps AND predicted flip probability < tau. k and tau selected on the training split (grid k in {2,3,5}, tau in {0.1,0.2,0.3}). Systems compared on all four datasets: settling detector vs. (a) no intervention, (b) one-shot k-step stability exit, (c) confidence early-exit, (d) verbosity/manifold steering, (e) fixed truncation matched to detector mean budget. Decisive metric: token reduction at equal accuracy — percent reduction vs. no intervention while accuracy stays within 1 point; the detector must specifically beat the one-shot stability exit on this metric. Secondary: missed-flip rate (exits before a beneficial correction), mean tokens, wall-clock speedup. Convincing result: >= 20% token reduction within 1 accuracy point on GSM8K and MATH500, with missed-flip rate at least 30% lower than one-shot exit at matched tokens. Indecision band: reduction in [10%, 20%] within 1 point, or missed-flip rate within 10% of one-shot exit — the flip-aware criterion adds little over one-shot stability; the dynamical characterization (Experiments 1-5) is then the standalone contribution. Negative result (< 10% reduction, or no improvement in missed-flip rate over one-shot exit): the settling detector does not deliver a usable, flip-aware advantage.

Experiment 7 (H2/H3 — Generality across data and scale): Transfer probes and the settling detector across datasets and the 1.5B/7B/14B/Qwen3-8B models without retraining. Decisive metric: transferred-probe accuracy relative to in-domain, and detector token-savings retention. Convincing result: transfer retains >= 80% of in-domain probe accuracy on at least three scales; savings hold within 10 relative percent. Indecision band: retention in [60%, 80%] — partly model-specific; scoped to per-model probes. Negative result (< 60% retention): the oscillation signal is idiosyncratic across models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Step-wise latent-answer decoding is only reliable for extractable answers, so we restrict to math/multiple-choice. Oscillation may be rare in some models or datasets, making settling-time a weak predictor (an informative negative result). The future-flip probe may be hard to calibrate and could exit prematurely on hard problems where a late flip is corrective (underthinking); the missed-flip metric and tau tuning address this trade-off explicitly. Switching may not be cleanly head-mediated, weakening the circuit-localization claim though the dynamical characterization stands independently. Damping-coefficient fitting on discrete, short trajectories is noisy; we mitigate by subsampling and reporting robust summary statistics. Detector gains may not exceed strong steering baselines, but the flip-aware settling criterion targets a documented failure of one-shot exit and is a standalone contribution. Results may be model-family and scale specific.

novelty.reasoning: Core claim is a dynamical-systems framing of step-wise answer switching as under-damped oscillation with a damping coefficient and flip-aware settling detector. Closest prior family is already rich: latent-answer backtracking, trajectory geometry/stability, hesitation loops, and early-answer/confidence-exit work. The genuine delta is mostly the specific oscillation/damping formalism plus a future-flip-aware stopping rule on verbal reasoning models. That is a meaningful packaging/measurement twist, but not a fundamentally new phenomenon.

The downstream change is concrete: better stopping rules for reasoning models. However, the practical scope is narrow, and the claimed gains depend on whether oscillation is common and whether the detector calibrates well across tasks/models. The so what is solid but not broad.
