Name: branch_worthiness_signal
Title: Does a Model Know When to Fork? An Internal Branch-Worthiness Signal for Per-Problem Parallel Compute Allocation
Short Hypothesis: A reasoning model's early hidden states, from a single greedy prefix, linearly encode a 'branch-worthiness' signal: whether the problem has multiple plausible competing solution paths that make parallel sampling (best-of-N / self-consistency) worthwhile, versus a single-basin problem where extra samples are wasted. This signal derives from the entropy of the model's internal candidate-answer distribution and can be read cheaply to allocate parallel budget per-problem, saving compute at fixed accuracy.
Related Work: Test-time scaling work allocates parallel budget per-problem using black-box predictors: T2 (2026) estimates optimal parallelism from latent representations; OptScale/OSCA/SCALE/DORA (2024-2025) derive resource-allocation rules; First Finish Search (2025) returns the first-completing trace; Latent-Trajectory signals (Vilas et al. 2025) predict per-trace success from representation dynamics. All of these either predict per-trace quality (post-hoc, needs the trace) or fit an opaque predictor for how many samples to draw. Separately, interpretability work (Distributional Reasoning in LLMs, 2024; How to Think Step-by-Step, 2024) shows middle layers hold a distribution over candidate intermediate/final answers via parallel pathways. No prior work connects these: we hypothesize that the *internal candidate-answer distribution entropy*, readable from a single short prefix before any full trace or sampling, is the mechanistic origin of branch-worthiness, and that it predicts the marginal value of parallel sampling per-problem. This is a mechanistic account plus a causal test (steering the entropy signal changes sampling utility), not another opaque allocation heuristic or per-trace success predictor.
Abstract: Parallel test-time scaling (best-of-N, self-consistency) improves reasoning accuracy but wastes enormous compute: many problems are 'single-basin' where all samples converge to the same answer, so extra samples add nothing, while a minority are genuinely multi-path where parallel exploration pays off. Existing methods choose the sample count per problem with opaque predictors and offer little mechanistic insight into what determines the value of forking. We hypothesize that a model's early hidden states already encode a branch-worthiness signal, rooted in the entropy of the internal candidate-answer distribution known to live in middle layers, and that this signal predicts the marginal accuracy gain of parallel sampling before any sampling is done. Across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we (1) measure per-problem parallel-sampling utility (accuracy gain from N=1 to N=k) as ground truth; (2) read the internal candidate-answer distribution from a short greedy prefix via logit-lens and trained linear probes and test whether its entropy predicts branch-worthiness better than prompt-length, difficulty probes, or output-confidence baselines; (3) localize the heads/layers carrying the distribution via activation patching and causally test whether steering the entropy up/down changes the actual utility of sampling; and (4) build a training-free per-problem allocator that reads the signal from a single prefix and sets N adaptively. We compare compute-at-fixed-accuracy against uniform-N, T2-style latent predictors, and confidence-based allocation. Our work reframes 'how many samples to draw' as reading a mechanistically-grounded internal signal.
Experiments:
Compute fits an academic node (<= 8xA100-80GB). Primary model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, frozen; only linear probes are trainable, interventions are activation edits. Scale sweep: R1-Qwen distills 1.5B/7B/14B and Qwen3-8B (smaller k for the 14B model to control cost). Sampling: temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 16k thinking tokens, seeds 0/1/2. Analysis restricted to extractable-answer items (math / multiple-choice). Datasets, used as released: GSM8K test (1319), MATH500 (500), AIME 2024+2025 (60), GPQA-Diamond (198); ground-truth utility (Experiment 1) is measured on a 400-item stratified subsample of GSM8K/MATH500 plus all AIME/GPQA to bound the N=16 sampling cost.

Experiment 1 (H1 — Branch-worthiness ground truth exists and budget is wasted under uniform-N): For each problem draw N=16 independent full samples; define parallel-utility = accuracy(self-consistency at N=16) minus accuracy(greedy N=1), and answer-diversity = entropy of the final-answer distribution over samples. Label single-basin (near-zero diversity, no utility) vs multi-path. Decisive metric: fraction of problems with parallel-utility <= 1 point (single-basin), i.e., budget wasted under uniform N=16. Convincing result: >= 40% of problems are single-basin, establishing large avoidable waste and a non-degenerate multi-path minority (>= 15%). Indecision band: single-basin fraction in [20%, 40%] — waste is modest; the allocator's headroom is limited and we say so. Negative result (< 20% single-basin, or < 5% multi-path): there is little to allocate over, undercutting the motivation.

Experiment 2 (H2 — Internal candidate-distribution entropy from a short prefix predicts branch-worthiness): Generate only a short greedy prefix (test lengths 32/64/128 tokens); at middle layers decode the internal candidate-answer distribution via (a) logit-lens at the last prefix position and (b) a trained linear probe predicting the entropy of eventual sampled answers, giving internal-entropy. Probe data: 40% of problems train, 60% held out, split so no problem is shared. Decisive metric: held-out rank correlation (Spearman) and AUROC of short-prefix internal-entropy vs. ground-truth parallel-utility / single-basin label. Convincing result: AUROC >= 0.75 for the single-basin vs multi-path label at prefix length <= 128 tokens, with Spearman > 0.4 against parallel-utility. Indecision band: AUROC in [0.62, 0.75] — the prefix signal is weak; branch structure may emerge only later and we report that. Negative result (AUROC < 0.62 at all tested prefix lengths): branch-worthiness is not readable from an early prefix, refuting H1/H2.

Experiment 3 (H1 — The cheap internal signal matches costlier predictors): Predict parallel-utility from short-prefix internal-entropy vs. (i) prompt length, (ii) a pre-generation difficulty probe, (iii) verbal/output confidence after a full greedy trace, (iv) a T2-style black-box latent predictor. Decisive metric: ranking AUROC (and regression R^2) of internal-entropy minus the best baseline that needs no full trace, and the gap to full-trace baselines. Convincing result: short-prefix internal-entropy is within 0.03 AUROC of the best full-trace predictor while using far less compute, and beats every no-full-trace baseline by >= 0.05 AUROC. Indecision band: within [0.03, 0.08] AUROC below the best full-trace predictor and only tied with difficulty probe — the signal is not distinctly better than plain difficulty; the causal test (Experiment 5) becomes decisive for the mechanistic claim. Negative result (worse than difficulty probe): internal-entropy is just a difficulty proxy, weakening the novelty.

Experiment 4 (H2 — Localizing the candidate-answer distribution): Use activation patching / head attribution to find middle layers/heads carrying the candidate-answer distribution; ablate them and measure degradation of the entropy readout. Decisive metric: drop in Experiment-2 probe AUROC under top-component ablation vs. equal-count random ablation. Convincing result: top-component ablation drops entropy-readout AUROC by >= 0.1 (vs. < 0.03 random), localizing the signal to a small component set. Indecision band: drop in [0.03, 0.1] — partially localized. Negative result (< 0.03): the signal is not localized to identifiable components.

Experiment 5 (H2 — Causal: entropy reflects branch structure): Steer the identified components to raise or lower internal-entropy on the prefix, then run N=16 sampling and measure realized answer-diversity, checking sample validity. Decisive metric: change in realized answer-diversity when steering entropy up vs. down (paired per problem). Convincing result: raising internal-entropy significantly increases realized diversity and lowering it collapses samples toward one answer (paired p < 0.01, monotone in steering magnitude), with < 5% invalid/degenerate samples. Indecision band: a significant but small effect (diversity change < 0.2 in normalized entropy units) or > 10% degenerate samples — the signal correlates with but may not cleanly cause branch structure. Negative result (no significant change or mostly degenerate samples): the entropy signal is a spurious correlate, not the mechanistic origin of branch-worthiness.

Experiment 6 (H3 — Adaptive allocator saves compute at fixed accuracy): For each problem, generate one short prefix, read internal-entropy, and set N via a monotone schedule (single-basin -> N=1; high entropy -> N=16). Schedule thresholds fit on the Experiment-2 training split only. Systems compared on all four datasets: allocator vs. (a) uniform-N self-consistency, (b) First Finish Search, (c) confidence-based allocation, (d) T2-style predictor. Decisive metric: compute (mean samples/tokens) at fixed accuracy — samples needed to match uniform-N=16 accuracy within 1 point. Secondary: full Pareto accuracy-vs-compute curve, accuracy at matched budget. Convincing result: allocator matches uniform-N=16 accuracy within 1 point using >= 40% fewer samples, and dominates or ties the best baseline on the Pareto frontier. Indecision band: 15-40% sample reduction, or a tie with T2 (< 5% sample difference at matched accuracy) — the allocator works but is not clearly superior; the mechanistic grounding (Experiments 2-5) is then the standalone contribution. Negative result (< 15% reduction or > 1 point accuracy loss to match budgets): the signal does not yield usable allocation savings.

Experiment 7 (H1 — Generality across data and scale): Transfer probe and allocator across datasets and the 1.5B/7B/14B/Qwen3-8B models without retraining. Decisive metric: transferred-probe AUROC relative to in-domain, and allocator sample-savings retention. Convincing result: transfer retains >= 80% of in-domain AUROC on at least three scales; savings hold within 10 relative percent. Indecision band: retention in [60%, 80%] — partly model-specific; scoped to per-model probes. Negative result (< 60% retention): branch-worthiness readout is idiosyncratic across models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The internal candidate-answer distribution is cleanest for extractable-answer tasks, so we restrict to math/multiple-choice. Short-prefix entropy may not capture branch structure that only emerges late in reasoning, weakening prediction (an informative negative result, and mitigated by testing several prefix lengths). Internal-entropy may correlate with plain difficulty, making it hard to distinguish from difficulty-probe baselines; the causal steering experiment and the direct comparison to difficulty probes address this. Steering entropy could produce degenerate or off-distribution samples, complicating the causal claim; we report sample validity. The allocator's gains may not exceed strong latent-predictor baselines like T2, but the mechanistic grounding (branch-worthiness as internal candidate-distribution entropy, causally validated) is a standalone contribution. Ground-truth utility estimation with k up to 16 is compute-intensive; we subsample problems and use smaller k for larger models. Results may be model-family and scale specific.

novelty.reasoning: Core claim is a mechanistic reinterpretation of existing test-time compute allocation: early hidden-state entropy as a branch-worthiness signal to predict when parallel sampling helps. The search summary indicates close prior work already predicts per-problem sample budget from hidden states / early decoding, including T2, OSCA/OptScale, and self-estimating BoN. The genuine delta is narrower: tying the predictor to an internal candidate-answer distribution in middle layers and adding causal steering/localization. That is more than a heuristic tweak, but it still sits within a crowded family and may reduce to a difficulty proxy.

The proposal's potential impact is strongest for inference-efficiency and reasoning-scaling researchers, especially on extractive reasoning tasks and model families where early branch-worthiness is stable. However, the practical gain may be modest if it only matches existing allocators, transfers poorly, or works only on curated tasks.

Name: narration_subspace_suppression
Title: Think in Shorthand: Separating a Narration Subspace from Computation to Suppress Performative Reasoning
Short Hypothesis: Reasoning models carry two largely separable residual-stream subspaces: a computation subspace that carries out and updates the latent answer, and a narration subspace that governs verbose, human-facing presentation of already-computed results. Overthinking is over-activation of the narration subspace after computation is effectively done. Suppressing the narration subspace (while leaving the computation subspace intact) makes the model 'think in shorthand,' cutting tokens with minimal accuracy loss, and does so more precisely than a single verbosity/length direction.
Related Work: Recent work establishes that CoT is often performative or unfaithful and that latent answers form early: Reasoning Theater (2026) probes performative CoT and early-exits; TTS / 'Can Aha Moments Be Fake?' (2025) labels steps decorative vs load-bearing and finds a single steerable TrueThinking direction; State over Tokens (2025) reframes tokens as externalized state; Causal Bypass / CMI (2026) shows answers can be causally independent of CoT text. Efficiency-steering work (Manifold Steering, CREST, ThinkEdit, ASC) steers along a single verbosity/length direction. All prior work either (a) treats decorative-vs-genuine as a per-step binary, (b) reads a single latent 'answer' or 'verbosity' direction, or (c) reactively early-exits. None hypothesizes or tests a *dimensional decomposition* of the residual stream into a computation subspace that must be preserved and a separable narration/presentation subspace that can be suppressed. Our contribution is (1) constructing and causally validating these two subspaces via contrastive activation collection (terse vs verbose renderings of identical computations) plus disentanglement, (2) showing overthinking corresponds to sustained narration-subspace activation after computation completes, and (3) a training-free intervention that projects out the narration subspace during generation, which is finer-grained than a single length direction because it preserves the orthogonal computation subspace by construction.
Abstract: Reasoning language models routinely 'overthink,' generating verbose chains of thought long after they have effectively solved a problem. Prior interpretability work explains this as performative or decorative reasoning and either labels individual steps or steers a single verbosity direction. We propose a sharper, dimensional account: the residual stream contains two largely separable subspaces—a computation subspace that performs and updates the latent answer, and a narration subspace that governs verbose, human-facing presentation of results already computed. We hypothesize that overthinking is sustained narration-subspace activation after computation is complete, and that suppressing the narration subspace while preserving the orthogonal computation subspace lets the model 'think in shorthand' with minimal accuracy loss. We construct the two subspaces via contrastive activation collection—prompting models to render identical computations tersely versus verbosely—followed by difference-of-means and orthogonalization to isolate a narration direction set that is, by construction, orthogonal to the components that carry the latent answer. Across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we verify the subspaces are separable by testing that suppressing narration does not degrade a latent-answer probe while suppressing computation does. We show narration-subspace activation stays high during overthinking after residual work (via truncate-and-resume) reaches zero. Finally, we introduce a training-free generation-time projection that removes the narration subspace and compare token savings at equal accuracy against verbosity steering, TTS-style pruning, and reactive early-exit. Our work reframes overthinking as an over-narration mode and offers a precise, interpretable efficiency mechanism.
Experiments:
Compute fits an academic node (<= 8xA100-80GB). Primary model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, frozen; only linear probes are trainable, interventions are activation projections. Scale sweep: R1-Qwen distills 1.5B/7B/14B and Qwen3-8B. Decoding: temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 16k thinking tokens, seeds 0/1/2 on every reported number. CoT segmented into steps; analysis restricted to extractable-answer items (math / multiple-choice). Datasets, used as released: GSM8K test (1319), MATH500 (500), AIME 2024+2025 (60), GPQA-Diamond (198); a held-out 300-problem set (disjoint from evaluation) is used to build the subspaces.

Experiment 1 (H1 — Constructing the narration subspace): Collect contrastive activation pairs by prompting the model to render the SAME worked computation tersely vs verbosely on the held-out set; compute per-layer difference-of-means vectors and assemble a low-rank narration subspace by SVD. Build an alternative narration signal from easy-vs-hard (more vs less performative) problems. Decisive metric: variance explained and rank of the narration subspace, and agreement (principal-angle alignment) between the terse/verbose subspace and the easy/hard subspace. Convincing result: a low-rank (<= 10-dim) narration subspace captures the terse/verbose contrast and aligns with the easy/hard signal (principal angles < 45 degrees on the top directions). Indecision band: alignment with top principal angles in [45, 60] degrees — the two narration signals only partly agree; we report the construction as prompt-dependent. Negative result (no low-rank structure or > 60 degree misalignment): a stable narration subspace cannot be constructed, undercutting the framing.

Experiment 2 (H1 — Separability from computation): Train a linear latent-answer probe (predicting the eventual final answer) as the computation readout on 40% of held-out problems; evaluate on the remaining 60%. Then compare probe accuracy under (a) projecting out the narration subspace, (b) projecting out a matched-rank random subspace, (c) projecting out the computation subspace (from the answer-probe weights). Report principal angles between narration and computation subspaces. Decisive metric: latent-answer probe accuracy drop under narration-subspace removal vs. under computation-subspace removal. Convincing result: narration removal drops probe accuracy by < 3 points (comparable to random-subspace removal) while computation removal drops it by > 20 points, with narration/computation principal angles > 60 degrees (near-orthogonal). Indecision band: narration-removal drop in [3, 8] points, or principal angles in [45, 60] degrees — the subspaces overlap partially; suppression will carry some accuracy risk and we report it. Negative result (narration removal drops probe > 8 points, or subspaces are not near-orthogonal): the subspaces are not separable, refuting H1 (an informative null).

Experiment 3 (H2 — Narration stays high after computation completes): Read narration-subspace activation magnitude at each step; measure residual work via truncate-and-resume (accuracy after forcing termination at step t). Decisive metric: out-of-sample R^2 (5-fold) of the post-completion narration-activation integral (activation after residual work hits zero) predicting wasted tokens, minus best competitor R^2 among trace length, absolute verbosity-direction projection, and a confidence probe. Convincing result: narration activation stays significantly elevated after residual work hits zero, and its post-completion integral beats the best competitor by >= 0.10 R^2 on at least three datasets. Indecision band: R^2 advantage in [0.02, 0.10] — narration activation is a useful but not dominant predictor. Negative result (advantage <= 0.02 or no sustained post-completion activation): overthinking is not specifically sustained narration, weakening H2.

Experiment 4 (H3 — Narration projection saves tokens, more precisely than a single direction): During generation, subtract the projection onto the narration subspace at selected layers (coefficient sweep). Coefficient and layer set selected on the held-out construction problems. Systems compared on all four datasets: narration-subspace projection vs. (a) no intervention, (b) single verbosity/length steering (ASC/Manifold-style), (c) TTS-style post-hoc step pruning, (d) Reasoning-Theater-style probe early-exit, (e) fixed truncation matched to mean budget. Decisive metric: token reduction at equal accuracy — percent reduction vs. no intervention while accuracy stays within 1 point; the key comparison is whether narration projection Pareto-dominates the single verbosity direction. Secondary: mean tokens, accuracy, wall-clock speedup. Convincing result: >= 25% token reduction within 1 accuracy point on GSM8K and MATH500, strictly above the single-direction baseline's accuracy-vs-token frontier (>= 5% more reduction at matched accuracy). Indecision band: reduction in [10%, 25%] within 1 point, or within 5% of the single verbosity direction at matched accuracy — the dimensional method works but is not clearly finer-grained; the separability analysis (Experiments 1-2) is then the standalone contribution. Negative result (< 10% reduction, or worse than the single direction): the subspace method adds nothing over prior steering.

Experiment 5 (H3 — Qualitative: shorthand, not damage): Inspect generations under narration suppression; an LLM-judge plus a human spot-check (200 traces, two annotators) rate whether derivation steps are preserved while decorative narration/verification asides are dropped. Decisive metric: fraction of suppressed traces judged to preserve all load-bearing derivation steps. Convincing result: >= 85% of suppressed traces preserve load-bearing steps while dropping narration, with inter-annotator agreement kappa > 0.6. Indecision band: preservation in [70%, 85%] — suppression sometimes removes substantive content. Negative result (< 70% preserve load-bearing steps): suppression damages computation, contradicting the shorthand claim.

Experiment 6 (H3 — Underthinking analysis): On the hardest quartile of items where narration may overlap genuine verification, measure accuracy drop vs. suppression strength and identify a safe operating point. Decisive metric: hard-item accuracy drop at the deployed suppression coefficient. Convincing result: hard-item accuracy drops < 1 point at the coefficient delivering the Experiment-4 savings. Indecision band: 1-3 point drop — a safety/savings tradeoff; report the curve. Negative result (> 3 point drop): narration suppression harms genuine verification, bounding H3.

Experiment 7 (H1/H3 — Generality across data and scale): Transfer the narration subspace across datasets and the 1.5B/7B/14B/Qwen3-8B models without recomputation. Decisive metric: separability (Experiment-2 probe-drop asymmetry) and token savings under a transferred subspace, relative to an in-domain subspace. Convincing result: transferred subspace retains the separability asymmetry and >= 80% of in-domain token savings on at least three scales. Indecision band: 60-80% retention — partly model-specific; scoped to per-model subspaces. Negative result (< 60% retention): the narration subspace is idiosyncratic across models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The clean separation of narration and computation subspaces may not hold—verification/narration can carry genuine computation, so suppressing narration might harm accuracy on hard problems (this trade-off is measured directly and a near-null result on separability is itself informative). Contrastive terse/verbose prompting may not elicit representations that match spontaneous overthinking, biasing the narration direction; we mitigate with an alternative easy-vs-hard difference signal and cross-validate. Latent-answer probes are reliable mainly for extractable answers, so we restrict to math/multiple-choice. The narration subspace may partially coincide with the single verbosity direction, in which case the dimensional framing yields little gain over prior steering (though the separability analysis remains a contribution). Projection at generation time can push activations off-distribution and introduce errors; coefficient sweeps and validity checks address this. Results may be model-family and scale specific.

novelty.reasoning: Core claim is a 2-subspace decomposition of residual stream into computation vs narration, with a causal separability test and generation-time suppression. That is a meaningful delta over prior single-direction verbosity steering and step-level decorative-vs-load-bearing labeling. However, the search summary already covers adjacent families: CoT unfaithfulness/causal bypass, functional metacognition subspaces, and shared/logical subspace steering. So the novelty is real but moderate: the main newness is applying a dimensional disentanglement framing specifically to narration suppression, not a fundamentally new phenomenon.

That matters to efficient-reasoning researchers and model steering folks. The proposal is not obviously a new application area or a broadly enabling capability change.

Name: importance_precommitment_gap
Title: Does a Model Know a Step Matters Before It Writes It? A Pre-Emission Importance Signal for Cheap, Faithful Reasoning Compression
Short Hypothesis: Reasoning models linearly encode, at the moment they begin a reasoning step, a pre-emission importance signal that predicts whether the step will turn out to be causally load-bearing (high counterfactual importance / 'thought anchor') or negligible. Because this signal is available before the step is generated, it can drive a training-free, attention-matrix-free budget allocator that spends full detail on anchor steps and compresses the rest, achieving better token-accuracy tradeoffs than post-hoc attention-based pruning.
Related Work: Thought Anchors (2025) and Can Aha Moments Be Fake?/TTS (2025) show only a small fraction of reasoning steps are causally load-bearing, but they measure importance retrospectively via resampling or corruption of already-generated steps. MI-Peaks (2025) finds 'thinking tokens' are information peaks, again identified during/after generation. Attention-based efficiency methods (DynTS, FROST, LazyEviction, G-KV, EpiKV 2026) prune or evict tokens using attention or representation-change signals computed after tokens exist; EpiKV notably argues attention is a noisy, expensive importance proxy and scores tokens by forward-pass representation change post-hoc. Preplan-and-Anchor (2025) uses attention to find anchors but for RL credit assignment, not prospective prediction. Crucially, NO prior work asks whether step importance is encoded PROSPECTIVELY, before the step is emitted, from a single forward pass at the step boundary, nor uses such a signal to allocate generation-time detail budget. Our contribution is (1) establishing that a cheap, attention-free, pre-emission linear probe predicts a step's eventual thought-anchor status, (2) causally validating it, and (3) turning it into a proactive detail-budget allocator that avoids materializing the attention matrix, unlike all attention-based baselines.
Abstract: Recent interpretability work shows that only a small minority of reasoning steps in a chain of thought are causally load-bearing 'thought anchors'; the rest are near-negligible. But every existing method identifies these anchors retrospectively, after the steps are generated, using resampling, corruption, or attention scores. We ask a sharper, forward-looking question: does a reasoning model already know, at the instant it starts a step, whether that step will matter? We hypothesize that the residual stream at a step boundary linearly encodes a pre-emission importance signal predicting the step's eventual counterfactual importance. Across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we first compute ground-truth per-step importance via resampling (thought-anchor counterfactual importance), then train a lightweight linear probe on pre-step activations to predict it, comparing against post-hoc attention-based and representation-change scores. We test whether the signal is causal by steering it and observing changes in the actual importance/length of the emitted step, and by localizing the components carrying it. We then convert the probe into a training-free, attention-matrix-free detail-budget allocator: at each step boundary the model spends a full-detail budget on predicted-anchor steps and a compressed budget (via prompted terseness or truncation-and-continue) on the rest. We evaluate token-accuracy tradeoffs against uniform compression, attention-based pruning (FROST/DynTS-style), and reactive eviction. Our work reframes efficient reasoning as prospective importance prediction and yields a cheap, deployable, interpretable allocator.
Experiments:
Compute fits an academic node (<= 8xA100-80GB). Primary model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, frozen; only linear probes are trainable, interventions are activation edits / prompt-budget controls. Scale sweep: R1-Qwen distills 1.5B/7B/14B and Qwen3-8B. Decoding: temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 16k thinking tokens, seeds 0/1/2 on every reported number. CoT segmented into sentence-level steps. Datasets, used as released: GSM8K test (1319), MATH500 (500), AIME 2024+2025 (60), GPQA-Diamond (198); resampling-based importance labels (Experiment 1) computed on a 400-item stratified subsample of GSM8K/MATH500 plus all AIME/GPQA to bound cost.

Experiment 1 (H1 — Ground-truth anchor sparsity): Compute per-step counterfactual importance via resampling (Thought-Anchors style: sample semantically-different replacement steps, continue, measure the shift in the final-answer distribution) and a second TTS-style corruption score. Threshold to label steps anchor vs negligible; 8 resamples/step. Decisive metric: median anchor fraction per dataset, and label agreement (kappa) between the resampling and corruption schemes. Convincing result: median anchor fraction < 0.35 (confirming sparsity) with scheme kappa > 0.6. Indecision band: anchor fraction in [0.35, 0.5] or kappa in [0.4, 0.6] — anchors are less sparse or labels noisy; downstream claims scoped accordingly. Negative result (fraction > 0.5 or kappa < 0.4): steps are not sparsely load-bearing, or labels unreliable, undercutting the premise.

Experiment 2 (H1 — Pre-emission importance is decodable): At each step boundary, extract residual activations BEFORE the step is generated (test the boundary and the first few step tokens) and train per-layer linear probes to predict the ground-truth importance label. Probe data: 40% of steps train, 60% held out, split by problem. Systems compared: pre-emission probe vs. (a) bag-of-words on prior text, (b) retrospective probe that sees the generated step (upper bound), (c) post-hoc attention-received score, (d) EpiKV-style representation-change score. Decisive metric: held-out AUROC of the pre-emission probe for anchor vs negligible. Convincing result: pre-emission AUROC >= 0.72, beating bag-of-words by >= 0.08 and within 0.05 of the best post-hoc score that requires the step to exist. Indecision band: AUROC in [0.6, 0.72], or no clear advantage over bag-of-words — the signal is weak or largely lexical; the allocator is unlikely to beat post-hoc methods and we say so. Negative result (AUROC < 0.6): importance is not pre-encoded at the boundary, refuting H1 (an informative negative — importance may form mid-step).

Experiment 3 (H2 — The signal is causal): Steer along the probe direction (up/down) at a step boundary and measure whether the emitted step's realized importance (resampling score) and length change, vs. norm-matched random/control directions; localize contributing components via activation patching. Decisive metric: change in realized step importance when steering up vs. down (paired), relative to control-direction steering. Convincing result: steering up significantly raises realized importance and length while steering down lowers them (paired p < 0.01, monotone), both clearly above control directions, with task accuracy held within 2 points. Indecision band: a significant but small effect (realized-importance change < 0.1 in normalized units) — the signal correlates with but does not clearly cause importance. Negative result (no significant change vs. control): the probe reads a correlate, not a causal importance signal, weakening H2.

Experiment 4 (H3 — Attention-free allocator beats attention-based pruning): At each step boundary read the pre-emission importance; predicted-anchor -> full generation, predicted-negligible -> compressed budget (terseness instruction / step-length cap / skip-and-continue). Threshold selected on the Experiment-2 training split. Systems compared on all four datasets: allocator vs. (a) no intervention, (b) uniform terseness, (c) fixed truncation matched to allocator budget, (d) FROST/DynTS-style attention pruning, (e) EpiKV/LazyEviction reactive eviction. Decisive metric: token reduction at equal accuracy — percent reduction vs. no intervention while accuracy stays within 1 point. Secondary: mean tokens, accuracy, wall-clock speedup, and confirmation the allocator never materializes the full attention matrix (a deployability advantage over attention-based baselines). Convincing result: >= 25% token reduction within 1 accuracy point on GSM8K and MATH500, matching or beating attention-based baselines on the accuracy-token frontier while avoiding attention-matrix materialization. Indecision band: reduction in [10%, 25%] within 1 point, or a tie with attention-based pruning (< 5% difference at matched accuracy) — the allocator is competitive but not clearly better on savings; the prospective-signal finding (Experiments 1-3) plus its cheaper compute profile remain the contribution. Negative result (< 10% reduction or > 1 point accuracy loss): the prospective signal does not yield a usable allocator.

Experiment 5 (H3 — Faithfulness / anchor preservation): Verify true anchors are preserved and quantify the cost of mis-compressing one. Decisive metric: recall of true anchors (fraction routed to full-detail budget) at the deployed threshold, and accuracy drop attributable to compressing a true anchor. Convincing result: anchor recall >= 0.9 at the deployed threshold with < 1 point accuracy loss from anchor mis-compression. Indecision band: anchor recall in [0.75, 0.9] — some anchors are compressed; report the recall/savings tradeoff. Negative result (recall < 0.75 or > 3 point loss): the allocator cannot protect anchors, bounding H3.

Experiment 6 (H1/H3 — Generality across data and scale): Transfer probe and allocator across datasets and the 1.5B/7B/14B/Qwen3-8B models without retraining. Decisive metric: transferred-probe AUROC relative to in-domain, and allocator token-savings retention. Convincing result: transfer retains >= 80% of in-domain AUROC on at least three scales; savings hold within 10 relative percent. Indecision band: retention in [60%, 80%] — partly model-specific; scoped to per-model probes. Negative result (< 60% retention): the pre-emission signal is idiosyncratic across models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Step importance may only be decidable mid-step rather than at the boundary, making pre-emission prediction weak; this would be an informative negative result and is partly mitigated by testing multiple boundary positions (first few tokens of a step). Resampling-based importance labels are noisy and compute-heavy; we subsample steps and use two labeling schemes for robustness. The signal may correlate with generic difficulty/position, blurring the distinction from simpler heuristics; we control with baselines and causal steering. Compressing predicted-negligible steps could still cascade errors on hard problems (underthinking); the anchor-recall metric and budget thresholds address this. Allocator gains may not exceed strong attention-based baselines, but the prospective, attention-free framing and its deployability (no attention-matrix materialization) are standalone contributions. Results may be model-family and scale specific.

novelty.reasoning: Core claim: a cheap linear probe on pre-step activations can predict whether the upcoming reasoning step will be causally load-bearing, and this signal can drive an attention-free detail-budget allocator. Closest prior family is Thought Anchors / TTS / MI-Peaks for importance labeling, plus ROI/meta-cognitive and budget-guidance work for budgeting. The genuine delta is the prospective, pre-emission prediction at step boundary and the deployability angle of avoiding attention matrices. This is meaningfully different from retrospective importance estimation, but the conceptual leap is moderate because it sits very close to prospective routing / meta-cognition and could reduce to difficulty/position proxies.

Name: shallow_token_depth_skip
Title: Most Reasoning Tokens Are Shallow: Training-Free Adaptive Depth via a Cheap Deep-Thinking Predictor
Short Hypothesis: In a reasoning model's chain of thought, the vast majority of generated tokens (connectives, narration, formatting, easy continuations) reach their final prediction in early-to-middle layers ('shallow tokens'), while only a sparse set of 'deep-thinking' tokens require the full stack. Whether the current token is shallow is predictable online from mid-layer activations, so a training-free adaptive-depth decoder can early-exit the shallow majority through the LM head while running full depth only on deep tokens, cutting compute at fixed accuracy.
Related Work: Adaptive-depth architectures (Mixture-of-Depths, Mixture-of-Recursions, Inner Thinking Transformer, Think-at-Hard, adaptive latent CoT) all REQUIRE training routers/adapters from scratch or fine-tuning. Interpretability work on depth usage (Guess-then-Refine 2025; Concept Depth 2024; Demystifying LLM Layers 2025) shows tokens converge at different depths but does not build a deployable decoder. 'Think Deep, Not Just Long' (2026) measures deep-thinking tokens (predictions revised in deep layers) and uses the deep-thinking ratio to SELECT good samples (test-time scaling), not to allocate per-token depth during generation. MTD/Divergence Steering (2025) measures computation density via a shallow-head KL and steers text style, not depth-skipping. KV-cache pruning (DynTS, EpiKV, LazyEviction) reduces memory over the sequence dimension, orthogonal to skipping layers on the current token. Classic early-exit LMs (e.g., CALM) exist for general LM but rely on confidence thresholds and typically need calibration training; none exploit the specific mechanistic structure that reasoning CoTs are dominated by shallow narration tokens, nor characterize which token TYPES are deep. Our contribution is threefold and distinct: (1) a mechanistic characterization that deep-thinking need in reasoning CoT is sparse, structured (concentrated on computation/answer tokens, not narration), and cheaply predictable mid-stack; (2) a fully training-free adaptive-depth decoder for existing reasoning models using a self-speculative check; (3) an efficiency evaluation showing token-wise depth skipping is complementary to step-level stopping methods.
Abstract: Reasoning language models generate long chains of thought, but not every token is computationally hard. Building on the 'guess-then-refine' view of transformer depth, we hypothesize that in reasoning traces the overwhelming majority of tokens—connectives, narration, formatting, and easy continuations—converge to their final prediction in early-to-middle layers, while only a sparse set of 'deep-thinking' tokens (arithmetic results, logical commitments, answer tokens) need the full stack. We first characterize this structure across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3): using logit-lens saturation and prediction-revision-in-deep-layers, we measure the per-token depth at which the argmax stabilizes and show deep-thinking need is sparse and concentrated on specific token categories rather than narration. We then test whether a token's deep-thinking need is decidable ONLINE from mid-layer signals, comparing a cheap mid-layer confidence/agreement check and a lightweight linear probe. Finally we build a fully training-free adaptive-depth decoder: at each token, run to a mid-layer checkpoint, and if the checkpoint prediction is confidently stable, exit through the LM head, skipping the remaining layers; otherwise complete full depth (a self-speculative verify step guards accuracy). We evaluate compute-at-fixed-accuracy against uniform full depth, fixed-layer early exit, and CALM-style confidence exit, and show the method is complementary to step-level early stopping. Our work turns a mechanistic depth observation into a deployable, interpretable efficiency mechanism for reasoning.
Experiments:
Compute fits an academic node (<= 8xA100-80GB). Primary model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, frozen; only a lightweight linear depth-probe is trainable, and the decoder itself is training-free. Scale sweep: R1-Qwen distills 1.5B/7B/14B and Qwen3-8B (with L layers each). Decoding: temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 16k thinking tokens, seeds 0/1/2 on every reported number. Datasets, used as released: GSM8K test (1319), MATH500 (500), AIME 2024+2025 (60), GPQA-Diamond (198).

Experiment 1 (H1 — Deep-thinking need is sparse and category-structured): For sampled traces, apply logit-lens at every layer and record each token's convergence depth (earliest layer after which the argmax equals the final output and stays stable); cross-check with the prediction-revised-in-deep-layers definition. Categorize tokens (function/connective, narration, numeric/operator, answer-region) via POS + regex. Decisive metric: fraction of tokens that converge by layer 2L/3, and the share of late-converging (deep) tokens falling in numeric/logical/answer categories vs narration. Convincing result: >= 70% of tokens converge by 2L/3, and >= 60% of deep tokens are numeric/logical/answer (not narration), with the two depth definitions agreeing (rank correlation > 0.5). Indecision band: convergence-by-2L/3 in [50%, 70%], or deep-token category concentration in [45%, 60%] — the structure is present but weak; the decoder's headroom is limited and we say so. Negative result (< 50% converge by 2L/3, or deep tokens spread evenly across categories): reasoning tokens are not predominantly shallow or not category-structured, refuting H1.

Experiment 2 (H2 — Deep-thinking need is decidable online mid-stack): Predict late-convergence from mid-layer state via (a) training-free mid-layer logit-lens top-1 margin/entropy and agreement with an adjacent layer, and (b) a lightweight linear probe on the mid-layer residual predicting whether the token changes by the final layer. Probe data: 40% of tokens train, 60% held out, split by problem; checkpoint layer swept. Decisive metric: held-out AUROC for predicting late-convergence at the best mid-layer checkpoint. Convincing result: AUROC >= 0.80 at a checkpoint no deeper than 2L/3, with the training-free confidence check within 0.05 AUROC of the probe. Indecision band: AUROC in [0.65, 0.80] — decidability is moderate; exit rates and savings will be modest. Negative result (AUROC < 0.65): deep-thinking need is not predictable mid-stack, so the decoder cannot exit safely, refuting H2.

Experiment 3 (H3 — Training-free adaptive-depth decoder cuts compute at fixed accuracy): Decode to checkpoint layer c; if the checkpoint LM-head prediction is confident (margin > tau) and agrees with layer c-1, exit and emit, else run full depth; a self-speculative safeguard periodically re-verifies a batch of exited tokens at full depth and adjusts tau. tau and c selected on the Experiment-2 training split. Systems compared on all four datasets: adaptive-depth decoder vs. (a) uniform full depth, (b) fixed exit at c layers for all tokens, (c) CALM-style confidence early exit, (d) random exit at matched rate. Decisive metric: average layers executed per token (FLOP proxy) at fixed accuracy — mean depth to match full-depth accuracy within 1 point; reported alongside true wall-clock. Secondary: fraction of tokens early-exited, accuracy, wall-clock speedup (both a KV-recompute variant and a checkpoint-KV-reuse variant, per the KV-consistency caveat). Convincing result: >= 30% reduction in average layers per token within 1 accuracy point on GSM8K and MATH500, beating fixed-layer exit and matching or beating CALM at equal accuracy, with a measurable (>= 15%) wall-clock speedup in at least one KV variant. Indecision band: layer reduction in [15%, 30%] within 1 point, or a tie with CALM (< 5% difference at matched accuracy), or FLOP savings that do not translate to wall-clock (< 5% speedup due to KV overhead) — the decoder is a modest or systems-limited win; the mechanistic characterization (Experiments 1-2) remains the standalone contribution. Negative result (< 15% layer reduction or > 1 point accuracy loss): shallow-token skipping does not yield usable savings.

Experiment 4 (H1 — Causal category check): Verify early-exited tokens are dominantly narration/connective and that forcing early exit on answer-region tokens is harmful. Decisive metric: accuracy drop when early exit is forced on answer-region tokens vs. on narration tokens at matched exit rate. Convincing result: forcing exit on answer-region tokens costs >= 10 accuracy points while forcing exit on an equal number of narration tokens costs < 2, confirming the depth need is causally tied to token category. Indecision band: answer-region forced-exit cost in [3, 10] points — depth need is only partly category-tied. Negative result (< 3 points on answer-region tokens): depth is not causally concentrated on computation tokens, weakening H1's mechanistic claim.

Experiment 5 (H3 — Complementarity with step-level stopping): Combine the token-wise depth decoder with a step-level early-stopping baseline and measure additive savings. Decisive metric: compute (FLOP proxy) at fixed accuracy for the combined method vs. either method alone. Convincing result: the combination saves >= 10% more compute at matched accuracy than the better single method, on the accuracy-compute Pareto frontier. Indecision band: additive saving in [3%, 10%] — the methods partly overlap. Negative result (< 3% additive, or accuracy loss when combined): the two axes are redundant, bounding the complementarity claim.

Experiment 6 (H3 — Sensitivity and hard-item safety): Sweep tau and checkpoint layer to trace the accuracy-vs-compute curve; report accuracy on the hardest items (AIME) and calibration drift across datasets without retuning. Decisive metric: AIME accuracy drop at the tau/c that deliver the Experiment-3 savings on GSM8K/MATH500 (transfer without retuning). Convincing result: AIME accuracy drops < 1 point under transferred thresholds. Indecision band: 1-3 point drop — per-dataset retuning is needed and reported. Negative result (> 3 point drop): thresholds do not transfer and hard items are unsafe, bounding H3.

Experiment 7 (H2/H3 — Generality across data and scale): Transfer the depth probe and thresholds across datasets and the 1.5B/7B/14B/Qwen3-8B models without retraining. Decisive metric: transferred-probe AUROC relative to in-domain, and decoder compute-savings retention. Convincing result: transfer retains >= 80% of in-domain AUROC on at least three scales; savings hold within 10 relative percent. Indecision band: retention in [60%, 80%] — partly model-specific; scoped to per-model probes/thresholds. Negative result (< 60% retention): the shallow-token signal is idiosyncratic across models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Standard transformer forward passes are not trivially layer-skippable at decode time because later layers' KV entries would be missing for future attention; we mitigate by exiting only the current token's residual through the head while still computing (or approximating/caching) the KV of skipped layers—this may limit realized speedup and must be measured carefully (we report both a FLOP proxy and true wall-clock, and test a variant that reuses checkpoint-layer KV). If KV inconsistency degrades downstream attention, gains may shrink (an informative systems finding). Deep-thinking need may be only weakly predictable at the checkpoint (the model may decide deep), yielding modest exit rates—still a publishable characterization. Logit-lens convergence depth is a proxy for computational need and may misclassify tokens; we cross-validate with two definitions. Forcing early exit could cascade errors on hard problems; tau sweeps and the self-speculative safeguard address this. Gains may not exceed CALM-style baselines, but the mechanistic characterization (sparse, category-structured, mid-stack-predictable deep-thinking in reasoning CoT) and its training-free, complementary deployment are standalone contributions. Results may be model-family and scale specific.

novelty.reasoning: Closest prior family is very strong: TIDE, LiteStage, CALM, FlexiDepth, LayerSkip/SpecEE already cover training-free per-token adaptive depth / early exit in pretrained LLMs. The deployable decoder here is largely the same mechanism (mid-layer confidence/consistency + early exit + fallback), so the core algorithmic delta is limited. The genuine newness is mostly in the characterization claim: reasoning CoT tokens are sparse and category-structured (numeric/logical/answer tokens vs narration), plus a causal category experiment and complementarity with step-level stopping. That is a narrower mechanistic contribution than a new decoder.

Name: language_detour_overthinking
Title: The Language Tax: Overthinking as a Pivot-Detour Overhead in Non-English Reasoning
Short Hypothesis: For the identical problem, reasoning models spend substantially more tokens when the question is posed in a low-resource / non-Latin-script language than in English, and this excess is not extra genuine reasoning but a 'pivot detour' overhead: tokens spent routing the input into an English-centered latent reasoning space (re-translating, restating, language-mixing) after the effective answer computation is already possible. This overhead is mechanistically driven by a language-specific representational component and can be causally reduced—cutting tokens with no accuracy loss—by ablating that component mid-generation.
Related Work: Multilingual reasoning work documents an accuracy gap favoring high-resource languages, attributes it to understanding failures, and mitigates it via translation/alignment for accuracy (Why Do Multilingual Reasoning Gaps Emerge 2025; SLAM 2025; Question Translation 2024; SoT 2025). Language-mixing work shows reasoning traces drift toward English/Han pivots, more so on harder/low-resource inputs, reflecting an English-centered latent pathway (Language Mixing in RLMs 2025; Large Reasoning Models Are (Not Yet) Multilingual Latent Reasoners 2026). Disentanglement work ablates language-specific hidden components to IMPROVE ACCURACY (When Less Language is More 2025). Efficiency/overthinking work (Stop Overthinking survey 2025; When More is Less 2025; TRACE 2025) is entirely English-only and studies verbosity/verification, not language. Crucially, no prior work (a) measures an EFFICIENCY (token/compute) gap across languages on matched problems, (b) decomposes non-English trace length into genuine-reasoning vs pivot-detour overhead, or (c) uses language-component ablation to REDUCE TOKENS at fixed accuracy. Our contribution unites the efficiency and multilingual literatures: we name and quantify language-dependent overthinking, attribute its excess specifically to a pivot detour, and turn the disentanglement direction (previously an accuracy tool) into an efficiency intervention.
Abstract: Reasoning language models 'overthink,' but studies of this waste are almost entirely English-only, while multilingual studies focus on accuracy gaps, not compute. We ask a simple, consequential question: for the exact same problem, does a model reason longer—and waste more—when the question is asked in a low-resource or non-Latin-script language than in English? We hypothesize a language tax: non-English prompts incur a pivot-detour overhead in which the model spends tokens routing the input into an English-centered latent reasoning space (re-translation, restatement, language-mixing) rather than doing extra genuine reasoning. Using matched multilingual math and science benchmarks (MGSM and translated MATH500/GPQA subsets across high- and low-resource, Latin and non-Latin scripts) on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we first measure per-language token counts on identical problems, controlling for tokenizer effects via character/word-normalized budgets. We then decompose each non-English trace into genuine-reasoning tokens versus pivot-detour tokens using truncate-and-resume (when does the correct answer become recoverable?) and language-of-token classification, and test whether the cross-language token gap is concentrated in the detour, not in reasoning depth. Mechanistically, we locate a language-specific representational component via probing and difference-of-means, and causally test whether ablating it mid-generation collapses the detour, reducing tokens at fixed accuracy—turning an accuracy-oriented disentanglement into an efficiency intervention. We compare against forced-English-reasoning and translate-first baselines on tokens-at-fixed-accuracy and latency. Our work reveals a hidden, equity-relevant compute cost paid by non-English users and offers an interpretable fix.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 — Cross-language efficiency gap at matched accuracy): Tests whether, on identical problems, models emit more reasoning tokens in non-English than in English. Data: MGSM (250 grade-school math problems, professionally translated into 11 languages, parallel by construction; use all 250 in English, French, German, Chinese, Bengali, Swahili, Telugu — 7 of 11, chosen to span high-resource Latin, high-resource non-Latin, and low-resource non-Latin) plus a 200-problem stratified subset of MATH500 (500 exist) and all 198 GPQA-Diamond problems, both translated with NLLB-200-3.3B and human-verified on a 100-problem subset per language to catch gross mistranslation. Models: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B, 7B, 14B and Qwen3-8B, all frozen (inference only); temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 16384 generated tokens, 3 seeds. Systems compared: the same model on the English vs each non-English rendering of the same problem. Decisive metric: median reasoning-token count per language as a ratio to English, computed within equal-accuracy strata (only problems solved in both languages, so the gap is not an accuracy artifact). Secondary: tokens per source character and per source word, to net out tokenizer fertility. Convincing result: median token ratio >= 1.25 for the three low-resource non-Latin languages, holding within matched-accuracy strata and after character-normalization. Indecision band: a token ratio in [0.95, 1.10] on the matched stratum means no meaningful gap and H1 is unsupported for that language; a ratio in (1.10, 1.25) is weakly suggestive and treated as inconclusive pending Experiment 2. Negative result (ratios <= 1.10, or the gap vanishing after character-normalization) would mean any raw token difference is tokenizer fertility rather than a language tax, undercutting the hypothesis.

Experiment 2 (H2 — The excess is pivot-detour overhead, not deeper genuine reasoning): Tests whether the cross-language token excess sits after the point where the answer is already computable, while genuine reasoning depth is language-invariant. Data: the MGSM 250 and MATH 200 problems from Experiment 1, restricted to problems the model solves in both English and the target language (to define a clean effective-solve step); expect ~150-200 usable MGSM problems per low-resource language given accuracy loss. Models: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B as primary, 1.5B and 14B for robustness, frozen. Method: (a) truncate-and-resume — at each decile of a trace, force '</think> The answer is' and greedily decode; the effective-solve step is the earliest decile whose forced answer is correct and stays correct thereafter, with genuine-reasoning tokens = tokens up to that step and overhead tokens = the remainder; (b) token-language tagging via fastText lid.176 plus Unicode-script heuristics, counting language-switch spans and restatement/re-translation spans. Decisive metric: the fraction of the English-vs-target token gap attributable to overhead tokens. Secondary: effective-solve step in normalized reasoning units (script-independent) compared across languages, and language-switch count per trace vs resource level. Convincing result: >= 70% of the token gap sits in overhead tokens, normalized effective-solve step differs by < 10% across languages, and switch counts rise monotonically as resource level falls. Indecision band: an overhead share of the gap in [50%, 70%) is partial support — the detour explains some but not most of the tax, reported as such and not as confirmation; below 50% means the excess is genuine extra reasoning and H2 fails. Negative result (overhead share < 50%, or the effective-solve step itself growing in non-English) would mean non-English prompts trigger genuinely longer reasoning, refuting the 'detour' framing while still documenting the gap.

Experiment 3 (H3 — A language-specific representational component drives the detour): Tests both an internal signature and the existence of an isolable component. Data: 2000 prompt/step residual states sampled from the MGSM+MATH traces (balanced English/non-English, high/low resource) for fitting, and a held-out 500 for evaluation. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, frozen; nothing is trained except a linear probe and a difference-of-means direction that we read off the residual stream. Part A (signature): logit-lens on intermediate-layer residuals during non-English generation, measuring the layer/step at which the internally predicted answer-token language switches to English/Han, and whether the overhead tokens from Experiment 2 coincide with that switch. Part B (location): a logistic linear probe and a difference-of-means vector for the English-vs-non-English direction at each of layers 8-20, choosing the layer that maximizes probe AUC. Decisive metric: language-probe AUC, and — after projecting the direction out — the drop in surface-language AUC against the retained accuracy of a separate latent-answer probe (reasoning content intact). Convincing result: language-probe AUC >= 0.85 at some middle layer; projecting the direction out drops surface-language AUC below 0.65 while the latent-answer probe stays within 3 points of baseline; and the logit-lens switch precedes >= 60% of overhead tokens. Indecision band: language-probe AUC in [0.70, 0.85) means the component is only partially linearly isolable — proceed to Experiment 4 but flag a reduced expected effect; AUC < 0.70 means no clean component and H3 fails. Negative result (no isolable direction, or projecting it out also destroying the latent answer) would mean the detour is entangled with reasoning and cannot be cleanly targeted, predicting that Experiment 4 trades accuracy for tokens.

Experiment 4 (H4 — Ablating the component reduces tokens at fixed accuracy): Tests the causal efficiency claim. Data: held-out MGSM 250 and GPQA 198 per language, never used to fit the direction. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (primary) and 14B (transfer), frozen; the only intervention is projecting out the Experiment-3 direction from the residual stream at the selected middle layers, applied only after the input-understanding phase (the first 10% of tokens left untouched); 3 seeds. Systems compared: (i) no intervention, (ii) our language-component ablation, (iii) forced-English-reasoning via system-prompt / decoding constraint, (iv) translate-to-English-first then reason, (v) a matched random-direction ablation of equal norm (control). Decisive metric: tokens-at-fixed-accuracy — the change in median reasoning tokens per language subject to accuracy not dropping beyond the noise band. Secondary: detour-token fraction (Experiment 2 method), language-mixing count, wall-clock latency, accuracy. Convincing result: our ablation cuts median tokens by >= 15% on the low-resource non-Latin languages with accuracy change within +/- 1.0 point, beating the random-direction control (expected < 5% token change or accuracy damage) and matching or beating forced-English / translate-first without their input-fidelity costs. Indecision band: an accuracy change in [-3.0, -1.0] points is the zone where savings are ambiguous — a token cut there is reported as an accuracy-cost trade, not a free reduction; an accuracy drop > 3.0 points counts as failure of the 'no accuracy loss' claim even if tokens fall; a token reduction in [5%, 15%) is a weak positive. Negative result (no token reduction beyond the random control, or reduction only with accuracy loss > 3 points) would refute the causal efficiency claim and, read with Experiment 3, tell us whether the failure is no-effect or entanglement.

Experiment 5 (H4 — Specificity and transfer): Tests that the intervention does not harm cases where understanding, not detour, is the bottleneck, and that one shared low-resource direction transfers. Data: the hardest-difficulty stratum (bottom accuracy tercile) of GPQA and MATH per language. Models: 7B and 14B, frozen. Systems: ablation vs no-intervention on the hardest strata; and a single shared low-resource direction (averaged across the three low-resource languages) applied per language vs the per-language directions. Decisive metric: hardest-strata accuracy under ablation (must not drop) and the token reduction retained under the shared direction. Convincing result: hardest-strata accuracy within +/- 1.0 point of no-intervention (no induced underthinking) and the shared direction retaining >= two-thirds of the per-language token savings. Indecision band: a hardest-strata accuracy drop in (1.0, 3.0] points flags that the intervention should be gated to mid-difficulty items; > 3.0 points means the component is functionally necessary on hard low-resource inputs and the ablation must be scoped away from them. Negative result would bound the intervention's applicability rather than refute the core hypothesis.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Translated benchmarks may introduce artifacts or altered difficulty; we mitigate with human-verified translations for a subset and report results on the parallel-by-construction MGSM separately. Tokenizer fertility confounds raw token counts; we control via character/word-normalized effort and matched-accuracy comparisons, but residual confounding is possible. The genuine-vs-detour split relies on truncate-and-resume, which is noisy and compute-heavy; we subsample steps and use two overhead definitions (resume-based and language-tag-based) for robustness. The pivot-detour hypothesis may be wrong—extra tokens could reflect genuinely harder understanding rather than a routing overhead, which would be an informative negative result and still a novel efficiency-gap characterization. Language-specific ablation could damage understanding on low-resource inputs (underthinking), especially where the detour is functionally necessary; the specificity and hardest-strata analyses guard against this and may reveal the intervention only helps mid-difficulty items. Effects may be model-family and script specific, and low-resource-language coverage in open models is limited.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims: (1) non-English prompts incur extra reasoning tokens beyond English on matched problems; (2) this excess is framed as removable 'pivot-detour' overhead rather than genuine reasoning; (3) a language-specific representational component causally drives it; (4) mid-generation ablation reduces tokens with no accuracy loss. The first two are close to existing multilingual reasoning and English-pivot literature; the specific causal decomposition and no-loss efficiency intervention are the main delta, but still adjacent to recent steering/overthinking and disentanglement work. Novelty is more in the mechanistic framing and intervention than in the phenomenon itself.
