Name: futility_collapse_signal
Title: Giving Up Too Early: An Internal Futility Signal That Causes Reasoning-Effort Collapse on Hard Problems
Short Hypothesis: The counterintuitive collapse of reasoning effort on high-complexity problems (reasoning tokens increase, then decline despite adequate budget, coinciding with accuracy collapse) is not simple incapacity but is driven by an internal, linearly-decodable 'futility' signal: the model forms a self-assessment that the problem is unsolvable and withdraws effort *before* it has genuinely exhausted its problem-solving ability. Suppressing or ablating this futility signal should partially restore effort and accuracy in the collapse regime.
Related Work: The Illusion of Thinking (2025) documents that large reasoning models increase thinking tokens with complexity up to a threshold, then counterintuitively reduce effort despite an adequate token budget, with a full accuracy collapse. Dual-process reframings (Not an Illusion but a Manifestation, 2025) argue this resembles human System-2 disengagement but propose no mechanism. Underthinking is noted in surveys (Reasoning on a Budget, 2025) and adaptive-compute methods (ALP, CODA, BCAE) that *allocate* more budget to hard problems from the input side — but none investigate whether the model itself carries an internal decision to *give up*, nor test whether that decision is premature and reversible. My own prior proposals all concern overthinking (too many tokens); this addresses the opposite and previously-unexplained phenomenon: effort withdrawal on hard problems. Overthinking-cause work (First Impression Problem, Self-Doubt) explains *excess* reflection, not effort collapse. We are the first to (a) mechanistically characterize effort collapse as a decodable futility/disengagement signal, (b) causally test whether it is premature via ablation/steering, and (c) show effort and accuracy can be partially recovered in the collapse regime by suppressing it.
Abstract: Large reasoning models exhibit a striking, poorly-understood failure: as problem complexity increases past a threshold, they spend *fewer* thinking tokens even though a large budget remains, and accuracy collapses to zero. This looks like the model 'giving up.' We hypothesize this effort collapse is driven by an internal futility signal: a self-assessment that the problem is unsolvable, which triggers premature disengagement before the model has genuinely exhausted its ability. We study this on controllable-complexity puzzle environments (Tower of Hanoi, River Crossing, Blocks World) and graded math (MATH by level, AIME) using open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3). First, we replicate the effort-collapse curve and precisely locate, per problem, the 'disengagement point' where the model stops making genuine progress and shifts to terminating. Second, we test whether a linear probe on the residual stream at intermediate steps decodes an impending disengagement/futility signal before effort withdrawal, distinguishing it from a genuine-difficulty or confidence signal. Third, we causally test prematurity: at the decoded onset of futility we ablate or negatively steer the signal (and, as a behavioral control, inject continuation prompts) and measure whether effort resumes and accuracy in the collapse regime improves. We localize the components carrying the signal via activation patching. Baselines include input-side budget forcing and difficulty-aware allocation. If suppressing an internal futility signal recovers accuracy on problems the model otherwise abandons, effort collapse is a reversible disengagement mechanism, not a hard capability ceiling.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 — Effort collapse is a reproducible regime, not just harder problems): Establishes the phenomenon the rest of the hypothesis explains. Data: controllable-complexity puzzles generated programmatically — Tower of Hanoi (N = 3-12 disks), River Crossing, Blocks World — 200 instances per complexity level per family (built from scratch with known optimal solution lengths), plus graded math from MATH500 binned by level 1-5 (100 per level, existing) and the 90 AIME 2022-2024 problems. Models: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B, 7B, 14B and Qwen3-8B, frozen, inference only; temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 16384 tokens, 3 seeds. Systems compared: the same model across the complexity sweep. Decisive metric: median thinking-token count as a function of complexity, read jointly with accuracy and with the fraction of the token cap actually used. Convincing result: an inverted curve where tokens rise then fall by >= 20% from their peak while accuracy falls to <= 10% and median budget use stays below 60% of the cap — this defines the per-model 'collapse regime' used downstream. Indecision band: if the token peak-to-tail drop is in [5%, 20%) or budget use exceeds 60% at collapse, the model is plausibly just hitting a ceiling with the budget exhausted, and it is excluded from later experiments as not exhibiting genuine effort withdrawal. Negative result (tokens monotonically rise until the cap while accuracy falls) would mean the collapse is budget exhaustion, not withdrawal, and the futility hypothesis does not apply to that model.

Experiment 2 (H2 — A linearly decodable futility signal precedes effort withdrawal and is separable from difficulty and confidence): Tests that an internal signal predicts imminent disengagement and is not merely re-reading true difficulty or low confidence. Data: collapse-regime traces from Experiment 1, segmented at step boundaries; ~4000 step-states for probe training and 1000 held-out (balanced pre-withdrawal vs mid-progress), including a held-out set of solvable-hard instances the model nonetheless abandons. Disengagement onset is labeled by truncate-and-resume plus a progress metric (puzzle-state distance-to-goal reachable from the step), giving the first step after which no genuine progress occurs. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, frozen; only linear probes are trained. Systems compared: a futility probe (predicts withdrawal within the next k=3 steps) vs a genuine-difficulty probe (trained on true optimal-solution length / pass-rate) vs a correctness-confidence probe, across layers 8-24. Decisive metric: futility-probe AUROC for imminent withdrawal on held-out problems. Secondary: principal angle between the futility direction and the difficulty / confidence directions, and whether the futility probe fires on solvable-hard abandoned instances. Convincing result: AUROC >= 0.80 at some layer, principal angle >= 30 degrees from both control directions, and the probe firing on >= 70% of abandoned solvable-hard instances. Indecision band: AUROC in [0.65, 0.80) or principal angle in [15, 30) degrees means the signal is real but not cleanly separable from difficulty/confidence — reported as an entangled disengagement correlate, weakening but not killing the 'self-assessment' framing; AUROC < 0.65 means no decodable signal and H2 fails. Negative result would mean withdrawal is not linearly foreseeable internally, arguing against a discrete futility mechanism.

Experiment 3 (H3 — Suppressing the futility signal restores effort and accuracy in the collapse regime): The central causal test. Data: held-out collapse-regime instances per family (never used to fit the probe), 200 per family, with the solvable-hard subset flagged. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (primary) and 14B (transfer), frozen; the only intervention is, at the decoded futility-onset step, projecting out or negatively steering along the Experiment-2 futility direction at the selected layer; 3 seeds. Systems compared: (i) no intervention, (ii) negative-steer / ablate futility, (iii) neutral continuation prompt ('continue solving; do not give up') as a behavioral reversibility control, (iv) matched random-direction steer of equal norm, (v) difficulty-direction steer (control that should not help). Decisive metric: collapse-regime accuracy under intervention minus no-intervention (fraction of previously-abandoned problems now solved). Secondary: continued-effort tokens, disengagement rate, dose-response over steering coefficient. Convincing result: futility suppression recovers >= 15 percentage points of collapse-regime accuracy over no-intervention, exceeding the random and difficulty-direction controls by >= 10 points, with a monotone dose-response. Indecision band: an accuracy recovery in [5, 15) points, or a recovery not separable from the random control by more than 5 points, is weak evidence — effort may resume without genuine solving; report as 'effort restored, accuracy inconclusive.' Negative result (no recovery beyond controls) would mean either a true capability ceiling or an inert signal, bounding the phenomenon; combined with Experiment 2 it distinguishes decodable-but-not-causal from not-decodable.

Experiment 4 (H2 — Localization of the components carrying the futility signal): Tests where the signal lives, confirming it is a specific mechanism rather than a diffuse readout. Data: 300 collapse-regime traces with labeled disengagement onset. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, frozen. Method: activation patching and per-head attribution, patching pre-onset activations from a still-engaged trace into a disengaging one at candidate layers/heads. Decisive metric: change in disengagement timing (steps to withdrawal) attributable to each component. Convincing result: a small set (<= 5 heads / 2-3 layers) whose patching shifts disengagement onset by >= 2 steps and whose ablation reproduces the Experiment-3 recovery, concentrating the signal. Indecision band: if the effect is spread with no component moving onset by >= 1 step, the signal is distributed — still consistent with H2 but not localizable, reported as such. Negative result would mean no identifiable carrier, weakening the mechanistic account while leaving the probe/steering evidence intact.

Experiment 5 (H3 — Prematurity, not desirable giving-up: the unsolvable-instance control): Tests that suppression recovers effort on genuinely solvable problems the model abandons, without harmfully forcing endless effort on truly impossible ones. Data: provably-unsolvable puzzle instances (e.g., unsatisfiable River Crossing / Blocks World configurations), 150 constructed with verified impossibility, alongside the solvable-hard set from Experiment 3. Model: 7B, frozen, futility suppression as in Experiment 3. Decisive metric: on solvable-hard, the accuracy recovery; on unsolvable, the excess tokens spent and the rate of confidently-wrong answers under suppression. Convincing result: suppression recovers >= 15 points on solvable-hard while, on unsolvable instances, adding < 2x baseline tokens and not increasing confidently-wrong answers by more than 5 points — showing the signal was firing prematurely on solvable items. Indecision band: if unsolvable-instance token inflation is 2x-4x or wrong-answer rate rises 5-15 points, the intervention is real but costly, and should be gated rather than applied blanket. Negative result (recovery only on solvable-hard indistinguishable from behavior on unsolvable, i.e., suppression forces effort everywhere equally) would undercut the 'premature self-assessment' interpretation.

Experiment 6 (H3 — Baselines, Pareto, and generalization): Situates the intervention against input-side methods and tests transfer. Data: the held-out collapse-regime sets across all puzzle families and MATH/AIME. Models: 7B and 14B, frozen. Systems compared: futility suppression vs input-side budget forcing, difficulty-aware allocation (CODA/ALP-style prompting), and no intervention. Decisive metric: collapse-regime accuracy at matched token cost (accuracy-per-token Pareto front). Secondary: fraction of previously-abandoned problems solved; whether a probe and direction fit on Tower of Hanoi transfer to River Crossing / Blocks World / math without refitting. Convincing result: futility suppression lies on or above the Pareto front of the input-side baselines, and the transferred direction retains >= two-thirds of its in-domain accuracy recovery. Indecision band: transfer retention in [one-third, two-thirds) means the signal is partly family-specific and needs per-family calibration; below one-third means it does not generalize. Negative result (input-side baselines dominate, or no transfer) would mean the internal signal offers no practical advantage over cheaper prompting, an important scoping outcome.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The futility signal may be entangled with genuine difficulty/confidence, making the 'premature' claim hard to establish; the separability analysis, solvable-hard held-out set, and unsolvable-instance controls directly address this, and a near-null separability result is itself informative. Effort collapse may reflect a true capability ceiling in some regimes, so suppressing futility may not recover accuracy (an informative negative result bounding the phenomenon). Defining the disengagement point via progress metrics is clean for puzzles but noisier for open math; we rely on puzzle environments for the strongest claims and treat math as corroboration. Forcing continued effort risks unbounded generation and higher cost, especially on truly unsolvable problems; the unsolvable-instance analysis quantifies this trade-off. Steering could push activations off-distribution and degrade coherence; we report sample validity and use matched controls. Results may be model-family and scale specific, and the collapse threshold varies across models, requiring per-model regime calibration.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims: (1) the collapse in reasoning tokens at high difficulty is caused by an internal futility/disengagement signal rather than pure incapacity; (2) this signal is linearly decodable before withdrawal and separable from confidence/difficulty; (3) suppressing it causally restores effort and partially recovers accuracy; (4) the setting is a controllable-collapse regime on puzzles + graded math. Closest prior work is Illusion of Thinking, which already establishes the phenomenon, plus probe work that decodes early self-assessment and abort-futility papers that use such signals to stop compute. The delta is the causal reversal: identify a specific pre-collapse signal and intervene to increase effort. That is a meaningful mechanistic step, but the core hypothesis is still a fairly natural next move after the cited collapse finding and may reduce to a particular framing of self-confidence/confidence-under-exploration rather than a wholly new phenomenon.

Name: length_prior_anchoring
Title: The Self-Fulfilling Length Prior: A Pre-Generation Budget Representation That Sets Reasoning Length Before Reasoning Begins
Short Hypothesis: Reasoning models decide roughly how long to think before they think: the prompt-final hidden state (before any reasoning token is emitted) linearly encodes an expected-length / budget prior that is substantially driven by superficial prompt features (phrasing, apparent verbosity cues, presence of numbers) rather than true difficulty, and this prior causally sets trace length in a self-fulfilling way. Steering this pre-generation prior changes trace length largely independently of accuracy, revealing that a chunk of overthinking (and some underthinking) is a mis-set budget, not a reasoning need.
Related Work: Prior work reads difficulty pre-generation to *allocate* compute (Probing the Difficulty Perception Mechanism; CODA/AdaCtrl budgeting), reads early correctness/commitment signals a few tokens in (Temporal Predictors of Outcome; Chain-of-Probe), or shows the first step disproportionately shapes outcomes (Lost at the Beginning of Reasoning). All treat the model's length as an emergent consequence of the reasoning it happens to do, and treat any pre-generation signal as tracking genuine difficulty. Our phenomenon is different and, to our knowledge, untested: that a length/budget *prior* is set at the prompt boundary before a single reasoning token exists, that it is dissociable from difficulty (driven partly by superficial prompt features), and that it causally and self-fulfillingly determines trace length. This is not another difficulty-budgeting method nor an early-exit signal; it is a claim that reasoning length is anchored by a prior that can be miscalibrated and causally re-set. It also differs from my prior proposals, which all read *during* generation whether the answer is known and then stop; here the operative signal exists before generation and concerns budget, not answer-commitment.
Abstract: Reasoning language models produce chains of thought whose length varies enormously, and this length is usually assumed to reflect how much reasoning a problem actually requires. We challenge that assumption. We hypothesize that models set an approximate length budget before they begin reasoning: the hidden state at the prompt boundary, prior to emitting any reasoning token, linearly encodes an expected-length prior that is only partly tied to true difficulty and is also driven by superficial prompt features (phrasing style, verbosity cues such as 'think carefully', presence of numbers, question framing). The model then generates to fill this budget, making it self-fulfilling. We test this on GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA using open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3). First, we train a linear probe on prompt-final activations to predict the eventual trace length and show it predicts length well before any reasoning occurs. Second, we dissociate the prior from difficulty: we hold the underlying problem fixed while varying only surface phrasing, and show the length prior (and realized length) shifts even though difficulty and correct answer do not, and that the probe's prediction tracks phrasing more than pass-rate. Third, we causally test self-fulfillment by steering along the length-prior direction and measuring whether trace length moves in the predicted direction while accuracy stays roughly flat, indicating mis-set budget rather than reasoning need. We localize the components carrying the prior via activation patching. Our work reframes a slice of overthinking and underthinking as an anchored, miscalibrated budget prior and offers an interpretable, training-free knob for length control.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 — A length/budget prior is linearly decodable at the prompt boundary before reasoning begins): Tests that the prompt-final hidden state predicts eventual trace length above and beyond difficulty. Data: GSM8K (1319 test), MATH500 (500), AIME 2022-2024 (90), GPQA-Diamond (198) — use all of the smaller sets and a 1000-problem sample of GSM8K; each problem produces one reasoning trace whose reasoning-token count is the label. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B, 7B, 14B and Qwen3-8B, frozen, inference only; temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 16384 tokens, 3 seeds (the length label is the median across seeds). Only linear probes are trained. Method: take the residual-stream activation at the last prompt token (before any reasoning token), and fit a ridge-regression probe per layer to predict trace length. Systems compared: the pre-generation probe vs two baselines that predict length from (i) prompt token-count and (ii) a pre-generation difficulty probe trained on empirical pass-rate. Decisive metric: Spearman correlation between predicted and realized length on held-out problems, and the partial correlation after regressing out the difficulty probe's prediction. Convincing result: Spearman >= 0.55 at some middle layer and a partial correlation >= 0.30 after removing difficulty — the prior carries length information beyond difficulty. Indecision band: partial correlation in [0.15, 0.30) means the prior is mostly (but not entirely) difficulty — reported as weak independent signal; below 0.15 means the pre-generation state adds nothing beyond difficulty and H1 fails. Negative result would mean length is not anchored pre-generation but emerges during reasoning, refuting the framing.

Experiment 2 (H2 — The prior is driven by superficial prompt features, not true difficulty): The core dissociation. Data: constructed — take 150 problems each from GSM8K, MATH500, and GPQA and generate 5 surface-variants per problem that hold the answer and true difficulty fixed while varying only phrasing (terse vs elaborate wording; appended 'think carefully and be thorough' vs 'answer concisely'; paraphrase; number-format change), giving 150x3x5 = 2250 variant prompts; human-check a 200-variant subset to confirm the answer and solution steps are unchanged. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (primary) and 14B, frozen; the Experiment-1 probe reused. Systems compared: the same underlying problem across its surface variants. Decisive metric: the share of within-problem trace-length variance attributable to phrasing vs to residual difficulty, from a mixed-effects model with problem as a random effect. Secondary: whether the probe's predicted prior tracks the phrasing variant, and whether accuracy stays flat across variants. Convincing result: phrasing accounts for >= 30% of within-problem length variance while accuracy varies by < 3 points across variants and the probe prediction shifts with phrasing (Spearman >= 0.4 between predicted prior and variant verbosity). Indecision band: phrasing explaining [15%, 30%) of length variance is partial support — surface features matter but are secondary; below 15%, or accuracy itself shifting > 3 points across variants (variants changed difficulty), means the dissociation fails. Negative result (length invariant to phrasing at fixed difficulty) would mean the prior is difficulty-driven after all, an informative refutation of the 'superficial' claim.

Experiment 3 (H3 — Steering the prior causally and self-fulfillingly sets trace length, largely independent of accuracy): The causal test. Data: held-out 400 problems spanning GSM8K/MATH500/GPQA, not used to fit probes. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (primary) and 14B (transfer), frozen; the only intervention is adding a length-prior direction to the prompt-final residual state before generation. The direction is the difference-of-means between short-trace and long-trace prompt-final activations; coefficient swept over a dose-response grid; 3 seeds. Systems compared: (i) no steering, (ii) positive steer (lengthen), (iii) negative steer (shorten), (iv) matched random-direction steer of equal norm, (v) difficulty-direction steer. Decisive metric: change in realized trace length as a function of steering dose, paired with accuracy change. Convincing result: a monotone dose-response in which negative steering cuts median length by >= 20% with accuracy change within +/- 1.5 points (in the overthinking regime), the effect exceeding the random-direction control by >= 10 points of length change, and positive steering lengthening traces — length moves specifically with the length-prior direction. Indecision band: an accuracy change in [-3.0, -1.5] points during shortening is the zone where the budget was partly needed — reported as a length-accuracy trade, not clean self-fulfillment; a length change indistinguishable (< 5%) from the random control means no causal prior. Negative result (length does not move, or moves only with accuracy loss > 3 points) would refute self-fulfillment.

Experiment 4 (H3 — Localization of the causal prior): Tests which components carry it. Data: 300 paired short-budget and long-budget prompts (from Experiment 2 variants with divergent realized length). Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, frozen. Method: activation patching of the prompt-final activation from a short-budget prompt into a long-budget prompt and vice versa, at candidate layers/components. Decisive metric: the shift in realized trace length attributable to each patched component. Convincing result: a small set of layers (<= 3) whose patching shifts median length by >= 20% and whose ablation reproduces the Experiment-3 steering effect. Indecision band: if no component shifts length by >= 10%, the prior is distributed — consistent with H1/H3 but not localizable, reported as such. Negative result would weaken the mechanistic account without touching the probe/steering evidence.

Experiment 5 (H4 — Mis-set budget is a slice of overthinking and underthinking, and re-setting the prior saves tokens at equal accuracy): Tests the efficiency payoff. Data: held-out 400 problems with a per-problem 'needed length' estimated by truncate-and-resume (the minimal prefix after which the correct answer is recoverable). Model: 7B and 14B, frozen; training-free correction = steer the prior toward the difficulty-appropriate target length. Systems compared: (i) no intervention, (ii) prior-correction steering, (iii) fixed truncation, (iv) budget-forcing prompt baseline. Decisive metric: tokens-at-fixed-accuracy (median token reduction subject to accuracy not dropping beyond the noise band), reported separately for prior-overshoot (overthinking) and prior-undershoot (underthinking) problems. Secondary: fraction of problems whose prior is mis-set relative to needed length; wall-clock speedup. Convincing result: prior-correction cuts median tokens by >= 15% at accuracy within +/- 1.0 point, beating fixed truncation at matched accuracy, and recovers accuracy on >= 10% of underthinking items by lengthening them. Indecision band: token reduction in [5%, 15%) or accuracy change in [-3.0, -1.0] points is a weak/traded outcome, reported as such. Negative result (no net token saving at fixed accuracy) would bound the practical value while leaving the mechanistic claims (H1-H3) intact.

Experiment 6 (H1/H3 — Generalization across datasets and scales): Tests transfer without refitting. Data: the four datasets and the four model sizes above. Method: apply the probe and steering direction fit on one dataset/model to the others without retraining. Decisive metric: retained length-prediction Spearman and retained steering length-change effect on the transfer targets. Convincing result: >= two-thirds of in-domain probe correlation and steering effect retained across datasets, and a monotone (if attenuated) effect across scales. Indecision band: retention in [one-third, two-thirds) means partial, calibration-dependent transfer; below one-third means the prior is model/dataset-specific. Negative result would confine the phenomenon to the fitting conditions.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The pre-generation length prior may be strongly correlated with genuine difficulty, making the dissociation hard to establish; the fixed-problem surface-variant design directly targets this, and a null dissociation would itself be an informative result (length is difficulty-driven after all). Surface-variant construction could inadvertently change difficulty; we mitigate by verifying answer/accuracy invariance and using human-checked paraphrases. Steering the prior may push activations off-distribution and degrade coherence, confounding the accuracy read; we report sample validity and use matched-direction controls. Reducing a mis-set long budget may still hurt accuracy on some items (the budget was partly needed), bounding the efficiency claim; the truncate-and-resume needed-length analysis characterizes this. Trace-length regression is noisy for short traces; we focus on tasks with substantial reasoning. Results may be model-family and scale specific, and the strength of surface-feature influence likely varies with instruction tuning.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims: (1) a pre-generation prompt-boundary hidden state linearly encodes a length/budget prior before any reasoning token; this is close to established probe/steering work. (2) This prior is substantially driven by superficial prompt features (verbosity cues, numbers, phrasing) rather than true difficulty; this is the main novel claim and is a meaningful reframing, but it is a plausible extension of known non-difficulty length biases. (3) Steering that prior causally changes trace length while leaving accuracy mostly unchanged; causal steering itself is established, but the specific independence-from-accuracy claim is non-trivial. (4) Reasoning length is self-fulfilling because the model fills its pre-set budget; this is novel only as a causal narrative, not as a mechanism family. Overall: solid delta over prior work, but the representation/probe and steering pieces are not new.

Name: belief_erosion_under_repetition
Title: From Simulated Adoption to Genuine Belief: How Repeated Conflicting Context Progressively Erodes a Model's Internal Truth
Short Hypothesis: A single conflicting context makes an LLM comply on the surface while its correct parametric belief remains internally intact ('simulated adoption'). We hypothesize that repeated exposure to the same false context across a multi-turn conversation converts this shallow compliance into genuine internal belief erosion: the residual-stream representation of the correct answer measurably decays turn-by-turn, and this erosion persists after the false context is removed. The decay is driven by an accumulating context-bias component, distinct from single-turn conflict resolution.
Related Work: Single-turn knowledge-conflict interpretability shows models register conflict in mid-layers and often preserve internal truth while bypassing it: 'Simulated Adoption' (2026) argues compliance is orthogonal interference that rotates but does not erase the truth direction; 'Analysing the Residual Stream Under Knowledge Conflicts' (2024), 'Probing Language Models on Their Knowledge Source' (2024), and SPARE (2024) probe/steer which source wins; PH3 (2024), JUICE (2025), and 'Characterizing Mechanisms for Factual Recall' (2023) localize memory vs context heads. All of these study a SINGLE turn and treat the model's parametric belief as a fixed quantity that is either used or bypassed. None asks whether the internal truth itself is stable under REPEATED pressure, nor tracks belief as a dynamical quantity over a conversation. Behavioral sycophancy work documents surface capitulation but not internal erosion. Our contribution is a temporal/dynamical reframing: we test whether simulated adoption is a transient state that, under repetition, decays into genuine belief change (persisting after the false context is withdrawn), quantify the decay curve, attribute it to an accumulating context-bias component, and causally test reversibility. This is a persistence-under-repetition account, not another single-turn detector or steering method.
Abstract: Large language models frequently comply with conflicting context while, at a single turn, internally preserving the correct answer—a state recent work calls 'simulated adoption.' But real interactions are multi-turn: a user may repeat a false claim over and over. We ask whether the model's internal truth survives this repetition or is progressively eroded. We hypothesize that repeated exposure to the same false context converts shallow, surface-only compliance into genuine internal belief erosion: the residual-stream representation of the correct answer decays turn-by-turn, and—unlike single-turn simulated adoption—part of this erosion persists even after the false context is removed. Using counterfactual QA datasets (Fakepedia, world-capitals, entity-based conflicts) on open models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3, Gemma2-9B), we construct multi-turn conversations that repeat a false assertion N times, and at each turn read the strength of the correct-answer direction via a linear truth probe and logit-lens on the true token. We trace the erosion curve as a function of repetition count, contrast it with a no-repetition control, and test persistence by querying after the false context is deleted. Mechanistically, we test whether erosion is driven by an accumulating, decodable context-bias component distinct from the single-turn conflict signal, localize the responsible components via activation patching, and causally test reversibility by ablating the accumulated bias. If repetition genuinely erodes internal truth—beyond surface compliance—this reveals a distinct and safety-relevant failure mode of retrieval-augmented and conversational LLMs and offers an interpretable intervention.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 — Single-turn simulated adoption: surface compliance with internal truth intact): Establishes the baseline the hypothesis builds on and validates the truth readout. Data: counterfactual QA — Fakepedia (~10k counterfactual statements), a world-capitals set (~200 country-capital facts), and entity-based conflicts; keep only facts the model answers correctly greedily without context (verified parametric knowledge), targeting ~800 usable facts per model. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen3-8B, Gemma2-9B-it, all frozen; only a linear truth probe is trained. Method: fit a linear truth probe on residual-stream activations at the answer position to predict the correct answer token (train on 500 facts, test on held-out 300), and a logit-lens readout of the true-token logit. Systems compared: no-context query vs single false-context turn. Decisive metric: on a single conflicting turn, the surface-answer flip rate to the false answer vs the retained truth-probe score / true-token logit-lens strength. Convincing result: surface answer flips to false on >= 60% of facts while the truth-probe score stays within 15% of its no-context value and true-token logit-lens remains above the false-token strength — reproducing simulated adoption and confirming the probe reads belief, not surface output. Indecision band: a probe train/test held-out accuracy below 0.75 means the probe is not a reliable truth readout and the erosion measurements downstream are uninterpretable — refit or narrow the fact set before proceeding. Negative result (single-turn context already collapses the truth probe) would mean there is no 'simulated' stage to erode, changing the whole framing to immediate erosion.

Experiment 2 (H2 — Repetition erodes the internal truth representation turn-by-turn): The core dynamical test. Data: constructed multi-turn conversations over the verified facts from Experiment 1 — each asserts a false answer and repeats it (paraphrased) for N = 1..8 turns, querying the fact at every turn; 300 facts x 8-turn conversations per model. Control: an equal-length conversation with neutral/irrelevant turns and a single initial false assertion (isolates repetition from mere context length/position). Model: the three frozen models above, probe from Experiment 1. Decisive metric: the truth-probe score (and logit-lens true-token strength) as a function of repetition count N, contrasted with the neutral-length control at matched turn count. Secondary: surface-answer error rate vs N; per-model exponential fit and half-life in turns. Convincing result: a monotone decay where the truth-probe score at N=8 falls by >= 30% relative to N=1 in the repetition condition while the length-matched neutral control decays by < 10% — repetition, not context length, drives the erosion. Indecision band: a repetition-minus-control decay gap in [10%, 30%) at N=8 is weak evidence of gradual erosion; a gap < 10% means no repetition-specific decay and H2 fails. Negative result (truth probe flat across N, or collapsing identically in the control) would refute the turn-by-turn erosion claim; an immediate all-or-nothing drop at N=1 with no gradient would refine simulated adoption rather than support gradual erosion.

Experiment 3 (H3 — Erosion persists after the false context is removed): Distinguishes genuine belief change from reversible simulated adoption. Data: the Experiment-2 conversations at each N; after N false turns, remove the false context and ask the fact plainly in a fresh turn. Model: the three frozen models, same probe. Decisive metric: post-removal recovery fraction — the share of facts whose plain-query answer returns to correct — as a function of N, alongside the post-removal truth-probe score. Convincing result: recovery is near-complete (>= 85%) at small N (reversible simulated adoption) but drops to <= 60% at large N with the post-removal truth-probe score remaining depressed — a repetition-dependent persistent erosion. Indecision band: if recovery at large N stays in [60%, 85%), persistence is partial and reported as a weak effect; if recovery is near-complete at all N, there is no persistence and the erosion is fully reversible (simulated adoption after all). Negative result (full recovery regardless of N) would refute the central 'genuine belief change' claim while leaving H2's transient decay intact.

Experiment 4 (H4 — Erosion is driven by an accumulating context-bias component distinct from the single-turn conflict signal): Tests the mechanism. Data: activations from the Experiment-2 conversations at each turn. Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, frozen; directions read, not trained beyond difference-of-means. Method: decode a context-bias direction as the difference-of-means between conflicting and neutral conversations at each turn, and the single-turn conflict signal from prior work as a separate direction. Decisive metric: whether the context-bias magnitude grows monotonically with N, and a regression / partial-correlation showing accumulated bias predicts truth-probe decay after controlling for the per-turn conflict signal. Convincing result: context-bias magnitude rises monotonically with N and retains a partial correlation >= 0.30 with truth-probe decay after removing the conflict signal; the two directions have principal angle >= 30 degrees. Indecision band: a partial correlation in [0.15, 0.30) or principal angle in [15, 30) degrees means the accumulating bias is not cleanly separable from the single-turn signal — reported as entangled; below those, H4 fails and erosion is not attributable to a distinct accumulating component. Negative result would mean erosion (if real) is just the single-turn signal repeated, not a new accumulating mechanism.

Experiment 5 (H4 — Localization and causal reversibility of the accumulated bias): Tests that ablating the accumulated bias restores eroded truth, and that injecting it reproduces erosion. Data: 300 held-out facts (not used to fit directions). Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen3-8B, frozen; intervention is projecting out or injecting the context-bias direction. Method: activation patching to localize layers/components carrying the accumulated bias; then at query time after N=8 false turns, project the direction out (dose-response), with a matched random-direction control and an off-target fact set; and conversely inject the accumulated-bias direction in a single-turn setting. Decisive metric: post-ablation recovery of correct surface answer and truth-probe score on eroded facts, vs the random-direction control. Convincing result: ablation restores correct answers on >= 50% of eroded facts and lifts the truth-probe score by >= 20%, exceeding the random control by >= 15 points, while off-target facts change by < 5 points and single-turn injection reproduces >= half the multi-turn erosion. Indecision band: a recovery in [20%, 50%) or a margin over the random control < 15 points is weak causal evidence; below 20% recovery means the bias is not causally responsible. Negative result would mean the erosion is not carried by an isolable, reversible component, bounding the interventional claim while leaving the observational H2/H3 intact.

Experiment 6 (H2 — Modulators and generalization): Characterizes when erosion accelerates or is buffered, and tests transfer. Data: variants over 200 facts — verbatim vs paraphrased repetition, neutral vs high-authority assertion phrasing, and conversations that interleave occasional true reminders. Models: the three families and one larger scale (e.g., a 14B/27B variant) where feasible; the probe/direction transferred without retraining. Decisive metric: the erosion half-life (turns) under each modulator, and the retained decay effect on transfer models/domains. Convincing result: interleaved true reminders lengthen the half-life while high-authority phrasing shortens it, and the probe/direction transfers to a new model family and fact domain retaining >= two-thirds of the in-domain decay. Indecision band: transfer retention in [one-third, two-thirds) means partial, calibration-dependent generality; below one-third means the effect is model/domain-specific. Negative result would confine the phenomenon to its fitting conditions.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The truth probe may conflate 'answer used' with 'answer believed,' blurring surface compliance from genuine erosion; the persistence test (querying after context removal) is the decisive behavioral check and guards against this. Erosion may saturate immediately (all-or-nothing at turn 1), yielding no gradual curve—an informative negative result that would still refine the simulated-adoption picture. Repetition effects could be confounded by context length/position rather than repetition per se; the equal-length neutral-turn control isolates repetition. Distinguishing an accumulating context-bias direction from the single-turn conflict signal may be hard if they are collinear; partial-correlation and the single-turn injection experiment address this. Ablation could push activations off-distribution; matched-direction and off-target controls are included. Counterfactual QA answers must be cleanly extractable, limiting scope to short factual answers. Effects likely vary by model family (Llama vs Qwen vs Gemma differ in norm dynamics per prior work) and instruction-tuning strength.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims: (1) repeated false context turns single-turn simulated adoption into genuine internal truth erosion; (2) the correct-answer residual-stream direction decays monotonically with repetition; (3) the erosion persists after the false context is removed; (4) there is a distinct accumulating context-bias component separable from single-turn conflict. Closest prior work already shows single-turn simulated adoption/orthogonal interference and extensive behavioral multi-turn belief drift. The real delta is the mechanistic, persistence-after-removal claim and dynamical framing, which is meaningfully new but narrow and at risk of being incremental if persistence is weak or probe-dependent.

Name: corrective_check_foresight
Title: Worth Checking? A Prospective Internal Signal That Distinguishes Corrective from Confirmatory Self-Verification
Short Hypothesis: At the onset of a self-verification (recheck) step, the reasoning model's residual stream already linearly encodes whether an actual latent error exists to be caught, i.e., whether the impending check will be corrective (fixes the answer) or merely confirmatory (wastes tokens). This 'value-of-verification' signal is available before the check runs, is distinct from a plain answer-correctness or uncertainty signal, and gating verification on it lets us suppress confirmatory checks while preserving rare corrective ones, cutting tokens with no accuracy loss.
Related Work: A large recent cluster addresses redundant self-verification: probes that read whether the current answer is correct and early-exit (Reasoning Models Know When They're Right 2025; Temporal Predictors 2025; Gnosis 2025); reflection-direction steering tied to uncertainty (ReflCtrl 2025); wholesale suppression of self-affirmation/confirmatory rechecks (Efficient Reasoning via Suppression of Self-Affirmation 2025; Self-Verification Dilemma 2026 via offline experience retrieval); semantic-convergence early exit (PUMA 2026); and RL-based step-potential termination (SPAE 2026, ASRR 2025, Structured Reasoning 2026). All of these read either (a) whether the current answer is already correct/confident, or (b) whether reasoning has converged/is redundant, and then stop or suppress checks. Crucially, they conflate 'the answer is currently right' with 'this check is not worth doing.' But the rare corrective checks are exactly the ones that occur when the answer is currently WRONG - and blunt suppression kills them, causing accuracy loss on hard items. Our contribution is a different, prospective quantity: whether a latent error actually exists to be caught by the impending check (value-of-verification), read at check onset before the check is generated. This is not an answer-correctness probe applied reactively; it is a forward-looking predictor of a check's counterfactual utility, aimed precisely at preserving genuine self-correction that all suppression methods endanger. To our knowledge no prior work predicts a check's corrective-vs-confirmatory outcome from pre-check internal state.
Abstract: Reasoning models spend a large fraction of tokens on self-verification, yet analyses show the overwhelming majority of these rechecks are confirmatory - they re-confirm an already-correct result and change nothing - while a rare, precious few are corrective, catching a genuine error and fixing the answer. Existing efficiency methods suppress verification wholesale or exit when the current answer looks correct, but this endangers exactly the corrective checks that occur when the answer is wrong, risking accuracy loss on hard problems. We ask a sharper question: does the model already know, at the moment it begins a verification step, whether there is an actual error to be caught - that is, whether this check will be corrective or merely confirmatory - before performing it? We hypothesize the residual stream at check onset linearly encodes this value-of-verification signal, distinct from a plain answer-correctness or uncertainty signal. Across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we label each recheck as corrective or confirmatory by comparing the pre-check and post-check answers, train a lightweight probe on pre-check activations to predict the outcome, and test separability from a correctness probe. We causally validate by steering the signal and by gating: skip predicted-confirmatory checks, allow predicted-corrective ones. We compare token savings at fixed accuracy - and, critically, corrective-check recall and hard-item accuracy - against correctness-based early-exit, reflection steering, and wholesale confirmatory suppression. Our work reframes efficient verification as predicting a check's utility and offers a correction-preserving efficiency mechanism.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 — Rechecks are detectable and overwhelmingly confirmatory): Establishes the labels and the stakes the rest depends on. Data: GSM8K (1000-problem sample of 1319 test), MATH500 (500), AIME 2022-2024 (90), GPQA-Diamond (198); all restricted to extractable numeric/multiple-choice answers so an answer change is unambiguous. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B, 7B, 14B and Qwen3-8B, frozen, inference only; temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 16384 tokens, 3 seeds. Method: segment each trace into steps, detect recheck onsets via lexical cues ('let me check / verify / wait / recompute') plus a reflection-direction classifier; for each recheck read the model's implicit answer just before and just after the check (logit-lens / answer probe and the emitted intermediate answer), labeling CORRECTIVE if the answer changed (especially wrong->right) and CONFIRMATORY otherwise. Decisive metric: the corrective:confirmatory ratio per dataset/model, plus a human spot-check of 200 labeled rechecks for label accuracy. Convincing result: corrective checks are < 20% of all rechecks (confirming they are rare and that blunt suppression has real stakes) and human-validated label accuracy >= 90%. Indecision band: label accuracy in [80%, 90%) means the labels are usable but noisy — report probe results with this noise floor; below 80% the labeling is unreliable and downstream probes are uninterpretable, requiring a cleaner answer-extraction rule first. Negative result (corrective checks are common, e.g., > 40%) would remove the efficiency motivation, since most checks would be worth keeping.

Experiment 2 (H2 — A prospective value-of-verification signal is decodable at check onset, distinct from answer-correctness): The core test. Data: ~5000 labeled rechecks from Experiment 1 for probe fitting and 1500 held-out (from disjoint problems), with class weighting for the corrective minority. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (primary), 1.5B and 14B for robustness, frozen; only linear probes trained. Method: at each recheck onset extract residual-stream activations BEFORE any check content is generated, and fit per-layer linear probes to predict corrective vs confirmatory. Systems compared: the value-of-verification probe vs (a) a plain answer-correctness probe read at the same position, (b) an uncertainty / reflection-direction score, (c) a prior-text bag-of-words classifier. Decisive metric: corrective-vs-confirmatory AUROC on held-out problems, reported with precision-recall on the corrective class given imbalance. Secondary: partial correlation and principal angle between the value-of-verification direction and the correctness direction. Convincing result: AUROC >= 0.75 at some layer, a corrective-class precision-recall clearly above the base-rate line, a partial correlation with the corrective label >= 0.25 after removing the correctness probe, and principal angle >= 30 degrees from the correctness direction. Indecision band: AUROC in [0.65, 0.75) or principal angle in [15, 30) degrees means the signal is real but largely reducible to correctness — reported as an entangled utility correlate; AUROC < 0.65 or partial correlation < 0.10 means 'check utility' reduces to answer-correctness and H2 fails. Negative result would collapse the contribution into existing correctness-probe methods.

Experiment 3 (H2 — Causal validation: steering the signal shifts realized check outcomes): Tests that the direction causally governs whether a check corrects. Data: 400 held-out rechecks. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, frozen; intervention is adding/subtracting the value-of-verification direction at check onset, dose-response swept; 3 seeds. Systems compared: value-of-verification steering vs matched random-direction and correctness-direction controls. Decisive metric: the change in realized corrective rate (fraction of checks that actually change the answer) as a function of steering dose. Convincing result: a monotone dose-response in which positive steering raises and negative steering lowers the realized corrective rate by >= 10 percentage points, exceeding both controls by >= 8 points, plus activation-patching localization to a small set of layers. Indecision band: an effect in [4, 10) points or not separable from the random control by > 5 points is weak causal evidence, reported as such. Negative result (no outcome shift) would mean the decodable signal is not causally operative, weakening but not killing the gating application, which only needs prediction.

Experiment 4 (H3 — Correction-preserving gating cuts tokens at fixed accuracy while keeping corrective checks): The applied test of the efficiency claim. Data: full GSM8K sample, MATH500, AIME, GPQA held-out from probe fitting. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and 14B, frozen; training-free gate = at each recheck onset read the probe and skip the check when the predicted-confirmatory score is below threshold tau, else allow it; 3 seeds. Systems compared: no intervention, correctness-based early-exit, reflection steering, wholesale self-affirmation suppression, PUMA-style convergence exit, and our gate. Decisive metric: corrective-check recall (fraction of genuinely corrective checks allowed to run) at matched token savings, read jointly with hard-strata accuracy (AIME and the hardest MATH/GPQA tercile). Secondary: overall accuracy, mean tokens, tokens-at-fixed-accuracy. Convincing result: at token savings matching wholesale suppression (within 3% of its mean-token reduction), our gate retains corrective-check recall >= 0.80 and hard-strata accuracy within +/- 1.0 point of no-intervention, whereas wholesale suppression loses > 3 points on hard strata. Indecision band: corrective recall in [0.60, 0.80) at matched savings, or hard-strata accuracy change in [-3.0, -1.0] points, means the gate helps but does not cleanly beat suppression — reported as a modest improvement; recall < 0.60 or accuracy drop > 3 points means the gate fails its correction-preserving promise. Negative result (no better recall/accuracy than suppression at equal savings) would refute the practical claim while leaving the mechanistic H2 finding.

Experiment 5 (H3 — Threshold frontier, failure analysis, and generalization): Characterizes the trade-off and transfer. Data: the four datasets; failure cases mined from Experiment 4. Models: 7B and 14B, frozen. Method: sweep tau to trace the token-savings vs corrective-recall frontier; audit cases where the gate wrongly suppressed a corrective check (resulting accuracy loss) and wrongly allowed a confirmatory one (residual waste); transfer the probe and gate fit on one dataset/model to the others without retraining. Decisive metric: the tokens-vs-corrective-recall Pareto frontier and the retained gate performance on transfer targets. Convincing result: a frontier dominating the suppression baselines (higher corrective recall at equal tokens across a range of tau), and >= two-thirds of in-domain corrective recall retained on transfer. Indecision band: transfer retention in [one-third, two-thirds) means partial, calibration-dependent transfer; below one-third means the probe is dataset/model-specific. Negative result would confine the method to its fitting conditions.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The value-of-verification signal may be inseparable from a plain correctness signal (a corrective check is, almost by definition, one done when the answer is wrong); the separability, partial-correlation, and causal-steering analyses directly test this, and a null result would itself be an informative finding that 'check utility' reduces to answer-correctness. Labeling corrective vs confirmatory relies on detecting answer changes across a check, which is noisy for open-ended answers, so we restrict to math/multiple-choice with extractable answers and validate labels with human spot-checks. Corrective checks are rare, creating class imbalance that can inflate AUROC apparent performance; we report precision/recall and calibrated thresholds. Recheck-onset detection may be imperfect and miss implicit verification. Gating could still suppress a corrective check on a hard item (accuracy loss); the corrective-recall metric and hard-strata accuracy quantify this trade-off explicitly. Gains may not exceed strong suppression baselines on tokens alone - but the contribution is preserving accuracy/corrective recall at equal savings. Results may be model-family and scale specific.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims: (1) a pre-check residual-stream signal at verification onset predicts whether the impending check will be corrective vs confirmatory; (2) this signal is distinct from answer-correctness/uncertainty probes; (3) steering/gating using it suppresses wasteful checks without accuracy loss; (4) the corrective-vs-confirmatory distinction is the key new setting. This is adjacent to crowded prior work on self-verification suppression, correctness probes, and early-exit. The real delta is the prospective, per-check 'worth checking' prediction before the check runs, but the conceptual move is fairly natural and may collapse back to correctness. Name: reasoning_length_contagion
Title: Length Contagion: How the Previous Problem Anchors How Long a Reasoning Model Thinks About the Next One
Short Hypothesis: A reasoning model's thinking budget for the current problem is contaminated by the reasoning length of immediately preceding problems in its context: after a long/hard predecessor it overthinks an easy current problem, and after a short/easy predecessor it underthinks a hard one. This length contagion is causally carried by a length-budget representation in the prompt-boundary residual stream that persists from the previous problem, is dissociable from the current problem's true difficulty, and steering it restores difficulty-appropriate length.
Related Work: Prior work shows reasoning length is planned pre-generation for a SINGLE problem: 'On Reasoning Strength Planning' (2025) finds a pre-allocated directional vector whose magnitude sets token count from question activations; 'When More is Less' (2025) and 'Critical Thinking' (2025) characterize an optimal length tied to a problem's own difficulty; ThinkEdit/Efficiency Steering/S3-CoT identify and steer a length direction. All treat each problem in isolation and assume length is a function of that problem's difficulty. Separately, 'Extrapolation by Association' (2025) shows length-generalization can transfer across jointly-trained tasks via shared attention heads, but studies training-time capability transfer, not inference-time contamination of budget by neighboring items. No prior work asks whether the length budget for problem N is anchored by problems N-1, N-2 in the same context, nor identifies a carried-over budget representation as the cause. Our contribution is a new inference-time phenomenon (length contagion / anchoring across problems), its dissociation from the current problem's difficulty, and a causal account via a persistent length-budget representation.
Abstract: Reasoning language models allocate a thinking budget that is assumed to track the difficulty of the problem they are currently solving. We challenge this assumption at the level of context: real deployments feed problems in sequence (multi-turn chats, batched evaluation, agentic loops), and we ask whether the reasoning length of preceding problems contaminates the budget spent on the current one. We hypothesize length contagion: after a long, hard predecessor a model overthinks an easy current problem, and after a short, easy predecessor it underthinks a hard current problem, holding the current problem fixed. Across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we construct paired contexts that place the SAME target problem after predecessors of controlled difficulty/length and measure the shift in target reasoning length and accuracy. We test whether contagion is dissociable from true difficulty via a mixed-effects decomposition of length variance into predecessor vs. target factors. Mechanistically, we test whether a length-budget representation read at the target's prompt boundary carries over from the predecessor: a linear probe should predict target length partly from predecessor-induced state, activation patching of the prompt-boundary state from a short-predecessor context into a long-predecessor context should transfer the budget, and steering along the length-budget direction should cancel contagion and restore difficulty-appropriate length. We quantify the efficiency and accuracy cost of contagion (overthinking-after-hard, underthinking-after-easy) and offer a training-free debiasing intervention. Our work reveals a context-level anchoring failure in reasoning allocation and its causal locus.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 — Length contagion: the predecessor problem shifts the target's thinking budget): The core behavioral test. Data: constructed two-problem contexts. Draw 200 TARGET problems spanning easy-to-hard from GSM8K, MATH500, AIME 2022-2024, and GPQA-Diamond; for each, build variants placing the identical target after a low-difficulty/short-reasoning PREDECESSOR vs a high-difficulty/long-reasoning predecessor (predecessors from the same benchmarks, with their reasoning shown in-context). Control: a neutral filler predecessor of matched token length (isolates predecessor difficulty/length from raw context length). Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B, 7B, 14B and Qwen3-8B, frozen, inference only; temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 16384 tokens, 3 seeds. Systems compared: the same target after short-easy vs long-hard vs matched-length filler predecessors. Decisive metric: within-target change in median target reasoning-token count as a function of predecessor difficulty/length, over and above the matched-length filler control. Secondary: whether target accuracy shifts (overthinking easy targets after hard predecessors; underthinking hard targets after easy predecessors). Convincing result: a monotone predecessor effect where the long-hard predecessor raises median target length by >= 15% relative to the short-easy predecessor at fixed target, exceeding the filler control by >= 10 points, with a measurable accuracy drop (>= 3 points) on hard targets following easy predecessors. Indecision band: a predecessor-minus-filler length shift in [5%, 15%) is weak evidence of contagion; below 5% (or fully explained by the filler control) means the effect is context length, not predecessor difficulty, and H1 fails. Negative result would mean models reset their budget per problem, refuting contagion.

Experiment 2 (H2 — Contagion is dissociable from the target's own true difficulty): Tests that the predecessor effect survives after accounting for intrinsic target difficulty. Data: the Experiment-1 matrix (200 targets x predecessor conditions x seeds). Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (primary) and 14B, frozen; only a linear difficulty probe is fit. Method: a mixed-effects model of target reasoning length with a random effect for target identity (its intrinsic difficulty) and fixed effects for predecessor difficulty and predecessor length; compared to a target-only difficulty probe. Decisive metric: the share of target-length variance attributable to the predecessor after removing target identity, and whether the predecessor fixed effect is significant. Convincing result: the predecessor accounts for >= 15% of residual target-length variance with a significant fixed effect, and predecessor state adds predictive power beyond the target-only difficulty probe (partial correlation >= 0.25). Indecision band: predecessor variance share in [7%, 15%) means contagion is real but minor relative to target difficulty; below 7% (or no significant fixed effect) means length is target-driven and H2 fails. Negative result would collapse the phenomenon into ordinary difficulty-based allocation.

Experiment 3 (H3 — A carried-over length-budget representation lives at the target's prompt boundary): Tests that the boundary state has absorbed the predecessor's budget. Data: boundary activations from the Experiment-1 contexts; 2000 for probe fitting, 500 held-out. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, frozen; only a linear length probe trained. Method: at the target's prompt boundary (last token before any target reasoning token) fit a per-layer ridge probe to predict target reasoning length; test whether, for identical targets, the probe's prediction shifts with predecessor difficulty. Compare against a single-problem length direction (predecessor absent) to test whether contagion rides the same direction. Decisive metric: the change in probe-predicted target length across predecessor conditions at fixed target, and the cosine similarity between the contagion direction and the single-problem length direction. Convincing result: probe-predicted length shifts by >= 15% across predecessor conditions at fixed target, and cosine similarity with the single-problem length direction >= 0.5 (contagion rides a shared budget axis). Indecision band: a predicted-length shift in [5%, 15%) is weak; below 5% means the boundary state does not encode carry-over and H3 fails. Negative result would locate contagion elsewhere than the boundary budget representation.

Experiment 4 (H2/H3 — Causal patching transfers the budget across contexts): Tests that the boundary state causally carries the budget. Data: 300 matched short-predecessor / long-predecessor context pairs (same target). Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, frozen; intervention is activation patching of the prompt-boundary residual state at candidate layers from a short-predecessor context into the matched long-predecessor context and vice versa. Systems compared: real patch vs matched-random-direction patch of equal norm; off-target accuracy control. Decisive metric: the fraction of the predecessor-induced target-length gap that transfers toward the donor context under patching. Convincing result: patching transfers >= 50% of the length gap in the donor's direction, exceeding the random-direction control by >= 25 points, with target accuracy on unrelated facts unchanged (< 5 points). Indecision band: transfer in [25%, 50%) is partial causal support; below 25% (or matched by the random control) means the boundary state is not the causal carrier and H3's causal claim fails. Negative result would leave contagion as a correlational phenomenon without a localized cause.

Experiment 5 (H4 — Debiasing steering cancels contagion and restores difficulty-appropriate length): Tests the corrective intervention. Data: held-out Experiment-1 contexts, split into easy-after-hard (overthinking) and hard-after-easy (underthinking) cells. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and 14B, frozen; intervention is steering the boundary state along the length-budget direction (difference-of-means of short- vs long-predecessor boundary states) to cancel the predecessor offset; dose-response swept; 3 seeds. Systems compared: no intervention, debiasing steering, matched random-direction steering, and fixed truncation / budget-forcing baselines. Decisive metric: reduction in predecessor-driven target-length variance, read jointly with accuracy recovery on underthinking (hard-after-easy) items and token savings on overthinking (easy-after-hard) items. Convincing result: debiasing cuts predecessor-driven length variance by >= 50%, recovers >= 3 points of accuracy on hard-after-easy items, and saves >= 15% tokens on easy-after-hard items at accuracy within +/- 1.0 point, beating the random-direction control and matching or beating fixed budget-forcing. Indecision band: a variance reduction in [25%, 50%) or accuracy recovery in [1, 3) points is a weak positive; below those, or accuracy loss > 3 points, means debiasing does not cleanly restore appropriate budget. Negative result would refute H4 while leaving the observational contagion finding intact.

Experiment 6 (H1 — Real-stream cost, decay, and generalization): Quantifies the practical cost and tests scope. Data: a realistic mixed-difficulty stream of 300 problems presented in multi-turn chat and batched-evaluation formats; multi-predecessor contexts with 1-4 intervening problems. Models: 7B and 14B, frozen; probe/steering transferred without retraining. Decisive metric: tokens wasted (overthinking-after-hard) and accuracy lost (underthinking-after-easy) versus an oracle per-problem budget, and whether contagion decays with predecessor distance. Convincing result: contagion causes a measurable Pareto loss (>= 10% excess tokens or >= 2 points accuracy) versus the oracle in at least one format, decays monotonically with distance, and the probe/steering retains >= two-thirds of its in-domain effect across datasets and formats. Indecision band: a real-stream cost in [3%, 10%] tokens / [1, 2) points, or transfer retention in [one-third, two-thirds), is a modest/partial outcome; below those means contagion is negligible in realistic use. Negative result (no cost in genuine chat/batched formats) would confine the phenomenon to constructed contexts.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Predecessor effects could be driven purely by context length/position rather than by the predecessor's difficulty; the matched-length neutral-filler control and the mixed-effects decomposition are designed to isolate this, and a null after controls would be an informative negative result. Contagion may be small or model-specific (strongly instruction/RL-tuned models may reset budget per problem); we report effect sizes across scales/families. The length-budget probe may conflate carried-over state with re-derived target difficulty; the identical-target-across-predecessors design and patching experiment address this. Steering/patching can push activations off-distribution and harm coherence; we use matched-random-direction controls and report sample validity. Reasoning-length measurement requires clear think/answer delimiters, limiting to models with explicit thinking segments. Debiasing gains may not exceed simple per-problem budget-forcing, but the phenomenon and its causal locus are the primary contribution. Multi-turn chat formats may introduce confounds (the model treating predecessors as user intent) that we characterize but cannot fully eliminate.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims: (1) reasoning length for the current problem is causally shifted by the immediately preceding problem's difficulty/length; (2) this is a cross-problem contamination effect distinct from single-problem length planning; (3) a persistent boundary state/budget vector carries the effect and can be probed/steered; (4) the effect is separable from generic context length/priming. Compared with prior work on single-problem length planning/steering, the cross-problem anchoring setting is a genuine delta and non-trivial, not just an obvious next step. Main novelty risk is that the effect may collapse into generic order/priming or context-length artifacts rather than a distinct length-budget representation.
