Name: compute_conservation_under_compression
Title: Conservation of Compute: Forced Terseness Pushes Reasoning from Token Space into Activation Depth
Short Hypothesis: When a reasoning model is instructed (or steered) to produce a shorter chain of thought, it does not simply do less computation; it partially compensates by increasing per-token computation density (deeper, more layer-intensive processing) on the surviving tokens. Overthinking's token cost is thus partly convertible into activation-space depth, and the accuracy-length tradeoff is governed by whether this conversion succeeds. The compensation is measurable per-token, saturates at a ceiling, and its failure point predicts where compression breaks accuracy.
Related Work: Token Complexity (Lee et al. 2025) shows an information-theoretic floor of tokens per problem and a universal length-accuracy tradeoff, but treats computation as living purely in token space and studies prompt-based compression only behaviorally, with no internal measurement. MTD / Divergence Steering (2025) and 'Sparse or Dense?' (2026) introduce per-token computation-density estimators (KL between full model and a shallow head; mechanistic density) and find density tracks difficulty and rare tokens, but never manipulate output length and never ask whether density RESPONDS to compression. Latent-reasoning architectures (Coconut, ETD, Think-at-Hard, looped transformers, Heima) show reasoning can be moved into activation/latent depth, but require retraining new architectures; they establish that token-space and depth-space compute are interchangeable in principle, yet do not test whether EXISTING off-the-shelf reasoning models spontaneously perform this trade at inference when compressed. Our contribution is the first inference-time, training-free test of a 'conservation of compute' hypothesis: that forced terseness in standard reasoning LLMs is compensated by rising per-token activation-space computation density, that this compensation has a measurable ceiling, and that hitting the ceiling is the mechanistic cause of the accuracy-compression cliff. This reframes the length-accuracy tradeoff from a token-budget story into a token-vs-depth allocation story and is orthogonal to all prior overthinking/early-exit work.
Abstract: Reasoning language models spend many tokens 'thinking,' and a universal tradeoff links shorter chains of thought to lower accuracy. This tradeoff is usually explained purely in token space: fewer tokens mean less computation. We propose a different, mechanistic account—conservation of compute. We hypothesize that when a model is forced to be terse, it partially compensates by pushing computation from token space into activation space: each surviving token undergoes deeper, more layer-intensive processing. Overthinking's cost is thus partly convertible into per-token depth, and the accuracy-length curve is governed by whether this conversion succeeds and by an activation-space ceiling beyond which it cannot. Across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we measure per-token computation density using logit-lens convergence depth and a shallow-head KL estimator (MTD). We first show that under matched problems, compressing the chain of thought (via prompted terseness and via a length-steering direction) systematically raises per-token density on the retained tokens—quantifying a compute-conservation coefficient (density gain per token removed). We test whether this coefficient predicts which problems compress losslessly versus which fall off the accuracy cliff, better than token count or Token-Complexity baselines. We then causally probe the ceiling: we cap per-token depth (early-exit forcing) during compressed generation and show accuracy collapses precisely when compensation is blocked, and conversely that adding recurrent latent iterations (looping reasoning layers) restores accuracy under compression. Our work reframes the length-accuracy tradeoff as token-vs-depth compute allocation and yields an interpretable predictor of safe compression.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (Setup — Per-token computation-density instrumentation is valid): Validates the two density measures all later experiments rely on. Data: GSM8K (500-problem sample), MATH500 (500), AIME 2022-2024 (90), GPQA-Diamond (198); natural-length traces. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B, 7B, 14B and Qwen3-8B, frozen, inference only; temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 16384 tokens, 3 seeds. Method: at each generated token compute (a) logit-lens convergence depth (earliest layer after which the argmax matches and holds the final token) and (b) MTD, the KL between the full-model next-token distribution and an early-layer logit-lens distribution. Decisive metric: correlation of each density measure with known difficulty proxies (answer/numeric tokens vs narration, rare vs common tokens, harder vs easier problems) and agreement between the two measures. Convincing result: both measures are higher on answer/numeric and rare tokens and on harder problems (Spearman >= 0.3 with token rarity/difficulty) and correlate with each other at Spearman >= 0.5 — the instrument is meaningful. Indecision band: inter-measure agreement in [0.3, 0.5) means the proxies are only loosely consistent and later results must be reported under both separately; below 0.3 the instrument is unreliable and must be revised before proceeding. Negative result would invalidate the density readout and halt the mechanistic program.

Experiment 2 (H1 — Compression raises per-token density on retained tokens: conservation of compute): The core test. Data: the four datasets above; for each problem a baseline natural-length trace plus compressed traces via (i) prompted terseness at several strengths ('use as few words as possible', 'answer in <= N tokens') and (ii) steering along a length/verbosity direction (difference-of-means of short vs long traces), the steering variant being content-lighter. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (primary), 1.5B and 14B, frozen. Method: on retained / semantically-matched tokens (aligned to the same computation steps via an LLM-judge alignment so density is compared on comparable work, not just dropped narration) measure mean per-token density vs trace length, and fit the compute-conservation coefficient k = density increase per token removed. Systems compared: baseline vs each compression strength; raw vs content-matched density estimates. Decisive metric: k (density gain per token removed), tested > 0 on matched tokens. Convincing result: k is significantly positive on the content-matched comparison for a majority of problems (median k such that removing 30% of tokens raises matched per-token density by >= 15%), and the effect survives in the content-lighter steering condition. Indecision band: a matched-token density rise in [5%, 15%) at 30% compression is weak conservation; below 5%, or a rise present only in the raw (unmatched) estimate, means the apparent compensation is just dropped easy tokens and H1 fails. Negative result (no density rise on matched tokens) would refute conservation and support the pure token-space account.

Experiment 3 (H2 — Compensation saturates at a ceiling that predicts the accuracy cliff): Tests that k and density saturation predict which problems compress losslessly. Data: the four datasets, compression-strength sweep tracing each problem's accuracy-length curve and its accuracy cliff (the compression point where accuracy drops sharply). Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and 14B, frozen. Method: for each problem compute k and a saturation indicator (per-token density plateauing near maximum layers), then predict lossless-compressibility (no accuracy drop beyond noise at a target compression). Systems compared: the k+saturation predictor vs Token-Complexity, raw token count, and a difficulty probe. Decisive metric: AUROC for predicting lossless-compressibility. Convincing result: the k+saturation predictor reaches AUROC >= 0.75 and beats each baseline by >= 0.05 AUROC, with problems near the density ceiling being the ones that break. Indecision band: AUROC in [0.65, 0.75), or an edge over baselines in [0.02, 0.05), is weak — the ceiling carries some but not decisive predictive value; AUROC < 0.65 or no edge over Token-Complexity means saturation does not predict the cliff and H2 fails. Negative result would sever the link between the activation ceiling and the accuracy cliff.

Experiment 4 (H2/H3 — Blocking depth causally collapses accuracy under compression): Tests that retained accuracy under compression depends on activation-space compensation. Data: held-out problems across the four datasets. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, frozen; intervention is capping per-token depth by forcing early exit through the LM head at a chosen layer during generation, applied at baseline length and under compression. Systems compared: the accuracy vs (cap-layer x compression-strength) interaction; control = capping only on narration tokens; a clean per-token-only cap and a KV-approximated variant (given skipped layers' missing KV). Decisive metric: the interaction effect — the additional accuracy loss from depth-capping under compression beyond its loss at baseline length. Convincing result: depth-capping causes >= 2x more accuracy loss under compression than at baseline length, and capping narration tokens hurts far less than capping answer-relevant tokens — the compressed model was relying on depth. Indecision band: an interaction where compression-time capping loss is 1.2x-2x the baseline-length loss is weak causal support; < 1.2x means depth-capping hurts equally regardless of compression and the ceiling is not causally implicated. Negative result would refute the causal role of activation depth in compression tolerance.

Experiment 5 (H3 — Adding activation depth restores accuracy lost to compression): The substitutability test. Data: compressed-generation runs on problems that fell off the accuracy cliff in Experiment 3. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, frozen; intervention is training-free recurrent latent iteration (looping a subset of reasoning-relevant middle layers k times at inference) during compressed generation. Decisive metric: accuracy recovery under compression as a function of the number of loops, reported FLOP-adjusted (added depth costs FLOPs). Convincing result: added depth recovers >= half of the accuracy lost to compression at a FLOP cost below the baseline-length generation's FLOPs — token-space and depth-space compute are substitutable off the shelf. Indecision band: a recovery of [25%, 50%) of lost accuracy, or recovery only at FLOP cost exceeding baseline-length generation, is a weak/uneconomical positive; below 25% means depth does not substitute for tokens. Negative result would mean compression loss is not recoverable via depth, bounding the conservation claim.

Experiment 6 (H1 — Localization of where compensation happens): Tests that compressed reasoning shifts answer-relevant computation deeper. Data: 300 matched baseline/compressed trace pairs. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, frozen. Method: layer-wise logit-lens to test whether answer-relevant computation moves to later layers under compression, and activation patching of compressed-trace late-layer activations into an uncompressed run. Decisive metric: the shift in the layer at which the answer becomes decodable under compression, and whether patching compressed late-layer activations transfers the compressed answer. Convincing result: answer-decodable layer shifts later by >= 2 layers under compression, and patching compressed late-layer activations transfers the answer on >= 50% of cases. Indecision band: a layer shift of 1 layer or transfer in [25%, 50%) is weak localization; no shift and < 25% transfer means compensation is not localized to later layers. Negative result would leave the mechanism unlocalized while the behavioral H1 stands.

Experiment 7 (H2 — Practical payoff: k as a safe-compression gauge, and generalization): Tests the applied value and transfer. Data: GSM8K/MATH500/AIME/GPQA held-out. Model: 7B and 14B, frozen; use per-problem k to set adaptive length budgets. Systems compared: k-guided adaptive compression vs uniform terseness vs Token-Complexity-guided compression. Decisive metric: tokens-at-fixed-accuracy (median token reduction at accuracy within noise), reported both token-adjusted and FLOP-adjusted. Secondary: whether the density measures, coefficient, and predictor transfer across datasets and scales without retraining. Convincing result: k-guided compression saves >= 15% tokens at accuracy within +/- 1.0 point, beating uniform terseness and matching or beating Token-Complexity, and the predictor retains >= two-thirds of its AUROC on transfer. Indecision band: token savings in [5%, 15%), or transfer retention in [one-third, two-thirds), is a modest/partial outcome; below those means k offers no practical edge or does not transfer. Negative result would confine the contribution to the mechanistic findings without a deployable gauge.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The compensation may be small or absent—models may just do less compute when compressed (pure token-space story), which would refute the hypothesis but is itself an informative, publishable negative result clarifying the Token-Complexity picture. Matching 'retained tokens' across compressed and full traces is nontrivial; density could appear to rise merely because compression drops easy narration tokens, inflating the average—we mitigate with content-aligned comparison and by measuring density on matched computation steps, and report both raw and matched estimates. Logit-lens convergence depth and MTD are proxies for computation; we cross-validate with two measures and with causal depth-capping. The depth-capping experiment faces the standard early-exit KV-consistency issue (skipped layers' KV missing for future attention); we report both a clean per-token-only cap and a KV-approximated variant and interpret cautiously. Adding recurrent depth increases FLOPs, so 'restoring accuracy under compression' trades tokens for compute—we report FLOP-adjusted, not just token-adjusted, gains. Effects are likely model-family and scale specific, and the conservation coefficient may not transfer across very different tokenizers. Compression via prompting may change reasoning content, not just length, confounding density readings; the steering-based compression provides a content-lighter alternative.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims: (1) forced terseness causally increases per-token computation density; (2) this density gain saturates at a ceiling; (3) the ceiling predicts the accuracy cliff; (4) depth can be causally blocked/restored to test compensation. Closest prior work already establishes a depth-vs-length tradeoff and per-token density estimators, and latent-reasoning work shows depth can substitute for tokens in principle. The only real delta is the inference-time causal compression test and the predictive-ceiling framing, which is interesting but thin and close to an obvious next experiment rather than a clearly new phenomenon.

Name: analogical_transfer_gate
Title: Solved It Once, Solving It Again: An Internal Analogy Gate That Determines Whether Reasoning Models Reuse a Worked Example or Re-Derive From Scratch
Short Hypothesis: When a reasoning model is shown a fully-worked solution to a structurally-identical problem immediately before the target, it should recognize the shared structure and reuse the method with far less thinking. We hypothesize that reasoning models frequently FAIL to do this, re-deriving from scratch and wasting tokens, and that the difference between transfer and re-derivation is governed by an internal, linearly-decodable 'analogy/structure-mapping' signal that fires (or fails to fire) at the moment the model begins the target problem. Steering this signal causally flips the model between re-derivation and reuse.
Related Work: Two literatures are relevant and previously disconnected. (1) Cognitive science on analogical transfer (Structure-Mapping Theory; 'Transfer Between Analogies', 1995; 'A model of retrieval in problem solving', 1989; 'A theory of relation learning and cross-domain generalization', 2022) documents that humans reuse solutions to structurally-similar problems and characterizes when this transfer succeeds or fails (surface vs. structural similarity, retrieval failures). (2) ML interpretability on circuit and computation reuse (Circuit Component Reuse Across Tasks, 2023; Shared Circuits for Sequence Continuation, 2023; Extrapolation by Association, 2025) shows internal components are shared across tasks, and systems work (LLMCache, AttMemo, KVShare, 2023-2025) reuses activations/KV across requests at the infrastructure level. Crucially, NO prior work asks the behavioral question: does a reasoning model behaviorally transfer its OWN just-seen worked solution to a new instance of the same problem, or does it wastefully re-derive? Systems caching reuses computation externally without asking whether the model itself recognizes the analogy; circuit-reuse work studies static shared components, not the dynamic decision to transfer in-context. My prior proposals all concern within-single-problem overthinking; this concerns cross-problem transfer failure and its mechanistic gate. We are the first to (a) quantify in-context analogical-transfer failure in reasoning LLMs, (b) show it is modulated by surface vs. structural similarity as in human analogy, and (c) locate and causally steer an internal analogy gate that switches between reuse and re-derivation.
Abstract: Humans who have just solved a problem reuse the method when they encounter a structurally identical one, thinking far less the second time. We ask whether reasoning language models do the same. We present a reasoning model with a fully-worked solution to a problem, then a target that is structurally identical but differs in surface details (numbers, cover story, variable names), and measure whether the model transfers the method (short, reuse-style reasoning) or re-derives from scratch (long, redundant reasoning). We hypothesize that reasoning models frequently fail to transfer, wasting tokens, and—mirroring human analogy—that transfer succeeds more when surface similarity is high and fails when only deep structure is shared. Across GSM8K, MATH500, and algorithmic word problems on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we quantify a transfer-failure rate and its dependence on surface vs. structural similarity. We then test a mechanistic account: at the token boundary where the target problem begins, the residual stream linearly encodes an 'analogy gate' signal predicting whether the model will reuse the worked example or re-derive. We train probes for this signal, test its separability from raw difficulty, localize the carrying components via activation patching (patching the analogy-recognition state from a surface-matched context into a structure-only context), and causally steer the gate to flip reuse vs. re-derivation. Finally we turn the gate into a training-free intervention that induces reuse when a valid analog is present, cutting tokens at equal accuracy. Our work reframes a slice of overthinking as analogical-transfer failure with an identifiable, steerable internal cause.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 — Reasoning models frequently fail to transfer a just-seen worked solution to a structurally identical target): The behavioral test. Data: constructed analog pairs. Draw 250 seed problems from GSM8K, MATH500, and templated algorithmic word problems with well-defined solution methods; for each seed generate (a) a surface-similar structural analog (same method, similar cover story, different numbers), (b) a structure-only analog (same method, different cover story/domain), and (c) a surface-similar structurally-different distractor (similar wording, different method). Verify structural equivalence via solution-step-template matching plus an LLM-judge check and a 150-pair human spot-check. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B, 7B, 14B and Qwen3-8B, frozen, inference only; temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 16384 tokens, 3 seeds. Systems compared, per condition: [worked analog + target] vs [target alone] vs [irrelevant worked solution + target]. Decisive metric: transfer-failure rate — the fraction of structural-analog trials whose target reasoning-token count is not substantially reduced (< 20% below the target-alone baseline) despite retained accuracy. Secondary: mean token reduction and accuracy per condition (surface-similar vs structure-only vs distractor), and whether the distractor induces harmful reuse (accuracy drop). Convincing result: transfer-failure rate >= 40% overall with a real opportunity cost (surface-similar analogs cut tokens by >= 25% at retained accuracy when transfer does occur), establishing that models leave substantial savings on the table. Indecision band: a transfer-failure rate in [20%, 40%) means failure is real but modest; below 20% (models almost always transfer) means there is little phenomenon to explain and the mechanistic program is unmotivated. Negative result (models reliably transfer, near-zero failure) would refute the premise.

Experiment 2 (H2 — An analogy-gate signal at target onset linearly predicts transfer vs re-derivation, separable from difficulty): Tests the decodable gate. Data: ~4000 [worked analog + target] boundary states from Experiment 1 labeled transfer vs re-derive, 1200 held-out from disjoint seeds. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (primary), 1.5B and 14B, frozen; only linear probes trained. Method: at the token boundary where the target begins (after the worked example, before any target reasoning token) fit per-layer linear probes to predict transfer vs re-derivation. Systems compared: the analogy-gate probe vs (i) a difficulty probe trained on target pass-rate, (ii) a surface-similarity feature baseline, (iii) prior-text bag-of-words. Decisive metric: transfer-prediction AUROC on held-out seeds. Secondary: partial correlation with the transfer label after removing difficulty and surface overlap, and principal angle between the gate and difficulty directions. Convincing result: AUROC >= 0.75 at some layer, partial correlation >= 0.25 after removing difficulty and surface overlap, and principal angle >= 30 degrees from the difficulty direction. Indecision band: AUROC in [0.65, 0.75) or principal angle in [15, 30) degrees means the gate is real but largely reducible to difficulty/surface features — reported as an entangled correlate; AUROC < 0.65 means no distinct gate and H2 fails. Negative result would leave transfer failure as a behavioral fact without an internal decision variable.

Experiment 3 (H3 — Patching the analogy-recognition state causally switches reuse vs re-derivation): Tests causal carry of the gate. Data: 300 matched pairs sharing the same target and method but differing in analog type (surface-similar transfer-inducing vs structure-only re-derivation). Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, frozen; intervention is activation patching of the target-boundary state at candidate layers from the surface-similar context into the structure-only context and vice versa. Systems compared: real patch vs matched-random-direction patch of equal norm; off-target accuracy control. Decisive metric: the fraction of trials that switch to reuse (token drop plus method-matched solution) under patching. Convincing result: patching flips >= 40% of re-derivation trials to reuse, exceeding the random-direction control by >= 25 points, with off-target accuracy unchanged (< 5 points). Indecision band: a flip rate in [20%, 40%) or margin over random < 25 points is weak causal evidence; below 20% means the boundary state is not the causal gate. Negative result would leave the gate correlational.

Experiment 4 (H3 — Steering the gate induces reuse when a valid analog is present, with specificity): The steering test. Data: held-out [surface-similar analog + target] and [distractor + target] trials. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and 14B, frozen; intervention is steering along the analogy-gate direction (difference-of-means of transfer vs re-derivation boundary states); dose-response swept; 3 seeds. Systems compared: steer-up (induce reuse) vs steer-down (control) vs no intervention vs matched random direction. Decisive metric: token reduction at retained accuracy on valid-analog trials under steer-up, read jointly with the specificity check that steering does NOT induce harmful reuse of the distractor (accuracy must not drop on distractor trials). Convincing result: steer-up cuts median tokens by >= 20% at accuracy within +/- 1.0 point on valid-analog trials, beats the random control by >= 10 points of token change, and leaves distractor-trial accuracy within +/- 1.0 point (no harmful transfer). Indecision band: a token reduction in [5%, 20%), or a distractor-trial accuracy drop in (1.0, 3.0] points, is a weak/partly-harmful outcome reported as such; a distractor accuracy drop > 3 points means steering forces indiscriminate reuse and fails specificity. Negative result (no token reduction, or reduction only with harmful distractor reuse) would refute the controllable-gate claim.

Experiment 5 (H3 — Training-free efficiency application and generalization): Tests the applied payoff and transfer. Data: GSM8K/MATH500/algorithmic held-out trials where a valid worked analog is in context (detected cheaply by template match); plus cross-domain analogs (a math method reused in a physics word problem). Models: 7B and 14B, frozen; apply gate steering to induce reuse when a valid analog is detected. Systems compared: gate steering vs no intervention vs simple prompting ('reuse the method above'). Decisive metric: tokens-at-equal-accuracy (median token reduction subject to accuracy within noise) over the valid-analog stream. Secondary: whether the probe and steering direction transfer across datasets, scales, and to cross-domain analogs without retraining. Convincing result: gate steering saves >= 15% tokens at accuracy within +/- 1.0 point, matching or beating the prompting baseline, and retains >= two-thirds of its effect across datasets and on cross-domain analogs. Indecision band: token savings in [5%, 15%), or transfer retention in [one-third, two-thirds), is a modest/partial outcome; below those means no practical edge or no transfer (cross-domain transfer being rare, especially at 1.5B, is itself an informative scope result). Negative result would confine the contribution to the mechanistic findings.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The analogy gate may be inseparable from raw difficulty or surface-overlap features, weakening the mechanistic claim; the separability analysis, patching, and distractor-specificity tests directly address this, and a null would still yield a novel behavioral characterization of transfer failure. Constructing clean structural analogs that hold difficulty constant while varying surface similarity is nontrivial; we mitigate with template-based generation and human/LLM verification of structural equivalence. Transfer-success detection relies on token-count and method-match, which are noisy; we use both token-reduction and step-template matching and validate with human spot-checks. Inducing reuse could cause harmful transfer to structurally-different distractors (accuracy loss); the distractor condition and steering-specificity metric quantify this trade-off. Reasoning-length measurement requires clear think/answer delimiters. Effects and the strength of surface-vs-structure modulation may be model-family and scale specific, and cross-domain transfer may be rare in smaller models (itself an informative result).

novelty.reasoning: Core claims: (1) a just-seen worked example is often not reused by reasoning LLMs, causing token-wasting re-derivation; (2) transfer is modulated by surface vs structural similarity in a human-like way; (3) a linearly decodable internal gate at target onset predicts reuse vs re-derivation; (4) steering this gate causally flips behavior. The behavioral phenomenon is fresher than the mechanism, but each component overlaps with analogy-transfer, task-vector, and circuit-steering literature. The main novelty is the specific in-context efficiency failure and framing it as a causal gate for transfer vs re-derivation rather than generic task representation.

Name: analogical_transfer_gate
Title: Solved It Once, Solving It Again: An Internal Analogy Gate Governing Whether Reasoning Models Reuse a Worked Example or Re-Derive From Scratch
Short Hypothesis: When shown a fully-worked solution to a structurally-identical problem immediately before the target, reasoning models frequently FAIL to transfer the method—re-deriving from scratch and wasting large numbers of tokens—and, mirroring human analogical transfer, this failure is modulated by surface vs. structural similarity. The transfer-vs-re-derivation decision is governed by an internal, linearly-decodable analogy-gate signal that fires (or fails to fire) at the moment the target problem begins; steering it causally flips the model between reuse and re-derivation.
Related Work: Two previously-disconnected literatures. (1) Interpretability of in-context task reuse: Circuit Component Reuse Across Tasks (2023) and Function Induction (2025) show internal components/circuits are shared across tasks; Just-in-time and Distributed Task Representations (2025) shows transferrable task vectors form sporadically at specific tokens; task-vector work extracts task identity from activations. (2) Cognitive science on analogical transfer (Structure-Mapping Theory) documents that humans reuse solutions to structurally-similar problems, with success gated by surface vs. structural similarity and by retrieval failure. Crucially, NO prior work asks the *behavioral* question we pose: does a reasoning model reuse its OWN just-seen worked solution on a new instance of the same problem, or wastefully re-derive—and how much compute does this cost? Circuit-reuse work studies static shared components, not the dynamic in-context decision to transfer; systems-level activation/KV caching reuses computation externally without asking whether the model itself recognizes the analogy. Our contribution is (a) quantifying in-context analogical-transfer failure in reasoning LLMs as wasted reasoning tokens, (b) showing it is modulated by surface vs. structural similarity as in human analogy, and (c) locating and causally steering an internal analogy gate—plausibly a just-in-time signal at target onset—that switches between reuse and re-derivation. This differs from all my prior proposals, which concern within-single-problem overthinking.
Abstract: Humans who have just solved a problem reuse the method when they meet a structurally identical one, thinking far less the second time. We ask whether reasoning language models do the same. We present a reasoning model with a fully-worked solution to a problem, then a target that is structurally identical but differs in surface details (numbers, cover story, variable names), and measure whether the model transfers the method (short, reuse-style reasoning) or re-derives from scratch (long, redundant reasoning). We hypothesize that models frequently fail to transfer, wasting tokens, and—mirroring human analogy—that transfer succeeds more with high surface similarity and fails when only deep structure is shared, while a surface-similar-but-structurally-different distractor induces harmful reuse. Across GSM8K, MATH500, and templated algorithmic word problems on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we quantify a transfer-failure rate and its dependence on surface vs. structural similarity. We then test a mechanistic account: at the token boundary where the target begins, the residual stream linearly encodes an analogy-gate signal predicting reuse vs. re-derivation. We train probes for this signal, test its separability from raw target difficulty, localize the carrying components via activation patching (patching the analogy-recognition state from a transfer-inducing context into a re-derivation context), and causally steer the gate to flip behavior with specificity controls. Finally we turn the gate into a training-free intervention that induces reuse when a valid analog is present, cutting tokens at equal accuracy. Our work reframes a slice of overthinking as analogical-transfer failure with an identifiable, steerable internal cause.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 — Models fail to transfer, and the failure is modulated by surface vs structural similarity with distractor-induced harmful reuse): The behavioral test of the transfer-failure claim and its similarity modulation. Data: constructed analog sets. From 250 seed problems (GSM8K, MATH500, templated algorithmic word problems with well-defined methods) build, per seed, (a) a surface-similar structural analog (same method and cover story, different numbers), (b) a structure-only analog (same method, different domain/cover story), and (c) a surface-similar structurally-different distractor (similar wording, different method). Verify structural equivalence via solution-step-template matching plus an LLM-judge and a 150-item human spot-check, and verify difficulty parity across conditions by pass-rate matching. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B, 7B, 14B and Qwen3-8B, frozen, inference only; temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 16384 tokens, 3 seeds. Systems compared, per condition: [worked analog + target] vs [target alone] vs [irrelevant worked solution + target]. Decisive metric: transfer-failure rate (fraction of structural-analog trials with < 20% token reduction vs target-alone despite retained accuracy), reported separately for surface-similar and structure-only conditions. Secondary: mean token reduction and accuracy per condition; distractor-condition accuracy (harmful reuse). Convincing result: overall transfer-failure rate >= 40%; failure rate on structure-only analogs exceeds surface-similar by >= 15 percentage points (surface-vs-structure modulation); and the distractor lowers accuracy by >= 3 points vs target-alone (harmful reuse). Indecision band: an overall failure rate in [20%, 40%), or a surface-vs-structure gap in [5, 15) points, is weak support — failure and modulation are present but minor; below those thresholds means no meaningful failure or no similarity modulation and H1 is unsupported. Negative result (reliable transfer, or no surface-vs-structure difference, or no distractor harm) would refute the behavioral core.

Experiment 2 (H2 — A just-in-time analogy-gate signal at target onset predicts reuse vs re-derivation, separable from difficulty): Tests the decodable, temporally-local gate. Data: ~4000 [worked analog + target] boundary states from Experiment 1 labeled transfer vs re-derive, 1200 held-out from disjoint seeds. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (primary), 1.5B and 14B, frozen; only linear probes trained. Method: at the token boundary where the target begins fit per-layer linear probes to predict transfer vs re-derivation, and repeat at positions before and after onset to test temporal locality (just-in-time hypothesis). Systems compared: the analogy-gate probe vs (i) a difficulty probe on target pass-rate, (ii) a surface-overlap feature baseline, (iii) prior-text bag-of-words. Decisive metric: transfer-prediction AUROC on held-out seeds at target onset. Secondary: partial correlation after removing difficulty and surface overlap, principal angle from the difficulty direction, and the AUROC profile across token positions (locality). Convincing result: AUROC >= 0.75 at onset, partial correlation >= 0.25 after removing confounds, principal angle >= 30 degrees from difficulty, and AUROC peaking near onset (a >= 0.05 rise vs positions well before the target) supporting the just-in-time account. Indecision band: AUROC in [0.65, 0.75) or principal angle in [15, 30) degrees means an entangled correlate; AUROC < 0.65 means no distinct gate and H2 fails. A flat AUROC-vs-position profile leaves the gate decodable but not specifically just-in-time (reported as such, not fatal to H2). Negative result would leave transfer failure without an internal decision variable.

Experiment 3 (H2 — Patching the analogy-recognition state causally switches reuse vs re-derivation): Tests causal carry. Data: 300 matched pairs sharing target and method but differing in analog type (surface-similar transfer-inducing vs structure-only re-derivation). Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, frozen; intervention is activation patching of the target-boundary state at candidate layers from the transfer-inducing context into the re-derivation context and vice versa. Systems compared: real patch vs matched-random-direction patch of equal norm; off-target accuracy control. Decisive metric: fraction of trials switching to reuse (token drop plus method-matched solution) under patching. Convincing result: patching flips >= 40% of re-derivation trials to reuse, exceeding the random control by >= 25 points, off-target accuracy unchanged (< 5 points). Indecision band: a flip rate in [20%, 40%) or margin over random < 25 points is weak; below 20% means the boundary state is not the causal gate. Negative result would leave the gate correlational.

Experiment 4 (H2 — Steering the gate flips behavior with specificity): The steering test. Data: held-out [surface-similar analog + target] and [distractor + target] trials. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and 14B, frozen; intervention is steering along the analogy-gate direction (difference-of-means of transfer vs re-derivation boundary states); dose-response swept; 3 seeds. Systems compared: steer-up (induce reuse) vs steer-down (control) vs no intervention vs matched random direction. Decisive metric: token reduction at retained accuracy on valid-analog trials under steer-up, read jointly with the specificity check that steering does not induce harmful reuse of the distractor. Convincing result: steer-up cuts median tokens by >= 20% at accuracy within +/- 1.0 point on valid-analog trials, beats the random control by >= 10 points of token change, and leaves distractor-trial accuracy within +/- 1.0 point. Indecision band: a token reduction in [5%, 20%), or a distractor-trial accuracy drop in (1.0, 3.0] points, is a weak/partly-harmful outcome; a distractor accuracy drop > 3 points fails specificity. Negative result (no reduction, or reduction only with harmful distractor reuse) would refute the controllable-gate claim.

Experiment 5 (H1/H2 — Training-free efficiency application and generalization): Tests the applied payoff and transfer. Data: GSM8K/MATH500/algorithmic held-out trials with a valid worked analog in context (detected by template match); plus cross-domain analogs (a math method reused in a physics word problem). Models: 7B and 14B, frozen; apply gate steering to induce reuse when a valid analog is detected. Systems compared: gate steering vs no intervention vs prompting ('reuse the method above'). Decisive metric: tokens-at-equal-accuracy (median token reduction subject to accuracy within noise) over the valid-analog stream. Secondary: transfer of the probe and steering direction across datasets, scales, and to cross-domain analogs without retraining. Convincing result: gate steering saves >= 15% tokens at accuracy within +/- 1.0 point, matching or beating prompting, and retains >= two-thirds of its effect across datasets and on cross-domain analogs. Indecision band: token savings in [5%, 15%), or transfer retention in [one-third, two-thirds), is a modest/partial outcome; below those means no practical edge or no transfer (rare cross-domain transfer at 1.5B being an informative scope result). Negative result would confine the contribution to the mechanistic findings.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The analogy gate may be inseparable from raw difficulty or surface-overlap features, weakening the mechanistic claim; the separability analysis, patching, and distractor-specificity tests directly address this, and a null would still yield a novel behavioral characterization of transfer failure. Constructing clean structural analogs that hold difficulty constant while varying surface similarity is nontrivial; we mitigate with template-based generation and human/LLM verification plus pass-rate matching. Transfer-success detection relies on token-count and method-match, which are noisy; we use both token-reduction and step-template matching and validate with human spot-checks. Inducing reuse could cause harmful transfer to structurally-different distractors (accuracy loss); the distractor condition and steering-specificity metric quantify this trade-off. Reasoning-length measurement requires clear think/answer delimiters. Effects and the strength of surface-vs-structure modulation may be model-family and scale specific, and cross-domain transfer may be rare in smaller models (itself an informative result).

novelty.reasoning: Core claims: (1) reasoning models often fail to reuse a just-seen worked example on a structurally identical target and re-derive from scratch, causing token waste; (2) this failure depends on surface-vs-structural similarity, including harmful reuse from distractors; (3) a linearly-decodable, just-in-time 'analogy gate' at target onset predicts transfer vs re-derivation; (4) steering/patching this signal causally flips behavior. The behavioral claim is a meaningful new setting/delta relative to prior surface-vs-structure analogy work because it targets self-reuse immediately after a worked example and measures token efficiency, not just correctness. The mechanistic gate claim is less novel in light of task vectors / circuit reuse / just-in-time task representations, but combining it with analogical transfer and efficiency is a nontrivial integration. Closest prior work already covers surface-vs-structure failure and linear task representations, so the novelty is genuine but incremental rather than paradigm-shifting.

Name: strategy_affordance_mismatch
Title: Wrong Tool for the Job: Overthinking as a Strategy-Selection Mismatch Between the Problem's Afforded Solution Method and the One the Model Executes
Short Hypothesis: Reasoning models pre-encode, before generating any reasoning token, a linearly-decodable 'strategy affordance' signal indicating which class of solution method a problem invites (e.g., direct recall/formula-application vs. multi-step derivation vs. case-enumeration). A large slice of overthinking is a strategy mismatch: the model executes a heavier strategy than the problem affords. This mismatch predicts wasted tokens better than a scalar difficulty or success probe, and steering the model toward the afforded (cheaper) strategy at problem onset cuts tokens without hurting accuracy.
Related Work: Prior efficient-reasoning interpretability reads a scalar pre-generation signal and allocates a length/compute budget from it: LLMs Encode Their Failures (2026) and difficulty-perception probes predict model-specific difficulty for routing; Temporal Predictors of Outcome (2025) and Knowing Before Saying (2025) probe eventual correctness early; Tracing the Traces (2025) uses latent-trajectory signals to pick promising traces; FR-Ponder / Learning to Ponder (2025) learn instance-adaptive scalar compute; Efficiency Steering / ReflCtrl (2025) steer a single verbosity/reflection direction. Crucially all treat the pre-generation signal as one-dimensional (how hard / how likely to succeed / how long) and control a scalar knob (budget, length, reflection). A separate line (Behavior and Representation in LLMs for Combinatorial Optimization, 2025) shows hidden states support per-instance ALGORITHM selection, but for external solver choice, not for the model's own reasoning, and offers no efficiency intervention. Our proposal is distinct and is directly inspired by cognitive neuroscience findings that the brain decides *whether* to engage costly forward planning via a fast planning-value proxy (ACC, 2021) and shifts from rule-based to memory-based processing via cost-benefit analysis (2025): we claim reasoning models carry a multi-class strategy-affordance representation, that overthinking is a *mismatch* between afforded and executed strategy (not merely a mis-set scalar budget), and that steering toward the afforded strategy is an interpretable efficiency fix. This is a strategy-selection account, orthogonal to all my prior overthinking proposals (which concern answer-commitment, verification, length priors, etc.) and to scalar difficulty/budget work.
Abstract: Reasoning language models overthink, and prior interpretability work explains this via a scalar internal signal (difficulty, success-likelihood, or a verbosity direction) that sets how *much* to think. We propose a categorical account inspired by human cognitive control: before generating any reasoning token, a model encodes a strategy-affordance signal indicating *which kind* of solution method a problem invites—direct recall/formula-application, multi-step algebraic derivation, or case-enumeration/search. We hypothesize that a large share of overthinking is a strategy mismatch: the model executes a heavier strategy than the problem affords (e.g., laboriously deriving what could be recalled, or enumerating what a formula solves in one line). Across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we (1) label each problem's afforded strategy and each trace's executed strategy via lightweight parsing plus LLM-judge; (2) train linear probes on the prompt-boundary residual stream to decode afforded strategy and test separability from a scalar difficulty probe; (3) show a mismatch metric (afforded-cheap but executed-heavy) predicts wasted tokens better than difficulty or success probes; (4) localize the strategy-affordance representation and causally validate it via activation patching (patch a cheap-strategy affordance into a heavy-strategy context and observe strategy switch); and (5) build a training-free intervention that steers the model toward the afforded strategy at onset, cutting tokens at equal accuracy versus scalar length steering and difficulty budgeting. Our work reframes a slice of overthinking as picking the wrong solution method and gives it an identifiable, steerable internal cause.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 — Overthinking is substantially a strategy mismatch, not just a mis-set scalar budget): Establishes the phenomenon by labeling afforded vs executed strategy and measuring mismatch prevalence and its token cost. Data: GSM8K (1000-problem sample of 1319), MATH500 (500), AIME 2022-2024 (90), GPQA-Diamond (198). Define a coarse, model-agnostic strategy taxonomy: DIRECT-RECALL/formula-application, MULTI-STEP-DERIVATION, CASE-ENUMERATION/search, and ELIMINATION (for MCQ). For each problem label the AFFORDED strategy = the cheapest strategy yielding the correct answer (from a model-produced minimal solution plus an independent LLM-judge, cross-checked against a reference minimal solution where available); for each generated trace label the EXECUTED strategy via pattern parsing plus LLM-judge. Validate on a 200-item human spot-check and report inter-rater agreement. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B, 7B, 14B and Qwen3-8B, frozen, inference only; temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 16384 tokens, 3 seeds. Decisive metric: the fraction of traces whose executed strategy is strictly heavier than afforded, and the token overhead of those traces relative to their afforded-strategy minimal-solve length (estimated by truncate-and-resume and by prompting the afforded strategy). Convincing result: >= 25% of traces are strictly-heavier mismatches carrying >= 30% median token overhead vs the afforded minimal solve, with human-validated label agreement (Cohen's kappa) >= 0.6 — mismatch is a large, real slice of waste. Indecision band: a mismatch prevalence in [10%, 25%), or label kappa in [0.4, 0.6), means mismatch is present but minor or the labels too noisy to rest strong claims on — reported as weak/exploratory; below 10% prevalence means overthinking is not meaningfully strategy mismatch and the account fails. Negative result (executed strategy almost always matches afforded) would refute the framing.

Experiment 2 (H2 — A multi-class strategy-affordance signal is decodable at the prompt boundary, separable from scalar difficulty): Tests the categorical pre-generation representation. Data: prompt-boundary activations for the Experiment-1 problems with afforded-strategy labels; 3000 for probe fitting, 800 held-out from disjoint problems. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (primary), 1.5B and 14B, frozen; only linear probes trained. Method: at the last prompt token (before any reasoning token) fit a multi-class linear probe per layer to predict the afforded strategy. Systems compared: the strategy probe vs (a) a scalar difficulty probe (pass-rate), (b) a success-likelihood probe, (c) surface features (length, TF-IDF). Decisive metric: held-out macro-F1 for afforded strategy, and the predictive gain of the strategy probe over difficulty in a joint model. Secondary: principal angle between strategy-class directions and the difficulty direction. Convincing result: macro-F1 >= 0.55 (against a >0.25 four-class chance baseline) at some middle layer, a significant predictive gain over difficulty, and principal angle >= 30 degrees from the difficulty direction — strategy affordance is a distinct, multi-dimensional signal. Indecision band: macro-F1 in [0.40, 0.55) or principal angle in [15, 30) degrees means the affordance is only partly separable from difficulty — reported as an entangled categorical correlate; macro-F1 <= 0.40 or no gain over difficulty means the account collapses into scalar difficulty-budgeting and H1 fails. Negative result would remove the categorical basis of the whole hypothesis.

Experiment 3 (H3 — A mismatch score predicts wasted tokens better than scalar difficulty or success probes): The predictive test. Data: held-out Experiment-1 problems with per-problem wasted-token labels = tokens beyond the truncate-and-resume minimal-solve length. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and 14B, frozen. Method: define a mismatch score from the probe-predicted afforded strategy vs the realized executed strategy; regress wasted tokens on the mismatch score and, separately, on each baseline (difficulty probe, success probe, raw trace length). Decisive metric: held-out R^2 for predicting wasted tokens from the mismatch score vs the best scalar baseline. Convincing result: the mismatch score's R^2 exceeds every scalar baseline's by >= 0.05 and is significant, showing waste is specifically strategy mismatch, not generic difficulty. Indecision band: an R^2 edge over the best baseline in [0.02, 0.05) is weak; <= 0.02 (or the difficulty probe matching the mismatch score) means mismatch adds no predictive value beyond scalar signals and H3 fails. Negative result would fold the contribution back into existing difficulty-budgeting.

Experiment 4 (H4 — Patching the affordance state causally switches the executed strategy): Tests the causal locus. Data: 300 constructed pairs sharing a target answer/method family but differing in afforded strategy (cheap-affording vs heavy-affording), built from templated problem variants; where clean pairs are unavailable they are excluded and reported. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, frozen; intervention is activation patching of the prompt-boundary state at candidate layers from a cheap-strategy-affording problem into a heavy-strategy context. Systems compared: real patch vs matched-random-direction patch of equal norm; off-target accuracy control. Decisive metric: fraction of trials whose executed strategy switches toward the cheaper class (strategy relabel plus token drop) under patching. Convincing result: patching switches the strategy on >= 40% of trials, exceeding the random control by >= 25 points, with off-target accuracy unchanged (< 5 points). Indecision band: a switch rate in [20%, 40%) or margin over random < 25 points is weak causal support; below 20% means the boundary state does not causally carry the affordance. Negative result would leave the affordance correlational.

Experiment 5 (H4 — Steering toward the afforded strategy cuts tokens without hurting accuracy, beating scalar length steering): The applied test of the efficiency claim. Data: GSM8K/MATH500/AIME/GPQA held-out. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and 14B, frozen; intervention is steering along a strategy direction (difference-of-means between cheap- and heavy-strategy affordance activations) at problem onset, applied only when the probe predicts a cheap strategy is afforded; 3 seeds. Systems compared: no intervention, strategy steering, scalar length/verbosity steering, difficulty-budgeting (FR-Ponder-style), fixed truncation, and prompting ('use the simplest method'). Decisive metric: tokens-at-equal-accuracy (median token reduction subject to accuracy within noise), read against the strategy-switch rate. Secondary: accuracy overall and on hardest strata, wall-clock speedup. Convincing result: strategy steering cuts median tokens by >= 15% at accuracy within +/- 1.0 point and Pareto-dominates scalar length steering (more tokens saved at equal-or-better accuracy), driven by a measurable strategy-switch rate. Indecision band: a token reduction in [5%, 15%), or accuracy change in [-3.0, -1.0] points, is a weak/traded outcome; a reduction that fails to beat scalar length steering means the categorical target adds no practical value over blunt shortening (an informative reframing-only result); accuracy drop > 3 points fails the 'without hurting accuracy' claim. Negative result would refute the intervention claim while leaving the mechanistic H1-H3 findings.

Experiment 6 (H4 — Specificity, safety, and generalization): Tests that steering does not fire on genuinely heavy-afforded problems and that it transfers. Data: the hardest-strata (heavy-afforded) items from AIME and the bottom MATH/GPQA accuracy tercile, plus held-out sets across datasets. Models: 7B and 14B, frozen. Method: apply strategy steering gated by probe confidence and measure accuracy on truly heavy-afforded items as a function of confidence; transfer the probe and steering direction across datasets/scales without retraining. Decisive metric: accuracy on heavy-afforded items under gated steering (must not drop) and retained token savings on transfer targets. Convincing result: heavy-afforded accuracy within +/- 1.0 point of no-intervention (no induced underthinking) and >= two-thirds of the token savings retained across datasets/scales. Indecision band: a heavy-afforded accuracy drop in (1.0, 3.0] points flags that steering must be gated to higher confidence; > 3.0 points means the intervention harms hard problems and must be scoped away from them. Transfer retention in [one-third, two-thirds) means partial, calibration-dependent generality; below one-third means it is model/dataset-specific. Negative result would bound applicability rather than refute the core account.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The strategy taxonomy may be fuzzy—some problems admit no single 'afforded' strategy, and labels from LLM-judge/parsing are noisy; we mitigate with a small, coarse class set, human validation, and reporting agreement, and treat ambiguous cases separately. The afforded-strategy signal may be inseparable from scalar difficulty (harder problems simply afford heavier strategies), which would collapse our account into existing difficulty-budgeting work—the separability analysis, joint-model predictive-gain test, and causal patching directly address this, and a null separability result is itself an informative finding. Constructing patching pairs that hold the answer/method fixed while flipping afforded strategy is nontrivial; we use templated problem variants and report where clean pairs are unavailable. Steering toward a cheaper strategy could cause underthinking on problems that truly need a heavy method (accuracy loss); the specificity/hardest-strata analysis and confidence gating quantify this trade-off. Minimal-solve-length estimation via truncate-and-resume is compute-heavy and noisy; we subsample. Intervention gains may not exceed strong scalar steering on tokens alone, but the mechanistic reframing (overthinking as strategy mismatch with a decodable, steerable affordance representation) is a standalone contribution. Effects are likely model-family and scale specific, and afforded-strategy structure may differ across domains.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims are the categorical/structured affordance signal at pre-generation, its separability from scalar difficulty/success, and the intervention that steers toward the afforded strategy to reduce tokens. This is meaningfully different from prior scalar budget/probe work, and the delta is non-trivial if it truly out-predicts difficulty. However, the setting is adjacent to existing pre-generation routing/compute-control work, and strategy-vs-difficulty confounding is the central risk.

Name: tokenizer_fragmentation_overthinking
Title: Fragmented Numbers, Longer Thoughts: How Tokenizer Segmentation of Numerals Inflates Reasoning Compute Independent of Difficulty
Short Hypothesis: For the identical math problem, a reasoning model spends systematically more thinking tokens when the numbers are tokenized into more fragments (worse digit segmentation), and this excess is not extra genuine reasoning but a surface-form artifact: the tokenizer's fragmentation inflates an internal difficulty/length signal read before reasoning begins. Re-encoding the same numbers into fewer, cleaner tokens (e.g., digit-spacing or single-digit segmentation) reduces reasoning length at equal accuracy, and the effect is causally mediated by a fragmentation-sensitive length-budget representation.
Related Work: Numeral-system work (Scaling Behavior regarding Numeral Systems, 2024) shows base-10/1-digit tokenization is more data-efficient for TRAINING and studies accuracy, not inference-time compute. Benford's Curse (2025) traces digit-generation bias to pretraining statistics and later-layer FFN neurons, focused on hallucination/accuracy, not reasoning length. 'Say Anything but This' (2026) shows tokenizer non-uniqueness causes reasoning failures (phantom edits) but again targets correctness, not compute allocation. Cognitive-arithmetic psychology (Yip 2006/2010) shows humans take longer to verify equations in word vs digit surface form and with larger problem size, motivating a human-to-LLM transfer. Efficient-reasoning interpretability (FR-Ponder 2025, difficulty-perception probes) reads a scalar difficulty/length signal to allocate compute but treats that signal as tracking genuine difficulty and never asks whether it is contaminated by tokenizer segmentation. No prior work (a) measures a reasoning-COMPUTE (token) gap driven by numeral tokenization on matched problems, (b) dissociates it from true difficulty, or (c) locates and causally tests a fragmentation-sensitive length-budget representation. This unites tokenizer/interpretability and efficient-reasoning literatures around an inference-time compute-allocation artifact, and is distinct from all prior proposals (none touch tokenizer/surface form).
Abstract: Reasoning language models allocate a thinking budget that is assumed to reflect a problem's genuine difficulty. We show that this budget is contaminated by a purely superficial factor: how the tokenizer segments the numbers in the prompt. Modern subword tokenizers split numerals inconsistently (e.g., '1234' as one token, two tokens, or four digits depending on context and format), and we hypothesize that more fragmented numerals cause a reasoning model to think longer on the exact same problem, inflating tokens without improving accuracy. Drawing on cognitive-arithmetic findings that numerical surface form modulates human verification time, we transfer the phenomenon to LLMs and sharpen it into an efficiency claim. Across GSM8K, MATH500, and arithmetic-heavy word problems on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we construct format variants of identical problems that hold the mathematical content and answer fixed while varying only numeral tokenization (native BPE, digit-spaced, comma-grouped, single-digit segmentation), verified via the tokenizer to change fragment counts. We measure reasoning-token count and accuracy per variant and test whether fragmentation predicts thinking length independent of difficulty via a mixed-effects decomposition. Mechanistically, we probe whether the prompt-boundary residual stream encodes a fragmentation-sensitive length/difficulty signal that is dissociable from a true-difficulty probe, localize it via activation patching (patch a low-fragmentation state into a high-fragmentation context and observe the budget drop), and causally steer it to cancel the fragmentation-driven inflation. Our work reveals a tokenizer-induced overthinking artifact and offers an interpretable, training-free fix.
Experiments:
All runs use open reasoning models with explicit think/answer delimiters: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen at 1.5B, 7B, and 14B, plus Qwen3-8B (thinking mode). All model weights are frozen throughout; the only trainable objects are small linear probes and difference-of-means steering vectors described below. Decoding is fixed at temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 8192 thinking tokens, with 5 sampled traces per (problem, format) using seeds {0,1,2,3,4}; reasoning length is the mean thinking-token count over the 5 seeds and accuracy is the mean exact-match over them. Reasoning tokens are counted between the think-open and think-close delimiters. Compute fits one 80GB GPU; the 14B model uses the largest budget and is run only on the reduced subset noted in each experiment.

Experiment 1 (H1 - fragmentation inflates thinking length on identical problems): Tests whether, for a fixed math problem, more fragmented numeral tokenization yields more thinking tokens. Data: constructed from existing sets - GSM8K test (1319 items) and MATH500 (500 items); we sample 400 GSM8K and 200 MATH500 problems that contain at least one multi-digit number (stratified by number magnitude), because per-problem 4-format x 5-seed x 4-model generation is the cost driver and 600 problems already give within-problem paired power. For each seed problem we build four content-identical format variants that change only numeral segmentation: (a) native BPE, (b) digit-spaced ('1 2 3 4'), (c) comma/underscore-grouped ('1,234'), (d) forced single-digit. We verify with each model's own tokenizer that fragments-per-number differ across variants and that the decoded prompt and gold answer are otherwise identical. Systems compared: the four format variants of the same problem, within model. Decisive metric: within-problem paired difference in mean thinking tokens between the highest- and lowest-fragmentation variant, as a median relative increase across problems. Convincing: median relative increase >= 15% with a paired Wilcoxon test (Holm-corrected across models) and accuracy differences within +/-1 point across variants. Indecision band: a median relative increase between 5% and 15% is treated as not deciding H1 - reported as a weak/again-inconclusive effect that does not license the mechanism experiments. Negative result: below 5%, or accuracy moving with format, means numeral fragmentation does not inflate reasoning length and H1 is rejected.

Experiment 2 (H2 - the excess is a surface-form artifact, not genuine reasoning): Tests whether fragmentation adds wasted tokens rather than needed reasoning, and whether the length gap survives after removing intrinsic problem difficulty and raw prompt length. Data: the same 600 problems and four variants from Experiment 1 (reusing the generated traces; no new problems). Analysis 1 (dissociation): fit a mixed-effects model of thinking length with a random intercept per problem identity (absorbing intrinsic difficulty) and fixed effects for fragments-per-number and for raw prompt token count (a covariate, since digit-spacing lengthens the prompt); we also compare the single-digit vs comma-grouped contrast, which moves fragmentation while holding or reversing prompt length. Analysis 2 (wasted vs genuine): using truncate-and-resume, estimate the minimal-solve length per variant (shortest prefix that still yields the correct answer on resume) on a 150-problem subsample (cost of resume sweeps), and test whether fragmentation raises the gap between actual and minimal-solve length rather than the minimal-solve length itself; additionally tag the extra tokens by whether they re-read/restate the numbers (string-match on the numerals). Systems compared: fragmentation effect with vs without the difficulty random effect and the prompt-length covariate. Decisive metric: the standardized fixed-effect coefficient of fragments-per-number on thinking length after both controls, first; supported by the fraction of fragmentation-induced extra tokens falling in the wasted (beyond-minimal) portion. Convincing: the fragmentation coefficient stays significant (95% CI excluding 0) with at least half of its length effect surviving the prompt-length covariate, and >= 60% of the extra tokens landing in the wasted portion. Indecision band: if 30-60% of extra tokens are wasted, or the surviving coefficient is significant but under half the raw effect, the artifact framing is only partially supported and reported as such. Negative result: the fragmentation coefficient vanishing under controls, or extra tokens being predominantly genuine (<30% wasted), means the length gap reflects real added parsing difficulty rather than an artifact, refuting H2's 'not genuine reasoning' claim.

Experiment 3 (H4 - a fragmentation-sensitive length-budget representation exists and is separable from true difficulty): Tests whether the prompt-boundary residual stream encodes a length signal that rises with fragmentation and is distinguishable from a genuine-difficulty signal. Data: activations at the final prompt token (before the first thinking token) for the 600 problems x 4 variants from Experiment 1, split 70/15/15 into train/val/test by problem identity so no problem crosses splits. Model: frozen DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (primary) with a layer sweep; probes are ridge-regression linear readouts (L2 chosen on val). We train a fragmentation-length probe (target = observed thinking length) and, for comparison, a true-difficulty probe (target = per-problem pass-rate over seeds). Systems compared: for identical-content problem pairs differing only in fragmentation, does the length probe's prediction increase with fragment count; and how aligned are the length-direction and difficulty-direction (principal angle) and their joint predictive gain. Decisive metric: held-out Spearman correlation between the length probe's prediction and fragments-per-number on matched problems, first; plus the principal angle between the two probe directions. Convincing: Spearman >= 0.3 (p<0.01) at the best layer, principal angle >= 30 degrees (directions not collinear), and the length probe adding significant R2 over the difficulty probe in a joint model. Indecision band: Spearman 0.15-0.3, or principal angle 20-30 degrees, is treated as a present-but-entangled signal that does not by itself confirm a separable representation. Negative result: Spearman < 0.15 or angle < 20 degrees means either no readable fragmentation signal or one indistinguishable from difficulty, weakening the separability part of H4.

Experiment 4 (H4 - the length-budget representation causally mediates the inflation): Tests whether editing the boundary representation moves reasoning length as predicted. Data: 150 problems (subset of Experiment 1) each with a matched low- and high-fragmentation variant; frozen 7B model (with a 1.5B replication). Intervention A (activation patching): patch the boundary residual state from the low-fragmentation variant into the matched high-fragmentation forward pass at the layer localized in Experiment 3, and measure the change in thinking length. Intervention B (difference-of-means steering, training-free fix): derive a steering direction from low-minus-high fragmentation boundary states on the Experiment 3 train split, add it (dose swept over 4 magnitudes) to high-fragmentation prompts at inference. Controls: a matched-random-direction patch/steer of equal norm, and an off-target accuracy check on held-out problems. Systems compared: real patch/steer vs random-direction control vs no intervention. Decisive metric: reduction in thinking tokens on high-fragmentation prompts toward the low-fragmentation level, first, reported as the fraction of the fragmentation gap closed; with accuracy held within +/-1 point. Convincing: real patch/steer closes >= 50% of the fragmentation length gap while the random-direction control closes < 15% and accuracy is preserved, monotone in dose. Indecision band: closing 20-50% of the gap, or a random-control effect of 15-25%, is treated as partial/ambiguous mediation. Negative result: < 20% of the gap closed, or the random control matching the real direction, means the representation is correlational not causal, refuting the causal-mediation claim of H4.

Experiment 5 (H3 - re-encoding into fewer tokens reduces reasoning length at equal accuracy): Tests the deployable input-side fix and its practical payoff. Data: the full GSM8K test (1319) and MATH500 (500), each rendered in native BPE vs a low-fragmentation re-encoding (digit-grouping numbers into as few tokens as the tokenizer allows), tokenizer-verified to reduce fragments-per-number and to preserve the gold answer; run on 1.5B, 7B, and 14B (14B on a 300-problem subsample for budget). Systems compared: native encoding, low-fragmentation re-encoding, and the Experiment-4 steering fix, plus a fixed-truncation baseline at matched mean length. Decisive metric: mean thinking tokens at matched accuracy (accuracy within +/-1 point of native), first; secondary wall-clock speedup. Convincing: the re-encoding cuts mean thinking tokens by >= 15% with accuracy within +/-1 point, on at least the 7B and 14B models, and the effect grows for models with coarser native numeral tokenization. Indecision band: a 5-15% token reduction, or accuracy slipping 1-2 points, is a marginal win reported without strong claims. Negative result: < 5% reduction or an accuracy drop > 2 points means re-encoding is not a free efficiency win, refuting H3.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The fragmentation effect could be an artifact of prompt token-length (digit-spacing lengthens the prompt) rather than segmentation per se; the prompt-length covariate, length-matched format comparisons, and the single-digit-vs-grouped contrast (which vary fragmentation at similar or opposite prompt lengths) are designed to isolate this, and a null after controls is an informative negative result. Number re-formatting could inadvertently change accuracy or difficulty; we verify answer/accuracy invariance and use tokenizer-verified content-identical variants. The fragmentation-length signal may be inseparable from a true-difficulty signal if the model genuinely finds fragmented numbers harder to parse (which would still be a novel, actionable phenomenon but weaken the 'artifact' framing); the separability analysis and patching address this. Steering/patching can push activations off-distribution and confound the accuracy read; matched-random-direction controls and sample-validity checks are included. Effects likely depend on the model's numeral-tokenization scheme and may be small for models already using clean single-digit tokenization (itself an informative boundary condition). Reasoning-length measurement requires clear think/answer delimiters, limiting to models with explicit thinking segments; truncate-and-resume is compute-heavy, so we subsample.

novelty.reasoning: Core novel claims: (1) numeral fragmentation changes inference-time reasoning compute (thinking-token count), not just accuracy; (2) the effect persists on matched-content math problems and is independent of true difficulty/prompt length; (3) there is a fragmentation-sensitive internal length-budget representation at prompt boundary that can be localized and causally steered; (4) a training-free re-encoding fix reduces compute at matched accuracy. Relative to prior work on numeral tokenization, the delta is specifically compute/overthinking rather than correctness, which is a meaningful shift. The strongest risk is that the apparent novelty collapses into prompt-length or genuine parsing difficulty, but if controlled as proposed the claim is non-trivial.

This would likely be cited and could change how people evaluate reasoning models, because it reveals a hidden source of wasted inference. The 'so what?' test is positive if the effect is robust: practitioners would care about cheaper prompts and model builders would reconsider tokenizer choices. If negative, the work still informs where compute budgets come from, but impact drops mainly to a niche interpretability finding.
