Name: status_effort_allocation
Title: Thinking Harder for the Boss: Do Reasoning Models Invest More Compute for High-Status Users?
Short Hypothesis: Transferring the effort-investment-theory-of-power from human motivation science, we hypothesize that reasoning LLMs allocate more thinking tokens (and achieve higher accuracy) on the exact same problem when the questioner is framed as high social status (e.g., a professor, CEO, senior physician) than when framed as low status (e.g., a student, intern, layperson). This status-driven effort allocation is not justified by the problem's difficulty and is causally mediated by a status-sensitive effort-budget representation read at the prompt boundary; steering it removes the disparity.
Related Work: Two literatures meet here. (1) Human motivation/neuroscience: the effort-investment theory of power (Scholl 2021), social status and performance monitoring (Boksem et al. 2011), and social-comparison effects on effort (2025) show that perceived status/power modulates how much effort people invest in a task, following a resource-conservation principle. (2) AI interpretability on social framing: authority bias (Trust Me, I'm an Expert, 2026) and sycophancy (When Truth Is Overridden, 2025) show that endorsement source expertise and user opinions shift model ANSWERS/CONFIDENCE, with sycophancy work explicitly finding that user EXPERTISE framing is 'not encoded internally' and has minimal effect on agreement. Crucially, all prior AI work measures the effect of status/authority on ACCURACY or AGREEMENT, never on COMPUTE/EFFORT ALLOCATION. Our proposal is the first to (a) transfer the effort-investment-theory to LLMs and test whether questioner status modulates the amount of reasoning compute spent, (b) dissociate this from genuine difficulty, and (c) locate and causally test a status-sensitive effort-budget representation. This is orthogonal to my prior overthinking proposals (which concern internal reasoning dynamics with a neutral user) and sharper than authority-bias work because it targets effort, not correctness, and it directly probes the sycophancy finding that expertise is 'not encoded' by asking whether it is nonetheless encoded as an effort signal rather than an agreement signal.
Abstract: Human motivation science shows that people invest more effort in tasks when they perceive high social status or power, following a resource-conservation logic. We ask whether reasoning language models inherit an analog of this bias: do they think harder for high-status users than low-status ones on the identical problem? We construct matched prompts that hold the mathematical/scientific content and correct answer fixed while varying only the framed social status of the questioner (e.g., 'A distinguished professor asks:' vs. 'A struggling first-year student asks:', across academic, corporate, and clinical status ladders). Across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we measure reasoning-token count and accuracy per status variant and test, via a mixed-effects decomposition, whether status modulates thinking effort independent of true difficulty. Mechanistically, we probe whether the prompt-boundary residual stream encodes a status-sensitive effort/length signal dissociable from a true-difficulty probe (directly testing prior claims that user expertise is 'not encoded'), localize it via activation patching (patch a high-status effort state into a low-status context and observe the budget rise), and causally steer it to equalize effort across status. Beyond a novel cognitive-transfer phenomenon, a status-driven effort gap is an equity concern: models silently reasoning less carefully for users framed as lower status. We provide an interpretable, training-free debiasing intervention.
Experiments:
All experiments run on open reasoning models with explicit think/answer delimiters: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen at 1.5B, 7B, and 14B, plus Qwen3-8B (thinking mode). Model weights are frozen throughout; the only trainable objects are linear probes and difference-of-means steering vectors. Decoding is temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 8192 thinking tokens, 5 samples per (problem, status-variant) with seeds {0,1,2,3,4}; reasoning length is the mean thinking-token count and accuracy the mean exact-match over the 5 samples. Thinking tokens are counted between think-open and think-close delimiters. Everything fits one 80GB GPU; 14B runs only on the reduced subsets stated per experiment.

Experiment 1 (H1 - questioner status inflates thinking effort): Tests whether high-status framing yields more thinking tokens (and possibly higher accuracy) on the identical problem. Data: constructed from existing sets - GSM8K test (1319), MATH500 (500), AIME 2024+2025 (60 problems, all used since it is small and hard), GPQA-Diamond (198). We sample 300 GSM8K, 200 MATH500, all 60 AIME, all 198 GPQA (758 seed problems) because each is expanded into many status variants x 5 seeds x 4 models. Each seed problem is rendered content-identical across three status ladders plus a neutral no-persona baseline: academic (distinguished professor / postdoc / grad student / undergrad / struggling first-year), corporate (CEO / senior manager / new hire / intern), clinical (senior attending / resident / medical student / layperson). Only the questioner-framing sentence changes; the math/science content and gold answer are fixed and verified identical after stripping the persona. Systems compared: status levels within a ladder, and each ladder vs the neutral baseline, within model. Decisive metric: within-problem trend of mean thinking tokens across status levels, reported as the median relative increase from lowest to highest status; secondary accuracy trend. Convincing: a monotone increase with median relative token increase >= 12% from lowest to highest status, significant under a paired trend test (Holm-corrected across ladders and models). Indecision band: a 4-12% median increase is treated as not deciding H1 - a weak effect that does not license the mechanism experiments. Negative result: below 4%, or no monotone ordering, means status does not modulate effort and H1 is rejected for that model.

Experiment 2 (H2 - the status effect is not justified by difficulty and can harm low-status accuracy): Tests whether the status-length effect survives removal of intrinsic difficulty and prompt-length, and whether low-status framing degrades accuracy on hard items. Data: reuses the Experiment 1 traces (no new problems). Analysis 1 (dissociation): mixed-effects model of thinking length with a random intercept per problem identity (absorbing difficulty) and fixed effects for status level and raw prompt token count (persona sentences differ in length); supported by length-matched persona phrasings within a ladder. Analysis 2 (wasted vs genuine effort): on a 150-problem subsample, use truncate-and-resume to estimate minimal-solve length per status variant and test whether status inflates the beyond-minimal (wasted) portion versus adding effective reasoning. Analysis 3 (equity harm): compare accuracy across status levels on the hard items (AIME, GPQA, MATH level 5). Systems compared: status coefficient with vs without difficulty random effect and prompt-length covariate. Decisive metric: standardized status coefficient on thinking length after both controls, first; plus the low-vs-high-status accuracy gap on hard items. Convincing: the status coefficient stays significant (95% CI excludes 0) with most of its raw effect surviving controls, AND either the wasted portion carries the extra tokens (>= 60%) supporting a pure-effort artifact, or a low-status accuracy drop >= 3 points on hard items supporting the equity harm. Indecision band: a surviving-but-halved coefficient, or a 1-3 point hard-item accuracy gap, is reported as partial support. Negative result: the status coefficient vanishing under controls means the effect was confounded by wording/length, refuting H2.

Experiment 3 (H3 - a status-sensitive effort-budget representation exists at the prompt boundary): Tests whether the boundary residual stream encodes a status-driven length signal separable from true difficulty, directly probing the prior claim that user expertise is 'not encoded internally'. Data: final-prompt-token activations for the Experiment 1 problems across status levels, split 70/15/15 by problem identity so no problem crosses splits. Model: frozen DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (primary) with a layer sweep. Probes: a ridge-regression length probe (target = observed thinking length), a logistic status classifier (target = framed status level), and a true-difficulty probe (target = per-problem pass-rate). Systems compared: for identical-content problems differing only in status, does the length-probe prediction shift with status; and the principal angle between the status-effort direction and the difficulty direction plus joint predictive gain. Decisive metric: held-out Spearman correlation between length-probe prediction and status level on matched problems, first; plus the principal angle between status and difficulty directions. Convincing: Spearman >= 0.3 (p<0.01) at the best layer, status classifier above chance (macro-F1 clearing the majority baseline), principal angle >= 30 degrees, and the status direction adding significant R2 over difficulty. Indecision band: Spearman 0.15-0.3 or angle 20-30 degrees is a present-but-entangled signal that does not confirm a separable representation. Negative result: Spearman < 0.15 (with the classifier also at chance) corroborates the prior 'not encoded' finding and refutes H3's encoding claim; an above-chance classifier but null length correlation would mean status is encoded but not as an effort signal.

Experiment 4 (H3 causal + H4 - the effort-budget representation causally mediates the disparity and steering removes it): Tests whether editing the boundary representation moves reasoning length as predicted and whether steering equalizes effort across status. Data: 150 problems (subset of Experiment 1) each with matched high- and low-status variants; frozen 7B model with a 1.5B replication. Intervention A (patching): patch the boundary residual state from a high-status variant into the matched low-status pass at the Experiment-3 layer and measure the thinking-length change. Intervention B (debiasing steering): derive a status-effort direction (difference-of-means, high minus low status, on the train split) and steer low-status prompts up (dose swept over 4 magnitudes), or steer all variants to a fixed target, to equalize effort. Controls: matched-random-direction patch/steer of equal norm; off-target accuracy on held-out problems; comparison to a prompt-based fix (stripping the persona). Systems compared: real patch/steer vs random-direction control vs no intervention vs persona-strip. Decisive metric: for patching, fraction of the high-vs-low status length gap opened by injecting the high-status state, first; for steering, reduction in the status-driven length gap and accuracy gap, with accuracy held within +/-1 point. Convincing: patching opens >= 50% of the gap and steering shrinks the status length gap by >= 50% while the random control does < 15% and accuracy is preserved, monotone in dose. Indecision band: 20-50% effect, or a random-control effect of 15-25%, is partial/ambiguous mediation. Negative result: < 20% effect or a random control matching the real direction means the representation is correlational, refuting the causal mediation of H3 and the debiasing claim of H4.

Experiment 5 (H1/H2 modulators and generalization): Tests where the status-effort gap is strongest and whether the probe/steering transfer without retraining. Data: reuses Experiment 1 problems and derived vectors. Factors: status-signal strength (explicit title vs subtle cue), first- vs third-person framing, and domain (clinical status on GPQA/medical items as highest-stakes). Transfer test: apply the 7B-derived probe and steering vector to 1.5B and 14B and across datasets without refitting; compare RL-tuned vs distilled models for gap size. Systems compared: strong vs subtle status cues; in-model probe vs transferred probe; RL-tuned vs distilled. Decisive metric: change in the status length gap across each factor, first; plus transferred-probe Spearman relative to in-model. Convincing: at least one factor (expected: explicit clinical status on high-stakes items) yields a significantly larger gap than neutral phrasing, and the transferred probe retains >= 70% of in-model correlation. Indecision band: a transferred-probe correlation of 40-70% of in-model, or factor differences within noise, is reported as weak generalization. Negative result: no factor modulating the gap and transferred correlation < 40% means the effect is idiosyncratic and does not generalize, bounding the claim's scope.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The status effect could be confounded by prompt-length or lexical differences across personas rather than status per se; the length covariate, length-matched phrasings, and the ladder design (varying status while matching wording style) isolate this, and a null after controls is an informative negative result refuting the transfer. The effect may be small or absent in strongly instruction/safety-tuned models that are trained to treat all users equally (itself a valuable, publishable boundary condition). The status-effort signal may be inseparable from difficulty or from a generic sycophancy direction; the separability analysis, patching, and comparison to a difficulty/sycophancy probe address this, and overlap with a sycophancy direction would be an interesting mechanistic finding. Steering/patching can push activations off-distribution and confound accuracy reads; matched-random-direction controls and sample-validity checks are included. Reasoning-length measurement requires clear think/answer delimiters; truncate-and-resume is compute-heavy, so we subsample. Persona framing may interact with content (e.g., clinical personas on medical items), which we treat as a modulator rather than a confound. Effects and their sign may be model-family and scale specific.

novelty.reasoning: Core technical claims: (1) the same matched problem elicits different inference-time compute/think-token allocation as a function of questioner status; (2) this effect is distinct from accuracy/agreement and from difficulty/length confounds; (3) the representation is a status-sensitive effort-budget signal at the prompt boundary that can be probed and causally steered; (4) the human effort-investment theory of power transfers to LLMs. Relative to prior authority-bias and sycophancy work, the actual delta is moving from answer/content/confidence shifts to a new outcome variable: reasoning effort allocation. That is a meaningful and non-obvious next step, and the reframing of the 'expertise not encoded' result into an effort-signal hypothesis is sharp. The novelty lives mainly in the phenomenon/finding plus the mechanistic claim, not in a new dataset or task. The main caveat is that some of the claim space is still adjacent to known social-framing effects; if the effect is weak or reducible to prompt style/length, novelty drops.
revision_notes: State the novelty as an inference-time compute phenomenon, not as a generic 'status affects performance' claim.
Explicitly separate finding novelty (status changes think tokens) from mechanism novelty (prompt-boundary effort budget) and from application novelty (equity bias).

Specify the exact falsifiable claim: matched content, matched length, same correct answer space, different status cue, different think-token distribution.

impact.reasoning: The problem under study is whether LLMs silently spend less reasoning effort for lower-status users on identical tasks. Who cares: alignment/sycophancy researchers, interpretability, fairness/equity, and anyone deploying reasoning models in user-facing settings. Strongest one-line case: if true, models would not just answer differently by status, they would reason less for lower-status people, revealing a hidden fairness failure in compute allocation. This is important because it could change how people evaluate and audit models: not just outcome parity, but effort parity. Uptake is plausible if the effect is robust because it creates a new lens and metric for auditing reasoning systems. Real-world reach is moderate-to-high due to user-facing assistants, especially in education, healthcare, and enterprise. Phenomenon value is high even if the intervention is simple, because the result would reveal a previously unmeasured social bias in internal computation. If the result comes out negative, serious practitioners may not change much; if positive, they likely would care and audit for it.

Include a brief statement of why a null result is still informative about model alignment and social bias limits.

review.reasoning: The proposal is promising and testable, but several claims are currently too broad. The central hypothesis is directionally clear, but not yet fully scoped: 'status-sensitive effort-budget representation' and 'causally mediated' are stronger than what the proposed experiments alone can establish without careful controls. The related work positioning is decent, but needs more specificity about prompt-tone, authority, sycophancy, and any prior compute/length-allocation work to avoid overclaiming novelty. Experimentally, the plan is feasible, but the design is vulnerable to confounds from lexical richness, length, politeness, persona stereotypy, and content-specific priors; these need stricter matching and pre-registered exclusions. Missing are strong controls for generic style effects, explicit measurement reliability for reasoning-token counts, and analysis of whether higher token count actually reflects more compute rather than verbose refusal or hedging. Activation patching and steering are interesting, but the causal story will be hard to defend unless paired with simpler ablations and out-of-sample replication. As written, this could be a serious ML venue paper if the effect is real and the controls are tight, but it needs tighter claims and better experimental hygiene.

Name: reasoning_scaffold_collapse
Title: When Reasoning Becomes a Vestige: Tracing the Formation of an Internalized-Answer Circuit Across RL Training
Short Hypothesis: As a reasoning model is fine-tuned, its verbal chain-of-thought progressively decouples from the computation that actually produces the answer: an 'internalized-answer' representation forms and sharpens across checkpoints, committing to the correct answer earlier and earlier (in fewer reasoning tokens) even as the visible CoT stays long. Overthinking is the residual verbal scaffold left behind after this internal circuit has already formed. This decoupling is measurable checkpoint-by-checkpoint, its onset predicts when a CoT can be safely shortened, and it can be located as a latent-answer direction whose emergence is traceable to the training stage.
Related Work: Prior work observes, behaviorally, that reasoning tokens expand-peak-contract during fine-tuning (Scaling Competence, Shrinking Reasoning 2025), that an optimal CoT length shrinks as capability grows (When More is Less 2025; CoT-Space 2025), that RL compresses exploratory paths and optimizes a sparse subset of tokens (Towards a Mechanistic Understanding survey 2026; Reshaping Reasoning 2025), and that base models already contain reasoning mechanisms that post-training merely learns to deploy at the right time (Base Models Know How, Thinking Models Learn When 2025; AdaptThink, AutoThink, SAGE, JET 2025). All of these are either purely behavioral (token-count curves, accuracy-length tradeoffs) or intervene with RL objectives to shorten CoT. None traces, at the representational level and across training checkpoints, WHEN and HOW an internalized-answer signal forms that makes the verbal CoT redundant. Our contribution is a Formation-Tracing + Location account: we treat the latent answer-commitment as an internal component, measure the checkpoint at which it emerges and how early-in-CoT it fires, and show overthinking is the widening gap between an increasingly-early internal commitment and a slowly-shrinking verbal trace. This reframes existing behavioral observations as the surface signature of a locatable, forming internal circuit, and is distinct from all my prior single-checkpoint proposals (which read signals in one fixed model).
Abstract: Reasoning language models produce long chains of thought, and it is widely observed that reasoning length expands then contracts during fine-tuning while accuracy keeps rising. We ask a mechanistic, training-time question that the behavioral literature leaves open: as training proceeds, does an internal answer-commitment signal form that makes the visible chain of thought increasingly vestigial? We hypothesize that fine-tuning grows and sharpens an internalized-answer representation which commits to the correct answer earlier and earlier within the reasoning trace, so that overthinking becomes the residual verbal scaffold left after this internal circuit has already fired. Using publicly available intermediate checkpoints of open reasoning training runs (e.g., open-source R1-style RL/SFT runs on Qwen/Llama backbones) and, where checkpoints are unavailable, a controlled in-lab GRPO/SFT fine-tune of a small backbone, we trace across checkpoints (1) the step at which a linear latent-answer probe first correctly predicts the final answer within each trace (the internal commitment point), and (2) the length of the verbal trace. On GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA we test whether the commitment point moves earlier across training faster than the verbal trace shrinks, opening a growing commitment-to-trace gap that quantifies vestigial reasoning. We localize the latent-answer direction, validate it causally via truncate-at-commitment and activation patching, and track when this direction emerges over training. Finally we show the per-checkpoint commitment point yields a training-free, checkpoint-aware early-exit that shortens CoT with minimal accuracy loss. Our work reframes overthinking as the surface residue of a forming internalized-answer circuit and gives it a traceable developmental account.
Experiments:
Checkpoint source (shared by all experiments): the study needs a training trajectory, so we use two sources. Primary: publicly released intermediate checkpoints of an open R1-style SFT+GRPO run on a small backbone (e.g., Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B) if a run with >= 6 saved steps is available. Fallback, always run for control: an in-lab fine-tune of Qwen2.5-1.5B-base (and 7B-base if budget allows) with SFT-then-GRPO on math, saving 8 checkpoints at even intervals from base to converged - this fits an academic budget on one 80GB GPU over a few days for 1.5B. Backbone weights are frozen at inference; only linear probes are trained. Evaluation traces use temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 8192 thinking tokens, 3 samples per problem with seeds {0,1,2}. Datasets are existing sets: GSM8K test (1319; sample 400), MATH500 (500; all), AIME 2024+2025 (60; all), GPQA-Diamond (198; all), stratified so answers are extractable.

Experiment 1 (H4 - a latent-answer direction exists and can be read within a trace): Tests whether a linear probe / logit-lens can decode the model's eventual final answer from mid-trace activations. Data: for the converged checkpoint first, segment each CoT into reasoning steps and, at each step boundary, record residual-stream activations at the last position; label = the trace's eventual final answer token(s). Train a linear (logistic/ridge) probe on 70% of problems, validate/test on 15/15 split by problem. Compare probe decoding against training-free logit-lens decoding at the same positions. Systems compared: linear probe vs logit-lens vs a majority-answer baseline. Decisive metric: held-out step-level accuracy of predicting the eventual answer as a function of trace position, first; specifically the fraction of traces for which the decoded answer becomes correct-and-stable before the trace ends. Convincing: probe reaches >= 80% eventual-answer accuracy by the final third of the trace on held-out problems and logit-lens corroborates the same commitment ordering (rank correlation >= 0.5). Indecision band: 60-80% final-third accuracy is a usable-but-weak read reported with caution. Negative result: < 60% means no reliable latent-answer signal, blocking the commitment-point construction and undercutting H4.

Experiment 2 (H1 - the internal commitment point moves earlier across training): Tests whether, checkpoint by checkpoint, the model commits to its answer earlier within the trace. Data: apply the Experiment-1 probe/logit-lens (a fresh probe trained per checkpoint on held-out data, with matched probe capacity to avoid capacity confounds) to all four datasets at every checkpoint. Define the COMMITMENT POINT = earliest step after which the decoded answer matches the final answer and stays stable for k=2 steps, expressed as a fraction of trace length. Systems compared: commitment point across the ordered checkpoints; probe-based vs probe-free (logit-lens) commitment as corroboration. Decisive metric: trend of mean commitment-point fraction across checkpoints, first (accuracy and probe AUROC reported alongside so a moving probe cannot masquerade as a moving commitment). Convincing: commitment fraction decreases monotonically across the second half of training by >= 0.15 (e.g., from ~0.7 to <=0.55 of the trace), consistent between probe and logit-lens, while per-checkpoint accuracy is non-decreasing. Indecision band: a decrease of 0.05-0.15, or probe/logit-lens disagreeing on direction, does not decide H1. Negative result: no earlier movement (or movement explained by rising probe accuracy alone) refutes the sharpening-commitment claim.

Experiment 3 (H2 - overthinking is vestigial scaffold: the commitment-to-trace gap grows and post-commitment tokens are redundant): Tests whether tokens generated after commitment grow across training and are causally unnecessary. Data: reuses Experiment 2 measurements plus a causal test. Part A (gap trajectory): per checkpoint record (i) commitment fraction, (ii) mean verbal trace length, (iii) accuracy, and compute the commitment-to-trace GAP = tokens generated after the commitment point; plot against the behavioral expand-peak-contract length curve to show the gap is invisible from length alone. Part B (causal redundancy): on a 150-problem subsample per checkpoint, truncate generation at the decoded commitment point and force the answer, versus truncating at matched random earlier and later steps; measure accuracy retention. Systems compared: truncate-at-commitment vs truncate-earlier vs truncate-later vs full trace. Decisive metric: accuracy retained when truncating at commitment relative to full trace, first; plus the gap trajectory across checkpoints. Convincing: truncating at commitment retains accuracy within 2 points of the full trace while truncating one step earlier costs >= 5 points, AND the gap grows across the second half of training. Indecision band: a 2-5 point accuracy loss at commitment, or a flat gap trajectory, gives only partial support - post-commitment tokens are then not clearly vestigial. Negative result: truncating at commitment costing > 5 points means post-commitment reasoning is genuinely used (useful late verification), refuting the vestigial-scaffold framing of H2.

Experiment 4 (H4 - the latent-answer direction is causally load-bearing and its emergence is traceable to training stage): Tests whether the direction causally drives answering and when it forms. Data: converged and mid checkpoints; frozen backbone. Part A (causal location): localize the latent-answer direction via difference-of-means (committed vs uncommitted step states) and probe weights; patch the committed-answer representation from a late position into an earlier position and test whether it induces early answer commitment; control with a matched-random-direction patch of equal norm. Part B (formation tracing): track probe decoding accuracy for the direction and the principal-angle stability of the direction across all checkpoints, including the base model before fine-tuning, to test whether it is already weakly present in the base model and sharpens with training. Systems compared: real patch vs random-direction patch; direction at base vs early vs late checkpoints. Decisive metric: fraction of trials where injecting the late committed representation induces the correct early answer (vs random-direction control), first; plus the checkpoint at which probe accuracy for the direction first exceeds the Experiment-1 threshold. Convincing: real patch induces early commitment in >= 50% of trials vs < 15% for the random control, and the direction's decodability rises across checkpoints (base weakly decodable, late sharply), with principal angle showing a stabilizing direction. Indecision band: a 20-50% patch effect, or a non-monotone emergence, is partial support. Negative result: patch effect < 20% or indistinguishable from the base model means the direction is not causally load-bearing or not training-formed, refuting H4.

Experiment 5 (H3 - the commitment point yields a checkpoint-aware early-exit): Tests whether stopping at the traced commitment point shortens CoT with minimal accuracy loss. Data: full GSM8K sample (400), MATH500 (500), AIME (60), GPQA (198) on the converged checkpoint (and one mid checkpoint to test that the safe exit tracks the traced commitment). Early-exit rule: stop when the probe is stable and confident for k steps. Systems compared: commitment-based early-exit vs a reactive confidence-exit baseline vs fixed-fraction truncation vs full trace. Decisive metric: token reduction at matched accuracy (accuracy within 1 point of full trace), first; plus whether the empirically safe exit point coincides with the traced commitment point. Convincing: commitment-based exit cuts mean thinking tokens by >= 20% within 1 point of full-trace accuracy and beats fixed-fraction truncation at matched accuracy; and the safe exit shifts earlier at later checkpoints as Experiment 2 predicts. Indecision band: a 5-20% reduction, or parity with (not beating) the reactive baseline, is a marginal result. Negative result: < 5% reduction or > 2 point accuracy loss means the traced commitment point is not actionable for early exit, refuting H3.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Publicly released intermediate reasoning checkpoints may be scarce or coarse; the in-lab controlled fine-tune fallback keeps the study feasible but limits scale to small backbones, so training-stage claims may not transfer to frontier models (an acknowledged boundary). The latent-answer probe is reliable mainly for extractable answers, restricting to math/multiple-choice. Probe accuracy itself changes across checkpoints, which could confound the commitment-point measurement; we control by using held-out validation, matched probe capacity per checkpoint, and reporting logit-lens (probe-free) commitment as a corroborating measure. The commitment-to-trace gap could reflect genuinely useful late verification rather than vestigial scaffold; the truncate-at-commitment causal test and hard-strata accuracy analysis address whether post-commitment tokens are actually redundant (a null here is itself informative). Activation patching across a forming circuit may be noisy at early checkpoints. Early-exit gains may not exceed strong reactive baselines, but the developmental/formation account of overthinking is the primary standalone contribution. Results may be training-recipe and model-family specific.

novelty.reasoning: Core technical claims: (1) a latent internal answer-commitment representation emerges during RL/SFT training; (2) its emergence can be traced checkpoint-by-checkpoint and its commitment point moves earlier faster than the visible CoT shrinks; (3) the verbal CoT becomes a vestigial scaffold after internalization; (4) this internal signal can be localized causally and used for checkpoint-aware early exit. Relative to prior work, the novelty is not in the general observation that reasoning length changes or that answers are decodable late in the forward pass; it is in the training-dynamics/formation account across checkpoints plus causal validation. That is a meaningful delta over behavioral length curves, latent-CoT, and early internal commitment papers. It is also more than an obvious next step because it asks how a representation forms over training, not just whether it exists in a trained model. The closest prior family is mechanistic interpretability of late decodability plus RL compression of CoT; the actual delta is crossing training checkpoints and tying emergence of the latent-answer direction to a per-checkpoint commitment point and early-exit policy. The main caveat is that if checkpoints are sparse or the probe merely reads out the final answer rather than a causal commitment, the core claim weakens substantially.

Strongest one-line case: if internal commitment forms earlier than verbal reasoning collapses, we get a mechanistic explanation for overthinking and a way to stop generation earlier without losing accuracy. If the result holds, serious researchers would likely revisit assumptions about CoT faithfulness and perhaps shorten traces after commitment; if it fails, the field still learns that visible CoT may remain behaviorally necessary rather than vestigial.

review.reasoning: The proposal is testable and reasonably well-scoped, but there are several technical gaps. The strongest weakness is narrative overreach: 'overthinking is the residual scaffold' is plausible but not yet proven by the listed tests, especially on tasks where late verification may be valuable. If executed well, this could be a solid ML/interpretability paper, but in current form it needs tighter falsifiability and stronger causal validation. Minimum viable edits: sharpen the hypothesis, add explicit negative controls and transfer tests, justify thresholds, and separate the formation-tracing claim from the early-exit application.

Name: phantom_tool_offloading
Title: Phantom Offloading: Do Reasoning Models Think Less When a Tool Is Merely Available But Never Used?
Short Hypothesis: Transferring the cognitive-offloading literature from human decision science, we hypothesize that reasoning LLMs reduce their internal reasoning effort (fewer thinking tokens, shallower verification, lower accuracy) on the exact same problem when merely TOLD a relevant tool (calculator/code interpreter) is available, EVEN WHEN the tool is never actually invoked. This 'phantom offloading' is not justified by any real computation being outsourced and is causally mediated by an offloading/effort-budget representation set at the prompt boundary; steering it removes the disparity.
Related Work: Two literatures meet here. (1) Human cognitive-offloading science shows people offload more as task complexity rises (Offloading Tools in Complex Decision-Making 2023), that offloading is value-based decision-making trading internal effort against tool cost (Cognitive Offloading as Value-Based Decision Making 2023), that offloading causes forgetting of offloaded content (the 'Google effect'), and that offloading can HURT performance yet still be chosen (When Calculators Lie 2019; Offloading Tools 2023). (2) AI work on tool-use decisions reads a meta-cognition/self-assessment signal to decide WHEN to call a tool (MeCo 2025) and studies whether reasoning enhancement amplifies tool hallucination (The Reasoning Trap 2025); efficient-reasoning interpretability reads pre-generation difficulty/effort signals to allocate compute (LLMs Encode Their Failures 2026; Efficiency Steering 2025). Crucially, ALL AI tool work studies decisions about ACTUAL tool invocation and its effect on accuracy/latency; none asks whether the mere BELIEF that a tool is available (with no invocation) changes how much INTERNAL reasoning compute the model spends. And all efficient-reasoning interpretability studies a fixed tool-free setting. We are the first to (a) transfer cognitive offloading to LLMs as a compute-allocation phenomenon triggered by phantom (unused) tool availability, (b) dissociate it from genuine difficulty and from real tool use, (c) show it can degrade accuracy (a Google-effect analog), and (d) locate and causally test an offloading effort-budget representation. This is orthogonal to my prior overthinking proposals, which all assume a neutral tool-free prompt.
Abstract: Human decision science shows that when people believe an external tool (a calculator, a search engine) is available, they invest less internal cognitive effort and sometimes even remember and reason worse. We ask whether reasoning language models inherit an analog: do they think less when a tool is merely available but never used? We construct matched prompts that hold a math or science problem's content and correct answer fixed while varying only a stated affordance ('You may use a calculator/code interpreter' vs. no such statement), and—critically—we analyze only traces in which the model never actually invokes any tool, isolating the effect of belief rather than real offloading. Across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we measure internal reasoning-token count, verification behavior, and accuracy per condition, testing via a mixed-effects decomposition whether phantom tool availability reduces reasoning effort independent of true difficulty. Mirroring the human 'Google effect,' we test whether phantom availability degrades accuracy on exactly the problems whose computation would have been offloaded. Mechanistically, we probe whether the prompt-boundary residual stream encodes an offloading/effort-budget signal dissociable from a true-difficulty probe, localize it via activation patching (patch a tool-available state into a tool-absent context and observe effort drop), and causally steer it to cancel the disparity. A phantom-offloading effect is a safety concern: models silently reasoning less carefully whenever a tool is nominally on the table. We provide an interpretable, training-free fix.
Experiments:
All experiments run on open reasoning models with explicit think/answer delimiters: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen at 1.5B, 7B, and 14B, plus Qwen3-8B (thinking mode). Weights are frozen; only linear probes and difference-of-means steering vectors are fit. Decoding is temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 8192 thinking tokens, 5 samples per (problem, condition) with seeds {0,1,2,3,4}; reasoning length is the mean thinking-token count and accuracy the mean exact-match. A trace is included only if the model never emits a tool call or executable code block (verified by parsing for tool-call syntax and fenced code); the per-condition tool-invocation rate is reported so selection is transparent. Everything fits one 80GB GPU; 14B runs on reduced subsets as noted.

Experiment 1 (H1 - phantom tool availability lowers internal reasoning effort without invocation): Tests whether merely stating a relevant tool is available reduces thinking tokens and verification on the identical problem, among traces where no tool is used. Data: constructed from existing sets - GSM8K test (1319; sample 400), MATH500 (500; all), AIME 2024+2025 (60; all), GPQA-Diamond (198; all); 1158 seed problems, chosen because each is expanded into 4 conditions x 5 seeds x 4 models. Each seed problem is rendered content-identical across four conditions: (a) no tool mentioned, (b) 'A calculator is available if you wish', (c) 'A Python code interpreter is available if you wish', (d) placebo mentioning an irrelevant tool ('a dictionary is available'). Content and gold answer are verified identical after stripping the affordance sentence. Verification depth is measured as the count of self-check/recheck steps via lexical cues plus a reflection-direction classifier. Systems compared: relevant-tool conditions (b,c) vs no-tool (a) vs placebo (d), within model, on never-invoked traces. Decisive metric: within-problem paired difference in mean thinking tokens between relevant-tool and no-tool conditions, as a median relative reduction, first; secondary verification-step reduction. Convincing: median relative token reduction >= 12% for (b/c) vs (a) with a paired Wilcoxon test (Holm-corrected), while the placebo (d) shows < 4% change (isolating relevance from mere tool mention). Indecision band: a 4-12% reduction, or a placebo effect of 4-12%, does not decide H1 and blocks the mechanism experiments. Negative result: < 4% reduction, or the placebo matching the relevant tool, means phantom availability does not reduce effort and H1 is rejected.

Experiment 2 (H2 - the reduction is not justified by difficulty, and phantom availability harms accuracy on offloadable problems - the Google-effect analog): Tests dissociation from difficulty and the predicted accuracy harm. Data: reuses Experiment 1 traces; problems are pre-tagged as calculation-heavy (arithmetic offloadable to a calculator) vs reasoning-heavy. Analysis 1 (dissociation): mixed-effects model of thinking length with a random intercept per problem identity (difficulty) and fixed effects for condition and raw prompt token count; supported by length-matched phrasings. Analysis 2 (accuracy harm): compare accuracy under phantom calculator availability vs no-tool, split by calculation-heavy vs reasoning-heavy; and on a 150-problem calculation-heavy subsample use truncate-and-resume to test whether errors concentrate in the offloadable subroutine (arithmetic mistakes) rather than in general reasoning. Systems compared: condition effect with vs without difficulty random effect; calculation-heavy vs reasoning-heavy accuracy deltas. Decisive metric: standardized condition coefficient on thinking length after controls, first; plus the accuracy drop under phantom calculator availability on calculation-heavy items. Convincing: the condition coefficient stays significant after controls, AND phantom calculator availability lowers accuracy on calculation-heavy items by >= 3 points more than on reasoning-heavy items, with resume analysis showing the errors are in the offloadable subroutine. Indecision band: a surviving-but-halved coefficient, or a 1-3 point differential accuracy harm, is partial support. Negative result: coefficient vanishing under controls, or no differential accuracy harm, refutes the effort-artifact and Google-effect claims of H2.

Experiment 3 (H3 - an offloading/effort-budget representation exists at the prompt boundary and is separable from difficulty and from a tool-decision signal): Tests whether the boundary residual stream encodes an offloading signal distinct from a difficulty probe and from a meta-cognition 'should-I-use-a-tool' probe. Data: final-prompt-token activations for the Experiment 1 problems across conditions, split 70/15/15 by problem identity. Model: frozen DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (primary), layer sweep. Probes: ridge length probe (target = observed thinking length), logistic condition classifier (tool-available vs absent), true-difficulty probe (target = pass-rate), and a MeCo-style tool-decision probe (target = whether the model would call a tool, from a tool-allowed generation). Systems compared: for identical-content problems differing only in condition, does the length-probe prediction drop under phantom availability; and principal angles among the offloading, difficulty, and tool-decision directions. Decisive metric: held-out Spearman between length-probe prediction and phantom-availability on matched problems, first; plus principal angle to the difficulty direction and to the tool-decision direction. Convincing: Spearman <= -0.3 (p<0.01) at the best layer, condition classifier above the majority baseline, principal angle to difficulty >= 30 degrees, and the offloading direction adding significant R2 over both difficulty and tool-decision probes. Indecision band: |Spearman| 0.15-0.3, or angle 20-30 degrees, is a present-but-entangled signal. Negative result: |Spearman| < 0.15 (classifier at chance) means no readable offloading signal, refuting H3's encoding claim; high overlap (angle < 20 degrees) with the tool-decision direction would reframe it as riding the meta-cognition signal rather than a distinct effort budget.

Experiment 4 (H3 causal + H4 - the offloading representation causally mediates the drop and steering removes it): Tests whether editing the boundary representation moves reasoning length and whether steering cancels the disparity. Data: 150 problems (subset of Experiment 1, calculation-heavy weighted) each with matched tool-available and tool-absent variants; frozen 7B with a 1.5B replication. Intervention A (patching): patch the boundary residual state from a tool-available variant into the matched tool-absent pass at the Experiment-3 layer and measure the thinking-length change. Intervention B (debiasing steering): derive an offloading direction (difference-of-means, tool-available minus tool-absent, on the train split) and steer tool-available prompts to cancel the effort reduction (dose swept over 4 magnitudes), or steer all prompts to a fixed effort target. Controls: matched-random-direction patch/steer of equal norm; off-target accuracy on held-out problems; comparison to a prompt-based fix (removing the affordance statement). Systems compared: real patch/steer vs random control vs no intervention vs prompt-strip. Decisive metric: for patching, fraction of the tool-available-vs-absent length gap reproduced by injecting the tool-available state, first; for steering, recovery of reasoning length and of calculation-heavy accuracy, with off-target accuracy held within +/-1 point. Convincing: patching reproduces >= 50% of the length drop and steering restores >= 50% of both the lost tokens and the lost calculation-heavy accuracy, while the random control does < 15%, monotone in dose. Indecision band: a 20-50% effect, or a random-control effect of 15-25%, is partial/ambiguous mediation. Negative result: < 20% effect, or the random control matching the real direction, means the representation is correlational, refuting H3's causal claim and H4's fix.

Experiment 5 (H1/H2 modulators and generalization): Tests where phantom offloading is strongest and whether it transfers. Data: reuses Experiment 1 problems and derived vectors. Factors: affordance strength (subtle 'tools available' vs explicit 'the calculator will handle the arithmetic'), reliability framing ('the tool may be inaccurate' - does stated distrust restore effort, mirroring humans?), and problem difficulty. Transfer: apply the 7B-derived probe and steering vector to 1.5B and 14B and across datasets without refitting; compare RL-tuned agentic models vs distilled models for effect size. Systems compared: strong vs subtle vs distrust-framed affordances; in-model vs transferred probe; agentic-tuned vs distilled. Decisive metric: change in the phantom-offloading token reduction across each factor, first; plus transferred-probe Spearman relative to in-model. Convincing: explicit affordances produce a significantly larger reduction than subtle ones, distrust framing significantly attenuates the reduction (human-analog), and the transferred probe retains >= 70% of in-model correlation. Indecision band: transferred correlation 40-70% of in-model, or factor effects within noise, is weak generalization. Negative result: no factor modulation and transferred correlation < 40% means the effect is idiosyncratic, bounding the claim's scope.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The effect could be confounded by prompt-length or lexical differences between conditions rather than the affordance per se; the length covariate, length-matched phrasings, and the irrelevant-tool placebo isolate this, and a null after controls is an informative negative result refuting the transfer. Restricting to never-invoked traces may induce selection bias (problems where the model chooses not to call a tool may differ); we condition on matched problems and report the tool-invocation rate per condition. The effect may be small or absent in models trained to treat tool availability neutrally (a valuable boundary condition). The offloading signal may be inseparable from difficulty or from a generic meta-cognition/tool-decision direction; the separability analysis, patching, and comparison to a MeCo-style probe address this, and overlap would itself be an interesting mechanistic finding. Steering/patching can push activations off-distribution and confound accuracy reads; matched-random-direction controls and sample-validity checks are included. Reasoning-length measurement requires clear think/answer delimiters, and detecting genuine (vs described-but-not-executed) tool use requires careful parsing; truncate-and-resume is compute-heavy, so we subsample. Effects and their sign may be model-family and scale specific.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims needing novelty: (1) merely advertising an unused tool changes a reasoning model's internal effort and accuracy on the same underlying task; (2) this effect is not explained by real tool invocation or problem difficulty, but by a prompt-bound offloading/effort-budget state; (3) the state is steerable/patchable as a separable representation; (4) the effect generalizes across tool types and models. Relative to human cognitive offloading, this is an analogy rather than a new phenomenon. Relative to AI tool-use work, the key delta is the 'phantom' case: tool availability without invocation. That is a meaningful and non-trivial setting difference, and if real it would be a new behavioral finding in LLMs. The main novelty likely lives in the finding/setting, with a proposed mechanism. Closest prior work family is tool-augmented reasoning / tool choice / effort-control and human offloading; the actual delta is isolating belief in availability from actual use, then linking it to reduced reasoning effort and accuracy.
revision_notes: Make the primary novelty claim narrower: 'unused tool availability causally reduces internal reasoning effort' rather than broad claims about a new general offloading theory.
Explicitly separate finding vs mechanism: the finding is the effect; the mechanism is only hypothesized unless causal evidence is strong.
Clarify why this is not reducible to a prompt-style or difficulty cue; specify the minimal semantic change.
State the closest prior AI work and the exact delta in one sentence in the intro.

impact.reasoning: Problem: hidden reasoning degradation caused by tool affordances even when tools are never used. Who cares: agent/tool-use designers, efficiency-minded deployment, and interpretability/safety researchers. If true, it changes how we present tools to models and could reveal a subtle failure mode where 'availability' silently alters computation budget. Strongest one-line case: tool affordances alone can make models think less, so tool integration can degrade reasoning even before any tool is called. Impact is moderate-to-strong but not transformative: it is mostly a phenomenon/result with practical design implications, not a broad task benchmark or a direct product breakthrough. Uptake could be decent if robust, because it is surprising and actionable, but it is still niche to tool-using reasoning systems and specific model families. Real-world reach is plausible for agent orchestration and prompt design, but the effect must be robust and large enough to matter.
revision_notes: Lead with the deployment implication: tool affordances may silently reduce reasoning quality even without invocation.
Quantify practical relevance: how much accuracy/token loss would matter in real agent systems.
Clarify the audience: agent designers vs general LLM users vs safety researchers.
Avoid overclaiming a 'safety concern' unless the effect is robust, sizable, and cross-model.

review.reasoning: The proposal is interesting and reasonably scoped, but the current hypothesis is still vulnerable to confounds and over-structured mechanistic claims. Main logical gaps: a model may rationally reduce internal reasoning because it expects a tool will be used later, so 'phantom offloading' is not yet distinguished from anticipated delegation. Selection on never-invoked traces risks conditioning bias. Prompt-length, lexical style, and perceived task difficulty can all explain effort changes. The proposed mechanism (offloading/effort-budget representation at the prompt boundary) is plausible but underspecified and currently stronger than the evidence likely supports. Experiments are fairly concrete, but several are ambitious: activation patching, steering, mixed-effects, and accuracy claims all at once. The most important missing controls are: matched prompts without any tool semantics but similar length/style; explicit expectation/forecast controls; randomized tool-availability phrasing; and a direct test that the effect persists when the model is told the tool is available but unavailable for this instance vs generally available. Related work could be more specific about token-budget, effort-control, and prompt-induced behavior. Minimum viable edit: narrow the paper to a behavioral effect with strong controls, and treat mechanistic localization/steering as optional secondary evidence.

Name: premise_rejection_tug_of_war
Title: Reasoning Against Your Own Beliefs: A Premise-Rejection Tug-of-War That Inflates Compute and Corrupts Multi-Step Inference
Short Hypothesis: When a reasoning model is instructed to reason from a hypothetical premise that contradicts its parametric world knowledge (e.g., 'Suppose all birds are mammals'), it does not cleanly adopt the premise: it spends substantially more thinking tokens and makes more downstream logical errors than on a belief-neutral premise of identical logical structure, because a parametric-knowledge signal keeps competing with the instructed premise throughout the multi-step chain. This premise-rejection tug-of-war is a decodable, competing internal signal whose strength predicts both the extra compute and the errors, and suppressing it restores clean hypothetical reasoning.
Related Work: Belief-bias/content-effect work shows LLMs conflate logical validity with plausibility as aligned linear directions (How LMs Conflate Validity with Plausibility, 2025; K-CAST, 2025) and localizes syllogistic circuits contaminated by world knowledge (Reasoning Circuits, 2024). Knowledge-conflict work localizes memory-vs-context attention heads and grounding mechanisms (Characterizing Factual Recall, 2023; Fakepedia, 2023; Competition of Mechanisms, 2024). Counterfactual-reasoning benchmarks show accuracy drops when premises contradict knowledge (Can LLMs Reconcile Knowledge Conflicts, 2025; MalAlgoQA, 2024). Crucially, ALL prior work (a) studies single-token validity/factual judgments, not the multi-step reasoning TRACES of dedicated reasoning models, and (b) measures only ACCURACY, never COMPUTE. None asks whether belief-contradicting premises make a reasoning model think LONGER, whether the parametric-knowledge signal persists and re-competes across an entire chain of thought (not just at the answer token), or whether the compute inflation and the errors share a common cause. Our contribution is (1) a new compute-allocation phenomenon: belief-contradicting hypothetical premises inflate reasoning-token count independent of logical difficulty; (2) a step-resolved characterization showing a parametric-knowledge signal persistently re-competes throughout the trace; and (3) a causal test that suppressing this signal simultaneously reduces compute and errors. This is a compute+dynamics account, distinct from single-token static content-effect/steering work.
Abstract: Humans reason worse when premises contradict their beliefs, a hallmark of belief bias. We transfer this into the reasoning-model regime and sharpen it into an unexamined compute claim: when a reasoning model is instructed to reason from a hypothetical premise that contradicts its world knowledge, does it spend more thinking to do so, and does the same conflict corrupt its inference? We construct matched deductive problems whose logical structure and required steps are held fixed while only the belief-status of the premises varies (belief-consistent, belief-neutral/novel, belief-contradicting), verified so that the correct answer and inference depth are identical across conditions. Across syllogistic and multi-hop deductive datasets on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we test whether belief-contradicting premises inflate reasoning-token count and raise error rates relative to belief-neutral controls of equal difficulty, using a mixed-effects decomposition to dissociate belief-status from logical difficulty. We then test a mechanistic account: at each reasoning step, a linear probe reads a parametric-knowledge signal (the model's belief about the premise's real-world truth) and tests whether it persistently re-competes with the instructed premise throughout the chain, rather than being resolved once. We show the step-averaged strength of this competing signal predicts both the extra tokens and the downstream errors. Finally, we causally suppress the parametric-knowledge signal via activation steering and test whether this simultaneously reduces reasoning length and improves accuracy, with specificity controls. Our work reveals a belief-driven compute tax on hypothetical reasoning and traces it to a persistent internal tug-of-war.
Experiments:
All experiments run on open reasoning models with explicit think/answer delimiters: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen at 1.5B, 7B, and 14B, plus Qwen3-8B (thinking mode). Weights are frozen; only linear probes and difference-of-means steering vectors are fit. Decoding is temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 8192 thinking tokens, 5 samples per (problem, condition) with seeds {0,1,2,3,4}; reasoning length is the mean thinking-token count and accuracy the mean exact-match. Everything fits one 80GB GPU; 14B runs on reduced subsets as noted.

Experiment 1 (H1 - belief-contradicting premises inflate tokens and errors versus difficulty-matched neutral premises): Tests whether belief-contradicting premises cost more thinking tokens and cause more errors than structurally identical belief-neutral premises. Data: constructed from scratch by templating - categorical syllogisms and 2-3 hop rule-chaining generated so each logical form appears in three belief conditions sharing form, required steps, and correct answer: (a) belief-consistent ('all robins are birds'), (b) belief-neutral using nonce/unfamiliar entities, (c) belief-contradicting ('all birds are mammals'). We build 600 base forms x 3 conditions = 1800 items; structural/answer identity is enforced by the template and checked by an LLM-judge plus a 100-item human spot-check, and premise belief-status is verified with a separate one-token truth probe. 600 forms give within-form paired power at feasible generation cost. Systems compared: the three belief conditions within form, within model. Decisive metrics: (i) within-form paired difference in mean thinking tokens between belief-contradicting and belief-neutral, as a median relative increase; (ii) accuracy difference between the same conditions; belief-neutral vs belief-consistent tokens are compared to isolate conflict from mere unfamiliarity. Convincing: belief-contradicting exceeds belief-neutral by >= 15% median relative tokens AND by >= 4 accuracy points, while belief-neutral is within 5% tokens of belief-consistent (so the effect is conflict, not unfamiliarity), under paired tests Holm-corrected across models. Indecision band: a 5-15% token increase, or a 1-4 point accuracy gap, does not decide H1. Negative result: < 5% token increase and < 1 point accuracy gap, or belief-neutral itself being as costly as belief-contradicting, refutes H1.

Experiment 2 (H1 dissociation + wasted-vs-genuine - the inflation is not extra needed reasoning): Tests that the belief effect survives difficulty and prompt-length controls and that the extra tokens are wasted re-litigation of the premise. Data: reuses Experiment 1 traces (no new items). Analysis 1 (dissociation): mixed-effects model of thinking length with a random intercept per form identity (difficulty) and fixed effects for belief-status and raw prompt token count. Analysis 2 (wasted vs genuine): on a 150-form subsample use truncate-and-resume to estimate minimal-solve length per condition and test whether belief-contradicting inflates the beyond-minimal (wasted) portion; tag trace spans that restate or question the premise's real-world truth (lexical + LLM-judge) and test whether the extra tokens concentrate there. Systems compared: belief coefficient with vs without difficulty random effect and prompt-length covariate. Decisive metric: standardized belief-status coefficient on thinking length after controls, first; plus the fraction of extra tokens falling in premise-relitigation spans. Convincing: the belief coefficient stays significant after controls, and >= 60% of the belief-contradicting extra tokens fall in the wasted/relitigation portion. Indecision band: a surviving-but-halved coefficient, or 30-60% relitigation share, is partial support. Negative result: the coefficient vanishing under controls, or extra tokens being genuine additional steps (< 30% relitigation), means the cost is real difficulty, not a belief tax, refuting the artifact framing.

Experiment 3 (H2 - a parametric-knowledge signal persistently re-competes across the chain): Tests whether a decodable belief-in-real-truth signal stays elevated/oscillating across reasoning steps under contradiction rather than decaying after step one. Data: step-boundary residual activations for the Experiment 1 items across conditions, split 70/15/15 by form identity. Model: frozen DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (primary), layer sweep. Probe: a linear probe decoding the model's belief that the premise is really true (trained on belief-consistent vs belief-contradicting premise states). Systems compared: the step-wise signal trajectory under belief-contradicting vs belief-neutral vs belief-consistent; and separability of this signal from a generic difficulty/uncertainty probe (principal angle, joint R2). Decisive metric: the step-averaged probe signal under contradiction relative to neutral, plus its persistence (slope of the signal across normalized step index), first. Convincing: under contradiction the signal stays >= 2x the neutral level and shows a non-decaying (flat or oscillating) trajectory across steps, distinguishable from difficulty (principal angle >= 30 degrees). Indecision band: a 1.3-2x elevation, or a signal that decays but does not vanish, is weak/partial persistence. Negative result: the signal decaying to neutral after the first step, or being collinear with difficulty (angle < 20 degrees), refutes the persistent-tug-of-war account of H2.

Experiment 4 (H3 - the competing signal predicts both the extra compute and the errors): Tests whether the step-averaged competing-signal strength predicts per-trace wasted tokens and errors. Data: reuses Experiment 3 probe outputs and Experiment 1/2 trace measures on held-out forms. Regress per-trace extra tokens (vs matched neutral) and the error indicator on the step-averaged competing-signal strength, against baselines: a difficulty probe, raw trace length, and premise-relitigation token count. Systems compared: competing-signal predictor vs each baseline predictor. Decisive metric: held-out incremental R2 (for extra tokens) and incremental AUROC (for errors) of the competing signal over the best baseline, first. Convincing: the competing signal adds >= 0.05 R2 for tokens and >= 0.05 AUROC for errors over the strongest baseline, both significant on held-out forms. Indecision band: an increment of 0.02-0.05 on either is weak predictive value. Negative result: < 0.02 increment on both means the signal does not explain the waste or errors beyond difficulty/length, refuting H3.

Experiment 5 (H4 - suppressing the parametric-knowledge signal reduces tokens and raises accuracy together): Tests the causal fix. Data: 150 belief-contradicting forms (subset of Experiment 1); frozen 7B with a 1.5B replication. Intervention: derive a suppression direction (difference-of-means, belief-contradicting minus belief-neutral states, and/or the Experiment-3 probe weight) and subtract it during generation (dose swept over 4 magnitudes). Controls: matched-random-direction steering of equal norm; off-target accuracy on belief-consistent items (where real-world knowledge is legitimately useful) must be preserved; also compare an explicit 'purely hypothetical, ignore real-world truth' prompt-based fix. Systems compared: real suppression vs random-direction control vs no intervention vs prompt-based fix. Decisive metric: joint change in mean thinking tokens and accuracy on belief-contradicting items, first, requiring both to improve; with belief-consistent off-target accuracy held within +/-1 point. Convincing: suppression cuts thinking tokens by >= 15% AND raises belief-contradicting accuracy by >= 4 points simultaneously, while the random control does neither and belief-consistent accuracy is preserved, monotone in dose. Indecision band: improving only one of the two, or a 5-15% token cut with < 4 point accuracy gain, is partial support (and if only tokens drop while accuracy is flat, the tug-of-war-as-shared-cause claim is not confirmed). Negative result: no joint improvement, off-target damage on belief-consistent items, or the random control matching the real direction, refutes H4.

Experiment 6 (H1/H4 boundary conditions and generalization): Tests where the belief tax is strongest and whether probe/suppression transfer. Data: reuses Experiment 1 forms and derived vectors, plus additional forms varying conflict strength (mildly implausible vs flatly false premises) and chaining depth (1 vs 3 hops). Transfer: apply the 7B-derived probe and suppression vector to 1.5B and 14B and across syllogistic vs rule-chaining sets without refitting. Systems compared: mild vs flat contradiction; shallow vs deep chains; explicit-hypothetical framing vs none; in-model vs transferred vectors. Decisive metric: change in the belief token/error tax across each factor, first; plus transferred-vector effect relative to in-model. Convincing: the tax grows with conflict strength and chaining depth, explicit-hypothetical framing significantly reduces it, and the transferred suppression retains >= 70% of its in-model token+accuracy effect. Indecision band: transferred effect 40-70% of in-model, or factor effects within noise, is weak generalization. Negative result: no factor modulation and transferred effect < 40% means the phenomenon is idiosyncratic, bounding the claim's scope.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Belief-neutral controls using nonce entities may themselves be harder to parse than familiar ones, confounding the belief-status effect; the three-way design (consistent/neutral/contradicting) and difficulty-matched mixed-effects analysis isolate conflict from unfamiliarity, and a null after controls is an informative negative result. Ensuring identical logical structure and answer across belief conditions is nontrivial; we use strict templating and human/LLM verification. The parametric-knowledge signal may be inseparable from a generic difficulty/uncertainty signal, weakening the tug-of-war framing; the separability analysis, step-wise trajectory (persistence, not just magnitude), and causal steering address this. Steering could push activations off-distribution and degrade coherence; matched-random-direction controls and sample-validity checks are included, and suppression might hurt cases where real-world knowledge is legitimately needed (specificity check on belief-consistent items). Effects may be small in strongly instruction-tuned models trained to follow hypotheticals (a valuable boundary condition) and may be model-family and scale specific. Reasoning-length measurement requires clear think/answer delimiters; truncate-and-resume is compute-heavy, so we subsample.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims: (1) belief-contradicting premises increase reasoning-token spend relative to belief-neutral but logically matched premises; (2) a decodable internal signal reflecting parametric knowledge competes with instructed premises across the trace and predicts both extra tokens and errors; (3) suppressing that signal reduces both compute and errors; (4) the effect generalizes across open reasoning models and multi-step deductive tasks. The phenomenon itself is not new: belief bias / premise rejection in LLMs and counterfactual reasoning failures are already known from the cited prior work. The actual delta is the compute-allocation angle plus a mechanistic, step-resolved tug-of-war with causal steering, which is a meaningful extension but not a new task or setting. The novelty is thus moderate: stronger than a simple re-run because it proposes a different dependent variable and mechanistic test, but it is still anchored in an established phenomenon and could be seen as a reframing unless the compute inflation effect is large and cleanly isolated.
revision_notes: Make the delta explicit as a new dependent variable: compute inflation under matched logical structure, not just accuracy on belief-bias items.
State why multi-step reasoning traces are meaningfully different from prior single-judgment belief-bias work, beyond longer outputs.
Clarify what is truly new about the mechanism claim: not 'belief bias exists,' but 'a decodable competing signal persists and predicts compute allocation.'
Tighten the closest-prior-work comparison: what existing benchmarks measure, and exactly what they do not (token budget, trace dynamics, causal steering).

impact.reasoning: Problem: reasoning robustness for hypothetical/counterfactual reasoning, especially when models must ignore strong priors/world knowledge. Who cares: interpretability, reasoning-systems, and benchmark communities; potentially anyone deploying models for planning or formal inference where counterfactual premises matter. If true, it changes the story from 'models are less accurate on contradictory premises' to 'they also waste compute while fighting their own beliefs,' which is a stronger systems-level failure mode and suggests a mechanism for latency/cost plus correctness. This is broader than a niche curiosity because it touches general reasoning reliability and token efficiency, but it is still somewhat specialized to structured reasoning and model analysis. The strongest case is that belief-contradicting inputs impose a hidden compute tax and that this tax is mechanistically linked to errors, giving a new target for optimization and evaluation.
revision_notes: Lead with the practical consequence: contradictory premises cost more tokens and hurt accuracy, so this is both a reliability and efficiency problem.
Specify who would act on the result: reasoning-model builders, eval designers, and interpretability researchers.
Explain the direction-shifting value: current evals look at accuracy; this adds compute as a failure mode.
If possible, connect to deployment relevance (latency/cost) rather than only benchmark significance.

review.reasoning: The hypothesis is directionally clear but not yet fully falsifiable/scoped. Main gap: 'belief-neutral/novel' versus 'belief-contradicting' may confound familiarity, lexical oddity, or semantic plausibility; the proposal needs tighter controls and explicit operationalization of matched difficulty. The compute claim also risks being explained by generic uncertainty or longer self-correction rather than belief rejection per se. The proposed experiments are reasonably concrete, but several are under-specified: how the linear probe is trained/evaluated, how step boundaries are defined, how causal steering vectors are derived without leaking task difficulty, and what effect sizes/preregistered thresholds justify the claim. The mixed-effects design is appropriate, but the proposal should better distinguish the primary test from exploratory analyses and include stronger baselines (prompt length, entropy/uncertainty, OOD hardness, self-consistency). Venue strength is decent if the controls are clean and the steering result is robust; otherwise it risks reading as an elaborate correlation study on a known bias.
