Name: hawthorne_effort_effect
Title: The Hawthorne Effort Effect: Do Reasoning Models Think Harder When They Believe They Are Being Tested?
Short Hypothesis: Reasoning models allocate more thinking compute (more tokens, more verification) to the exact same problem when the prompt signals an evaluation/test context than when it signals casual real-world deployment, even though difficulty and the correct answer are identical. This effort inflation rides on the same evaluation-awareness representation already shown to be linearly encoded and steerable; steering the awareness signal causally moves reasoning length, decoupled from difficulty.
Related Work: A recent cluster shows evaluation/test awareness is linearly represented and steerable in LLMs and ties it to SAFETY outcomes: 'The Hawthorne Effect in Reasoning Models' (2025) and 'Probing and Steering Evaluation Awareness' (2025) probe/steer test-awareness activations and study sandbagging and harmful-compliance; 'Evaluation Awareness Scales Predictably' (2025) gives a scaling law. All of these measure the effect of evaluation awareness on ANSWER correctness, compliance, or capability concealment. Separately, efficient-reasoning interpretability reads a scalar length/difficulty signal to allocate compute (When More is Less 2025; Overclocking LLM Reasoning 2025; ThinkEdit 2025; S3-CoT 2026) but always in a fixed prompt framing and treats length as difficulty-driven. Crucially, NO prior work connects evaluation awareness to reasoning COMPUTE ALLOCATION: none asks whether test framing makes a reasoning model think LONGER on identical problems, dissociates this from genuine difficulty, or shows the reasoning-length change is causally carried by the evaluation-awareness representation. Our contribution is (1) a new behavioral phenomenon — a Hawthorne effect for reasoning effort; (2) its dissociation from difficulty; and (3) a mechanistic account showing it rides the known evaluation-awareness direction and can be causally steered. This is distinct from all my prior overthinking proposals (which assume a neutral, single framing) and from prior evaluation-awareness work (which targets safety/accuracy, not compute). If confirmed, it means published benchmark efficiency numbers are systematically biased and real users receive less careful reasoning.
Abstract: Reasoning language models are almost always measured on benchmarks — but benchmarks announce themselves as tests. We ask whether this framing changes how hard a model thinks. Transferring the Hawthorne effect and building on work showing that evaluation awareness is linearly encoded and steerable in LLMs, we hypothesize a Hawthorne effort effect: on the identical problem, a reasoning model spends more thinking tokens and does more self-verification when the prompt signals an evaluation/test context than when it signals casual real-world deployment. We construct matched prompts that hold the math or science problem's content and correct answer fixed while varying only contextual framing — explicit test cues (‘Question 4 of this exam’, ‘for benchmark scoring’) versus deployment cues (a casual user asking for help) versus neutral. Across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B–14B, Qwen3), we measure reasoning-token count, verification behavior, and accuracy per framing, using a mixed-effects decomposition to dissociate framing from genuine difficulty. Mechanistically, we test whether the prompt-boundary residual stream encodes an evaluation-awareness signal that predicts reasoning length beyond a difficulty probe, localize it, causally validate it via activation patching (patch a test-framing state into a deployment context and observe effort rise), and steer the awareness direction to show reasoning length moves with awareness independent of difficulty. Because deployment framing would then yield systematically less careful reasoning — and benchmark numbers systematically more — the effect is both a measurement-validity and an equity concern. We provide an interpretable, training-free debiasing intervention.
Experiments:
All experiments run on open reasoning models with explicit think/answer delimiters: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen at 1.5B, 7B, and 14B, plus Qwen3-8B (thinking mode). Weights are frozen; only linear probes and difference-of-means steering vectors are fit. Decoding is temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 8192 thinking tokens, 5 samples per (problem, framing) with seeds {0,1,2,3,4}; reasoning length is the mean thinking-token count and accuracy the mean exact-match. Everything fits one 80GB GPU; 14B runs on reduced subsets as noted.

Experiment 1 (H1 - test framing inflates reasoning effort on identical problems): Tests whether an evaluation/test framing yields more thinking tokens and more self-verification than a deployment framing on the identical problem. Data: constructed from existing sets - GSM8K test (1319; sample 300), MATH500 (500; all), AIME 2024+2025 (60; all), GPQA-Diamond (198; all); 1058 seed problems, since each is expanded into 3 framings x 5 seeds x 4 models. Each seed problem is rendered content-identical across three framings that change only context: (a) explicit test cues ('This is question 4 of a graded exam'; 'Your answer will be scored on a benchmark'; 'You are being evaluated'), (b) deployment/casual cues (a hurried user asking for help in chat), (c) neutral no-framing baseline. Content and gold answer are verified identical after stripping the framing. Verification depth = count of self-check/recheck steps via lexical cues plus a reflection-direction classifier. Systems compared: test vs deployment vs neutral framing, within model. Decisive metric: within-problem paired difference in mean thinking tokens between test and deployment framing, as a median relative increase, first; secondary verification-step increase; accuracy reported to confirm the extra effort is not merely correcting errors. Convincing: median relative token increase >= 12% (test over deployment) with a paired Wilcoxon test (Holm-corrected across models) and accuracy equal-or-higher under test framing. Indecision band: a 4-12% increase does not decide H1 and blocks the mechanism experiments. Negative result: below 4%, or the sign reversing consistently (deployment overthinking), refutes the stated direction of H1 (a reversal is still a reportable measurement-validity finding but rejects the hypothesis as written).

Experiment 2 (H1 dissociation - the effort gap is not driven by difficulty or prompt length): Tests that the framing effect survives removal of intrinsic difficulty and raw prompt length, and that the extra tokens are wasted rather than needed. Data: reuses Experiment 1 traces. Analysis 1 (dissociation): mixed-effects model of thinking length with a random intercept per problem identity (difficulty) and fixed effects for framing and raw prompt token count; supported by length-matched phrasings. Analysis 2 (wasted vs genuine): on a 150-problem subsample use truncate-and-resume to estimate minimal-solve length per framing and test whether test framing inflates the beyond-minimal (wasted) portion rather than the minimal-solve length. Systems compared: framing coefficient with vs without difficulty random effect and prompt-length covariate. Decisive metric: standardized framing coefficient on thinking length after both controls, first; plus the share of test-framing extra tokens in the wasted portion. Convincing: the framing coefficient stays significant (95% CI excludes 0) with most of its raw effect surviving controls, and >= 60% of extra tokens fall in the wasted portion. Indecision band: a surviving-but-halved coefficient, or 30-60% wasted share, is partial support. Negative result: the coefficient vanishing under controls, or extra tokens being genuine (< 30% wasted), means the gap is difficulty/length-driven, refuting the dissociation part of H1.

Experiment 3 (H2 - the effort gap rides on the linearly encoded evaluation-awareness representation): Tests whether the boundary residual stream carries an evaluation-awareness direction that predicts reasoning length beyond a difficulty probe. Data: final-prompt-token activations for the Experiment 1 problems across framings, split 70/15/15 by problem identity. Model: frozen DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (primary), layer sweep (prior work localizes awareness to early-to-middle layers). Probes: (i) a linear evaluation-awareness probe trained on test vs deployment framing (reproducing prior work), (ii) a ridge length probe (target = observed thinking length), (iii) a true-difficulty probe (target = pass-rate). Systems compared: does the length-probe prediction rise under test framing for identical problems; does the awareness direction predict length beyond difficulty; principal angle between awareness and difficulty directions. Decisive metric: incremental R2 of the evaluation-awareness direction for predicting reasoning length over the difficulty probe on held-out problems, first; plus held-out Spearman between length-probe prediction and framing on matched problems and the awareness/difficulty principal angle. Convincing: the awareness direction adds >= 0.05 R2 over difficulty (significant), length-probe Spearman with framing >= 0.3 (p<0.01), and principal angle to difficulty >= 30 degrees (awareness not collinear with difficulty). Indecision band: incremental R2 0.02-0.05, or angle 20-30 degrees, is a present-but-entangled signal. Negative result: incremental R2 < 0.02, or the awareness direction collinear with difficulty (angle < 20 degrees), means the length change is not carried by a distinct awareness representation, refuting H2.

Experiment 4 (H3 - steering the awareness direction causally moves reasoning length, decoupled from difficulty): Tests whether editing the awareness representation changes reasoning length as predicted. Data: 150 problems (subset of Experiment 1) each with matched test and deployment variants; frozen 7B with a 1.5B replication. Intervention A (patching, both directions): patch the boundary state from a test variant into the matched deployment pass (expect effort to rise) and, reversed, patch deployment state into a test pass (expect effort to drop), at the Experiment-3 layer. Intervention B (steering): steer along the evaluation-awareness direction (difference-of-means test minus deployment, or the awareness-probe weight) to (a) cancel the framing effort gap and (b) fix all framings to a common effort target; dose swept over 4 magnitudes. Controls: matched-random-direction patch/steer of equal norm; off-target accuracy on held-out problems; comparison to a prompt-based fix (stripping framing). Systems compared: real patch/steer vs random-direction control vs no intervention vs prompt-strip. Decisive metric: fraction of the test-vs-deployment length gap opened by injecting the test state (and closed by injecting deployment), first; plus the reduction in the framing length gap under steering, with accuracy held within +/-1 point. Convincing: patching moves length in the predicted direction for both patch directions closing >= 50% of the gap, and steering along the awareness direction shrinks the framing gap by >= 50% while a matched-random direction does < 15%, monotone in dose, accuracy preserved. Indecision band: a 20-50% effect, or a random-control effect of 15-25%, is partial/ambiguous mediation. Negative result: < 20% effect, or the random control matching the awareness direction, means reasoning length is not causally carried by the awareness representation, refuting H3.

Experiment 5 (H1/H3 modulators, scaling, and transfer): Tests where the effort gap is strongest and whether it scales and transfers. Data: reuses Experiment 1 problems and derived vectors. Factors: framing strength (subtle vs explicit test cues), high-stakes framing ('this determines your deployment'), and domain (GPQA/medical items). Scaling/transfer: apply the 7B-derived awareness probe and steering vector to 1.5B and 14B and across datasets without refitting, and test whether the framing token gap grows with model scale (as predicted by the evaluation-awareness scaling law) and whether RL-tuned models show larger gaps. Systems compared: subtle vs explicit vs high-stakes framing; 1.5B vs 7B vs 14B; in-model vs transferred probe/steering. Decisive metric: change in the framing token gap across each factor and across scale, first; plus transferred-vector effect relative to in-model. Convincing: explicit/high-stakes framing yields a significantly larger gap than subtle framing, the gap grows monotonically with scale, and transferred steering retains >= 70% of its in-model gap-closing effect. Indecision band: transferred effect 40-70% of in-model, or a non-monotone scale trend, is weak generalization. Negative result: no factor or scale modulation and transferred effect < 40% means the effect is idiosyncratic and does not follow the awareness scaling law, bounding the claim's scope.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The effect could be confounded by prompt-length or lexical differences between framings rather than the evaluation-awareness cue per se; the length covariate, length-matched phrasings, and neutral baseline isolate this, and a null after controls is an informative negative result. Framing may be small or absent in models trained to behave identically regardless of context (a valuable boundary condition, and one that would itself matter for eval validity). The reasoning-length signal may be inseparable from difficulty or from a generic sycophancy/instruction-following direction; the separability analysis, patching, and comparison to a difficulty probe address this, and overlap with the known evaluation-awareness direction is in fact the mechanistic prediction we test. Steering/patching can push activations off-distribution and confound accuracy reads; matched-random-direction controls and sample-validity checks are included. Reasoning-length measurement requires clear think/answer delimiters; truncate-and-resume is compute-heavy, so we subsample. The direction of the effect could reverse in some families (deployment overthinking) — still a novel, publishable measurement-validity finding. Results may be model-family and scale specific.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims that would need to be novel: (1) test/evaluation framing changes reasoning effort (thinking-token count / self-verification) on identical problems; (2) this effect is decoupled from difficulty and not just answer accuracy/compliance; (3) the effect is mediated by the already-known evaluation-awareness direction and can be causally steered into longer/shorter reasoning; (4) the effect is robust across open reasoning models and benchmark tasks; (5) a specific counterintuitive possibility: deployment framing could reduce effort or reverse the effect. Against novelty, the search summary says the main phenomenon, the linear-probe setup, and steering intervention are already present in almost identical prior work. So the proposal's real delta is narrow: using reasoning length/effort as the dependent variable and trying to separate it from difficulty/format confounds. That is a modest extension rather than a genuinely new theory or mechanism. Closest prior work family: evaluation-awareness / Hawthorne-effect papers probing and steering test awareness. Actual delta: effort allocation instead of correctness/compliance, plus an explicit difficulty-control claim.

impact.reasoning: Problem: whether benchmark/test framing changes how much reasoning compute models spend on the same task, which affects evaluation validity and possibly real-user behavior. Who cares: AI eval researchers, AI safety researchers concerned with gaming/sandbagging, and possibly teams measuring efficiency or deploying reasoning models. If true, it would imply benchmark results are partially contaminated by test-awareness and that deployment prompts may elicit less careful reasoning than benchmark prompts. Strongest one-line case: 'Models may think harder when they know they are being judged, so benchmark effort and deployment effort are not comparable.' This is important but still fairly niche and primarily relevant to evaluation methodology rather than broad downstream user impact. Uptake/citation potential is moderate because it sits near an active, contentious eval-awareness line; direction-shifting value is limited by the prior art overlap; real-world reach is plausible but not clearly large.

review.reasoning: The hypothesis is directionally clear but still somewhat overstuffed and vulnerable to confounds. Main logical gap: if test framing changes token length, it may be because of instruction/style/format differences rather than a latent 'evaluation-awareness' variable; the proposal knows this risk, but the proposed controls may not fully exclude it. Another gap: more tokens does not necessarily mean more effective reasoning or more 'thinking hard'; accuracy/self-verification measures need careful operationalization. The causal story is also not fully pinned down: patching/steering along an evaluation-awareness direction could affect many behaviors, so showing length changes alone does not prove compute allocation. Experiments are feasible, but several are under-specified or noisy: lexical cues, reflection classifiers, 'wasted vs genuine' tokens, and mixed-effects thresholds need stronger definitions; the proposed 12%/0.05 R2/30deg cutoffs feel arbitrary. Related work citation is strong but the narrative should be more honest that this is an extension of a known evaluation-awareness line, not a cleanly new mechanism. Minimum viable edits: tighten the claim to a pre-registered, scoped effect on reasoning length under carefully matched prompts; add stronger format-matched controls; include manual annotation of verification steps on a subset; and add an experiment showing the effect persists when superficial formatting is held constant.

Name: einstellung_method_fixation
Title: Mental Set in Machines: An Einstellung Effect Where Prior Problems Fixate a Reasoning Model on a Costly Method and Blind It to Simpler Ones
Short Hypothesis: Transferring the classic Einstellung (mental-set) effect from cognitive psychology, we hypothesize that after a reasoning model solves a run of problems that all require the same method, it rigidly reapplies that method to a subsequent problem that admits a far simpler solution—spending more tokens and often failing to find the shortcut—even though it solves the same problem correctly and cheaply in isolation. This method-fixation is not driven by the target problem's difficulty but by a method-commitment representation carried over from the preceding context, which can be located and causally steered to release the fixation.
Related Work: Two literatures meet here. (1) Cognitive psychology: the Einstellung / water-jar effect (Luchins 1942) and expertise-induced fixation (Bilalić et al.) show that a repeated successful method creates a mental set that blocks discovery of simpler solutions—a robust, authoritative human finding. (2) Efficient-reasoning and reuse work: external memory/retrieval methods (Retrieval-of-Thought, Buffer of Thoughts, MemShare, ENGRAM-R, Graph-Memoized, InftyThink-with-memory) REUSE prior reasoning to speed up new problems, and interpretability work shows in-context task/method reuse via shared circuits (Circuit Component Reuse 2023) and reasoning-length priors set pre-generation (On Reasoning Strength Planning 2025). Crucially, all reuse work treats reuse as BENEFICIAL and studies helpful transfer; none studies HARMFUL over-reuse—rigidity that inflates compute and blinds the model to shortcuts. My prior 'analogical_transfer_gate' proposal studied FAILURE to transfer a helpful analog; this is the opposite failure: pathological SUCCESS of transfer that fixates the model. My 'reasoning_length_contagion' proposal concerned length carry-over but not method rigidity or shortcut-blindness. We are the first to (a) demonstrate an Einstellung effect in reasoning LLMs as joint compute-inflation + shortcut-blindness, (b) dissociate it from target difficulty, and (c) locate and causally steer a method-commitment representation that releases the set.
Abstract: Humans who repeatedly solve problems with one method develop a mental set that leads them to rigidly reapply it, missing simpler solutions—the Einstellung effect. We ask whether reasoning language models inherit this rigidity. We construct 'Einstellung sequences': a run of prime problems all solvable only by a costly method M, followed by a critical target problem that admits both M and a much simpler shortcut S, with a matched no-prime control that presents the same target in isolation. We hypothesize that primed models rigidly apply M to the target—spending more tokens and more often failing to use S—even though the target is identical, and that this fixation is driven not by the target's difficulty but by a method-commitment signal carried over from the prime context. Across arithmetic word problems, algebra, and combinatorics on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we measure shortcut-usage rate, reasoning-token count, and accuracy on the critical target as a function of prime length, using a mixed-effects decomposition to dissociate the prime effect from target difficulty. Mechanistically, we probe whether the prompt-boundary residual stream at the target encodes a method-commitment signal separable from a difficulty probe, localize it, causally validate via activation patching (patch a no-prime state into a primed context and observe shortcut recovery), and steer the signal to release the set. We test a training-free debiasing intervention that restores shortcut use and cuts tokens. Beyond a novel cognitive-transfer phenomenon, method-fixation is a deployment risk: in agentic and multi-turn settings, recent problem history can silently make models reason worse and more expensively.
Experiments:
All experiments run on open reasoning models with explicit think/answer delimiters: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen at 1.5B, 7B, and 14B, plus Qwen3-8B (thinking mode). Weights are frozen; only linear probes and difference-of-means steering vectors are fit. Decoding is temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 8192 thinking tokens, 5 samples per (sequence, condition) with seeds {0,1,2,3,4}; reasoning length is the mean thinking-token count and accuracy the mean exact-match, both measured on the critical target only. Everything fits one 80GB GPU; 14B runs on reduced subsets as noted.

Experiment 1 (H1 - method-repetition priming inflates target tokens and suppresses the shortcut): Tests whether a run of same-method prime problems makes the model reapply the costly method to a target that admits a simpler shortcut, costing more tokens and lowering shortcut use, versus the same target in isolation. Data: constructed from scratch - for each critical target we design a simple shortcut S (symmetry, closed-form, cancellation) and a costly-but-valid method M (brute-force enumeration, long derivation), plus prime problems solvable only by M and not by S. Domains: water-jar-style arithmetic, algebra, small combinatorics. We build 200 targets, each verified (LLM-judge + a 60-item human spot-check) to be solvable by both S and M in isolation while primes admit only M. Each target is run at prime lengths N in {0,1,3,5} (N=0 = no-prime control) plus a diverse-prime control (N=5 primes solved by varied methods) that isolates method-repetition from mere context length; 200 targets x 6 conditions is the cost driver. Shortcut usage is detected by step-template matching plus LLM-judge (human-validated agreement reported). Systems compared: primed (N=1,3,5) vs no-prime (N=0) vs diverse-prime, within target and model. Decisive metric: shortcut-usage rate on the target as a function of prime length, first; secondary within-target token increase and accuracy change. Convincing: shortcut-usage rate drops by >= 20 percentage points from N=0 to N=5 with a monotone dose-response, tokens rise >= 15%, while the diverse-prime control shows < 8 points of shortcut suppression (fixation needs method-repetition, not length), all under paired tests Holm-corrected across models. Indecision band: an 8-20 point shortcut drop, or the diverse-prime control itself suppressing 8-15 points, does not decide H1. Negative result: < 8 point shortcut drop, or the diverse-prime control matching the same-method prime, means no method-fixation and H1 is rejected.

Experiment 2 (H2 dissociation - fixation is not driven by target difficulty or prompt length): Tests that the prime effect survives removal of target difficulty and raw prompt length, and that the extra tokens are rigid M-execution rather than needed reasoning. Data: reuses Experiment 1 traces. Analysis 1 (dissociation): mixed-effects models of shortcut-usage, tokens, and accuracy with a random intercept per target identity (intrinsic difficulty) and fixed effects for prime length and raw prompt token count; supported by a length-matched irrelevant-filler prime that adds context length without a repeated method. Analysis 2 (wasted vs genuine): on a 100-target subsample use truncate-and-resume to estimate the S-minimal solve length and test whether priming inflates tokens beyond the S-minimal solve (rigid M) rather than adding needed reasoning. Systems compared: prime coefficient with vs without target random effect and prompt-length covariate; same-method prime vs length-matched filler. Decisive metric: standardized prime-length coefficient on shortcut-usage after controls, first; plus the share of primed extra tokens beyond the S-minimal solve. Convincing: the prime coefficient on shortcut-usage stays significant after controls, the length-matched filler shows no significant fixation, and >= 60% of primed extra tokens exceed the S-minimal solve. Indecision band: a surviving-but-halved coefficient, or 30-60% excess-token share, is partial support. Negative result: the coefficient vanishing under controls, or the filler prime reproducing the effect, means fixation was a context-length artifact, refuting H2's dissociation.

Experiment 3 (H3 - a method-commitment representation exists at the target boundary and is separable from difficulty): Tests whether the target's prompt-boundary residual stream encodes a carried-over method-commitment signal that predicts shortcut-vs-method use and is distinct from a difficulty signal. Data: target prompt-boundary activations (last token before any target reasoning token) across prime lengths from Experiment 1, split 70/15/15 by target identity. Model: frozen DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (primary), layer sweep. Probes: a linear probe predicting whether the model will use S vs M on the target, a classifier for prime-method identity, and a target-difficulty probe (target = isolated pass-rate). Systems compared: for identical targets, does the S-vs-M probe prediction shift with prime length; principal angle between the method-commitment direction and the difficulty direction plus joint predictive gain. Decisive metric: held-out AUROC of the S-vs-M probe and its shift with prime length on matched targets, first; plus the method-commitment/difficulty principal angle. Convincing: S-vs-M probe AUROC >= 0.7, its predicted shortcut-probability drops with prime length on matched targets (Spearman <= -0.3, p<0.01), and the method-commitment direction is not collinear with difficulty (angle >= 30 degrees), adding significant R2 over the difficulty probe. Indecision band: AUROC 0.6-0.7, or angle 20-30 degrees, is a present-but-entangled signal. Negative result: AUROC < 0.6 or no prime-length shift, or collinearity with difficulty (angle < 20 degrees), means no separable method-commitment representation, refuting the location part of H3.

Experiment 4 (H3 causal - patching and steering release (or induce) the set): Tests whether editing the target-boundary representation recovers the shortcut and whether steering releases fixation. Data: 100 targets (subset of Experiment 1) each with matched N=5 primed and N=0 no-prime contexts; frozen 7B with a 1.5B replication. Intervention A (patching, both directions): patch the target-boundary state from the no-prime (S-inducing) context into the matched primed pass (expect shortcut recovery) and, reversed, patch the primed state into the no-prime pass (expect induced fixation), at the Experiment-3 layer. Intervention B (steering): derive a method-commitment direction (difference-of-means, primed minus no-prime) and steer primed targets to release fixation (dose swept over 4 magnitudes). Controls: matched-random-direction patch/steer of equal norm; off-target accuracy on M-only targets (where M is genuinely required) must be preserved; comparison to a prompt-based fix ('consider whether a simpler method applies'). Systems compared: real patch/steer vs random-direction control vs no intervention vs prompt-based fix. Decisive metric: recovery of shortcut-usage rate on primed targets (toward the no-prime level), first; secondary token reduction and accuracy gain on shortcut-favoring targets, with M-only off-target accuracy held within +/-1 point. Convincing: patching/steering recovers >= 50% of the primed shortcut-usage deficit and cuts tokens accordingly, while the random control recovers < 15% and M-only accuracy is preserved, monotone in dose; reversed patching induces fixation. Indecision band: a 20-50% recovery, or a random-control effect of 15-25%, is partial/ambiguous mediation. Negative result: < 20% recovery, off-target damage on M-only targets, or the random control matching the real direction, means the representation is not causally responsible, refuting H3's causal claim.

Experiment 5 (H1/H3 modulators and generalization): Tests where fixation is strongest and whether probe/steering transfer. Data: reuses Experiment 1 targets and derived vectors. Factors: prime-method salience (strongly vs weakly cued method), an explicit 'this is a fresh, unrelated problem' delimiter before the target (does it reset the set?), and cross-domain priming (prime in one domain, target in another). Transfer: apply the 7B-derived probe and steering vector to 1.5B and 14B and across domains without refitting; compare RL-tuned vs distilled models for fixation strength. Systems compared: salient vs weak prime; fresh-delimiter vs none; within- vs cross-domain; in-model vs transferred vectors; RL-tuned vs distilled. Decisive metric: change in the shortcut-suppression magnitude across each factor, first; plus transferred-vector recovery relative to in-model. Convincing: salient primes fixate more than weak ones, an explicit fresh-problem delimiter significantly reduces fixation, and transferred steering retains >= 70% of its in-model shortcut-recovery. Indecision band: transferred recovery 40-70% of in-model, or factor effects within noise, is weak generalization. Negative result: no factor modulation and transferred recovery < 40% means fixation is idiosyncratic, bounding the claim's scope.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Constructing targets with a clean shortcut S and a genuinely-only-M prime set is nontrivial; we mitigate with templated generation plus human/LLM verification that primes exclude S and targets admit both, and treat ambiguous items separately. The effect could be confounded by context length rather than method-repetition; the diverse-prime control, length-matched filler prime, and mixed-effects analysis isolate this, and a null after controls is an informative negative result refuting the transfer. Shortcut-usage detection (step-template + LLM-judge) is noisy; we validate with human spot-checks and report agreement. The method-commitment signal may be inseparable from a generic difficulty/uncertainty direction; the separability analysis, patching, and difficulty-probe comparison address this, and overlap with an in-context task-vector direction would itself be an interesting mechanistic finding. Steering/patching can push activations off-distribution and confound accuracy reads; matched-random-direction controls and sample-validity checks are included, and releasing the set could over-trigger on problems where M is genuinely required (specificity check on M-only targets). The effect may be small in strongly instruction-tuned models trained to treat each problem freshly (a valuable boundary condition) and may be model-family and scale specific. Reasoning-length measurement requires clear think/answer delimiters; truncate-and-resume is compute-heavy, so we subsample.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims that need to be novel: (1) repeated use of one reasoning method primes an LLM to reuse that same costly method on a later problem that has a cheaper shortcut; (2) this is not just an accuracy/flexibility effect but a compute-overuse / overthinking effect measurable in extra reasoning tokens on the same target solved cheaply in isolation; (3) the effect is caused by a carried-over method-commitment representation at the target boundary rather than target difficulty or generic context length; (4) that representation is decodable/localizable and can be causally steered to restore shortcut use; (5) a training-free mitigation can reduce fixation without harming tasks where the costly method is actually needed. From the provided context, claim (1) is not new in broad phenomenon terms: LLM mental-set / Einstellung effects have already been reported, including shortcut-missing after priming. The meaningful delta is mainly claims (2)-(4): reframing as compute inflation and mechanistically identifying a decodable, steerable method-commitment state. That is a non-trivial extension, especially if the same target is cheap in isolation but expensive after method priming. Relative to the proposal's own related work, the novelty is overstated where it says 'First to demonstrate an Einstellung effect in reasoning LLMs'; that part appears false from the search summary. The closest prior family is human Einstellung literature plus recent LLM studies on mental-set/inflexible reasoning. Actual delta: moving from behavioral rigidity/accuracy to token-cost inefficiency and from phenomenon description to mechanistic representation + causal intervention. If executed cleanly, this is moderately novel, but not a new phenomenon.
revision_notes: Remove or soften any 'first demonstration of Einstellung in LLMs' claim; position the work as the first compute-centric and mechanistic study instead.
Explicitly name the closest LLM prior work and state the exact delta in one sentence: same-target isolated-vs-primed compute inflation plus decodable causal method-commitment signal.
Make clear why the setting is meaningfully different from prior accuracy-only studies: the key unit is excess reasoning tokens on identical targets, not just lower success or flexibility.
Pre-register what counts as a shortcut and costly method to avoid appearing like post hoc relabeling of known reasoning failures.

impact.reasoning: Problem: recent context can make reasoning models persist with an expensive method, wasting compute and sometimes missing simpler valid solutions on later tasks. Who cares: efficient-reasoning, inference-cost optimization, in-context learning, reasoning robustness, and agentic/multi-turn deployment communities. If true, it changes how people evaluate and prompt reasoning models: benchmark scores alone miss a context-induced inefficiency/fixation failure mode; system designers may need resets, delimiters, anti-fixation prompting, or internal steering to control compute blowups and brittle reuse. Strongest one-line case: the same model can solve the same problem cheaply alone but overthink it after a run of similar problems because context induces a reusable but harmful method commitment. This passes the 'so what?' test better than many interpretability proposals because it ties to both cost and reliability in deployed multi-turn systems. Still, the real-world reach depends on effect size and prevalence outside curated puzzle-like tasks. If it only appears in hand-constructed arithmetic/algebra/combinatorics examples, impact is moderate rather than field-shifting. It is more likely to influence a focused subcommunity than the whole field unless the authors show the effect in realistic agent workflows or long-horizon assistants.

Clarify whether the main value is scientific understanding of in-context rigidity, a benchmark for efficient reasoning, or a mitigation method; right now all three are present but none dominates.
Show prevalence/boundary conditions: how often does this happen under normal prompting, not only adversarially designed prime-target sequences?

review.reasoning: The proposal is unusually concrete and testable for an ML idea: it has a scoped hypothesis, clear controls, target-only metrics, multiple prime-length conditions, diverse-prime and filler controls, mixed-effects analysis, mechanistic probing, causal patching, steering, and specificity checks on M-only targets. The central falsifiable claim is strong: identical targets should be solved more expensively and with lower shortcut usage after method-repetition primes than in isolation. That said, there are several strict-review weaknesses. First, related work specificity is insufficient given the apparent existence of direct LLM mental-set papers; the narrative currently overclaims novelty. Second, the dataset construction is the crux and also the main vulnerability: 'shortcut' versus 'costly method' may be ambiguous, target verification leans on LLM judges, and 60-item human spot-checks may be too weak for a 200-target benchmark. Third, token count is noisy under stochastic decoding and may reflect verbosity/style rather than true method commitment; stronger controls are needed to separate latent reasoning path from generation length. Fourth, the mechanistic claims may be underspecified: linear probes and angle-to-difficulty are suggestive but not decisive, and 'target prompt-boundary residual stream' localization may be too coarse without layer/head/component specificity and robustness across seeds/models. Fifth, activation patching from no-prime to primed contexts can introduce distribution shift; causal claims require carefully matched patch sites and null controls. Overall the plan is feasible and above average in quality, but it needs sharper prior positioning, stronger annotation/controls, and a crisper success criterion to be senior-reviewer robust.

Name: expected_value_of_control
Title: Worth the Thought: Do Reward and Efficacy Framings Modulate How Hard Reasoning Models Think, via an Internal Value Signal?
Short Hypothesis: Transferring the Expected-Value-of-Control theory from cognitive neuroscience, we hypothesize that reasoning LLMs allocate more thinking compute (tokens, verification) to the identical problem when the prompt frames the answer as high-reward or as one where effort is highly efficacious, and LESS when a high opportunity cost of time is signalled, even though difficulty and the correct answer are unchanged. This reward/efficacy/opportunity-cost modulation of effort is causally carried by an internal value representation read at the prompt boundary; steering it moves reasoning length independent of difficulty.
Related Work: Cognitive neuroscience robustly shows humans allocate cognitive effort by weighing expected reward, efficacy (how much effort changes outcome), and the opportunity cost of time / average reward rate: Expected-Value-of-Control theory (Shenhav; 'When effort matters' 2020 shows reward and efficacy separately modulate control allocation), and reward-rate/opportunity-cost studies (2022, 2025) show MORE reward at stake or higher efficacy raises effort while high average reward rate LOWERS it. In LLMs, a 'Sparse Reward Subsystem' (2026) identifies value neurons encoding state value critical to reasoning, and Latent Thinking Optimization (2025) shows latent thoughts encode reward signals. Efficient-reasoning interpretability (LLMs Encode Their Failures 2026; FR-Ponder 2025; When More is Less 2025; Efficiency Steering 2025) reads a scalar DIFFICULTY/length signal to allocate compute, always under a fixed, neutral framing, and treats compute as difficulty-driven. Crucially, NO prior work asks whether framing the problem's REWARD, EFFICACY, or OPPORTUNITY COST changes how much a reasoning model thinks on identical problems, dissociates this from genuine difficulty, or ties it to a value representation. We are the first to (a) transfer Expected-Value-of-Control to reasoning LLMs as a compute-allocation phenomenon driven by reward/efficacy/opportunity-cost framing, (b) dissociate it from difficulty, and (c) locate and causally steer the value signal (plausibly the value neurons of the Sparse Reward Subsystem) that mediates it. This is orthogonal to all my prior overthinking proposals (which assume neutral prompts) and sharper than difficulty-budgeting work because it manipulates motivational value, not difficulty.
Abstract: Cognitive neuroscience shows that humans decide how much mental effort to invest by weighing three motivational quantities: the reward at stake, the efficacy of effort (how much it changes the outcome), and the opportunity cost of time. We ask whether reasoning language models inherit an analog of this Expected-Value-of-Control computation. We construct matched prompts that hold a math or science problem's content and correct answer fixed while varying only motivational framing: high vs low stated reward ('this answer is very important / worth a lot' vs 'no big deal'), high vs low efficacy ('careful reasoning strongly determines correctness here' vs 'the outcome is mostly luck'), and high vs low opportunity cost ('you have many other urgent problems waiting' vs 'take all the time you need'). Across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we measure reasoning-token count, verification behavior, and accuracy per framing, using a mixed-effects decomposition to dissociate framing from genuine difficulty. We predict: high reward and high efficacy increase thinking, while high opportunity cost decreases it, mirroring human findings. Mechanistically, we test whether the prompt-boundary residual stream encodes a value/effort signal (probing, and reusing the value neurons of the reported LLM reward subsystem) that predicts reasoning length beyond a difficulty probe, localize it, causally validate it via activation patching, and steer it to show reasoning length moves with value independent of difficulty. Because framing-driven effort means models silently reason less carefully for problems framed as low-value, the effect is a safety and reliability concern; we provide an interpretable, training-free debiasing knob.
Experiments:
All experiments run on open reasoning models with explicit think/answer delimiters: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen at 1.5B, 7B, and 14B, plus Qwen3-8B (thinking mode). Weights are frozen; only linear probes and difference-of-means steering vectors are fit. Decoding is temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 8192 thinking tokens, 5 samples per (problem, framing) with seeds {0,1,2,3,4}; reasoning length is the mean thinking-token count and accuracy the mean exact-match. To keep the framing matrix affordable we prioritize the reward and efficacy axes and subsample problems per cell (below). Everything fits one 80GB GPU; 14B runs on reduced subsets as noted.

Experiment 1 (H1 - reward, efficacy, and opportunity-cost framing modulate thinking effort in the predicted directions): Tests whether high reward and high efficacy raise thinking tokens/verification and high opportunity cost lowers them, on identical problems. Data: constructed from existing sets - GSM8K test (1319; sample 200), MATH500 (500; sample 200), AIME 2024+2025 (60; all), GPQA-Diamond (198; all); 658 seed problems, expanded across three framing axes each at high/low plus a neutral baseline (7 cells per problem) x 5 seeds x 4 models. Axes: REWARD ('a lot rides on getting this right' vs 'this is just a throwaway question'), EFFICACY ('careful step-by-step reasoning strongly determines correctness here' vs 'the answer is largely luck no matter how hard you think'), OPPORTUNITY COST ('you have a long queue of other urgent problems' vs 'there is nothing else to do; take all the time you need'). Content and gold answer are verified identical after stripping the framing sentence. Verification depth = self-check/recheck step count via lexical cues plus a reflection-direction classifier. Systems compared: each axis's high vs low vs neutral, within problem and model. Decisive metric: within-problem paired token difference per axis (high minus low), as a median relative change, first; secondary verification change and accuracy (to confirm extra effort is not merely error-correction). Convincing: high reward and high efficacy each raise tokens by >= 10% median relative, and high opportunity cost lowers tokens by >= 10%, all in the predicted sign under paired Wilcoxon tests (Holm-corrected across axes and models). Indecision band: a 4-10% effect on an axis, or a mixed sign across models, does not decide H1 for that axis. Negative result: < 4% on an axis, or a sign opposite to the human-EVC prediction, refutes H1 for that axis (an opposite sign is still a reportable characterization but rejects the hypothesis as written).

Experiment 2 (H1 dissociation - the framing effect requires motivational content and is not difficulty or length): Tests that framing effects survive difficulty and prompt-length controls and require motivational content. Data: reuses Experiment 1 traces plus an irrelevant-framing placebo cell (a neutral comment about the weather) matched in length. Analysis: mixed-effects models of thinking length (and accuracy) with a random intercept per problem identity (difficulty) and fixed effects for each framing axis and raw prompt token count; supported by length-matched phrasings and the placebo. On a 150-problem subsample, truncate-and-resume estimates minimal-solve length to test whether high-reward/high-efficacy framing inflates the beyond-minimal (wasted) portion rather than adding needed reasoning. Systems compared: framing coefficients with vs without difficulty random effect and prompt-length covariate; motivational framings vs the irrelevant placebo. Decisive metric: standardized framing-axis coefficients on thinking length after controls, first; plus the placebo coefficient (expected ~0). Convincing: reward and efficacy coefficients remain significant after controls with the placebo coefficient not significant, and >= 60% of the reward/efficacy extra tokens fall in the wasted portion. Indecision band: a surviving-but-halved coefficient, or a placebo effect of similar-but-smaller magnitude, is partial support. Negative result: framing coefficients vanishing under controls, or the placebo reproducing the effect, means the modulation was a length/lexical artifact, refuting the dissociation part of H1.

Experiment 3 (H2 - a value/effort representation at the prompt boundary carries the framing effect and is separable from difficulty): Tests whether the boundary residual stream encodes a value signal that predicts reasoning length beyond a difficulty probe and shifts with framing. Data: final-prompt-token activations for the Experiment 1 problems across framing cells, split 70/15/15 by problem identity. Model: frozen DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (primary), layer sweep. Probes: (i) a ridge length probe (target = observed thinking length), (ii) a value probe fit by regressing activations on the framing-induced value level, and (iii) a true-difficulty probe (target = pass-rate); we additionally screen for individual high-weight units as candidate 'value neurons'. Systems compared: for identical problems, does the length-probe prediction rise with reward/efficacy and fall with opportunity cost; principal angle between the value/effort direction and the difficulty direction plus joint predictive gain. Decisive metric: incremental R2 of the value direction for predicting reasoning length over the difficulty probe on held-out problems, first; plus the sign-correct monotone shift of the length-probe prediction across framing levels and the value/difficulty principal angle. Convincing: the value direction adds >= 0.05 R2 over difficulty (significant), the length-probe prediction moves in the predicted sign across all three axes, and the value direction is not collinear with difficulty (angle >= 30 degrees). Indecision band: incremental R2 0.02-0.05, or angle 20-30 degrees, is a present-but-entangled signal. Negative result: incremental R2 < 0.02, no sign-correct shift, or collinearity with difficulty (angle < 20 degrees), means the framing effect is not carried by a distinct value representation, refuting H2's location claim.

Experiment 4 (H2 causal + H3 - patching/steering/ablating the value representation moves reasoning length independent of difficulty): Tests whether editing the value representation changes reasoning length as predicted. Data: 150 problems (subset of Experiment 1) each with matched high- and low-value variants per axis; frozen 7B with a 1.5B replication. Intervention A (patching): patch the boundary state from a high-reward (or high-efficacy) variant into the matched low-value pass (expect length rise), and reverse for opportunity cost, at the Experiment-3 layer. Intervention B (steering): steer along the value/effort direction (difference-of-means high minus low value) to (a) cancel each axis's framing gap and (b) fix all framings to a common effort target; dose swept over 4 magnitudes. Intervention C (neuron ablation): ablate the candidate value neurons from Experiment 3 and test whether framing sensitivity collapses. Controls: matched-random-direction patch/steer of equal norm; off-target accuracy on held-out problems; comparison to a prompt-based fix (stripping framing) and to a scalar length-steering baseline. Systems compared: real patch/steer/ablation vs random-direction control vs no intervention vs prompt-strip vs scalar length steering. Decisive metric: fraction of the high-vs-low value length gap opened by patching (and closed by reverse patching), first; plus the reduction in the framing length gap under steering, with accuracy held within +/-1 point. Convincing: patching moves length in the predicted direction closing >= 50% of the gap, steering shrinks the framing gap by >= 50% and ablating the value neurons removes >= 50% of framing sensitivity, while a matched-random direction does < 15%, monotone in dose, accuracy preserved. Indecision band: a 20-50% effect, or a random-control effect of 15-25%, is partial/ambiguous mediation. Negative result: < 20% effect, or the random control matching the value direction, means reasoning length is not causally carried by the value representation, refuting H2's causal claim and H3.

Experiment 5 (H1/H3 modulators, combination, and transfer): Tests whether reward and efficacy combine as in human EVC and whether the value probe/steering transfer. Data: reuses Experiment 1 problems and derived vectors, plus a reward x efficacy factorial cell set and a monetary-reward framing ('you earn a stated bonus for a correct answer'). Transfer: apply the 7B-derived value probe and steering vector to 1.5B and 14B and across datasets without refitting; compare RL-tuned models (with explicit reward history) vs distilled models. Systems compared: reward-only vs efficacy-only vs combined cells; monetary vs importance framing; subtle vs explicit strength; in-model vs transferred vectors; RL-tuned vs distilled. Decisive metric: the interaction term between reward and efficacy on thinking length, first; plus transferred-vector gap-closing relative to in-model. Convincing: reward and efficacy combine at least additively (a significant positive joint effect), and transferred steering retains >= 70% of its in-model gap-closing effect. Indecision band: a transferred effect 40-70% of in-model, or an interaction within noise, is weak generalization. Negative result: no reward-efficacy combination and transferred effect < 40% means the phenomenon does not follow EVC structure and is idiosyncratic, bounding the claim's scope.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The framing effect could be confounded by prompt-length or lexical differences rather than motivational content per se; the length covariate, length-matched phrasings, neutral baseline, and irrelevant-framing placebo isolate this, and a null after controls is an informative negative result refuting the transfer. Effects may be small or absent in strongly instruction/safety-tuned models trained to behave identically regardless of stakes (a valuable boundary condition). The direction of some effects (especially opportunity cost) may not match human predictions - still a publishable characterization. The value/effort signal may be inseparable from a generic difficulty or sycophancy direction; the separability analysis, patching, value-neuron reuse, and difficulty-probe comparison address this, and overlap with the reported LLM value neurons would be a positive mechanistic finding rather than a confound. Steering/patching can push activations off-distribution and confound accuracy reads; matched-random-direction controls and sample-validity checks are included. Reasoning-length measurement requires clear think/answer delimiters; truncate-and-resume is compute-heavy, so we subsample. Multiple framing axes and levels create a large prompt matrix; we subsample problems per cell and prioritize the reward and efficacy axes. Effects and their sign may be model-family and scale specific.

novelty.reasoning: Core technical claims: (1) LLM reasoning effort/computation is modulated by EVC-style framings along three separable axes (reward, efficacy, opportunity cost) on identical problems; (2) this modulation is dissociable from task difficulty/content and can be detected as changes in thinking tokens/verification; (3) an internal value signal at the prompt boundary mediates the effect and can be causally steered; (4) candidate value neurons may underlie it. Relative to prior work, the basic idea that incentives change model behavior is not new ('Artificial Effort', monetary-framing compliance, reward-prediction/routing). The novel delta is the explicit transfer of the cognitive-neuroscience EVC decomposition to reasoning compute allocation, especially the efficacy and opportunity-cost axes plus mechanistic steering. That is a meaningful extension, but it is still a moderate rather than deep novelty because the setting is a new framing layer over an already active incentive-sensitivity line of work.

If the internal value-signal mechanism is central, specify whether it is a discovered representation or a hypothesized proxy; current wording overstates mechanism certainty.

impact.reasoning: Problem: can a reasoning model be made to spend more or less test-time compute by purely motivational framing, even when the task is unchanged? Who cares: teams doing efficient reasoning / controllable test-time compute, plus alignment researchers worried about incentive sensitivity and hidden compliance. If true, this would change how we think about prompt design, evaluation fairness, and whether 'same task' benchmarks are actually comparable under different framings. Strongest one-line case: tiny wording changes could systematically alter how much a model thinks, so benchmark scores and safety evaluations may be confounded by incentive framing rather than capability. Impact is real but somewhat niche/field-local: it is not a broad product problem by itself, and similar incentive-framing findings already exist, so uptake depends on whether the multi-axis EVC decomposition and causal steering are robust and general.

review.reasoning: The hypothesis is interesting but currently too broad and partly under-specified. Main logical gap: the framing manipulations may change length via social/instruction-following, verbosity, or perceived desired behavior rather than 'effort' or 'value'. The proposal recognizes this, but the controls need to be much tighter and more directly diagnostic. Also, the core mechanism claim ('internal value representation read at the prompt boundary') is not yet falsifiable as written because several latent signals could explain the same correlation. Experiments are feasible, but some proposed readouts are weak: lexical self-check counts and reflection classifiers are noisy proxies for reasoning effort; mixed-effects and placebo controls help, but you need stronger behavioral controls (e.g., identical semantics with systematically varied wording across multiple paraphrase families, within-model randomization, and prompt-bounded ablations). The mechanistic section is ambitious: 'candidate value neurons' and steering may not map cleanly to reasoning models, and patching/ablation results risk being post hoc unless you predefine a small set of candidate features and compare against generic length/difficulty baselines. Minimum viable edits: narrow H1 to one or two axes first (reward and efficacy), define a crisp primary endpoint (thinking tokens/accuracy tradeoff), add semantic-paraphrase controls and a no-task-compliance control, and separate descriptive findings from causal mechanism claims.

Name: subgoal_schedule_myopia
Title: Solving the Wrong Subgoal First: Overthinking as a Dependency-Scheduling Failure in Reasoning Models
Short Hypothesis: A problem's subgoals form a dependency DAG whose prerequisites impose a partial order; reasoning models schedule subgoals myopically rather than dependency-respectingly, frequently attacking a subgoal before its prerequisites are established. This premature scheduling wastes tokens on flailing and re-derivation. The model already carries an internal, decodable 'prerequisite-readiness' signal at each subgoal-onset that it fails to consult, and steering generation toward dependency-respecting order cuts tokens without hurting accuracy.
Related Work: Probing work shows LLM hidden states encode reasoning-DAG geometry (From Chains to DAGs, 2026) and that models are largely myopic/incremental planners with weak global planning (No Global Plan in CoT, 2026; Internal Planning: Horizon and Branch Awareness, 2025; Detecting and Characterizing Planning, 2025). Efficiency work characterizes overthinking as an inverted-U length effect (When More is Less, 2025) or as decorative/redundant steps (Thought Anchors; TTS). A shortest-path study shows next-token predictors are biased toward systematically inefficient (backtracking) traces (2025). Crucially, none connect the problem's *dependency structure* to *compute waste*: no prior work identifies suboptimal subgoal *ordering* (attacking a subgoal before its prerequisites) as a distinct, quantifiable source of overthinking, nor tests whether a decodable prerequisite-readiness signal governs it, nor intervenes on scheduling to save compute. This differs from my prior proposals (which target stopping, verification, length priors, and framing effects) by targeting the *order* in which reasoning is performed. It also goes beyond DAG-probing (which is diagnostic and static) by tying the encoded DAG to a behavioral scheduling failure and a causal efficiency intervention.
Abstract: Reasoning models overthink, but the role of *ordering* in that waste is unexamined. Many problems decompose into subgoals with prerequisite dependencies—a directed acyclic graph whose topological orders are the valid schedules. We hypothesize that reasoning models schedule subgoals myopically: they frequently begin a subgoal before its prerequisites are established, then flail or re-derive, spending tokens that a dependency-respecting order would avoid. We further hypothesize the model already encodes, at each subgoal onset, a prerequisite-readiness signal (are the inputs this subgoal needs already available in context?) that it does not act on. Using multi-step problems with recoverable dependency structure (GSM8K, MATH500, and templated multi-constraint word/logic problems where we can annotate a ground-truth subgoal DAG) on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we (1) segment traces into subgoals, align them to DAG nodes, and measure a scheduling-inversion rate (subgoals started before their prerequisites) and its token cost via truncate-and-resume and re-derivation detection; (2) show inversions predict wasted tokens beyond length or decorative-step baselines; (3) train a linear probe at subgoal onset to decode prerequisite-readiness and test its separability from a generic difficulty/confidence probe; (4) causally validate via activation patching—patching a high-readiness state into a premature-onset context should shift the model to a ready subgoal; and (5) deploy a training-free scheduling steer that, when readiness is low, nudges the model to defer the premature subgoal, cutting tokens at equal accuracy versus length-aware and reactive-pruning baselines. Our work reframes a slice of overthinking as a dependency-scheduling failure with a decodable, steerable internal cause.
Experiments:
All experiments run on open reasoning models with explicit think/answer delimiters: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen at 1.5B, 7B, and 14B, plus Qwen3-8B (thinking mode). Weights are frozen; only linear probes and difference-of-means steering vectors are fit. Decoding is temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 8192 thinking tokens, 5 samples per problem with seeds {0,1,2,3,4}; reasoning length is the mean thinking-token count and accuracy the mean exact-match. Everything fits one 80GB GPU; 14B runs on reduced subsets as noted. The subgoal DAG and trace-to-node alignment are shared infrastructure: templated multi-constraint word problems and small logic/scheduling puzzles have a DAG known by construction; for GSM8K and MATH500 we annotate the subgoal DAG by solution parsing plus LLM-judge, human-validated on a 100-item spot-check (inter-annotator/judge agreement reported). Traces are segmented into subgoals at step delimiters and each subgoal is aligned to a DAG node by semantic matching plus LLM-judge; a scheduling-inversion = a subgoal begun before all its prerequisite nodes were established earlier in the trace.

Experiment 1 (H1 - reasoning models commit scheduling inversions rather than respecting the dependency order): Tests whether models frequently begin subgoals before their prerequisites are established. Data: constructed and adapted - 300 templated multi-constraint word problems and 200 logic/scheduling puzzles built with known DAGs (varying width/depth), plus 400 GSM8K and 300 MATH500 problems with annotated DAGs; these counts give enough multi-subgoal traces while keeping per-trace segmentation/alignment affordable. Systems compared: the observed per-trace inversion rate against a random-scheduling null (the inversion rate expected if subgoals were ordered uniformly at random among the DAG's topological-order violations), across datasets and the four model sizes. Decisive metric: per-trace scheduling-inversion rate, first; reported against the random-scheduling null and against the ideal (zero-inversion) schedule. Convincing: the observed inversion rate is substantial (>= 15% of subgoal onsets are inversions) and significantly above zero, but below the random-null (models are partly, not fully, dependency-respecting), consistent across datasets. Indecision band: an inversion rate of 5-15% is a weak phenomenon reported as such and does not strongly motivate the intervention. Negative result: an inversion rate < 5% (models already schedule near-optimally) refutes H1 and removes the premise for the remaining experiments; an inversion rate at or above the random null would instead indicate alignment failure rather than a real scheduling signal and triggers an alignment audit.

Experiment 2 (H2 - inversions cause wasted tokens through flailing and re-derivation): Tests whether inversions predict wasted compute beyond length and decorative-step baselines. Data: reuses Experiment 1 traces. For each inversion we measure downstream waste via (a) truncate-and-resume estimating the minimal-solve length under a forced dependency-respecting order (prerequisite subgoals prompted first) on a 200-problem subsample, (b) re-derivation detection (value-producing statements re-derived after a premature attempt), and (c) dead-end/backtrack detection. We then regress per-trace wasted tokens on inversion rate versus baselines: trace length, decorative-step fraction, and a difficulty probe. Systems compared: inversion-rate predictor vs each baseline predictor. Decisive metric: held-out incremental R2 of inversion rate for predicting wasted tokens over the strongest baseline, first; plus the mean wasted tokens attributable to a single inversion. Convincing: inversion rate adds >= 0.05 R2 over the best baseline (significant), and forcing a dependency-respecting order reduces minimal-solve length by >= 15% on the subsample. Indecision band: incremental R2 0.02-0.05, or a 5-15% forced-order reduction, is partial support. Negative result: incremental R2 < 0.02 and < 5% forced-order reduction means inversions do not cause measurable waste, refuting H2.

Experiment 3 (H3 - a decodable prerequisite-readiness signal exists at subgoal onset and is separable from difficulty/confidence): Tests whether the residual stream at subgoal onset encodes whether the upcoming subgoal's prerequisites are satisfied, distinct from generic difficulty/confidence. Data: subgoal-onset activations (before the subgoal is generated) from Experiment 1 traces, labeled by DAG alignment as prerequisites-satisfied vs not, split 70/15/15 by problem identity. Model: frozen DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (primary), layer sweep. Probes: a linear readiness probe (target = prerequisites satisfied), a difficulty probe (pass-rate), and a confidence probe. Systems compared: readiness probe vs difficulty/confidence probes; principal angles among their directions and joint predictive gain. Decisive metric: held-out AUROC of the readiness probe, first; plus its principal angle to the difficulty and confidence directions. Convincing: readiness AUROC >= 0.7 at the best layer, the readiness direction not collinear with difficulty or confidence (angle >= 30 degrees to each), adding significant R2 over both - establishing that readiness is decodable even at onsets the model then treats as inversions (an unconsulted signal). Indecision band: AUROC 0.6-0.7, or angle 20-30 degrees, is a present-but-entangled signal. Negative result: AUROC < 0.6, or collinearity with difficulty/confidence (angle < 20 degrees), means there is no distinct readiness signal, refuting H3.

Experiment 4 (H3 causal - patching readiness redirects the model to a ready subgoal): Tests whether the readiness representation causally governs which subgoal is attacked. Data: 150 premature-onset contexts (subset of Experiment 1) where a dependency-ready subgoal is also available; frozen 7B with a 1.5B replication. Intervention: patch a high-readiness state (from a context where a ready subgoal is available) into the premature-onset context at the Experiment-3 layer and test whether the model switches to a dependency-ready subgoal (inversion avoided, tokens dropped). Controls: matched-random-direction patch of equal norm; off-target accuracy on held-out problems preserved. Systems compared: real readiness patch vs random-direction control vs no intervention. Decisive metric: fraction of premature onsets redirected to a dependency-ready subgoal under patching, first; secondary token reduction, with accuracy held within +/-1 point. Convincing: real patching redirects >= 50% of premature onsets and reduces tokens while the random control redirects < 15% and accuracy is preserved, monotone in dose. Indecision band: a 20-50% redirection, or a random-control effect of 15-25%, is partial/ambiguous mediation. Negative result: < 20% redirection or the random control matching the real direction means readiness is correlational not causal, refuting H3's causal reading.

Experiment 5 (H4 - a scheduling steer cuts tokens at equal accuracy): Tests the training-free intervention. Data: full templated set (300), puzzles (200), GSM8K sample (400), MATH500 sample (300) on the 7B model (with 1.5B and 14B-subsample replications). Online, at each subgoal onset the readiness probe is read; when it predicts low readiness (an impending inversion), a steer is applied - steering along the readiness direction, or injecting a terse 'first establish prerequisites' cue - to defer the premature subgoal. Systems compared: scheduling steer vs no intervention vs length-aware filtering vs reactive pruning vs decorative-step skipping vs fixed truncation. Decisive metric: token reduction at matched accuracy (accuracy within 1 point of no-intervention), first; secondary inversion-rate reduction and wall-clock speedup, on overall and hardest strata. Convincing: the scheduling steer cuts mean thinking tokens by >= 15% within 1 point of baseline accuracy and beats the length-aware and reactive-pruning baselines at matched accuracy, with a measurable inversion-rate drop. Indecision band: a 5-15% token reduction, or parity with (not beating) the strongest baseline, is a marginal result. Negative result: < 5% reduction or > 2 point accuracy loss means scheduling steering is not an efficiency win, refuting H4.

Experiment 6 (H4 specificity and generalization - beneficial-exploration guard and transfer): Tests that suppressing inversions does not remove genuinely useful exploration, and whether probe/steer transfer. Data: reuses Experiment 5 runs plus a hand-labeled subset where an apparent inversion is beneficial exploration (the model probes a subgoal to discover its prerequisites). Transfer: apply the 7B-derived readiness probe and steer to 1.5B and 14B and across datasets without refitting; correlate inversion rate with DAG width/depth. Systems compared: steer with vs without the beneficial-exploration guard threshold; in-model vs transferred probe/steer; low- vs high-width/depth DAGs. Decisive metric: accuracy on beneficial-exploration items under the guarded steer, first; plus transferred-probe AUROC relative to in-model and the inversion-rate/DAG-complexity correlation. Convincing: the guarded steer preserves beneficial-exploration accuracy within 1 point of no-intervention while still cutting tokens elsewhere, transferred probe retains >= 70% of in-model AUROC, and inversion rate rises with DAG width/depth. Indecision band: transferred AUROC 40-70% of in-model, or a beneficial-exploration accuracy loss of 1-3 points, is weak/partial. Negative result: the guard failing to protect beneficial exploration (> 3 point loss) or transferred AUROC < 40% means the intervention is unsafe or idiosyncratic, bounding H4's scope.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Annotating a ground-truth subgoal DAG for open math is noisy; we anchor the strongest claims on templated problems and puzzles with known structure, using GSM8K/MATH500 as corroboration with human-validated annotations. Aligning generated subgoals to DAG nodes is imperfect; we use semantic matching + LLM-judge with agreement reporting. Some scheduling 'inversions' may be legitimate exploration (probing a subgoal to learn its prerequisites), so suppressing them could hurt accuracy; the failure analysis and steer thresholds explicitly guard this, and finding that inversions are largely beneficial would be an informative negative result. The readiness signal may be inseparable from generic difficulty/confidence, weakening the mechanistic framing; the separability analysis and causal patching address this. Steering could push activations off-distribution and introduce errors; matched-random-direction controls and sample-validity checks are included. Intervention gains may not exceed strong length-aware or pruning baselines, but the scheduling-failure diagnosis (a named, quantifiable, dependency-structured source of overthinking) is a standalone contribution. Results may be model-family and scale specific, and reasoning-length measurement requires clear think/answer delimiters; truncate-and-resume is compute-heavy, so we subsample.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims that need to be novel: (1) reasoning models exhibit a systematic subgoal-ordering failure, i.e. they begin subgoals before prerequisites are established; (2) this yields measurable token waste/overthinking beyond generic length or redundancy effects; (3) a decodable prerequisite-readiness signal exists at subgoal onset and is not consulted; (4) intervening on scheduling/order (not just stopping or pruning) reduces tokens without accuracy loss; (5) the phenomenon is distinct from external multi-call agent planning and from prior DAG probing. The closest prior family is agent/planning work on task decomposition, DAG plans, dependency scheduling, and probing for reasoning-DAG geometry / weak global planning. The actual delta is moving the claim inside a single CoT trace and tying it to a causal, decodable readiness signal plus an efficiency intervention. That is a meaningful shift, not just a new benchmark. Main novelty risk: some parts may collapse to a rebranding of known myopia/global-planning weaknesses, unless the paper cleanly shows a distinct, quantifiable inversion phenomenon and causal readiness gating.
revision_notes: Make the novelty hinge on one crisp, falsifiable definition of 'subgoal inversion' and show it is not reducible to length, backtracking, or generic planning weakness.
Explicitly separate this from external agent-planning / multi-call scheduling in the related work and in the contribution statement.
State the closest prior work family and the exact delta in one sentence: within-trace dependency-order failure + decodable readiness + compute-saving intervention.
Be careful not to overclaim 'first' unless you can show the phenomenon and intervention are both new, not just the framing.

impact.reasoning: The problem is important to efficient reasoning and interpretability: wasted tokens during CoT is a real cost, and a dependency-aware explanation for overthinking would matter to model providers and reasoning researchers. Who cares: people optimizing inference cost, interpreting reasoning traces, and building planners/agents. Strongest one-line case: 'A large share of overthinking is not extra thinking but thinking in the wrong order, and fixing order saves compute without hurting accuracy.' Impact is real but not broad-general-purpose unless the token savings are substantial and transfer across models/tasks. It is more phenomenon-/mechanism-valued than immediately product-shifting. Uptake is plausible if the paper gives a clean diagnostic and an actionable steering method, but it remains somewhat niche to reasoning-model internals rather than end-user tasks.
revision_notes: Quantify practical significance early: expected token savings, accuracy parity, and cost reduction on representative models.
Frame the user-facing consequence as inference efficiency on reasoning models, not just an internal interpretability story.
Highlight whether the intervention is training-free and model-agnostic; that affects adoption.
If possible, include a simple cost/latency conversion to make the impact concrete.

review.reasoning: The proposal has a coherent hypothesis, but several methodological gaps could undermine it. The biggest issue is operationalizing ground-truth subgoal DAGs and aligning generated steps to nodes; this is central and currently under-specified. A second gap is causal interpretation: a linear probe on readiness may just recover difficulty/confidence or generic progress, so separability controls need to be very strong. Third, the claim that inversions cause wasted tokens needs a clean counterfactual; truncate-and-resume and re-derivation detection may be noisy and confounded by prompt length, solution style, and model verbosity. Fourth, the steering intervention risks being an opaque prompt hack unless it is shown to specifically alter ordering rather than just shorten outputs. The experiments are ambitious and mostly feasible, but several are too many for a paper unless the core tests are prioritized. Venue strength depends on whether the paper can nail one robust diagnostic + one causal intervention with strong controls on templated tasks and one corroborating real benchmark. Minimum viable edit: narrow to one or two datasets with known/validated DAGs, one main metric (inversion rate and token waste), one probe, and one intervention, plus thorough ablations against length, confidence, difficulty, and exploration.
