Name: conciseness_capability_entanglement
Title: The Conciseness Cliff: Why Global Brevity Steering Fails Because the Concise Direction Is Entangled with Difficulty-Appropriate Elaboration
Short Hypothesis: Training-free brevity steering has a sharp accuracy cliff not because the steering strength is mis-tuned, but because the 'concise-reasoning' direction is geometrically entangled with a 'difficulty-appropriate elaboration' capability in the same activation subspace: pushing toward brevity necessarily suppresses the model's own signal for when a problem needs more thinking. Disentangling brevity from this elaboration component yields steering that compresses easy reasoning while preserving hard-problem elaboration, eliminating the cliff.
Related Work: A wave of training-free brevity-steering methods treat conciseness as a single (often linear) direction to inject: ASC (steer residual stream, KL-bounded strength), Efficiency Steering (single contrastive direction), FlowSteer (nonlinear flow-matching transport), STU-PID (PID-controlled adaptive strength), and GLoRE (long-CoT is a general, transferable capability across domains). All of these either (a) assume brevity is a clean, universally-good direction and manage only its magnitude, or (b) add an external controller/classifier to modulate strength reactively. None asks WHY fixed steering has an accuracy cliff at the mechanistic level, nor whether the brevity direction is intrinsically coupled to the model's internal 'how much to elaborate' signal. GLoRE shows the long-CoT capability is a general encoded direction; we hypothesize the concise direction partially anti-aligns with a difficulty-appropriate elaboration capability, so global steering is not merely too strong but structurally destructive on hard problems. Our contribution is a mechanistic account of the failure mode (entanglement), a geometric measurement of it (principal angles / overlap between the brevity direction and an elaboration-capability direction), and a disentangled steering intervention that removes the harmful component — distinct from all prior 'steer harder / steer adaptively' methods.
Abstract: Training-free brevity steering promises to cut reasoning tokens with no retraining, but every method shares a fragile behavior: past a threshold, accuracy collapses sharply, especially on hard problems. Prior work manages this only by tuning or adaptively controlling the steering magnitude. We propose a mechanistic explanation: the 'concise-reasoning' steering direction is geometrically entangled with a difficulty-appropriate elaboration capability the model uses to decide how much to think, so pushing toward brevity does not merely shorten output — it suppresses the internal signal that hard problems need more reasoning. This predicts an asymmetric cliff (harmless on easy problems, destructive on hard ones) and explains why global steering is brittle. Across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we (1) reproduce the brevity direction (ASC/Efficiency-Steering style) and map the accuracy-vs-strength cliff stratified by difficulty; (2) extract an elaboration-capability direction (contrasting hard-solved-with-long-reasoning vs easy-solved-short traces) and measure geometric overlap/anti-alignment with the brevity direction via principal angles; (3) causally test entanglement by projecting the brevity direction into the elaboration-orthogonal subspace and steering; and (4) show disentangled steering compresses easy reasoning while preserving hard-problem elaboration, flattening the cliff versus ASC, Efficiency Steering, and STU-PID. Our work reframes the brevity-accuracy tradeoff as a representational entanglement problem and offers an interpretable, training-free fix.
Experiments:
All experiments run on open reasoning models with explicit think/answer delimiters: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen at 1.5B, 7B, and 14B, plus Qwen3-8B (thinking mode). Weights are frozen; only difference-of-means steering directions and linear probes are fit. Decoding is temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 8192 thinking tokens, 5 samples per problem with seeds {0,1,2,3,4}; accuracy is mean exact-match and length the mean thinking-token count. Difficulty strata are set by empirical per-problem pass-rate plus benchmark-provided levels: GSM8K and MATH500 (levels 1-2) as the easy strata, AIME 2024+2025 and GPQA-Diamond (and MATH500 level 5) as the hard strata. Everything fits one 80GB GPU; 14B runs on reduced subsets as noted.

Experiment 1 (H1 - the brevity-steering accuracy cliff is asymmetric, hitting hard problems earlier): Tests whether a reproduced brevity direction produces a sharper, earlier accuracy cliff on hard problems than easy ones. Data: existing sets used as is - GSM8K test (1319; sample 400 for the easy stratum), MATH500 (500; all, stratified by level), AIME 2024+2025 (60; all), GPQA-Diamond (198; all). The brevity direction is extracted by difference-of-means over paired verbose/concise traces on a held-out 300-problem calibration set (ASC / Efficiency-Steering protocol), disjoint from the evaluation sets. Systems compared: increasing steering strength (a sweep of >= 8 magnitudes) within each difficulty stratum. Decisive metric: the steering strength at which each stratum's accuracy drops 5 points from its unsteered baseline (the cliff onset), first; plus the mean-token reduction at that strength. Convincing: the hard-stratum cliff onset occurs at a steering strength at least 2x smaller than the easy-stratum onset (the predicted asymmetry), replicated on at least the 7B and 14B models. Indecision band: a hard/easy onset ratio between 1.3x and 2x is weak asymmetry that does not firmly establish H1. Negative result: a ratio below 1.3x (the cliff hits both strata at similar strength) means the cliff is not difficulty-asymmetric, refuting H1 and pointing to a pure magnitude/off-distribution cause.

Experiment 2 (H2 location - an elaboration-capability direction exists and predicts difficulty-appropriate length): Tests whether a difference-of-means 'difficulty-appropriate elaboration' direction can be extracted and validated. Data: correctness-conditioned contrastive pairs from the Experiment 1 sets - hard problems solved correctly with long reasoning vs easy problems solved correctly with short reasoning - to isolate elaboration from mere errors; per layer difference-of-means gives the elaboration direction, with a 70/15/15 split by problem identity. Model: frozen DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (primary), layer sweep. Validation: (i) steering along the elaboration direction should lengthen reasoning preferentially on problems the model treats as hard; (ii) a probe along it should predict per-problem reasoning length beyond a raw difficulty probe (pass-rate). Systems compared: elaboration probe vs raw difficulty probe. Decisive metric: incremental R2 of the elaboration direction for predicting reasoning length over the difficulty probe on held-out problems, first; plus the hard-vs-easy differential lengthening when steering along it. Convincing: the elaboration direction adds >= 0.05 R2 over difficulty and lengthens hard-problem reasoning significantly more than easy-problem reasoning. Indecision band: incremental R2 0.02-0.05 is a present-but-weakly-distinct direction. Negative result: incremental R2 < 0.02 (the elaboration direction is indistinguishable from raw difficulty) undercuts the entanglement claim's second term and weakens H2.

Experiment 3 (H2 geometry - the brevity direction is anti-aligned with the elaboration direction): Tests whether the two directions overlap geometrically rather than being orthogonal. Data: the brevity direction (Experiment 1) and elaboration direction (Experiment 2) per layer on the 7B model (with 1.5B and 14B for stability). Systems compared: the brevity/elaboration principal angle (and signed cosine) against a matched-random-direction null distribution of equal dimension. We also decompose the brevity direction into its projection onto the elaboration direction (candidate harmful component) and its orthogonal complement (candidate benign compression component). Decisive metric: the cosine overlap (signed) between brevity and elaboration relative to the random-direction null, first. Convincing: the brevity direction is significantly anti-aligned with elaboration (negative cosine whose magnitude exceeds the 99th percentile of the random-null overlap) at the layers where steering is applied. Indecision band: an overlap magnitude between the 90th and 99th percentile of the null is weak entanglement. Negative result: overlap within the null (below the 90th percentile) means the directions are effectively orthogonal, refuting the entanglement mechanism of H2 (and implying the cliff is a pure magnitude effect).

Experiment 4 (H2 causal - the elaboration-parallel component of brevity causes the cliff): Tests whether the harmful damage comes specifically from the entangled component. Data: 200 problems spanning easy and hard strata (subset of Experiment 1); frozen 7B with a 1.5B replication. Systems compared, all at matched dose sweeps: (a) steering along the full brevity direction, (b) along the elaboration-orthogonal component only, (c) along the elaboration-parallel component only, plus matched-random-projection controls of equal norm. Decisive metric: hard-stratum accuracy drop per unit compression for each component, first (i.e., accuracy cost at matched token savings). Convincing: the parallel component (c) reproduces most (>= 60%) of the full direction's hard-stratum accuracy damage while giving little compression, and the orthogonal component (b) delivers comparable compression to the full direction with a hard-stratum cliff onset at least 2x later, both beyond the random-projection controls. Indecision band: the parallel component carrying 30-60% of the damage is partial support for the entanglement-causes-cliff claim. Negative result: the parallel component causing < 30% of the damage, or the orthogonal component not deferring the cliff, means the cliff is not driven by the entangled component, refuting the causal core of H2.

Experiment 5 (H3 - disentangled steering compresses easy reasoning while preserving hard elaboration, flattening the cliff): Tests the training-free fix. Data: full GSM8K sample (400), MATH500 (500), AIME (60), GPQA (198) on the 7B model (with 1.5B and 14B-subsample replications). Intervention: steer along the elaboration-orthogonal brevity component, optionally difficulty-gated using the elaboration probe. Systems compared: disentangled steering vs no steering vs full-direction ASC vs Efficiency Steering vs STU-PID vs fixed truncation (FlowSteer included only if reproducible in budget). Decisive metric: hard-stratum cliff position (steering strength at which hard-stratum accuracy drops 5 points) for disentangled vs full-direction steering, first; plus token-reduction-at-equal-accuracy overall and per stratum. Convincing: disentangled steering Pareto-dominates full-direction steering - at matched overall token savings its hard-stratum accuracy drop is smaller by >= 3 points and its cliff onset is >= 2x later - and it matches or beats STU-PID at equal accuracy. Indecision band: a 1-3 point hard-stratum accuracy advantage, or parity with (not beating) STU-PID, is a marginal win. Negative result: no Pareto improvement over full-direction steering (hard-stratum advantage < 1 point) means disentangling does not remove the cliff, refuting H3.

Experiment 6 (H3 generalization - the fix and the entanglement geometry transfer across datasets and scales): Tests whether the directions and intervention transfer without recomputation and whether the geometry is stable. Data: reuses Experiment 1-5 directions. Transfer: apply the 7B-derived brevity and elaboration directions and the disentangled intervention to 1.5B and 14B and across datasets without recomputing them; measure the brevity/elaboration overlap across the four models. Systems compared: in-model vs transferred directions; overlap geometry across model families. Decisive metric: the disentangled intervention's cliff-flattening advantage under transferred directions relative to in-model, first; plus the cross-model consistency of the anti-alignment sign. Convincing: transferred directions retain >= 70% of the in-model hard-stratum advantage and the anti-alignment sign is consistent across all four models. Indecision band: transferred advantage 40-70% of in-model, or the sign consistent on three of four models, is weak generalization. Negative result: transferred advantage < 40% or an inconsistent anti-alignment sign means the entanglement geometry is model-specific and the fix does not transfer, bounding the claim's scope.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The brevity and elaboration directions may turn out to be largely orthogonal (no entanglement), refuting the mechanistic claim — this would be an informative negative result showing the cliff is purely a magnitude/off-distribution effect, and prior adaptive-strength methods (STU-PID) already suffice. The elaboration direction may be inseparable from a raw difficulty direction; we control by comparing predictive gain over a difficulty probe and by using correctness-conditioned contrasts. Projecting the brevity direction into a subspace may itself push activations off-distribution and reduce compression benefit, narrowing the Pareto gain; we sweep and report validity. Difficulty stratification for open math is noisy; we use empirical pass-rates and benchmark-provided levels. Reproducing FlowSteer/other baselines may be infeasible in an academic budget; we prioritize ASC, Efficiency Steering, and STU-PID as the core comparisons. Results may be model-family and scale specific, and the entanglement magnitude may vary with instruction/RL tuning. Reasoning-length measurement requires clear think/answer delimiters.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims: (1) the brevity/concise-reasoning steering direction is entangled with a latent 'difficulty-appropriate elaboration' capability; (2) the observed accuracy cliff is caused by suppressing that capability rather than by mis-set steering strength alone; (3) projecting out the elaboration component yields better compression-accuracy tradeoff and removes the cliff; (4) this entanglement is measurable geometrically (angles/overlap) and causally via component-wise steering; (5) the effect transfers across open reasoning models. Relative to the crowded prior work on FlowSteer/ASC/STU-PID, the novelty is not in concise steering itself, nor in adaptive/nonlinear fixes, but in a mechanistic explanation of why the cliff happens. That is a plausible new explanation/finding, but it is close to prior observations that stronger brevity steering harms robustness/specificity. The setting is meaningfully different only if the disentanglement is shown to be a specific internal factor rather than another reparameterization of steering strength. The core claim is non-trivial, but the space already contains evidence of the cliff and several methods that implicitly address it, so novelty is moderate rather than high. Closest prior family: inference-time brevity steering with linear/nonlinear/adaptive intervention. Actual delta: causal/mechanistic decomposition of the briefness direction into harmful and benign components tied to difficulty-aware elaboration.

The phenomenon-value is decent, but direction-shifting impact is limited because the prior art already noticed the cliff and has working fixes; this mainly clarifies and refines that line of work rather than opening a new domain.

Name: verification_recency_gradient
Title: Checking Least Where It Matters Most: A Verification-Effort Gradient That Leaves Late Reasoning Steps Fragile
Short Hypothesis: Reasoning models allocate progressively less self-verification effort to later steps of a chain of thought (a verification recency gradient), yet late steps are exactly where an injected error is most likely to corrupt the final answer (late-stage fragility). This mismatch is not a capability ceiling but an allocation failure: the model carries a decodable, monotonically-decaying internal 'verification-engagement' signal, and reallocating verification effort toward late steps repairs fragility at little extra cost.
Related Work: Two threads collide in the recent literature but have never been unified. (1) ASCoT (2025) documents 'Late-Stage Fragility': errors injected late in a CoT corrupt the final answer far more than identical early errors, contradicting the cascading-failure view; it fixes this with an external position-weighted correction pipeline. Snowball-error and Deductive-Verification work (2023-2026) instead assume early errors dominate and add step-verifiers. (2) NLDD/Reasoning-Horizon (2026) and Thought Anchors (2025) show late steps often have low or negative causal influence and that planning/uncertainty (early) steps carry the most counterfactual importance. Serial-position and Lost-in-the-Middle work (2025) shows primacy/recency biases in input processing. NONE of these ask whether the model's OWN self-verification effort is distributed unevenly across chain position, nor connect a verification-effort gradient to late-stage fragility as its cause. All prior fixes are external (verifiers, correction managers, position-weighted reward). Our contribution is (a) a new behavioral phenomenon: a monotonic verification-effort decay across the chain that anti-aligns with the fragility profile; (b) a mechanistic account via a decodable, decaying verification-engagement signal; and (c) a training-free internal reallocation that repairs late fragility, distinct from external correction pipelines. This is also orthogonal to my prior proposals, which concern stopping, decorative steps, recompute, uncertainty staleness, and framing effects, not the positional distribution of verification effort.
Abstract: Recent work reveals a paradox in chain-of-thought reasoning: errors introduced late in a reasoning chain are far more likely to corrupt the final answer than early ones (late-stage fragility), even though late steps often carry little causal influence. We propose an explanation that unifies these findings: reasoning models spend less self-verification effort as the chain progresses, so the model checks least exactly where a mistake is most catastrophic. We call this the verification recency gradient. Across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we first quantify per-position verification behavior (rate of rechecks/backtracks/self-affirmations, detected via lexical cues plus a reflection-direction classifier) and show it decays monotonically with normalized chain position. We independently measure a fragility profile via controlled error injection at each position (ASCoT protocol) and show it rises late, so effort and fragility are anti-aligned. We then test a mechanistic account: a linear probe on the residual stream at each step boundary decodes a verification-engagement signal that decays with position and predicts both local verification behavior and local fragility, separably from a difficulty or confidence probe. We causally validate via activation patching (patching an early high-engagement state into a late position increases verification and reduces late fragility) and via a training-free intervention that steers verification engagement upward on late steps, testing whether it repairs fragility with minimal added tokens. Our work reframes late-stage fragility as a positional verification-allocation failure with a decodable, steerable internal cause.
Experiments:
All experiments use open reasoning models run with fixed decoding (temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95 for generation-based measurements; greedy for deterministic re-runs) and are repeated over 3 generation seeds (0,1,2); all model weights are frozen throughout (no fine-tuning anywhere in this proposal) except linear probes, which are the only trainable parameters. Model families and scales: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen at 1.5B, 7B, and 14B, plus Qwen3-8B (thinking mode). Datasets, all public with clear think/answer delimiters: GSM8K test (1319 items), MATH500 (500 items), AIME 2024+2025 (60 items total), GPQA-Diamond (198 items). Unless stated, we sample generations per item and segment the chain-of-thought into steps by the models' native newline/step delimiters; 'normalized position' bins each step into deciles of its fractional location in the chain so chains of different length are comparable.

Experiment 1 (H1 — verification recency gradient): Tests whether self-verification effort decays monotonically across normalized chain position. Data: existing sets used as-is (GSM8K 1319, MATH500 500, AIME 60, GPQA 198); we generate 3 chains per item per model. Verification events per step are detected by two independent methods for robustness: (a) a fixed lexical-cue lexicon ('let me check/verify/re-examine/wait/recompute/actually/double-check'), and (b) a reflection-direction classifier — a logistic-regression probe on the mean residual-stream activation of a step (mid-depth layer), trained on 800 human-or-LLM-labeled verification/non-verification steps held out from a separate 200-step test set on which we report the classifier's AUROC (usable only if AUROC >= 0.75; if 0.65-0.75 we report lexical results as primary; below 0.65 we drop method (b)). Systems compared: the four models across the four datasets, and within chain-length strata (short/medium/long tertiles) to rule out length confounds. Decisive metric FIRST: the slope of per-step verification rate regressed on normalized position (deciles), with 95% bootstrap CI over items. Convincing positive result: negative slope with CI excluding 0 in >=3 of 4 models on >=3 of 4 datasets, replicated across both detection methods and within each length stratum. Indecision band: any model whose slope CI half-width exceeds |slope| (i.e., CI overlaps 0) OR |slope| < 0.01 verification-events per decile is treated as 'no detectable gradient' for that model — if the majority of model/dataset cells fall in this band the gradient claim is unsupported. Negative result (flat or positive slope): the verification recency gradient does not exist, and H1 — and with it the paper's central premise — fails; we would report this as a null characterization.

Experiment 2 (H2 — late-stage fragility and anti-alignment): Tests whether an injected error late in the chain corrupts the final answer more than an identical-magnitude error early, and whether the fragility profile anti-aligns with the Experiment-1 effort profile. Data: existing sets, adapted by controlled error injection following the ASCoT protocol — for each item and each position decile we inject one semantically-plausible corruption (perturb a number, operation, or logical connective via templated rules), keep only injections an LLM-judge rates as locally coherent, then resume generation from the corrupted step. Compute budget forces subsampling: 300 GSM8K, 300 MATH500, all 60 AIME, all 198 GPQA, 3 seeds. Systems compared: fragility across position deciles, and per error type. Decisive metric FIRST: fragility(position) = final-answer accuracy drop caused by a magnitude-matched injected error at that position; and the Spearman correlation rho between fragility(position) and verification-rate(position) from Experiment 1. Convincing result: fragility rises with position (positive slope, CI excluding 0) AND rho <= -0.5 with CI excluding 0 in >=3 of 4 models. Indecision band: |rho| < 0.3, or fragility-slope CI overlapping 0 — in this band effort and fragility are not shown to be anti-aligned and the 'checks least where it matters most' framing is not established. Negative result (fragility flat or falling with position, or rho >= 0): the mismatch does not exist; H2 fails and the mechanistic/intervention experiments are not warranted.

Experiment 3 (H3 — allocation failure, not capability ceiling): Tests whether the effort decay survives after controlling for late steps being genuinely easier or having fewer error opportunities. Data: reuse Experiment-1 chains plus a per-step local-difficulty measure (truncate-and-resume: from each step boundary, measure residual work as expected tokens-to-answer and resume accuracy on 200 items/dataset) and a per-step error-opportunity count (number of numeric/logical tokens available to corrupt). Systems compared: raw effort-vs-position slope versus the slope of a regression of verification rate on position that additionally conditions on local difficulty and error-opportunity count. Decisive metric FIRST: the partial slope of verification rate on position after conditioning on difficulty and opportunity, with 95% CI. Convincing result: partial slope remains negative with CI excluding 0 and retains >=50% of the raw slope's magnitude — the decay is not explained by difficulty/opportunity, supporting 'allocation failure'. Indecision band: partial slope magnitude between 20% and 50% of raw with CI touching 0 — partially confounded, reported as such. Negative result (partial slope not distinguishable from 0, <20% of raw): the decay is difficulty-driven, i.e. a rational allocation rather than a failure; H3 fails and we report an informative null that reframes the phenomenon as justified.

Experiment 4 (H4 — decodable, monotonically-decaying verification-engagement signal): Tests whether a single linear direction in the residual stream decodes local verification behavior, decays with position, and predicts local fragility beyond difficulty and confidence probes. Data: step-boundary activations from Experiment-1 chains, labeled with (i) whether the next step verifies (from Experiment 1) and (ii) whether the step is fragile (from Experiment 2). Split by item into 70/15/15 train/val/test; the probe (logistic regression, L2, one direction per layer) is the only trainable component; layer sweep over all layers, 3 seeds. Systems compared: the verification-engagement probe versus a difficulty probe and a confidence/uncertainty probe trained on the same activations. Decisive metric FIRST: test AUROC for decoding local verification, plus (a) correlation of the probe's projection with normalized position and (b) incremental AUROC for predicting fragility when the engagement probe is added to a model already containing difficulty+confidence probes. Convincing result: verification-decoding AUROC >= 0.70; projection-vs-position correlation <= -0.4 (CI excluding 0); incremental fragility AUROC gain >= 0.03 with CI excluding 0; and principal angle between engagement and confidence directions large enough that they are not collinear (>= 20 degrees). Indecision band: decoding AUROC 0.60-0.70, or incremental gain 0.01-0.03, or principal angle 10-20 degrees — signal present but weak/entangled, reported as suggestive not established. Negative result (AUROC ~0.5, no position decay, no incremental gain, angle < 10 degrees): there is no separable decaying engagement signal; H4 fails and the causal/steering experiments lose their basis.

Experiment 5 (H4 causal — patching engagement rescues late steps): Tests whether the engagement signal is causal, not merely correlational, by activation patching. Data: 200 items/dataset with injected late errors (from Experiment 2). Intervention: patch the residual-stream state at the engagement-carrying components (localized by activation patching across layers/positions) from an EARLY high-engagement step into a LATE step boundary; frozen weights. Systems compared: (i) no patch, (ii) engagement patch, (iii) matched random-direction patch of equal norm, (iv) off-target control measuring accuracy on uncorrupted items. Decisive metric FIRST: change in late-step fragility (probability an injected late error is caught/corrected) under the engagement patch versus controls, with dose-response over patch strength. Convincing result: engagement patch raises catch/correct rate by >= 5 absolute points with CI excluding 0, a monotone dose-response, no comparable effect from the random-direction patch, and off-target accuracy preserved within 1 point. Indecision band: effect 2-5 points, or a random-direction patch producing >=50% of the engagement effect — causality not cleanly established. Negative result (no effect, or non-specific effect matched by random direction): the signal is not causal for verification; H4's causal claim fails though the decoding result may still stand.

Experiment 6 (H5 — training-free late-step reallocation repairs fragility at little cost): Tests whether steering engagement upward on the late portion of the chain repairs late fragility more token-efficiently than alternatives. Data: full evaluation sets (GSM8K 1319, MATH500 500, AIME 60, GPQA 198), 3 seeds; fragility re-measured by re-running the Experiment-2 injection under each condition on the same 300/300/60/198 subset. Intervention: add the Experiment-4 engagement steering direction (difference-of-means, high minus low engagement) to the residual stream on the last 20-30% of steps (or when the position probe fires); frozen weights; steering coefficient swept. Systems compared: (a) no intervention, (b) uniform engagement boosting across all positions, (c) external ASCoT-style position-weighted correction, (d) prompt-only ('carefully re-check your final steps'), (e) our late-targeted steering. Decisive metric FIRST: late-fragility reduction at matched accuracy, and tokens-at-fixed-accuracy (added tokens needed to reach a target accuracy). Convincing result: late-targeted steering reduces late fragility by >= 5 absolute points while adding fewer tokens than uniform boosting (>=20% fewer at equal fragility reduction) and matching or beating the external pipeline on accuracy — establishing 'repairs fragility at little extra cost'. Indecision band: fragility reduction 2-5 points, or token savings vs uniform boosting < 10% — the efficiency advantage is not established and H5's 'little extra cost' claim is unsupported at that operating point. Negative result (no fragility reduction, or more tokens than uniform boosting for equal gain, or worse than prompting): reallocation does not help; H5 fails, though Experiments 1-2 (the phenomenon) remain standalone contributions.

Experiment 7 (H5 specificity — no over-correction): Tests that late-step boosting does not induce harmful oscillation/underthinking on easy items or degrade early verification. Data: the 40% easiest items (by Experiment-3 difficulty) from each set. Decisive metric FIRST: over-correction rate (fraction of originally-correct easy items flipped to wrong under the intervention) and change in early-position verification rate. Convincing result: over-correction rate <= 2% and early verification unchanged within noise. Indecision band: over-correction 2-5% — a real but tolerable cost, reported alongside the Experiment-6 gains. Negative result (over-correction > 5% or early verification degraded): the intervention trades late fragility for new easy-item errors, bounding its usefulness.

Experiment 8 (H4/H5 generalization — transfer without retraining): Tests whether the engagement probe and steering direction transfer across datasets and scales. Data: probe/direction fit on one dataset+model, applied unchanged to the others. Decisive metric FIRST: cross-dataset decoding AUROC and cross-dataset late-fragility reduction under transferred steering, plus the correlation across the four models between gradient steepness (Experiment-1 slope) and fragility severity (Experiment-2 slope). Convincing result: transferred AUROC within 0.05 of in-domain, transferred fragility reduction >= half the in-domain effect, and steepness-vs-severity correlation >= 0.5. Indecision band: transferred effect between one-quarter and one-half of in-domain, or steepness-severity correlation 0.3-0.5 — partial transfer, reported as scale/family-specific. Negative result (no transfer, correlation ~0): the signal and gradient are idiosyncratic per model/dataset, which we report as a characterization of the phenomenon's boundaries.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Verification-event detection is noisy (lexical + classifier); we validate against human-labeled steps and report agreement, and use two detection methods for robustness. The effort decay could be legitimately justified if late steps are genuinely easier or less error-prone; the difficulty-control and residual-work analyses address this, and a null after controls (decay is difficulty-driven) would be an informative negative result. Error-injection fragility is sensitive to how 'matched' injected errors are across positions; we use templated, magnitude-matched perturbations with LLM-judge coherence checks and report per-error-type results. The verification-engagement signal may be inseparable from a generic uncertainty/confidence direction; the separability analysis and causal patching guard against this, and overlap would still be a mechanistic finding. Steering late engagement could trigger over-verification/oscillation (added tokens or new errors); the specificity and over-correction analyses and dose sweeps quantify this trade-off. Reasoning-length/position measurement requires clear think/answer delimiters; error injection and truncate-and-resume are compute-heavy, so we subsample. The intervention may not beat strong external correction baselines on accuracy alone, but the phenomenon (verification effort anti-aligned with fragility) and its decodable, steerable internal cause are standalone contributions. Effects may be model-family and scale specific, and the direction of the gradient could vary across architectures (itself a publishable characterization).

novelty.reasoning: Core novel claims are: (1) a monotonic positional decay in self-verification effort within CoT, (2) a decodable residual-stream "verification-engagement" signal that tracks this decay, and (3) a training-free internal steering fix that reallocates verification late. Relative to ASCoT and nearby verifier/causal-influence work, the delta is not just a new setting but a new mechanistic account plus internal control. The main risk to novelty is that the signal may collapse into generic confidence/uncertainty, and the phenomenon may reduce to a re-description of known recency/causal-importance effects.

Name: dimensional_consistency_blindspot
Title: Right Number, Wrong Unit: An Internal Dimension Representation That Reasoning Models Encode But Fail to Consult
Short Hypothesis: Reasoning models internally encode the physical DIMENSION/unit-type of each quantity they manipulate (length vs time vs mass vs concentration), separately from its magnitude, but frequently fail to consult this representation at the moment a dimensionally-inconsistent operation is committed (adding incompatible units, dropping a conversion, reporting the wrong unit). This know-but-dont-check gap is decodable, causally real, and most dangerous in safety-critical domains like medication dosing; a cheap dimensional-consistency monitor built from the internal representation catches unit errors the model itself misses.
Related Work: Recent interpretability work shows LLMs linearly encode numerical LOG-MAGNITUDE (LLMs Know More About Numbers than They Can Say 2026; Number Representations as Human Mental Number Line 2025) and that irrelevant numerical context perturbs these magnitude representations (Interpreting Multi-Attribute Confounding 2025; Probing for Arithmetic Errors 2025). All of this concerns MAGNITUDE (how big a number is) and arithmetic correctness, never the physical DIMENSION/unit-TYPE of a quantity or dimensional consistency of operations. Separately, a large human-science education literature documents that unit/dimensional-analysis errors are pervasive and catastrophic in physics, engineering, and medicine (Using Math in Physics: Dimensional Analysis 2021; Check Your Work: Dimensional Homogeneity 2023; Metric Unit Conversion 2018), and that dimensional homogeneity is a powerful, underused error check. No prior work asks whether LLMs maintain an internal dimension representation, whether they use it to enforce dimensional consistency, or where dimensional errors originate mechanistically. We transfer the human-science phenomenon of dimensional-blindness into LLMs and into the highest-stakes domain (medication dosing), reframing the known know-but-cant-say magnitude gap as a know-but-dont-CHECK gap for units. This is a new phenomenon (dimensional-consistency blindness), a new internal representation (unit-type, distinct from magnitude), and a safety-critical decision-auditing angle, distinct from all prior magnitude/arithmetic probing.
Abstract: Human students and even engineers routinely make dimensional errors—adding a length to a time, forgetting a unit conversion, reporting an answer in the wrong unit—and dimensional-consistency checking is a classic remedy. We ask whether reasoning language models exhibit the same blind spot and, mechanistically, why. We hypothesize that models internally encode the physical DIMENSION (unit-type: length, time, mass, concentration, dose-per-mass, etc.) of each quantity they handle, separately from its numerical magnitude, but frequently fail to consult this representation at the point where a dimensionally-inconsistent operation is committed. We test this on templated unit-conversion and multi-step physics/engineering word problems, and—where the stakes are highest—on medication-dosing scenarios (mg vs mg/kg vs mL, unit-conversion traps) using open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3). We first quantify a dimensional-error rate and show it is distinct from magnitude/arithmetic errors: models often compute the right number but attach or combine the wrong units. We then train lightweight linear probes at reasoning-step boundaries to decode the unit-type of the current working quantity, test that this dimension representation is separable from the magnitude representation, and show it is often internally correct even on steps where the model commits a dimensional error—the know-but-dont-check gap. We localize the representation and causally validate it via activation patching (patch the correct unit-type in and observe the error avoided) and steering. Finally we build a training-free dimensional-consistency monitor that reads the internal unit-type at each step and flags incompatible operations, catching dosing errors the model misses at low token cost. Our work reveals a safety-critical dimensional blind spot and traces it to an unconsulted internal representation.
Experiments:
All experiments use open reasoning models with frozen weights (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B/7B/14B and Qwen3-8B thinking mode); the only trainable parameters anywhere are linear probes. Generation uses temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, 3 seeds (0,1,2). Because no public benchmark annotates per-step unit-types, we CONSTRUCT three sets with ground-truth dimension labels by construction and reuse their templates across all experiments: (S1) templated unit-conversion chains (km/h->m/s, nested SI-prefix conversions) — 1500 items generated from ~30 templates; (S2) multi-step physics/engineering word problems with known intermediate dimensions and correct final unit — 1000 items adapted from open physics-problem templates; (S3) medication-dosing scenarios (dose from weight in kg, concentration in mg/mL, dose in mg/kg, with g<->mg and mL<->L conversion traps) — 800 items from ~20 clinician-reviewed templates. Steps are segmented by native delimiters. 'Current working quantity' and its true unit-type are known from the template generator, removing annotation ambiguity.

Experiment 1 (H2 — dimensional-error phenomenon distinct from magnitude): Tests that models commit dimensional errors that are separate from arithmetic errors, i.e. often the right number with the wrong unit. Data: S1(1500), S2(1000), S3(800), 3 generations each. Each error is classified DIMENSIONAL (wrong unit-type / incompatible combination / missing conversion / wrong final unit) vs MAGNITUDE (right units, wrong number) by template-based parsing plus an LLM-judge, with human spot-checks on 300 items (report Cohen's kappa; parsing is primary if kappa>=0.7). Systems compared: the four models across the three sets. Decisive metric FIRST: the fraction of all errors that are dimensional AND numerically-correct ('right number, wrong unit'). Convincing result: this fraction is >= 15% of errors in >=3 of 4 models on >=2 of 3 sets, establishing dimensional errors as a non-trivial, distinct failure class. Indecision band: 5-15% — present but marginal, reported as a minor failure mode weakening the paper's premise. Negative result (< 5%, i.e. nearly all errors are arithmetic): there is no separate dimensional blind spot; the central premise fails and the mechanistic experiments are not pursued. We report dosing (S3) separately for its safety stakes.

Experiment 2 (H1 — dimension encoded separately from magnitude): Tests that a linear direction decodes the unit-type of the current working quantity, distinct from its magnitude. Data: step-boundary activations from Experiment-1 traces, labeled by true unit-type (classes: length/time/mass/volume/concentration/dose-per-mass/dimensionless/other); item-level 70/15/15 split; probe = multinomial logistic regression, L2, one per layer, layer sweep, 3 seeds. Systems compared: the unit-type probe versus a reproduced log-magnitude regressor on the same activations; and a critical lexical control — a probe trained where the unit STRING ('mg') is not token-adjacent and tested across notations/synonyms (mg vs milligram) to rule out reading the literal token. Decisive metric FIRST: unit-type classification accuracy (macro-F1) on held-out items, and the principal angle between the unit-type subspace and the magnitude direction. Convincing result: macro-F1 >= 0.70 (well above the majority-class baseline reported alongside), principal angle >= 30 degrees (not collinear with magnitude), and F1 drops by < 0.10 under the cross-notation lexical control. Indecision band: F1 0.55-0.70, or angle 15-30 degrees, or a lexical-control drop of 0.10-0.25 — dimension is encoded but weakly or partly lexically, reported as such. Negative result (F1 near majority baseline, or angle < 15 degrees, or F1 collapses under the lexical control): there is no abstract dimension representation separate from magnitude/token identity; H1 fails.

Experiment 3 (H2 — know-but-dont-check gap): Tests that on steps where the model commits a dimensional error, the internal unit-types of the input operands are nonetheless often correct. Data: from Experiment-1, the subset of steps flagged as dimensional errors (target >= 500 such steps aggregated across models/sets; if fewer, we report power limits) plus a matched set of correct steps. Read the Experiment-2 unit-type probe on the input operands just before the erroneous operation. Decisive metric FIRST: probe accuracy on the operands of error-committing steps (the internal unit-type is correct even though the executed operation is invalid). Convincing result: operand unit-type probe accuracy on error steps >= 0.60 and within 0.15 of its accuracy on correct steps — i.e. the information was available but unused, quantifying the gap. Indecision band: error-step probe accuracy 0.45-0.60 — the model may partly not know the units, blurring know-vs-dont-check; reported as ambiguous. Negative result (probe accuracy near chance on error steps): the model does NOT internally know the correct units when it errs, so this is a capability gap, not a consultation gap; H2's 'know-but-dont-check' framing fails (though the phenomenon and probe stand).

Experiment 4 (H3 — causal reality of the dimension representation): Tests that the unit-type representation causally controls whether the model commits the dimensional error. Data: 400 about-to-err steps identified in Experiment 3. Intervention: activation-patch the correct unit-type representation (from a matched correct-unit context) into the localized components at the erring step; frozen weights; dose-response over patch strength. Systems compared: (i) no patch, (ii) correct-unit patch, (iii) matched-random-direction patch of equal norm, (iv) off-target control on unrelated correct items. Decisive metric FIRST: reduction in dimensional-error rate at the patched step under the correct-unit patch versus controls. Convincing result: correct-unit patch cuts the dimensional-error rate by >= 10 absolute points with CI excluding 0, a monotone dose-response, no comparable effect from the random-direction patch, and off-target accuracy preserved within 1 point. Indecision band: 3-10 points, or random-direction patch reproducing >=50% of the effect — causality not cleanly shown. Negative result (no reduction, or non-specific): the representation is not causal for the error; H3 fails.

Experiment 5 (H5 — training-free dimensional-consistency monitor): Tests that a monitor reading the internal unit-type catches unit errors the model misses, more cheaply than prompting or post-hoc checking. Data: full S1/S2/S3, 3 seeds. Monitor: at each step boundary, read the Experiment-2 probe on the operands; flag when an operation combines incompatible dimensions or the running dimension diverges from the target answer's dimension, optionally triggering a unit-check re-derivation. Systems compared: (a) no monitor, (b) 'check your units' self-verification prompt, (c) the repurposed arithmetic-error probe from prior work, (d) an LLM-judge post-hoc checker, (e) our internal-representation monitor. Decisive metric FIRST: dimensional-error catch rate (recall of true dimensional errors) at matched false-flag rate on correct traces, plus corrected-answer rate after re-derivation and added tokens. Convincing result: the internal monitor achieves >= 15 points higher recall than the best baseline at equal false-flag rate (<= 5%), while adding fewer tokens than the post-hoc LLM checker. Indecision band: recall advantage 5-15 points, or false-flag rate 5-10% — useful but not decisively better, reported at its operating point. Negative result (no recall advantage, or false-flag rate > 10%): the internal representation gives no practical monitoring benefit; H5 fails though H1-H3 remain.

Experiment 6 (H4 — safety-critical dosing focus): Tests that the phenomenon and the monitor matter most in medication dosing. Data: S3 (800), with the subset of scenarios whose traps yield order-of-magnitude (10x) dosing errors from g/mg or mL/L confusion isolated. Decisive metric FIRST: catch rate of 10x dosing errors by the internal monitor versus baselines, and the residual dangerous-error rate after the monitor. Convincing result: the monitor catches >= 80% of 10x dosing errors at <= 5% false-flag, cutting residual dangerous errors by >= half relative to no monitor. Indecision band: catch rate 50-80% — meaningful but insufficient for the safety framing, reported with the residual failure modes catalogued. Negative result (< 50% caught): the monitor does not deliver the safety benefit the hypothesis claims for dosing; H4's practical claim fails. These are synthetic scenarios and are not clinical validation.

Experiment 7 (H1/H2 generalization and scale): Tests whether the probe and monitor transfer without retraining and whether the know-but-dont-check gap shrinks with scale. Data: probe/monitor fit on one set+model, applied unchanged to the others and across 1.5B->14B. Decisive metric FIRST: cross-set unit-type F1 and cross-set monitor recall under transfer, and the trend of the Experiment-3 gap (encode-well-but-consult-poorly) across model scale. Convincing result: transferred F1 within 0.10 of in-domain, transferred recall >= half the in-domain value, and a monotone shrink of the consultation gap from 1.5B to 14B. Indecision band: transfer at one-quarter to one-half of in-domain, or a non-monotone but downward scale trend — partial generalization, reported as scale/family-specific. Negative result (no transfer, flat scale trend): the representation and gap are idiosyncratic per model/set, reported as a boundary characterization.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Identifying the 'current working quantity' and annotating ground-truth unit-types at each step is nontrivial; we mitigate with templated problems (known dimensions by construction), parsing plus LLM-judge, and human validation with reported agreement. The unit-type representation may be inseparable from magnitude or from surface token identity of the unit string (a probe could just read the literal 'mg' token rather than an abstract dimension); we control by testing generalization across notations/synonyms (mg vs milligram), across problems where the unit token is not adjacent, and via the separability analysis and causal patching—if the signal is purely lexical that is an informative negative result. Dimensional errors may be rarer in strong models, limiting statistical power (itself a boundary-condition finding on the know-but-dont-check gap vs scale). The patching intervention could push activations off-distribution and introduce new errors; matched-random-direction controls and validity checks are included. The monitor may over-flag on legitimately dimensionless or context-dependent quantities (e.g., ratios), inflating false positives; we tune thresholds and report precision. Medication-dosing scenarios are synthetic and should not be treated as clinical validation—they demonstrate the failure mode, not a deployable clinical tool. Results may be model-family and scale specific, and reasoning-step segmentation requires clear delimiters.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims: (1) LMs encode physical unit-type/dimension separately from magnitude; (2) they often 'know but don't check' this representation at the commit point of a dimensionally invalid operation; (3) this can be causally demonstrated via patching/steering; (4) a lightweight monitor can detect unit-consistency errors, especially in dosing. Relative to prior work, the delta is real vs behavioral unit-error benchmarks and magnitude-only probing, but the idea is still a fairly natural extension of existing representation/probing and error-taxonomy lines. Novelty is strongest in the proposed representation/mechanism, not the task setting.

If true, serious researchers in interpretability and numerical reasoning would likely care, and the safety angle gives it broader reach. Still, the application domain is somewhat narrow and the dosing experiments are synthetic, so the real-world impact is meaningful but not field-shifting on its own.

Name: notation_mode_economy
Title: Thinking in Prose When Symbols Would Do: A Notation-Mode Representation That Sets a Surface-Form Compute Tax in Reasoning Models
Short Hypothesis: Reasoning models default to a verbose natural-language 'narration mode' for computations that could be expressed in a far terser symbolic/equational mode carrying the identical logical content, incurring a surface-notation compute tax independent of the problem's genuine reasoning depth. Which mode the model uses is set by a linearly-decodable notation-mode representation at the prompt boundary, before any reasoning token is emitted, and steering it toward the symbolic mode cuts tokens with minimal accuracy loss on symbol-amenable problems.
Related Work: Two literatures meet but never connect. (1) Notation/paradigm-choice work shows that natural-language vs symbolic reasoning changes ACCURACY and proposes external meta-selectors to pick a paradigm per problem (HybridMind 2024; Chain-of-Reasoning/CoR 2025; H-STAR 2024; Adaptive LLM-Symbolic Reasoning 2025; LLMs are In-Context Semantic rather than Symbolic Reasoners 2023). (2) CoT-compressibility work shows non-result 'glue' tokens are largely removable and that CoT tokens act like program variables (Chain-of-Thought Tokens are Computer Program Variables 2025; KisMATH 2025), and efficiency-steering work shows verbose vs concise paths are linearly separable and steerable (Efficiency Steering 2025; When More is Less 2025). Crucially, NO prior work (a) frames the model's SPONTANEOUS choice of surface notation as an inference-time COMPUTE tax measured on matched problems, (b) shows the model defaults to verbose narration even when a terse symbolic derivation carries the identical computation, (c) dissociates notation-mode from genuine reasoning depth, or (d) locates and causally steers a pre-generation notation-mode representation that sets it. Paradigm-selection work uses external selectors and targets accuracy, not internal cause or compute; compressibility work shows tokens CAN be removed post-hoc but does not identify a controllable internal mode. This is distinct from all my prior proposals (which concern answer-commitment, verification, length priors, framing, scheduling, dimensional units), which never touch surface-notation economy.
Abstract: Reasoning language models produce long chains of thought, and it is assumed their length reflects how much reasoning a problem requires. We identify a different, largely orthogonal source of waste: the SURFACE NOTATION the model chooses to think in. The same computation can be written as verbose natural-language narration ('First, we take the total number of apples, which is forty-two, and then we subtract the twelve that were given away...') or as a terse symbolic derivation ('42 - 12 = 30'), and we hypothesize that reasoning models default to the verbose narration mode even when the symbolic mode would carry identical logical content in a fraction of the tokens, incurring a notation compute tax independent of genuine reasoning depth. We further hypothesize that which mode is used is set before generation by a linearly-decodable notation-mode representation at the prompt boundary. Across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we (1) quantify per-problem notation verbosity (narration-to-symbol token ratio) and estimate the token savings of an equivalent symbolic rendering via matched terse re-derivations; (2) show the tax is dissociable from reasoning depth via a mixed-effects decomposition and truncate-and-resume minimal-solve length; (3) train linear probes on prompt-boundary activations to decode the notation mode and test separability from a difficulty probe; (4) causally validate via activation patching (patch a symbolic-mode state into a narration context and observe a mode switch); and (5) deploy a training-free notation-mode steer that induces symbolic reasoning on symbol-amenable problems, measuring tokens-at-equal-accuracy versus verbosity steering and terseness prompting. Our work reframes a slice of overthinking as a surface-notation choice with an identifiable, steerable internal cause, and maps the boundary where symbolic terseness starts to cost accuracy.
Experiments:
All experiments use frozen open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B/7B/14B, Qwen3-8B thinking mode); linear probes are the only trainable parameters. Generation: temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, 3 seeds (0,1,2). Datasets used as-is: GSM8K test (1319), MATH500 (500), AIME 2024+2025 (60), GPQA-Diamond (198). Chains are segmented into steps by native delimiters; each step is labeled narration / symbolic / mixed by regex (operators, equations, inequalities) plus an LLM-judge, with human spot-checks on 300 steps (report kappa; regex primary if kappa>=0.7). A per-problem 'symbol-amenability' label (does the solution reduce to a chain of equations/derivations?) is assigned by the same parser+judge.

Experiment 1 (H1 — notation compute tax): Tests whether models default to verbose narration on problems a terser symbolic derivation would solve with identical logical content. Data: all four sets, 3 generations each; for correct traces on symbol-amenable problems we build a matched terse symbolic re-rendering by prompting the model to rewrite ITS OWN correct solution as a compact symbolic derivation, keeping only rewrites the LLM-judge (plus human check on 200) certifies reach the same answer via the same step structure — rewrites that alter the reasoning are excluded, not counted as savings. Decisive metric FIRST: notation tax = narration tokens minus matched-symbolic tokens, as a fraction of narration tokens, on symbol-amenable problems. Convincing result: median tax >= 30% on symbol-amenable problems in >=3 of 4 models, with models emitting narration-dominant traces on a majority of highly symbol-amenable problems. Indecision band: median tax 10-30% — a real but modest tax, reported as limited. Negative result (< 10%, or models already default to symbolic): there is no surface-notation tax; H1 fails and the remaining experiments are not warranted.

Experiment 2 (H2 — dissociation from reasoning depth): Tests that the tax is tokens-per-step notation overhead, not extra genuine steps. Data: Experiment-1 traces. Analysis: a mixed-effects regression of reasoning-token count with a random effect for problem identity (intrinsic difficulty / step count) and a fixed effect for realized notation mode; plus truncate-and-resume minimal-solve step count on 200 items/dataset as a proxy for genuine depth; plus a within-problem contrast of narration-heavy vs symbol-heavy sampled generations of the SAME problem at equal accuracy. Decisive metric FIRST: the fixed-effect coefficient of notation mode on token count after absorbing problem identity, and the within-problem token gap at equal accuracy. Convincing result: notation mode retains a significant token effect (CI excluding 0) after problem identity is absorbed, and narration-heavy generations use >= 25% more tokens than symbol-heavy ones on the same problems at equal accuracy, while minimal-solve step counts are indistinguishable between modes. Indecision band: notation-mode token effect present but < 10% of total variance explained, or within-problem gap 10-25% — dissociation weak, reported as partly entangled with depth. Negative result (no notation effect beyond problem identity, or step counts differ by mode): the tax is really reasoning depth in disguise; H2 fails and the phenomenon collapses into existing verbosity work.

Experiment 3 (H3 — pre-generation notation-mode representation): Tests that a linear direction at the prompt boundary (last prompt token, before any reasoning token) decodes the notation mode the trace will use, separably from difficulty and length. Data: prompt-boundary activations from Experiment-1 traces, labeled narration-dominant vs symbolic-dominant and by realized narration-to-symbol ratio; item-level 70/15/15 split; logistic-regression / ridge probe per layer, layer sweep, 3 seeds. Systems compared: notation-mode probe versus a difficulty probe (trained on per-problem pass-rate) and a length probe (trained on total token count), via principal angles and joint-model predictive gain. Decisive metric FIRST: AUROC for predicting narration-vs-symbolic mode from the pre-generation state. Convincing result: AUROC >= 0.70, principal angle to both the difficulty and length directions >= 30 degrees, and notation mode adds >= 0.03 AUROC beyond a difficulty+length model. Indecision band: AUROC 0.60-0.70, or angle 15-30 degrees, or incremental gain 0.01-0.03 — decodable but entangled, reported as suggestive. Negative result (AUROC ~0.5, or collinear with difficulty/length): mode is not an independent pre-generation representation; H3 fails.

Experiment 4 (H3 causal — patching flips the mode): Tests that the notation-mode representation causally sets the surface notation. Data: 300 symbol-amenable problems with both a narration context and a symbolic-solved context. Intervention: activation-patch a symbolic-mode prompt-boundary state into the narration context for the same problem at the localized components; frozen weights; dose-response; plus the reverse patch (symbolic->narration) for bidirectionality. Systems compared: (i) no patch, (ii) symbolic patch, (iii) matched-random-direction patch of equal norm, (iv) off-target accuracy control. Decisive metric FIRST: drop in narration-to-symbol ratio (and token count) under the symbolic patch versus controls, with answer preserved. Convincing result: symbolic patch lowers the narration-to-symbol ratio by >= 30% and cuts tokens with answer preserved, monotone in dose, not reproduced by the random-direction patch, off-target accuracy within 1 point; reverse patch raises narration. Indecision band: ratio drop 10-30%, or random-direction patch giving >=50% of the effect — causality not clean. Negative result (no mode switch, or non-specific): the representation is not causal; H3's causal claim fails.

Experiment 5 (H4 — training-free notation-mode steer): Tests that steering toward symbolic mode cuts tokens with minimal accuracy loss on symbol-amenable problems. Data: full GSM8K/MATH500/AIME/GPQA, 3 seeds; steering direction = difference-of-means between symbolic-dominant and narration-dominant prompt-boundary states; applied at problem onset when the Experiment-3 probe predicts symbol-amenability; coefficient swept. Systems compared: (a) no intervention, (b) blunt verbosity/length steering, (c) terseness prompting ('use compact symbolic notation'), (d) external paradigm-selection prompting, (e) fixed truncation, (f) our targeted notation-mode steer. Decisive metric FIRST: tokens-at-equal-accuracy on symbol-amenable problems, and whether the targeted steer Pareto-dominates blunt verbosity steering (fewer tokens at no worse accuracy). Convincing result: targeted steer cuts tokens by >= 20% at accuracy within 1 point of no-intervention on symbol-amenable problems, and Pareto-dominates blunt verbosity steering on the token-accuracy frontier. Indecision band: token savings 8-20%, or accuracy loss 1-3 points — a modest, non-dominant gain, reported at its operating point. Negative result (no token savings at equal accuracy, or dominated by verbosity steering): the steer offers no benefit over existing methods; H4 fails though the phenomenon (H1-H3) stands.

Experiment 6 (H4 boundary — where terseness costs accuracy): Tests the claim's scope limit that steering helps on symbol-amenable problems by mapping where symbolic terseness hurts. Data: hard AIME/GPQA and non-symbol-amenable MATH500 problems. Decisive metric FIRST: accuracy drop vs steering strength across symbol-amenability strata. Convincing result: accuracy loss stays within 1 point on symbol-amenable easy/medium problems but grows on hard/non-amenable ones, delimiting a safe operating regime and showing narration is load-bearing where symbolic terseness fails. Indecision band: accuracy loss 1-3 points on symbol-amenable problems — the safe regime is narrow, reported as such. Negative result (accuracy loss large even on symbol-amenable easy problems): the intervention is unsafe to deploy; the scope of H4 shrinks to near-empty.

Experiment 7 (H3/H4 generalization and scale): Tests transfer without retraining and whether stronger models already default to terser notation. Data: probe/steer fit on one set+model, applied unchanged to the others and across 1.5B->14B. Decisive metric FIRST: cross-set mode-decoding AUROC and cross-set tokens-at-equal-accuracy under transferred steering, plus the trend of the Experiment-1 notation tax across model scale. Convincing result: transferred AUROC within 0.05 of in-domain, transferred token savings >= half the in-domain effect, and a monotone decline of the notation tax with scale (a notation analog of simplicity bias). Indecision band: transfer at one-quarter to one-half of in-domain, or a non-monotone but downward scale trend — partial generalization. Negative result (no transfer, flat scale trend): mode and tax are idiosyncratic per model/set, reported as a boundary characterization.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Classifying notation mode (narration vs symbolic vs mixed) is noisy; we mitigate with parsing plus LLM-judge and human spot-checks, reporting agreement. Producing a matched terse symbolic rendering that provably carries the IDENTICAL computation is nontrivial and could drop genuinely necessary reasoning; we verify same-answer and same-step-structure via LLM-judge and human validation, and treat cases where symbolic rendering changes the reasoning as excluded. The notation-mode signal may be inseparable from a difficulty or length signal (harder problems may genuinely warrant narration), which would collapse the phenomenon into existing verbosity work; the separability analysis, mixed-effects dissociation, and causal patching directly test this, and a null separability result is itself an informative finding. Narration may be load-bearing on hard problems (it scaffolds intermediate state), so steering toward symbolic terseness could cause underthinking; the boundary analysis and per-stratum accuracy quantify this trade-off and may show the intervention only helps symbol-amenable, easy-to-medium problems. Steering/patching can push activations off-distribution and confound accuracy reads; matched-random-direction controls and sample-validity checks are included. Intervention gains may not exceed strong verbosity-steering baselines on tokens alone, but the mechanistic reframing (a surface-notation compute tax with a decodable, steerable pre-generation mode representation) is a standalone contribution. Reasoning-length/notation measurement requires clear think/answer delimiters; truncate-and-resume and matched re-rendering are compute-heavy, so we subsample. Effects may be model-family and scale specific.

novelty.reasoning: The proposal's main practical claim—that prose reasoning is token-inefficient relative to symbolic notation—is not novel and is strongly anticipated by prior efficiency, formatting, and symbolic-reasoning work. The genuine novelty is narrower and mechanistic: reframing spontaneous notation choice as a distinct inference-time compute tax on matched computations, claiming a pre-generation notation-mode representation separable from difficulty/length, and proposing causal steering/patching of that internal mode. That is a nontrivial delta over prompting, external selectors, RL compression, and generic verbosity steering, but the proposal risks collapsing into an already-known verbosity/conciseness axis unless the separability claim holds convincingly.

impact.reasoning: The problem under study is excess inference-time token use from choosing verbose narration over equivalent symbolic derivations. That matters mainly to efficient-reasoning and interpretability researchers, and potentially to practitioners optimizing latency/cost. However, the direct practical payoff is limited because simpler prompting/RL/selectors already reduce verbosity, so a positive result may not strongly change deployed systems unless the internal steering method clearly outperforms them or reveals a broader principle about reasoning control. The strongest impact case is as a phenomenon/mechanism paper: if notation mode is a real pre-generation latent state, it could sharpen how the field thinks about reasoning style versus actual computation.

Quantify the practical stakes more concretely: expected cost/latency reduction ranges and which deployment settings care.
Clarify the target audience hierarchy: mechanistic interpretability first, efficient inference second, practical deployment third.
Show why internal notation-mode control would matter beyond existing prompting/RL baselines—e.g., robustness, controllability, transfer, or scientific insight.
Emphasize whether the main value is phenomenon discovery rather than immediate systems gains, and align claims accordingly.

review.reasoning: The proposal is unusually concrete and testable for an ML idea, with explicit models, datasets, controls, thresholds, and negative-result criteria. The central hypothesis is reasonably falsifiable. Still, there are major technical vulnerabilities. 'Identical computation' under symbolic rewrite is hard to verify and could become subjective. The notation labels may be noisy and entangled with problem type, answer format, length, or difficulty. Mixed-effects plus minimal-solve proxies may not truly isolate reasoning depth. AUROC/probe-angle evidence is suggestive but not sufficient for a distinct latent factor, and activation patching could still act through generic verbosity/style circuits. The dataset choices also mix domains where symbolic notation is naturally more or less appropriate, which may confound the core claim. If executed very well it could be viable for a serious ML venue as a mechanistic empirical paper, but it needs sharper controls and more defensible operationalization.
