Name: diagnostic_order_anchoring
Title: First Symptom, Wrong Diagnosis: Premature Hypothesis Commitment as the Mechanism of Symptom-Order Anchoring in Clinical Reasoning Models
Short Hypothesis: For a fixed set of clinical findings pointing to a single correct diagnosis, reasoning LLMs reach different final diagnoses depending only on the ORDER in which symptoms are presented, anchoring on the diagnosis best supported by the earliest symptoms. This order effect is mechanistically caused by a decodable 'leading-hypothesis' representation that forms after the first few symptoms and resists updating when later, more specific symptoms arrive; steering/resetting this representation removes the order-induced misdiagnoses.
Related Work: Human clinical-reasoning research robustly documents symptom-order anchoring: early symptoms bias the initial hypothesis and later evidence is distorted toward it (Order effects in diagnostic reasoning, 2012; Effect of presentation order in clinical decision making, 1997; Evidence for Anchoring Bias During Physician Decision-Making, 2023; Information Distortion, 2013). LLM anchoring work shows numeric/framing anchors shift output distributions (Anchors in the Machine, 2025; CBEval, 2024; Anchoring bias experimental study, 2025) and locates positional/MCQ 'A'-anchoring circuits (Anchored Answers, 2024), while The First Impression Problem (2025) shows an internal preliminary guess triggers overthinking via excessive attention to the question. Crucially, NONE (a) studies symptom-PRESENTATION-ORDER anchoring in the multi-step DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS of dedicated reasoning models, (b) shows order alone flips the FINAL diagnosis on content-identical cases in a safety-critical domain, or (c) ties this to a decodable leading-hypothesis representation that forms early and fails to update. Prior LLM anchoring uses artificial numeric anchors and single-turn outputs; prior clinical-order work is behavioral in humans. We transfer the human clinical phenomenon into reasoning LLMs and give it a mechanistic (Location + Causal Intervention) account, distinct from all my prior overthinking-efficiency proposals.
Abstract: Physicians who see a patient's symptoms in a different order can reach a different diagnosis, a robust human anchoring effect where early findings dominate. We ask whether reasoning language models inherit this, and mechanistically why, in the high-stakes setting of differential diagnosis. We construct clinical cases whose full symptom set unambiguously supports one correct diagnosis, then present the identical findings in different orders: an order whose leading symptoms favor a plausible-but-wrong competitor diagnosis versus an order whose leading symptoms favor the correct one, plus randomized orders. Across curated diagnostic benchmarks (e.g., MedQA-derived vignettes, NEJM-style case reports, and templated multi-symptom cases with controlled hypothesis structure) on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3, and a medical-tuned model), we measure whether the final diagnosis and accuracy shift with symptom order alone, using a mixed-effects decomposition to isolate order from case content. Mechanistically, we test that after the first few symptoms the residual stream linearly encodes a leading-hypothesis representation predicting the eventual diagnosis, that this representation is set early and updates too little when later contradicting symptoms arrive, and that its early strength predicts order-induced misdiagnosis. We localize it via probing and causally validate via activation patching (patch the correct-order leading-hypothesis state into a wrong-order case and observe the diagnosis correct) and steering. Finally we test a training-free 'hypothesis-reset' intervention applied after symptom intake that cancels the order effect. Because symptom order is arbitrary in real clinical notes, this reveals an order-driven misdiagnosis risk with a decodable, steerable internal cause.
Experiments:
All experiments use frozen open models: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B/7B/14B, Qwen3-8B (thinking mode), and one medical-tuned open model (e.g. OpenBioLLM-8B); linear probes are the only trainable parameters. Generation: temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, 3 seeds (0,1,2). We CONSTRUCT cases whose full symptom set S unambiguously supports one CORRECT diagnosis but whose early-presentable subset is also consistent with a plausible COMPETITOR diagnosis, and present the identical findings in different orders. Sources: (T) templated controlled-hypothesis vignettes (strongest control) — 600 cases from ~30 templates; (M) MedQA-derived vignettes adapted so the full findings are diagnostic — 300 cases; (N) NEJM-style case reports adapted — 150 cases. Clinical validity and unambiguity are checked by an expert-guided rubric plus LLM-judge, with human spot-check on 200 cases; ambiguous cases are analyzed separately. Diagnosis extraction uses LLM-judge matching with human spot-check (report kappa).

Experiment 1 (H1 — symptom-order anchoring flips the diagnosis): Tests whether symptom order alone changes the final diagnosis on content-identical cases. Data: each case in orderings (a) competitor-leading (early symptoms favor the wrong diagnosis; disambiguating symptoms last), (b) correct-leading, (c) 3 randomized orders. Decisive metric FIRST: within-case final-diagnosis accuracy and competitor-misdiagnosis rate as a function of ordering. Convincing result: competitor-leading order lowers accuracy by >= 8 absolute points and raises competitor-misdiagnosis by >= 8 points versus correct-leading on identical findings, in >=3 of the models on the templated set and replicated on >=1 adapted set. Indecision band: accuracy/misdiagnosis gap 3-8 points — a weak effect, reported as limited. Negative result (no gap, diagnosis invariant to order): symptom-order anchoring does not occur; H1 fails and the mechanistic experiments are not pursued.

Experiment 2 (H1 — dissociation from content, length, position): Tests that the effect is symptom-content-order, not case difficulty, prompt length, or the position of the disambiguating symptom. Data: Experiment-1 orderings plus matched-length filler and randomized disambiguating-symptom position. Analysis: mixed-effects model of accuracy/misdiagnosis with random effect for case identity and fixed effect for ordering. Decisive metric FIRST: the ordering fixed effect after absorbing case identity and controlling length/position. Convincing result: ordering effect survives (CI excluding 0) with case identity absorbed and is not explained by length or disambiguating-symptom position. Indecision band: ordering effect present but CI half-width comparable to the effect after controls — unresolved. Negative result (effect vanishes after controls): the phenomenon is a position/length artifact; H1 fails.

Experiment 3 (H2 — decodable early leading-hypothesis): Tests that after the first k symptoms the residual stream linearly encodes a leading hypothesis that predicts the eventual diagnosis even when wrong. Data: residual-stream activations after the first k symptoms (before the full set), from Experiment-1 cases; probe (multinomial logistic) per layer, item-level 70/15/15 split, layer sweep, 3 seeds. Decisive metric FIRST: AUROC/accuracy for predicting the FINAL diagnosis from the early state, and separability from a difficulty/uncertainty probe (principal angle). Convincing result: early-state prediction of the final diagnosis reaches macro-F1 >= 0.60 (well above majority baseline), higher in competitor-leading order (early commitment to the wrong diagnosis), and the leading-hypothesis direction is separable from difficulty (angle >= 30 degrees). Indecision band: macro-F1 0.45-0.60, or angle 15-30 degrees — decodable but weak/entangled. Negative result (early state does not predict the final diagnosis above baseline): there is no early leading-hypothesis representation; H2 fails.

Experiment 4 (H2 — under-updating when late evidence arrives): Tests that in competitor-leading order the leading-hypothesis representation under-updates when a late disambiguating symptom favoring the correct diagnosis arrives, and that the under-update predicts misdiagnosis. Data: probe-decoded leading-hypothesis trajectory across symptoms, competitor-leading vs correct-leading. Decisive metric FIRST: the shift in the probe readout at the late disambiguating symptom (competitor-leading vs correct-leading), and the incremental R^2 of the under-update magnitude in predicting order-induced misdiagnosis over difficulty/length baselines. Convincing result: the representation shifts markedly less toward the correct diagnosis in competitor-leading order (CI excluding 0), and under-update magnitude adds >= 0.05 R^2 over baselines. Indecision band: incremental R^2 0.02-0.05 — a weak mediator. Negative result (equal updating in both orders, or no predictive link): under-updating is not the mechanism; H2's mechanistic claim fails.

Experiment 5 (H2 causal — patching the leading hypothesis): Tests that the leading-hypothesis representation causally sets the final diagnosis. Data: 300 cases in matched competitor-leading and correct-leading orders. Intervention: activation-patch the correct-leading leading-hypothesis state into the matched competitor-leading case (same findings) at localized components; frozen weights; dose-response; reverse patch to induce misdiagnosis. Systems compared: (i) no patch, (ii) correct-leading patch, (iii) matched-random-direction patch of equal norm, (iv) off-target case accuracy control. Decisive metric FIRST: correction of the final diagnosis under the patch versus controls. Convincing result: the correct-leading patch corrects >= half the competitor-leading misdiagnoses with CI excluding 0, monotone in dose, not reproduced by the random-direction patch, off-target accuracy within 1 point; reverse patch induces misdiagnosis. Indecision band: correction of 20-50% of misdiagnoses, or random-direction patch giving >=50% of the effect — causality not clean. Negative result (no correction, or non-specific): the representation is not causal; H2's causal claim fails.

Experiment 6 (H3 — training-free hypothesis-reset): Tests that resetting the leading-hypothesis representation after symptom intake removes the order effect without overwriting correct early commitments. Data: full T/M/N sets, 3 seeds, competitor-leading order. Intervention: after all symptoms are presented but before commitment, steer the leading-hypothesis representation toward a neutral/uncommitted state (subtract the early-anchor component); coefficient swept. Systems compared: (a) no intervention, (b) prompt reset ('reconsider all findings without regard to order'), (c) presenting all symptoms simultaneously (order-free oracle), (d) re-ordering to correct-leading (oracle), (e) our activation reset. Decisive metric FIRST: reduction in the order-induced accuracy gap and competitor-misdiagnosis rate, with a specificity check on correct-leading cases. Convincing result: the reset removes >= half the order-induced accuracy gap (approaching the order-free oracle), beats the prompt reset, and does not reduce accuracy on correct-leading cases by more than 1 point (specificity). Indecision band: gap removal 20-50%, or a 1-3 point accuracy cost on correct-leading cases — partial, reported at its operating point. Negative result (no gap reduction, or correct cases harmed): the reset does not work; H3 fails though H1-H2 stand.

Experiment 7 (generalization and hypothesis count): Tests transfer without retraining and whether more competitors worsen anchoring. Data: probe/reset fit on one set+model, applied unchanged to the others and across scales; cases with >2 competitor diagnoses. Decisive metric FIRST: cross-set order-effect reduction under the transferred reset, and whether anchoring grows with the number of competitor hypotheses. Convincing result: transferred reset retains >= half its in-domain effect, anchoring worsens monotonically with competitor count (mirroring human findings), and medical-tuning shifts the effect in a characterizable direction. Indecision band: transfer at one-quarter to one-half of in-domain, or no clear competitor-count trend — partial generalization. Negative result (no transfer): the effect is idiosyncratic per model/set, reported as a boundary characterization. Vignettes are synthetic/adapted demonstrations, not clinical validation.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Constructing cases where the FULL symptom set is unambiguously diagnostic yet early subsets favor a competitor is nontrivial and requires clinical validity; we anchor strongest claims on templated controlled-hypothesis cases and use adapted MedQA/NEJM vignettes with expert/LLM-judge verification, treating ambiguous cases separately. The order effect could be a position/length artifact rather than symptom-content-order per se; matched-length filler, randomized disambiguating-symptom position, and the mixed-effects analysis isolate this, and a null after controls is an informative negative result. The leading-hypothesis representation may be inseparable from a generic difficulty/uncertainty signal; the separability analysis, under-update trajectory (not just magnitude), and causal patching address this. Steering/patching can push activations off-distribution and harm accuracy; matched-random-direction controls and validity checks are included, and the reset must not overwrite genuinely correct early commitments (specificity check on correct-leading cases). The effect may be small in strong or medical-tuned models trained to weigh all findings (a valuable boundary condition). Clinical vignettes are synthetic/adapted demonstrations of the failure mode, not clinical validation of a deployable tool. Diagnosis extraction requires reliable parsing/matching; we use LLM-judge with human spot-checks. Results may be model-family and scale specific.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims: (1) symptom presentation order alone can flip the final diagnosis in content-identical differential-diagnosis cases; (2) this is driven by an early decodable 'leading-hypothesis' state that forms after the first few symptoms; (3) the state under-updates when late disambiguating evidence arrives; (4) causal patching/steering can reverse the bias and a training-free reset mitigates it. The setting is different enough from prior LLM anchoring work because it moves from artificial numeric/MCQ anchors and behavioral clinical-bias studies to mechanistic probing in multi-step medical reasoning. Relative to related work, the delta is non-trivial: a content-identical order flip plus mechanistic localization, not just a prompt-level bias effect. Closest prior family is clinical symptom-order anchoring in humans and LLM anchoring/first-impression studies; the actual delta is mechanistic + causally intervened order anchoring in reasoning models on differential diagnosis.

Name: tokenizer_fragmentation_overthinking
Title: Fragmented Numbers, Longer Thoughts: A Tokenizer-Induced Compute Tax in Reasoning Models
Short Hypothesis: For the identical math problem, a reasoning model spends systematically more thinking tokens when its numbers are tokenized into more fragments (worse digit segmentation), and this excess is not extra genuine reasoning but a surface-form artifact: fragmentation inflates a length/difficulty signal read at the prompt boundary before reasoning begins. Re-encoding the same numbers into fewer, cleaner tokens reduces reasoning length at equal accuracy, and the effect is causally mediated by a fragmentation-sensitive length-budget representation.
Related Work: Overthinking is widely studied via steerable verbosity/reflection directions (Efficiency Steering, CREST, Manifold Steering, ReflCtrl, STU-PID), uncertainty/self-doubt (ReflCtrl, Self-Doubt), neuron-based early exit (NEAT), and batch-mode resource competition (DRQA). The First Impression Problem ties overthinking to excessive attention to the input question. All treat the pre-generation length/difficulty signal as tracking genuine difficulty and study a fixed textual form. Numeral-tokenization work (Scaling Behavior of Numeral Systems; Benford's Curse) studies training efficiency and accuracy/hallucination, not inference-time compute; tokenizer non-uniqueness work (Say Anything but This) targets correctness. No prior work measures a reasoning-COMPUTE gap driven by numeral tokenization on matched problems, dissociates it from true difficulty, or locates/causally tests a fragmentation-sensitive length-budget representation. This is a distinct inference-time compute-allocation artifact uniting tokenizer and efficient-reasoning literatures.
Abstract: Reasoning language models allocate a thinking budget assumed to reflect a problem's genuine difficulty. We show this budget is contaminated by a superficial factor: how the tokenizer segments the numbers in the prompt. Modern subword tokenizers split numerals inconsistently ('1234' as one, two, or four tokens depending on format), and we hypothesize that more fragmented numerals cause a model to think longer on the exact same problem, inflating tokens without improving accuracy. Across GSM8K, MATH500, and arithmetic-heavy word problems on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we construct content-identical variants that hold the mathematical content and answer fixed while varying only numeral tokenization (native BPE, digit-spaced, comma-grouped, single-digit segmentation), verified via the tokenizer to change fragment counts. We measure reasoning-token count and accuracy per variant and test whether fragmentation predicts thinking length independent of difficulty via a mixed-effects decomposition, controlling for raw prompt length. Mechanistically, we probe whether the prompt-boundary residual stream encodes a fragmentation-sensitive length/difficulty signal dissociable from a true-difficulty probe, localize it, causally validate via activation patching (patch a low-fragmentation state into a high-fragmentation context and observe the budget drop), and steer it to cancel the inflation. Our work reveals a tokenizer-induced overthinking artifact and offers a simple, training-free fix (re-encoding numbers) plus a mechanistic account.
Experiments:
All experiments use frozen open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B/7B/14B, Qwen3-8B thinking mode); linear probes are the only trainable parameters. Generation: temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, 3 seeds (0,1,2). Seed problems come from existing sets used as-is: GSM8K test (1319), MATH500 (500), and arithmetic-heavy word problems (300 items). For each seed we CONSTRUCT content-identical variants that change ONLY numeral tokenization — (a) native BPE, (b) digit-spaced ('1 2 3 4'), (c) comma/underscore-grouped ('1,234'), (d) single-digit forced segmentation — and confirm via the model's own tokenizer that fragment counts differ while decoded meaning and the correct answer are identical. Compute forces subsampling of the trace-heavy conditions to 400 GSM8K, 400 MATH500, and all 300 word problems, each in all four encodings, 3 seeds.

Experiment 1 (H1 — fragmentation inflates thinking length): Tests whether higher numeral fragmentation increases reasoning tokens on the same problem at equal accuracy. Data: the four encodings above. Decisive metric FIRST: within-problem reasoning-token count as a function of numeral fragment count, at matched accuracy. Convincing result: reasoning tokens rise monotonically with fragment count by >= 15% median from the least- to most-fragmented encoding while accuracy stays within 1 point, in >=3 of 4 models on >=2 of 3 sources. Indecision band: token inflation 5-15% — a modest tax, reported as limited. Negative result (no inflation, or accuracy changes so it is not equal-accuracy): tokenizer fragmentation does not inflate compute; H1 fails and the mechanistic experiments are not pursued.

Experiment 2 (H1 — segmentation, not prompt length): Tests that the effect is fragment count, not raw prompt length. Data: Experiment-1 variants, exploiting that single-digit vs grouped encodings vary fragmentation at similar or opposite prompt lengths. Analysis: mixed-effects model of reasoning length with random effect for problem identity and fixed effects for fragment count and raw prompt length. Decisive metric FIRST: the fragment-count fixed effect after absorbing problem identity and prompt length. Convincing result: fragment-count effect survives (CI excluding 0) with problem identity and prompt length absorbed, and holds in length-matched format contrasts. Indecision band: fragment-count effect present but its length-matched contrast CI overlaps 0 — possibly length-driven. Negative result (effect vanishes after length control): the phenomenon is a prompt-length artifact, an informative null; H1's segmentation claim fails.

Experiment 3 (H1 — wasted, not genuine reasoning): Tests that the extra tokens are wasted, not genuine number-parsing reasoning. Data: 200 items/source with truncate-and-resume minimal-solve length per variant, plus lexical tagging of number re-reading/restatement. Decisive metric FIRST: the increase in WASTED tokens (beyond minimal solve) with fragment count, and rate of number re-reading. Convincing result: fragmentation inflates wasted tokens and number-restatement (CI excluding 0) while minimal-solve length is unchanged. Indecision band: minimal-solve length itself rises 5-15% with fragmentation — fragmented numbers are genuinely a bit harder to parse, weakening the 'artifact' framing (reported as such). Negative result (minimal-solve rises as much as total): the extra compute is genuine parsing difficulty, not a surface artifact; the 'artifact' claim fails though the phenomenon stands.

Experiment 4 (H2 — fragmentation-sensitive length signal at the prompt boundary): Tests that the prompt-boundary residual stream encodes a length signal that rises with fragmentation for identical problems, dissociable from true difficulty. Data: prompt-boundary (last prompt token, pre-reasoning) activations from Experiment-1 variants; a length-predicting probe (ridge) and a true-difficulty probe (trained on pass-rate) per layer, item-level 70/15/15 split, layer sweep, 3 seeds. Decisive metric FIRST: the shift in the length-probe prediction for identical problems between low- and high-fragmentation encodings, and the principal angle between the fragmentation-length direction and the true-difficulty direction. Convincing result: the length-probe prediction rises monotonically with fragment count for identical problems (CI excluding 0), correlates with Experiment-1 token inflation, and the fragmentation-length direction is separable from true difficulty (angle >= 30 degrees). Indecision band: probe shift present but correlation with token inflation |r| < 0.3, or angle 15-30 degrees — weakly evidenced/entangled. Negative result (no probe shift for identical problems): no fragmentation-sensitive length representation; H2 fails.

Experiment 5 (H4 — causal mediation by patching): Tests that the fragmentation-sensitive representation causally drives the extra compute. Data: 300 problems in both low- and high-fragmentation encodings. Intervention: activation-patch the prompt-boundary state from the low-fragmentation variant into the matched high-fragmentation context (same problem) at localized components; frozen weights; dose-response; reverse patch for bidirectionality. Systems compared: (i) no patch, (ii) low-fragmentation patch, (iii) matched-random-direction patch of equal norm, (iv) off-target accuracy control. Decisive metric FIRST: reduction in reasoning length toward the low-fragmentation level under the patch versus controls, accuracy preserved. Convincing result: the low-fragmentation patch removes >= half the fragmentation-driven inflation with CI excluding 0, monotone in dose, not reproduced by the random-direction patch, off-target accuracy within 1 point; reverse patch inflates length. Indecision band: removal 20-50% of the inflation, or random-direction patch giving >=50% of it — causality not clean. Negative result (no reduction, or non-specific): the representation is not causal; H4 fails.

Experiment 6 (H3 — re-encoding fix and debiasing steer): Tests that reducing fragmentation cuts reasoning length at equal accuracy. Data: full evaluation sets, 3 seeds, high-fragmentation native inputs. Systems compared: (a) no intervention, (b) input-side re-encoding of numbers into fewer tokens (deployable preprocessing fix), (c) fragmentation-length debiasing steer (difference-of-means between low- and high-fragmentation boundary states, applied at problem onset), (d) fixed truncation. Decisive metric FIRST: tokens-at-equal-accuracy relative to the native-fragmentation baseline. Convincing result: both the re-encoding fix and the steer cut tokens by >= 15% at accuracy within 1 point of native. Indecision band: token savings 5-15%, or a 1-3 point accuracy cost — a modest gain, reported at its operating point. Negative result (no token savings at equal accuracy): neither fix delivers the benefit; H3 fails though H1-H2 stand.

Experiment 7 (practical payoff and generalization): Tests the deployment payoff and transfer. Data: a mixed problem stream, and probe/steer fit on one set+model applied unchanged to the others and across 1.5B->14B. Decisive metric FIRST: total tokens wasted on the stream by native fragmentation versus an oracle low-fragmentation encoding, and cross-set transfer of the fix. Convincing result: native fragmentation wastes >= 10% of stream reasoning tokens recoverable by input-side digit grouping, transfer retains >= half the in-domain savings, and the effect is stronger for models with coarser numeral tokenization. Indecision band: recoverable waste 3-10%, or transfer at one-quarter to one-half of in-domain — a small but real win. Negative result (no recoverable waste, no transfer): the effect is negligible or idiosyncratic per model, reported as a boundary characterization (models already using clean single-digit tokenization may show no effect).
Risk Factors and Limitations: The fragmentation effect could be an artifact of prompt token-length (digit-spacing lengthens prompts) rather than segmentation per se; the length covariate, length-matched comparisons, and single-digit-vs-grouped contrasts isolate this, and a null after controls is an informative negative result. Number re-formatting could inadvertently change accuracy/difficulty; we verify answer/accuracy invariance and use tokenizer-verified content-identical variants. The fragmentation-length signal may be inseparable from a true-difficulty signal if the model genuinely finds fragmented numbers harder to parse (still a novel, actionable phenomenon but weakening the 'artifact' framing); the separability analysis and patching address this. Steering/patching can push activations off-distribution and confound accuracy reads; matched-random-direction controls and sample-validity checks are included. Effects likely depend on the model's numeral-tokenization scheme and may be small for models already using clean single-digit tokenization (an informative boundary condition). Reasoning-length measurement requires clear think/answer delimiters; truncate-and-resume is compute-heavy, so we subsample.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims are: (1) numeral fragmentation changes inference-time thinking-token length on content-identical math problems at matched accuracy; (2) this excess compute is driven by a prompt-boundary fragmentation/difficulty signal rather than true task difficulty; (3) the signal is decodable and causally patchable; (4) simple re-encoding reduces reasoning length without hurting accuracy. The underlying fact that fragmented numerals hurt performance is known, but the compute-tax framing, matched-accuracy setup, and mechanistic budget-signal claim are new and non-trivial. Closest prior family is numeral-tokenization work on accuracy/efficiency plus overthinking/verbosity steering work; the delta is shifting from accuracy loss to inference compute inflation and a causal mechanism for it.

impact.reasoning: The problem is wasted inference compute in reasoning models caused by tokenizer-induced numeral fragmentation. Who cares: efficient-reasoning researchers, tokenizer designers, and deployers of math/reasoning models paying token costs. If true, it changes preprocessing/tokenization choices and suggests a cheap deployment-time fix. The strongest case is that some 'thinking tokens' are not evidence of harder problems but are avoidable overhead introduced by surface form. Impact is meaningful but bounded: it matters most for math-heavy workloads and models using subword numerals, and less if the effect is small or disappears with better tokenizers.

Name: novelty_satiation_gating
Title: Bored of Its Own Ideas: A Novelty-Satiation Signal That Prematurely Collapses Exploration in Reasoning Models
Short Hypothesis: Transferring the curiosity/novelty-satiation phenomenon from human exploration science, we hypothesize that when a reasoning model generates candidate solution ideas within one chain of thought, an internal novelty signal decays as similar ideas accumulate, and once this signal drops below threshold the model stops proposing genuinely new approaches—committing early to a familiar strategy even on problems that require a different one. This premature exploration collapse is caused by a decodable, monotonically-satiating novelty representation whose early decay predicts failure; steering the novelty signal back up restores exploration and improves accuracy on problems the model otherwise abandons after one idea.
Related Work: Recent work shows LLMs explore poorly because they 'think too fast'—relying on early uncertainty-driven strategies and neglecting later empowerment signals, with SAE analysis showing uncertainty is represented in early layers (Large Language Models Think Too Fast To Explore Effectively, 2025); episode/anatomy analyses (ThinkARM, ReJump, Cognitive Foundations, 2025) show exploration is a critical branching point where correct solutions route into monitoring/re-analysis while incorrect ones continue execution or terminate; and The Illusion of Thinking (2025) documents effort collapse on hard problems. Curiosity work characterizes information-seeking and novelty-driven exploration in humans and RL (Computational mechanisms of curiosity, 2019; Curiosity-driven exploration, 2021) and even measures curiosity questionnaires in LLMs (Why Did Apple Fall, 2025). Crucially, NONE studies a within-trace NOVELTY-SATIATION dynamic—whether the model's drive to propose NEW ideas decays as it generates redundant ones, whether that decay is a decodable internal signal, and whether it CAUSES premature exploration collapse and failure. Prior exploration-in-LLMs work is behavioral (episode taxonomies) or locates static uncertainty representations; it never ties a satiating novelty signal to when the model stops generating diverse candidate strategies, nor causally reverses it. This differs from my prior overthinking proposals (which target stopping/verification/length under too-MUCH thinking) by targeting under-exploration—giving up idea-generation too soon—and its satiation mechanism.
Abstract: Humans keep exploring as long as new information feels novel, and satiate—stop seeking—once novelty fades. We ask whether reasoning language models exhibit an analog within a single chain of thought: as they generate candidate solution ideas, does an internal novelty drive decay with each redundant idea, causing them to stop proposing genuinely new approaches and commit prematurely to a familiar strategy? We call this novelty-satiation gating and hypothesize it is a distinct cause of reasoning failure: on problems whose first-considered strategy is wrong, a satiated model abandons idea-generation before reaching the approach that works. Across math (MATH500, AIME), science (GPQA), and open-ended exploration puzzles (a Little-Alchemy-2-style discovery task) on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we first segment traces into candidate-idea proposals, measure idea diversity over the trace, and show diversity decays and idea-generation halts earlier on failed than solved problems requiring strategy switches. We then test a mechanistic account: a linear probe on the residual stream at each idea boundary decodes a novelty/satiation signal that decays monotonically as similar ideas accumulate, is separable from a generic uncertainty or difficulty probe, and whose early decay predicts failure. We localize it, causally validate via activation patching (patch a high-novelty state into a satiated context and observe a fresh, distinct idea), and test a training-free 'novelty-refresh' steer that restores exploration when the signal collapses early. Our work reframes a class of reasoning failure as premature novelty satiation with a decodable, steerable internal cause.
Experiments:
All experiments use frozen open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B/7B/14B, Qwen3-8B thinking mode); linear probes are the only trainable parameters. Generation: temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, 3 seeds (0,1,2). Datasets: MATH500 (500) and AIME 2024+2025 (60) used as-is; GPQA-Diamond (198) as-is; and a CONSTRUCTED Little-Alchemy-2-style discovery puzzle (open-ended combination task where distinct 'ideas' = distinct combinations tried) — 300 instances from a procedural generator with known solution depth. We additionally CONSTRUCT a 'strategy-switch-required' set (300 items, templated so the obvious first strategy is wrong and a different approach is needed). Candidate ideas are segmented by lexical cues ('maybe try', 'alternatively', 'what if we use') plus an LLM-judge that clusters proposals into distinct strategy classes, validated by human spot-check on 300 traces (report kappa; on the discovery puzzle and strategy-switch set distinct ideas are well-defined by construction). Compute forces subsampling of judge-heavy analyses to 300 items/dataset.

Experiment 1 (H1 — novelty decays as redundant ideas accumulate): Tests whether idea diversity decays and idea-generation halts within a trace. Data: traces on MATH500/AIME/GPQA/discovery-puzzle. Measures: per-trace idea-diversity trajectory (new distinct strategies introduced per idea-boundary) and the halt point (last boundary introducing a novel strategy). Decisive metric FIRST: the slope of new-distinct-strategies per idea-boundary across the trace (the diversity-decay slope). Convincing result: diversity introduces new strategies at a monotonically decaying rate (negative slope, CI excluding 0) in >=3 of 4 models on >=3 of 4 datasets, with a well-defined halt point before trace end. Indecision band: slope CI overlapping 0, or |slope| below one new strategy per 10 boundaries — no clear satiation dynamic, reported as absent for that cell. Negative result (flat or increasing diversity): novelty does not satiate within traces; H1 fails and the remaining experiments are not pursued.

Experiment 2 (H2 — early satiation predicts failure, distinct from effort collapse): Tests that on problems whose obvious first strategy is wrong, failed traces satiate earlier than solved ones, and that satiation is distinct from simply spending fewer tokens. Data: the strategy-switch-required set plus first-strategy-wrong items identified from Experiment 1. Analysis: mixed-effects model of success on satiation timing (halt point, late-trace diversity) controlling for problem identity/difficulty; comparison against a total-token 'effort-collapse' baseline. Decisive metric FIRST: the effect of satiation timing on success after absorbing problem identity, and its incremental predictive power over total tokens. Convincing result: earlier satiation predicts failure (CI excluding 0) on strategy-switch problems and adds >= 0.05 AUROC over the total-token baseline, while on first-strategy-correct problems satiation is harmless. Indecision band: incremental AUROC 0.02-0.05 — satiation weakly distinct from effort collapse. Negative result (satiation timing does not predict success beyond total tokens): satiation is just effort collapse; H1/H2's distinctness claim fails.

Experiment 3 (H3 — decodable, monotonic, separable satiation signal): Tests that a linear direction at each idea boundary decodes next-idea novelty, decays monotonically with accumulated redundancy, is separable from uncertainty and difficulty, and its early decay predicts failure. Data: idea-boundary residual activations labeled by whether the NEXT idea is strategically novel vs redundant; item-level 70/15/15 split; logistic-regression probe per layer, layer sweep, 3 seeds. Systems compared: the novelty probe versus a generic uncertainty/confidence probe and a difficulty probe, via principal angles and joint predictive gain. Decisive metric FIRST: AUROC for next-idea novelty, the slope of the probe's within-trace satiation curve, and the incremental AUROC of the early satiation-slope for predicting final failure over uncertainty+difficulty. Convincing result: novelty-decoding AUROC >= 0.70, a monotone within-trace satiation curve (negative slope, CI excluding 0), principal angle to both uncertainty and difficulty >= 30 degrees, and early satiation-slope adds >= 0.03 AUROC for failure over uncertainty+difficulty. Indecision band: AUROC 0.60-0.70, or angle 15-30 degrees, or incremental gain 0.01-0.03 — decodable but weak/entangled. Negative result (AUROC ~0.5, flat curve, collinear with uncertainty/difficulty): there is no distinct satiating novelty signal; H3 fails.

Experiment 4 (H3 causal — patching restores a fresh idea): Tests that the novelty representation causally controls whether a new distinct strategy is produced. Data: 300 satiated idea boundaries (probe below threshold) from unsolved traces. Intervention: activation-patch a high-novelty state (from an early non-satiated context) into the satiated boundary at localized components; frozen weights; dose-response. Systems compared: (i) no patch, (ii) high-novelty patch, (iii) matched-random-direction patch of equal norm, (iv) off-target accuracy control. Decisive metric FIRST: the rate at which the model then proposes a genuinely NEW distinct strategy (not a repeat) under the patch versus controls. Convincing result: the high-novelty patch raises the new-distinct-strategy rate by >= 15 absolute points with CI excluding 0, monotone in dose, not reproduced by the random-direction patch, off-target accuracy within 1 point. Indecision band: increase 5-15 points, or random-direction patch giving >=50% of the effect — causality not clean. Negative result (no new-strategy increase, or non-specific): the representation is not causal; H3's causal claim fails.

Experiment 5 (H4 — novelty-refresh steer recovers abandoned problems): Tests that steering novelty up when early satiation is detected on an unsolved problem restores exploration and improves accuracy more token-efficiently than alternatives. Data: full MATH500/AIME/GPQA/discovery/strategy-switch sets, 3 seeds. Intervention: novelty steering direction (difference-of-means between high- and low-novelty idea-boundary states) applied online when the probe detects early satiation on a still-unsolved problem; coefficient swept; gated on unsolved-state. Systems compared: (a) no intervention, (b) self-consistency / higher-temperature resampling at matched extra compute, (c) prompting ('consider a completely different approach'), (d) effort-forcing 'don't give up' nudge, (e) our targeted novelty-refresh. Decisive metric FIRST: accuracy on strategy-switch-required and first-strategy-wrong problems at matched extra tokens (tokens-at-fixed-accuracy), plus idea-diversity recovery. Convincing result: novelty-refresh raises accuracy on abandoned problems by >= 5 absolute points at fewer added tokens than resampling (>=20% fewer for equal accuracy gain) and beats prompting/effort-forcing. Indecision band: accuracy gain 2-5 points, or token savings vs resampling < 10% — a modest, non-dominant gain, reported at its operating point. Negative result (no accuracy gain, or dominated by resampling): the steer offers no benefit; H4 fails though H1-H3 stand.

Experiment 6 (H4 specificity — no wasteful exploration on easy items): Tests that unsolved-state gating prevents the steer from over-triggering where the first strategy is correct. Data: first-strategy-correct items across datasets. Decisive metric FIRST: accuracy change and added tokens on first-strategy-correct items under the gated steer. Convincing result: accuracy unchanged within 1 point and added tokens < 5% on first-strategy-correct items (the steer stays dormant). Indecision band: 5-15% added tokens on easy items — a tolerable but real cost, reported alongside Experiment-5 gains. Negative result (accuracy drop or > 15% token inflation on easy items): the steer induces wasteful exploration/overthinking, bounding its usefulness.

Experiment 7 (generalization and scale): Tests transfer without retraining and the scale trend. Data: probe/steer fit on one dataset+model, applied unchanged to the others and across 1.5B->14B. Decisive metric FIRST: cross-dataset novelty-decoding AUROC and cross-dataset accuracy recovery under the transferred steer, plus whether larger/RL-tuned models satiate later (satiation-slope vs scale). Convincing result: transferred AUROC within 0.05 of in-domain, transferred accuracy recovery >= half the in-domain effect, and a monotone later-satiation trend with scale. Indecision band: transfer at one-quarter to one-half of in-domain, or a non-monotone scale trend — partial generalization. Negative result (no transfer, flat scale trend): the signal and satiation are idiosyncratic per model/dataset, reported as a boundary characterization.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Segmenting and clustering 'candidate ideas' into distinct strategies is noisy; we mitigate with lexical cues plus LLM-judge clustering and human spot-checks, anchoring the strongest claims on the discovery-puzzle and templated strategy-switch problems where distinct ideas are well-defined. Novelty satiation may be inseparable from a generic uncertainty or difficulty signal (a satiated model may simply be confident/stuck), which would weaken the distinct-mechanism claim; the separability analysis, monotonic within-trace satiation curve (a dynamical, not just magnitude, signature), and causal patching directly test this, and a null is an informative negative result. The phenomenon may only appear on problems requiring strategy switches; on first-strategy-correct problems early commitment is beneficial (this is the intended specificity, not a flaw). Steering could push activations off-distribution or induce wasteful exploration/overthinking on easy items; unsolved-state gating, matched-random-direction controls, and the specificity analysis quantify this trade-off. The novelty-refresh steer may not beat strong resampling baselines on accuracy alone, but the mechanistic reframing (a satiating novelty signal causing premature exploration collapse) is a standalone contribution. Reasoning-trace segmentation requires clear think/answer delimiters; LLM-judge clustering is compute-heavy, so we subsample. Effects may be model-family and scale specific.

novelty.reasoning: The core delta is a within-trace, decodable novelty-satiation mechanism for reasoning models, with causal patching and a steerable control signal. That is meaningfully new relative to prior work on training-time diversity collapse, uncertainty/effort collapse, and behavioral exploration studies. The setting shift to inference-time idea generation is substantial enough to make the claim novel if the signal is truly separable from uncertainty/difficulty.
